artigo.texto: Two of the biggest users of pallets, the manufacturing and construction sectors, face a mixed economic bag in 2027. But just like this year, some unknowns could really change the economic picture the way the conflict in the Middle East and the spike in energy prices have done this year. Let’s look at all the key variables to help you develop a picture that can inform your short-term plans for 2027. Key Predictions – Overall Economic Picture “Generally speaking, outside of data centers and related energy projects, it’s going to remain a sluggish construction environment for many contractors,” said Anirban Basu, chairman and CEO of Sage Policy Group (sagepolicy.com). “Warehouse, office and housing construction has dwindled.” Manufacturers can look forward to a fairly benign operating environment in 2027. “We look for a moderate acceleration in growth,” said Bernard Yaros Jr., lead U.S. economist at Oxford Economics (oxfordeconomics.com). But the biggest story of 2026 may not drive the economy in 2027. Yaros commented, “The worst of the energy price spike is tentatively over, federal spending on defense will increase, and businesses will spend money rebuilding their inventories.” Oxford Economics expects real GDP to grow by 2.5% in 2027, a small increase from the 2.2% expected when 2026 numbers are finally tallied. While the economy will likely avoid a recession, its growth rate remains among the most sluggish of the past 10 years. Even so, it is sufficiently strong to provide businesses with a solid springboard for generating profits. (Gross domestic product, the total value of the nation’s goods and services, is the most commonly utilized measure of economic growth. “Real” GDP subtracts the effects of inflation. Economists say an increase of 2% to 3% in real GDP reflects the nation’s “natural growth rate,” which supports business activity and maintains full employment while avoiding inflation). Support for the favorable GDP numbers is coming from the consumer and business quarters, noted Yaros: “Gains in financial wealth are powering the spending of well-to-do households, while the AI infrastructure buildout has turbocharged business investment.” Housing Angst High interest rates make mortgages more expensive and thus dampen the housing industry, a significant driver of the nation’s economic health and of demand for pallets. For house shoppers, competition for available funds is keeping borrowing rates high. Mortgage rates are closing in on 7% toward the end of 2026. “Global demand for credit is coming from places like China and the U.S. to support their budget deficits as well as from the private sector to support the rollout for artificial intelligence,” said Bill Conerly, principal of his own consulting firm in Lake Oswego, Oregon (conerlyconsulting.com). “Families shopping for mortgages are competing for loans with companies like SpaceX and Anthropic, as well as the U.S. and Chinese Treasuries, while the global supply of savings has not increased much.” Additional downward pressure on sales is coming from the increasing price tags on available homes. “We are looking for median prices of existing homes to increase 3.7% in 2027 after increasing 1.7% in 2026 and 1.9% in 2025,” said Yaros. Little wonder that for the second year running, single-family homebuilders are contending with a significant inventory of unsold homes, which needs to be worked down before too many new ones come on the market. “I continue to be not too optimistic about residential construction,” said Conerly. “We’re not going to see mortgage rates coming down. People say we need more housing, but the fact is our population is hardly growing, and with restrictions on immigration population growth will stay fairly low.” Forecasts from Oxford Economics put numbers on the phenomenon. “We look for housing starts to fall by 2.4% in 2027, after falling 1.4% in 2026 and 1% in 2025,” said Yaros. Multifamily builders are also facing slow rental growth and high rental vacancy rates. Meanwhile, labor constraints continue to affect builders, especially amid the crackdown on unauthorized immigration. Commercial Construction Manufacturers also create products for the commercial side of construction, and there the story is much happier, at least for the burgeoning sector that serves the growth of AI. “On the commercial side, I think we will continue to see strong demand for data centers,” said Conerly. “Despite the political opposition, there will be plenty of communities around the country that will look favorably on the tax revenue they can get from having data centers in their community.” A further positive impetus is that the hyperscalers who are driving the investment—the Amazons and Metas and Microsofts of the world—do not seem to be sensitive to interest rates or material costs. What’s good for the data center world, though, does not seem to be helping the rest of the non-residential sector. “The economy is just not growing so quickly that we need a lot more retail stores,” said Conerly. “We’re also a bit overbuilt in industrial and warehouse space. We’ll build some offices in the suburbs but not much in the downtowns with exceptions like New York and San Francisco.” The overall construction sector will need to deal efficiently with the current soft construction market. “Backlog may shrink and payments may be delayed,” warned Basu. “All the more reason to have a talk with one’s banker about extending lines of credit to ensure sufficient financial flexibility to get through the year.” There’s going to be a lot more work for those professionals in construction firms who provide estimating and marketing services, added Basu. “Because each project will attract more competition, prudent contractors will be wise to send out more bids.” This trend may also hold true in the new pallet market where there is excess capacity chasing constrained volumes. What we do Overview: how the EBRD operates Across three continents, the EBRD supports the transition to successful market economies. Work with us Overview: how you can work with the EBRD We draw on three decades of regional knowledge and financial expertise to tailor our products and approaches to each client's needs. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) is providing a €30 million loan to Tenevo Solar Technologies for the development of a major battery energy storage project in south-eastern Bulgaria. The financing is being complemented by €30 million in parallel funding from Raiffeisen Bank International AG (RBI). The €60 million package will finance the construction and operation of a battery energy storage system (BESS) at Tenevo, one of the largest battery storage projects in Bulgaria. The new facility will have a power capacity of 246 MW and be able to store 512.5 MWh of electricity. The BESS facility will be co-located with an existing 242 MWp solar photovoltaic (PV) plant (also financed by the EBRD and RBI), and a 65 MW battery installation capable of storing 260 MWh of electricity. It will increase energy storage capacity at the site, enhancing grid stability and supporting the integration of additional clean energy into Bulgaria’s power system. Tenevo Solar Technologies is a long-standing client of the EBRD. Previously the Bank provided €50 million to build and operate the fully merchant Tenevo solar PV plant. The project was supported by first loss risk cover deployed under the EBRD’s InvestEU Framework for Sustainable Transition. As Bulgaria accelerates its energy transition and reduces its reliance on fossil fuels, renewable energy generation and battery storage are becoming increasingly important for the decarbonisation of the power sector, improving flexibility and strengthening energy security. The rapid growth of battery storage capacity, which is exceeding 6.2 GW / 19 GWh according to latest estimates, is one of the country’s most significant energy transition achievements, positioning Bulgaria among the regional leaders in terms of renewable energy integration and decarbonisation. From 2023, the EBRD worked with Bulgaria’s Ministry of Energy on the design of grant schemes, competitive allocation and technical verification to support renewable energy and electricity storage projects under the country’s Recovery and Resilience Plan. September 2026 marked the successful completion of these crucial schemes, which have transformed Bulgaria’s renewable energy market. Manuela Naessl, EBRD Head of Bulgaria, said: “Bulgaria has made remarkable progress in deploying battery storage, and this project is another important step in that journey. By increasing the system’s flexibility and helping to integrate more renewable energy, Tenevo will contribute to a more resilient, secure and sustainable power sector. Supporting investments of this kind is central to the EBRD’s commitment to Bulgaria’s green transition.” The EBRD is a leading institutional investor in Bulgaria, having invested almost €5.3 billion in the country through 330 projects to date, with a strong focus on private sector development, competitiveness and the green economy transition. artigo.texto: JDEnergy Named BNEF Tier 1 Energy Storage Manufacturer for Seventh Consecutive Quarter XI'AN, China, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- JDEnergy has retained its place on BloombergNEF's (BNEF) Tier 1 Energy Storage Manufacturer list for Q4 2026, marking its seventh consecutive appearance. With BNEF raising its assessment standards and placing greater emphasis on project bankability and proven delivery records, JDEnergy's continued inclusion reflects its established project track record in the international energy storage market. JDEnergy specialises in string PCS technology, with a product portfolio spanning modular eBlock energy storage systems and prefabricated BESS solutions featuring string PCS architecture. This architecture enables independent control of individual battery strings, helping improve energy utilisation, system efficiency and availability while simplifying maintenance. The solutions serve a range of applications, including utility-scale energy storage, commercial and industrial (C&I) facilities, and solar-plus-storage projects. JDEnergy has obtained multiple international certifications covering product safety, grid code compliance and technical performance. Its systems are designed to comply with local grid codes and regulatory requirements and operate under different environmental conditions across Europe, the Americas and Asia-Pacific. JDEnergy has delivered energy storage products to more than 15 countries and regions, supporting applications such as grid flexibility, renewable energy integration and industrial energy management. Its growing international project portfolio reflects the company's experience in meeting diverse technical requirements and customer needs. Local technical support is an important part of JDEnergy's international operations. Working with regional partners, JDEnergy provides technical coordination, commissioning support and after-sales services to help customers navigate local grid requirements and maintain reliable system operation. This combination of standardised products and local expertise supports project delivery and long-term operation. As energy storage markets mature, developers and investors are placing greater emphasis on system reliability, operational performance, lifecycle costs and long-term returns. JDEnergy plans to further expand its presence in key international markets, working with local partners to deliver commercially viable energy storage projects and support the integration of renewable energy into power systems. About JDEnergy JDEnergy is a leader in smart energy storage across the value chain, offering integrated products and services for utility-scale and C&I applications. With capabilities spanning R&D, manufacturing, system integration, project delivery and intelligent operation, JDEnergy is committed to accelerating the deployment of energy storage and supporting the global transition toward a cleaner, more reliable and more sustainable power system. artigo.texto: Data centers are the digital steel of the AI century. America can't stop building them. COMMENTARY | In defense of the industry that will power America's next century. I grew up in Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, a steel town that knows what losing an industry costs. When the mill closed, the jobs and the tax base went with it. Families watched storefronts empty and kids move away. Data centers sound far from the kitchen table. They are not. They are where artificial intelligence lives, and every advance below runs on one. Start with science. The Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, launched in November 2025, connects DOE's 17 national laboratories and their supercomputers into one AI discovery platform, aiming to double the productivity of American science within a decade. The order behind it says America is "in a race for global technology dominance." Then the taxpayer. Through ATARC, I hear firsthand how government officials are using AI to serve the American people. Our fraud working group brings oversight officials and industry together to stop improper payments in Medicare, Medicaid, SNAP and Social Security before the money goes out the door. At our October forum in Reston, inspectors general also focused on how AI and shared data can spot risks faster. Then cancer, which touches nearly every family. In Sweden's MASAI trial of more than 105,000 women, AI-supported mammography found 29% more cancers than standard screening. Sybil, built at MIT and Massachusetts General Hospital, predicts lung cancer risk up to six years out from a single CT scan. This is the space race of our time, and America is canceling launches. The Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, citing Heatmap data, reports that at least $260 billion in planned U.S. data center investment has been canceled after local opposition this year, costing more than 2 million construction jobs, while China keeps building. Loudoun County, Virginia, shows what is at stake. It is the world's largest data center market and has the nation's highest median household income. Its roughly 233 data center buildings generated $1.2 billion in property taxes in fiscal 2026 — 39% of the county budget — which has helped cut homeowners' rates. Replacing that revenue would take roughly 63 more cents on today's 80.5-cent rate. Just as Silicon Valley grew up around the chip, a data center ecosystem has grown up in Loudoun: electricians, construction crews, network and cybersecurity professionals, suppliers and a community college degree in data center operations. Not every voice against this industry is a neighbor. In August, X reported roughly 200 accounts tied to a suspected Chinese bot farm pushing Americans to oppose data centers. Most opposition is homegrown, but Beijing knows what is at stake, and so should we. So let me be blunt: local zoning is paramount. If a community does not want a data center next to its homes, it does not go there. Period. The race will be won by building where communities welcome the investment, not by steamrolling neighborhoods. The administration's job is to make those projects possible, and the biggest barrier is power. Speed permitting for generation and transmission, clear the way for advanced nuclear and make the biggest users pay the full cost of their power so households never subsidize hyperscalers. Which brings me home. The Wall Street Journal has reported on a $2 billion plan to turn Aliquippa's long-closed mill site into a power plant and AI data centers. For towns like mine, the bigger risk is another generation of empty mill sites. Aliquippa's mills made the steel that built America's century. Data centers are the digital steel that will build the next one. Respect the neighbors. Power the grid. Keep making digital steel. Tom Suder is the founder and president of the Advanced Technology Academic Research Center (ATARC), a GovExec company.

artigo.texto: - The VCM is tracking more than 30 local and international project developers focusing on emissions reduction projects, including methane capture and nature-based solutions. - Saudi Arabia's aim to achieve net-zero emissions by 2060 is supported by its Circular Carbon Economy framework and a developing voluntary carbon market. - Challenges for the carbon market include ensuring liquidity, transparency, and maintaining credit quality amidst varying prices for different projects. RIYADH: Saudi Arabia’s carbon market is evolving from a platform supporting climate action into a channel for financing projects and reducing emissions, with the Voluntary Carbon Market Co. having traded more than 15 million carbon credits over three years, equivalent to SR350 million ($93.3 million) in financing directed toward climate projects worldwide. This comes as demand for carbon credits in the domestic market exceeds supply, according to the company’s CEO, Fadi Saadeh, who spoke to Al-Eqtisadiah. Saadeh said the platform facilitated trades of more than 2.5 million carbon credits in 2024 at a price of SR37.5 per tonne, adding that the market is working to stimulate domestic demand and attract developers and investors to projects that generate credits through emissions reduction or removal. Saadeh said in a 30-minute interview via Microsoft Teams that the company is tracking more than 30 project developers locally and internationally, whose projects range from methane capture and waste treatment to nature-based solutions, direct air capture and the use of low-carbon concrete. With domestic demand for carbon credits exceeding supply, he said the market needs to expand its project pipeline and diversify credit sources to meet the needs of Saudi companies seeking to manage their emissions. This expansion comes as Saudi Arabia seeks to translate its target of achieving net-zero emissions by 2060 into practical tools for financing and emissions management through its Circular Carbon Economy, or CCE, framework and the development of a voluntary carbon market. The company operates with the support of the Public Investment Fund and Saudi Tadawul Group, aiming to link financing with climate projects and develop market infrastructure for carbon trading. The challenge extends beyond supplying sufficient carbon credits to building a market that is credible and capable of attracting investment, supported by clear standards for measuring actual emissions reductions and verifying the climate impact of projects. The Kingdom is pursuing this agenda amid broader changes in global climate markets, with growth in energy-related emissions worldwide slowing to around 0.4 percent, while countries in the Middle East have begun developing regulatory frameworks to address emissions, according to the CEO. Against this backdrop, the carbon market is emerging as a potential channel for directing financing toward climate projects, although its growth will depend on expanding supply, maintaining credit quality, and sustaining corporate demand. Interview with Saadeh Q: How do you assess the Middle East and Saudi Arabia’s position in global carbon emissions, and what competitive advantage does Riyadh have in carbon markets? Globally, we are seeing some progress in carbon markets. For example, growth in energy-related carbon emissions slowed to around 0.4 percent this year. In the Middle East, however, progress remains relatively slow, although countries in the region are beginning to introduce regulations to support these efforts. In Saudi Arabia, the Voluntary Carbon Market Co. was established to help develop the market and establish its standards. Over the three years since the company was established, we have successfully traded more than 15 million tonnes of carbon credits, equivalent to approximately SR350 million directed toward financing climate projects worldwide. In Saudi Arabia, we focused first on building demand for carbon credits. We are now seeing growing interest, alongside an increase in the number of projects and developers that could become suppliers of credits in the Saudi market. We are tracking more than 30 project developers locally and internationally. Their projects span different sectors and environments, from waste landfills to nature-based solutions and advanced technologies such as direct air capture. These projects are spread across different parts of the country, giving Saudi Arabia a significant opportunity to become a major hub in the Middle East and a leading market for carbon credits and investment in them globally. Q: To what extent have voluntary carbon markets demonstrated their economic effectiveness in reducing emissions? How are carbon credit prices determined in Saudi Arabia compared with global markets? Carbon credits are a tool for strengthening corporate climate action. Companies need to develop sustainability strategies aimed at reducing their emissions, and we at VCM help companies in Saudi Arabia and the Middle East develop these strategies. There will always be emissions that are difficult to reduce or avoid. Carbon credits can therefore be one of the tools that help companies progress toward net zero by investing in climate projects through the purchase of credits. Globally, a significant part of the impact on carbon markets comes from direct carbon-pricing mechanisms, such as compliance markets, which currently cover more than 29 percent of emissions. Saudi Arabia has announced plans to launch a carbon compliance market. Globally, carbon credit retirements exceeded issuances for the first time in the first half of 2026, with retired credits exceeding 100 million tonnes. One of the main differences between global and regional markets is the expansion of forward carbon credit purchase agreements in global markets. We are seeing strong interest in these transactions from major companies such as Google and Microsoft, while this trend is developing more slowly in regional and domestic markets. Q

artigo.texto: Jaipur Discom and GEAPP Launch Sodium-Ion Battery Pilot 02 Nov 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share Jaipur Discom and global not-for-profit organisation GEAPP have launched a pilot project to assess sodium-ion battery storage for renewable power at the distribution transformer level in Jaipur. The initiative aims to help manage peak electricity demand and improve the use of energy generated by rooftop solar installations in Rajasthan. The entities have invited industry proposals to develop a 250 kilowatt-hour (kWh) battery energy storage system at KL Saini Stadium in the Mansarovar area of Jaipur. The request for proposal was issued during the second day of a national conference of electricity distribution companies being held in the city. The project will examine whether storing electricity closer to consumers can help maintain supply during periods of high demand and reduce pressure on local transformers. It will also assess sodium-ion batteries as an alternative to lithium-ion technology, including their performance under Rajasthan’s climatic conditions. Jaipur Discom will provide the project site, technical personnel and operational data. GEAPP will support system design, performance monitoring and technical work, while also training engineers from the distribution company. The pilot is intended to generate operational evidence from a working electricity network rather than relying solely on estimates. Rajasthan Energy Secretary and Discoms Chairperson Arti Dogra said the impact of rising demand during peak hours was first experienced at the distribution transformer level. She said the project would assess the ability of battery storage to ease transformer loads, store rooftop solar power and improve distribution network performance. GEAPP India Country Head Tanya Singhal said energy storage would become increasingly important to India’s electricity grid and that distribution companies needed dependable technology options beyond lithium-ion batteries. The organisations will share the pilot’s findings with electricity distribution companies across the country to support future decisions on energy storage systems. artigo.texto: MARCY, N.Y. -- A proposed battery energy storage facility has sparked strong opposition from residents at a public hearing held by the Town of Marcy Zoning Board of Appeals. The meeting took place at the Marcy Municipal Building, where many residents voiced concerns about the project. The proposed facility would be located at 9318 Cavanaugh Rd., across from the Marcy Beverage Center on River Road. Gridi Marcy Cavanaugh, the company behind the project, would need a use variance to build three separate battery energy storage systems at the site. Each system would have a capacity of 5 megawatts. Company representatives attended the hearing to answer questions from the board, local first responders and residents who oppose the project. "I've gotten a lot of contact from constituents in the Marcy area. They have concerns over this battery storage facility, whether it's going to devalue their property, safety concerns for our fire department. I have not received one phone call or contact in favor of this," said Oneida County Legislator Victoria Celia. Maynard assistant fire chief Randy Caldwell said, "Anytime we're dealing with lithium batteries. There's always concerns. The extinguishment of those it's not easily done. Sometime. Sometimes you just have to let them burn out. There are some agents that you can apply, but those are difficult fires." The board voted to accept the application for the use variance, but it will be at least 62 days before any decision is made.

artigo.texto: Tamil Nadu Approves 100 Per Cent Charge Waiver for BESS 02 Nov 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share The Tamil Nadu state cabinet has approved the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Policy 2026 after detailed discussions, with the policy aimed at accelerating the installation of battery storage across power generation and transmission networks. It covers projects with a capacity of 1 MW and above and seeks to improve renewable energy utilisation while reducing the curtailment of electricity generated from renewable sources. The policy recognises two categories of battery storage systems: standalone BESS and co-located BESS. Standalone BESS refers to independent systems with a capacity of more than 1 MW, which can be connected to transmission or distribution networks or to private consumer networks. Standalone projects will be eligible for a 100 per cent waiver of applicable transmission and wheeling charges. The systems can be used to meet peak-hour demand, support grid operations and provide other services approved under the policy. Co-located BESS refers to storage systems integrated with solar, solar-hybrid or other renewable energy projects with a capacity of more than 1 MW. These systems will store electricity produced by associated renewable energy plants and supply it during peak-demand periods or whenever required. Co-located BESS projects linked to existing or new solar, wind or hybrid projects will also receive a 100 per cent waiver of applicable transmission and wheeling charges. The policy will apply to all BESS projects for which applications are submitted on or after the date of notification, as well as projects commissioned on or after April 1, 2027. By covering both independent storage installations and systems paired with renewable energy projects, the policy establishes a common framework for deploying BESS across the state’s electricity network. The incentives are intended to support storage use during periods of peak demand and help renewable power reach the grid when it is needed. artigo.texto: From Readiness to Investment: Global Article 6 Forum Connects Host and Buyer Countries to Strengthen Carbon Market Cooperation November 3, 2026 Category The Global Article 6 Forum concluded in Seoul after four days of exchange among governments from eight buyer and enabler countries, and sixteen host countries, alongside carbon project developers, financiers, donors and academia. From 20 to 23 October 2026, the Forum gave actors across the carbon market landscape a shared platform to work through practical questions of international cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement as countries move from readiness to results. Hosted by the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) as part of Global Green Growth Week (GGGW) 2026, the Forum marked an evolution of the Community of Practice for Article 6 Implementing Countries (CoP-ASIC). Established under the Supporting Preparedness for Article 6 Cooperation (SPAR6C) program, CoP-ASIC has convened country practitioners annually since 2023. In Seoul, collaboration with GGGI’s Carbon Transaction Facility (CTF) helped extend the community from four to more than twenty countries actively pursuing Article 6 cooperation. Strengthening International Cooperation The expansion of CoP-ASIC reflects a central lesson: carbon markets are not only about rules and systems, but also about the relationships and trust that allow host countries, buyers, investors and project developers to cooperate to achieve climate targets. Building those relationships, through honest exchange about practical challenges, shared learning and a clearer understanding of country priorities, is essential to turning climate ambition into credible projects and benefits. More than twenty sessions translated country experience and insights into dialogue with market actors on actionable co-created solutions towards Article 6 readiness and implementation. Participants discussed practical challenges of moving towards carbon project pipeline development, including host-country strategies regarding additionality and corresponding adjustments, market interoperability, credit demand, and upfront financing. The sessions identified where stronger coordination and financing approaches are needed, and were complemented by interactive trainings on Article 6 operationalization. In his final day remarks, GGGI Executive Director Sang-Hyup Kim placed the Forum within the wider theme of GGGW 2026, “Powering Green Transformation: Technology, Finance and Global Cooperation at Scale.” He said: “Carbon markets, when built on integrity and effective governance, can mobilize finance where it is needed most, raise climate ambition, and support sustainable development across our member countries. They are a vital instrument of green growth, which lies at the heart of GGGI’s mandate.” Fenella Aouane, GGGI’s Managing Director and Head of Carbon Finance, highlighted the value of bringing the wider Article 6 community together. “Some of the most insightful moments of this Forum have been during conversations off this stage. I especially value the questions and discussions about getting funding on the ground – because that is where the most impact is and why we are all here to exchange ideas and solutions towards our shared challenges. We have supported host countries so they can lead the way to setting their own rules and translate Article 6 to how best it works for them, so barriers to carbon finance can be tackled effectively and transparently in each country.” Four Days of Learning and Exchange Day 1: CoP-ASIC Annual Meeting The fourth CoP-ASIC Annual Meeting brought together SPAR6C countries (Colombia, Thailand, Zambia and Pakistan) to discuss implementation experience, including progress on readiness, emerging strategic approaches and operational challenges. A highlight was the session “Sustaining SPAR6C Results Beyond 2027,” where participants discussed how capacities, networks and institutional arrangements can continue beyond the program’s end and shape a lasting legacy in partner countries and beyond. The SPAR6C 2025 achievement video was also screened and can be viewed here. Day 2: Capacity Development and Practical Exchange The second day was devoted to interactive learning and peer exchange, with workshops and applied discussions on the strategic and financial dimensions of Article 6. Highlights included workshops for host countries on corresponding adjustments, and on financing and contracting Article 6 activities featured in SPAR6C Toolbox’s Guide Six. The day also featured the research poster exhibition and award ceremony for third and final cohort of the SPAR6C Research Mentoring Program, where Masters and PhD students gained thesis support, networking and career opportunities as well as hands-on mentoring. Days 3 and 4: Conference, Market Dialogue and Knowledge Exchange On the third and fourth days of the Forum, participation opened to a wider group of carbon market stakeholders including governments, private sector actors, financiers and partners who met to discuss strategic choices, up-front financing challenges, blending of carbon and climate finance and broader market developments under Article 6. Sessions addressed emerging and cross-cutting themes and future collaboration across CoP-ASIC and the wider Article 6 community, including “Advancing Blue Carbon and Marine-Based Article 6 Cooperation,” “Advancing Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) in Mitigation Activities” and “Leveraging Carbon Finance for Adaptation Goals in Climate-Vulnerable Countries.” The conference closed with Buyer, Enabler and Host Countries Roundtables, that were a candid exchange among the three groups on the opportunities and challenges shaping Article 6 implementation, particularly for safeguarding and promoting benefit-sharing between countries. Together with country partners and the broader ecosystem, GGGI continues to support transparent and effective carbon market cooperation aligned with the Paris Agreement

artigo.texto: Form Energy Leading developer; first utility-scale projects underway According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Iron Air Battery market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global Iron Air Battery market is entering a pivotal commercialization phase, transitioning from laboratory-scale demonstrations to early multi-megawatt deployments. Iron-air chemistry, which stores energy by reversibly converting iron to iron oxide (rust), offers a compelling value proposition for long-duration energy storage (LDES) applications requiring 8 to 100+ hours of discharge. Its reliance on abundant, low-cost iron feedstock and water-based electrolytes fundamentally alters the cost-per-stored-energy equation compared to lithium-ion and flow batteries, which face material cost volatility and scaling constraints for extended durations. The primary demand architecture is bifurcating: front-of-the-meter grid-scale storage for renewable firming, transmission deferral, and capacity services, and behind-the-meter industrial resilience where safety and cycle-life insensitivity are prioritized. However, the technology remains largely unproven at multi-megawatt scale over decade-long operational lifetimes, and project bankability hinges on demonstrating multi-thousand-cycle durability and securing performance warranties. Supply chain logic diverges from lithium-ion, avoiding critical mineral dependencies but introducing new scale-up challenges in air electrode engineering and bipolar plate manufacturing. This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of the Iron Air Battery market from 2026 to 2035, covering deployment demand, technology positioning, manufacturing exposure, project economics, and competitive structure. The baseline scenario for the Iron Air Battery market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates a steep but uneven growth trajectory, characterized by early-stage commercialization followed by accelerated deployment as durability and bankability are proven. The market is projected to expand at a robust compound annual growth rate, with the market index rising from 100 in 2025 to a significantly higher level by 2035. This outlook is underpinned by the urgent need for cost-effective long-duration storage to support grid decarbonization, particularly in regions with high renewable penetration and constrained transmission infrastructure. The baseline assumes that leading developers successfully scale manufacturing, achieve multi-thousand-cycle durability in real-world conditions, and secure performance warranties backed by credible balance sheets. Demand will initially be concentrated in front-of-the-meter utility-scale projects, driven by LDES procurement mandates and investment tax credits in North America and Europe, before expanding into Asia-Pacific as manufacturing localizes. However, the path to 2035 is not without headwinds: the market faces competition from declining lithium-ion costs for mid-duration applications, nascent regulatory standards, and the inherent challenge of scaling a novel electrochemistry. The baseline scenario expects the first wave of commercial multi-megawatt systems to be commissioned by the late 2020s, with cumulative deployments accelerating through the early 2030s as project economics improve and supply chains mature. By 2035, iron-air batteries are expected to capture a meaningful share of the LDES market, particularly in applications requiring 100+ hours of storage, where their low marginal cost of energy capacity provides a distinct advantage over lithium-ion and flow batteries. Electric utilities and grid operators represent the largest and most critical end-use sector for iron-air batteries, driven by the need to firm high-penetration renewable grids and defer transmission investments. Currently, utilities are conducting pilot projects and early commercial procurements, primarily in North America and Europe, to validate iron-air performance over multi-day cycles. Through 2035, demand will shift from demonstration to large-scale deployment as utilities seek to replace gas peakers and provide capacity during extended low-renewable periods. Key demand-side indicators include renewable penetration rates, capacity auction prices, and LDES procurement mandates. The mechanism is straightforward: as variable renewables exceed 50% of generation, the grid requires storage durations of 100+ hours to bridge multi-day weather events, a niche where iron-air's low cost per stored energy unit provides a decisive advantage over lithium-ion. Utilities are also attracted by the safety profile and absence of critical mineral dependencies, which reduce supply chain risk and insurance costs. By 2035, utilities are expected to account for the majority of iron-air deployments, with projects scaling from tens of megawatts to hundreds of megawatts. Current trend: Rapid growth as utilities procure multi-day storage for renewable firming and capacity services.. Major trends: Rising renewable penetration driving need for multi-day storage, LDES procurement mandates and capacity auctions, Transmission deferral and non-wires alternatives, and Declining cost of renewable generation enabling arbitrage. Representative participants: Form Energy, Fluence Energy, Siemens Energy, General Electric, and Sumitomo Electric Industries. Renewable energy developers and independent power producers (IPPs) are increasingly co-locating iron-air battery storage with wind and solar farms to firm output and capture arbitrage opportunities. Currently, developers are evaluating iron-air for projects requiring multi-day firming, particularly in regions with high curtailment and negative pricing. Through 2035, demand will accelerate as developers seek to maximize project revenues by providing firm, dispatchable renewable power, which commands premium prices in power purchase agreements. K

artigo.texto: For a long time, an inverter had one primary job: keep essential appliances running when the power went out. Customers typically looked at three things when choosing one: how much load it could handle, how long the backup would last and how reliably it performed. That is beginning to change. As India expands its renewable energy capacity and adopts energy storage across more applications, the role of the inverter is evolving. It is no longer simply a backup device. It is becoming an important part of how electricity is converted, managed and delivered across homes, businesses and larger power systems. This shift has implications for the entire energy storage industry. The focus can no longer be on how much energy a battery can store alone. We also need to consider how efficiently that energy is converted, when it is used and how reliably the system performs under real-world conditions. India’s energy transition is changing the role of the inverter India’s growing renewable energy capacity brings an important challenge. Solar power generation depends on sunlight, while electricity demand follows its own pattern. The hours when solar generation is highest do not always coincide with the hours when electricity is needed most. Energy storage can help bridge this gap. It allows electricity to be stored when it is available and used when demand rises or generation falls. Beyond backup, storage can support peak-demand management, improve the utilisation of renewable energy and add flexibility to the power system. The scale of the opportunity is significant. According to the Central Electricity Authority’s National Electricity Plan, India’s projected energy storage requirement is 411.4 GWh by 2031–32, including 236.22 GWh of battery energy storage. These are projected requirements rather than installed capacity, but they give us a sense of the infrastructure India may need in the coming years. For the power electronics industry, this changes the conversation. The challenge is no longer limited to converting the direct current stored in a battery into alternating current for everyday use. Systems must also manage changing loads, operate efficiently and respond reliably to different electrical conditions. A battery is only as useful as the system around it Much of the discussion around energy storage focuses on battery chemistry, capacity, cycle life and charging performance. These are important considerations, but they tell only part of the story. The inverter, battery management system, control logic and protection mechanisms all influence how effectively stored energy is used. If these components are not designed to work together, the system may not deliver the performance a customer expects, even if the battery itself is capable. Consider a commercial facility that generates solar power during the day but experiences higher electricity demand in the evening. The value of its storage system depends on more than the amount of energy stored. It also depends on how efficiently the system charges and discharges, manages changing loads and minimises conversion losses. The same principle applies to homes, shops, offices and industrial facilities, although each application has different requirements. This is why we need to evaluate an inverter as part of an integrated energy storage system, rather than as an independent product. The shift from backup power to smarter energy management Customers are becoming more interested in how an energy storage system performs in everyday use, not simply how long it can provide backup during an outage. Can it handle changes in load? Is it compatible with the intended battery configuration? How does it respond to fluctuations in the electricity supply? Can its performance be monitored? What happens when operating temperatures or energy requirements change? These are practical questions, and the answers will increasingly influence buying decisions. I believe system integration will become one of the strongest differentiators in this market. The inverter, battery, controls and protection systems must work together as a reliable unit. Monitoring and diagnostic features can add value by helping users understand performance, identify potential issues and make informed maintenance decisions. However, adding software or connectivity does not automatically make a product better. Digital features are useful only when they are supported by sound engineering, reliable hardware and meaningful performance data. The objective should be straightforward: make energy systems more reliable, efficient and easier to manage. Grid-forming inverters and the next stage of grid stability One of the important developments in power electronics is the growing attention being paid to grid-forming inverter technology. As renewable energy and battery storage account for a larger share of electricity systems, maintaining stable grid voltage and frequency becomes an increasingly important engineering challenge. Grid-forming inverters are designed to establish and support aspects of grid behaviour, depending on their capabilities and the conditions in which they operate. India’s regulatory and technical discussions are also moving in this direction. Developments involving the Central Electricity Authority and proposed grid-connectivity requirements for renewable energy and storage projects reflect the growing importance of inverter capabilities in future power systems. The specific requirements, however, depend on the applicable regulations and the nature of each project. This is an important distinction. Adding more generation and storage capacity is necessary, but the electricity system must also be able to manage that capacity reliably. Grid-forming technology is particularly relevant to larger grid-connected applications. A residential inverter does not necessarily need the same capabilities as a utility-scale system. artigo.texto: Marvell compra Lumentum por US$ 115 bilhões em aposta no mercado de data centers para IA Fabricante de chips personalizados vai intensificar a concorrência com a rival de maior porte Broadcom, em meio à expansão dos investimentos em inteligência artificial A Marvell Technology anunciou nesta segunda-feira (2) um acordo para adquirir a fabricante de componentes ópticos Lumentum por US$ 115 bilhões, em uma transação inteiramente em ações, incluindo dívidas. Com a operação, a fabricante de chips personalizados intensifica a concorrência com a rival de maior porte Broadcom, em meio à expansão dos investimentos em inteligência artificial (IA). O negócio, anunciado hoje, é um dos maiores de 2026 e está entre as apostas corporativas mais ousadas até agora no boom da IA, que executivos do setor de chips esperam que sustente a demanda da indústria por muitos anos. Ao adquirir a Lumentum, uma empresa com cerca de metade de seu tamanho, a Marvell aposta que o boom de gastos com IA das grandes empresas de tecnologia veio para ficar e que a demanda por componentes ópticos usados para transmitir dados em alta velocidade continuará superando a oferta. Pelos termos do acordo, a Marvell pagará US$ 1.132 por ação da Lumentum, por meio de troca de ações, o que representa um prêmio de 23,9% em relação à última cotação de fechamento anterior à divulgação das negociações, em 28 de outubro. A operação atribui à Lumentum um valor de mercado de US$ 102,54 bilhões. Segundo a Marvell, a aquisição ampliará para US$ 550 bilhões o mercado total endereçável da companhia resultante da combinação dos negócios. As ações da empresa subiam 0,29% no pré-mercado, enquanto as negociações com os papéis da Lumentum foram suspensas. No início deste ano, a Nvidia, gigante dos chips de IA, investiu US$ 2 bilhões em cada uma das duas companhias. Há apenas três anos, a Marvell era uma fabricante de chips relativamente desconhecida. Desde então, porém, seu valor de mercado disparou para mais de US$ 170 bilhões, graças ao seu papel em ajudar gigantes da tecnologia, como a Amazon, a desenvolver chips de IA personalizados e tecnologia de rede para data centers. O acordo firmado nesta segunda-feira também pode fortalecer ainda mais a Marvell em sua disputa com a rival Broadcom, que há muito tempo é a principal parceira de chips personalizados do Google, de propriedade da Alphabet, e oferece aos clientes uma gama mais ampla de hardware de IA para data centers. A Marvell conquistou uma de suas maiores vitórias em agosto, ao assinar um acordo para fornecer chips que atuam em conjunto com os processadores de IA do Google, com um valor de vendas de até US$ 120 bilhões até o ano fiscal de 2033, concedendo ao gigante das buscas o direito de adquirir uma participação de US$ 12,2 bilhões.

artigo.texto: Mecpower Solutions, Navitas Solar Plan 5 GWh BESS Facility 02 Nov 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share Mecpower Solutions and Navitas Solar have collaborated to establish a 5 GWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) manufacturing facility in Karjan, Gujarat. The proposed facility is expected to begin operations in the first quarter of FY2027-28, according to an announcement by Navitas Solar. The companies said the project would support rising demand for integrated energy storage solutions across India’s renewable energy sector. The collaboration combines Mecpower Solutions’ capabilities in renewable energy project development, engineering and execution with Navitas Solar’s integrated manufacturing expertise. The proposed facility is intended to bring together manufacturing, project deployment and system integration capabilities. The companies plan to develop scalable storage solutions for utility-scale, commercial and industrial renewable energy applications, while supporting their respective engineering, procurement and construction deployments and utility-scale projects. BESS facilities are becoming an important part of renewable energy infrastructure because they can help manage the intermittency of solar and wind generation, improve grid stability and enable more efficient use of renewable power. The companies said the collaboration would strengthen domestic energy storage capabilities in line with India’s long-term renewable energy objectives. Setul Shah, director of Mecpower Solutions, said the facility would strengthen the company’s position across the energy storage value chain by combining manufacturing with its engineering, procurement and construction and independent power producer businesses. He said the project was intended to support the development of more flexible and reliable renewable power systems. Ankit Singhania, director of Navitas Solar, said domestic manufacturing would help strengthen India’s clean-energy supply chain and address the requirements of utility-scale storage projects. He added that the partnership would extend Navitas Solar’s manufacturing capabilities into energy storage and contribute to scalable solutions for India’s power sector. artigo.texto: PICKENS — Pickens County Council approved the first reading Monday of an ordinance establishing a six-month moratorium on data centers, giving county officials additional time to research the facilities and consider regulations governing their development. The measure, approved on first reading in title only, was amended to include a specific definition of what constitutes a data center. The ordinance would still need to go through two more readings and a public hearing before it can be finalized. Before taking up the proposed moratorium, council heard a presentation from Frank Hollman, a senior attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, who discussed potential impacts of data centers and considerations local governments should address when evaluating proposals. Hollman said data centers can raise significant local concerns. Among the issues he highlighted were transparency about a facility’s operations and energy demands, air pollution from on-site power generation, water consumption, wastewater treatment, noise and vibrations. He pointed to a proposed development in Spartanburg County, where he said the public was told a proposed development was not a data center and that its electricity consumption would be comparable to the previous operation. He said the facility was actually expected to use 470 megawatts of electricity, compared with 13 megawatts previously. “It happened in that instance. It’s happened elsewhere where things would be permitted in phases, so at first it appears like it’s a much smaller facility when it gets its initial approvals, and then boom, you learn later it’s eight times larger than was initially proposed,” Hollman said. He recommended establishing requirements for water use, wastewater pretreatment, noise limits, setbacks and landscaping before a facility is approved and construction begins. “The final point I think is all this needs to be set out in an ordinance up front and not negotiated after the construction is already begun and the problems are rising,” Hollman told council, adding communities can find themselves in difficult situations when those considerations are not addressed early in the process. Council on the moratorium After the presentation, the proposed moratorium was brought forward for consideration. Chairman Alex Saitta said Councilman Scott Lang had previously referred the data center issue to the county’s Development Standards Ordinance (DSO) Committee, while Councilwoman Claiborne Linvill had proposed the six-month moratorium to allow time to develop an ordinance. Saitta said he wanted the committee to receive direction from council members about what they would like a future data center ordinance to look like. He offered a complete prohibition as one possible approach. Linvill cautioned against adopting a moratorium without first establishing a clear definition of a data center. She said data centers come in different sizes and serve different purposes, pointing out Clemson University has two data centers and that smaller facilities may be necessary for businesses, medical facilities and educational institutions. “In order for us to have a moratorium, in order to be discussing, we need to know what it is we’re talking about,” Linvill said. She initially recommended one of three definitions provided by county staff, suggesting an option that would consider a facility’s primary use and establish exceptions for smaller operations. Councilman Chris Bowers then offered an amendment adopting a broader definition, describing a data center as any facility, building, structure or site primarily used to house computer systems, servers, data storage, networking equipment, high-performance computing, cryptocurrency mining infrastructure and associated power substations, backup generators, cooling systems and battery storage. The definition also includes cloud computing, which was added through a later amendment. Incidental server or IT equipment areas subordinate to a primary commercial, educational, governmental, healthcare or residential use would be excluded. Bowers said the definition would provide a starting point while allowing council to continue researching the issue. Linvill said additional considerations — including square footage, energy consumption thresholds and appropriate locations — could be discussed as the county works through the process. She also expressed interest in holding a public meeting to gather input on what residents would like to see addressed. Council approved the amended motion and first reading of the six-month moratorium.

artigo.texto: O fundo que controla a AP-9 entra no negócio das baterias elétricas na Galiza com um projeto de 22 milhões O grupo neerlandês Return, que é participado pelo fundo de pensões APG (dono da Audasa), promove um sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias de 40 megawatts de potência em Chantada (Lugo) Novo nome próprio na corrida pelos sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias em Galiza. BESS Development 11, filial do grupo holandês Return, projeta a implementação de instalações com 40,16 megawatts de potência instalada e uma capacidade de armazenamento energético de 152,395 MWh no concelho lucense de Chantada. Com a denominação de BESS Belesar, este grupo holandês promove a construção dessas instalações para as quais prevê um investimento total de cerca de 22,4 milhões de euros, conforme consta na documentação em posse da Xunta de Galiza, que submeteu o projeto a um processo de informação pública. A neerlandesa Return, que se autodefine como “fornecedor independente líder de armazenamento de energia em toda a Europa”, obteve em julho de 2025 as autorizações de acesso e conexão para colocar em funcionamento este sistema de armazenamento que será implantado sobre 1.024 metros quadrados de superfície. O projeto nasce com o objetivo de “armazenar energia nos momentos de maior produção e injetá-la na rede em períodos de alta demanda” e assim atenuar os picos irregulares na produção que sofre o sistema elétrico com a presença cada vez maior das fontes de geração renovável. O BESS Belesar ocupará assim 15% de um terreno de 6.683 metros quadrados e nele implantará 27 contentores CATL EnerX LFP de 5,644 MWh cada um. “A energia gerada pela planta chegará até a subestação coletora SET Soilán II 220/30 kV que está localizada a nordeste da planta no município de Chantada. A nova subestação coletora será compartilhada por vários promotores renováveis e evacuará a energia gerada através de uma linha subterrânea de 220kV até a subestação SE Belesar 220kV, propriedade da Red Eléctrica de España”, explica a companhia no projeto de execução elaborado pela Ingenor Iberia. A sombra do fundo APG após seu ganho com a AP-9 BESS Belesar é o primeiro projeto que a Return implementa em solo galego. Sua entrada ocorre em um momento marcado pela injeção de 300 milhões de euros que recebeu do fundo de pensões neerlandês APG. Galiza não é território desconhecido para esta firma, que desde 2024 atua como principal acionista da Itínere (dona da Audasa, concessionária da AP-9, e da Autoestradas de Galiza, que controla a AG-55 e a AG-57). Por meio dessa injeção de 300 milhões de euros, o APG entrou no capital da Return com uma participação minoritária. «O investimento do APG está alinhado com a estratégia de seu cliente de apoiar infraestruturas limpas e conectadas que gerem rentabilidade estável a longo prazo, ao mesmo tempo que impulsionam os objetivos de zero emissões líquidas, em benefício do ABP e seus participantes. O armazenamento de energia em baterias em grande escala é fundamental para integrar de forma confiável as energias renováveis e aliviar a congestão da rede», afirmou na ocasião Bart Saenen, diretor sênior de investimentos do APG. «A plataforma integrada da Return, sua visão de longo prazo nas relações e seu portfólio de projetos com riscos reduzidos a tornam um parceiro sólido para fortalecer a resiliência da rede elétrica em toda a Europa», defendia Saenen sobre esta companhia que no início de outubro colocou em funcionamento sua maior instalação até o momento. Trata-se do BESS Antares, um sistema de armazenamento de energia elétrica por baterias com 100 megawatts de potência e 200 MWh de capacidade, localizado no município neerlandês de Waddinxveen. Os outros projetos da Return na Espanha BESS Antares tem 2,5 vezes a potência do BESS Belesar e é o principal ativo de uma Return que atualmente constrói 450 megawatts e tem a Espanha no seu foco. A empresa alcançou no final de 2024 um acordo com a Benbros Energy para desenvolver mais de 500 megawatts em projetos de armazenamento na Espanha e já em 2026 firmou outros dois contratos-chave com a Engie e a Aquila Clean Energy para expandir sua presença no país. Com esta última, adquiriu projetos de 80 megawatts de potência para construir na Catalunha e em Astúrias, com os quais poderá armazenar o excedente de eletricidade gerado durante os períodos de alta produção solar e eólica, e liberá-lo quando aumentar a demanda e se atingir as horas de pico. Com a Engie, por sua vez, a Return acordou a implementação de três projetos de armazenamento de energia em baterias localizados no País Basco e dotados de uma potência combinada de 55 MW. “A Return desenvolverá, possuirá e operará os ativos, enquanto a Engie otimizará a carteira nos mercados grossistas e de serviços auxiliares da Espanha. O contrato tem duração de dez anos e prevê-se que as operações comerciais comecem no final de 2027”, explicava a empresa, que agora tramita seu primeiro projeto em Galiza. Não alterei nenhuma palavra. Apenas uni dois saltos de linha soltos que havia dentro das citações (“ao nordeste / da planta” e “na ocasião / Bart Saenen”). artigo.texto: Geral Putin determina que data centers privados na Rússia reservem 10% da capacidade para o país Medida é tomada em resposta a ataques ucranianos a data centers russos realizados nas últimas semanas. O presidente russo, Vladimir Putin, assinou nesta segunda-feira (2) um decreto que determina que proprietários russos de data centers não estatais reservem 10% do espaço físico e da capacidade das estruturas para ajudar a manter a infraestrutura digital da Rússia. Esse mecanismo permitiria que as autoridades russas acessassem rapidamente a capacidade disponível dos centros de dados, caso necessário. Nas últimas semanas, data centers da Rússia foram alvos de ataques de drones ucranianos, que alvejaram instalações operadas pelas empresas de tecnologia Yandex e Sberbank. Putin instruiu o Ministério do Desenvolvimento Digital a realizar um inventário da capacidade disponível e do espaço físico em data centers privados em toda a Rússia. Uma comissão governamental especial, a ser criada pelo decreto, terá poderes para ordenar a liberação da capacidade reservada, sendo obrigatório que os operadores disponibilizem o acesso em até 24 horas após a decisão. O decreto também permite o uso temporário de centros de dados localizados no exterior, sujeito à aprovação do Serviço Federal de Segurança (FSB, na sigla em russo).

artigo.texto: VinEnergo has commissioned a rooftop solar power system integrated with a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in the Vung Ang Economic Zone in Ha Tinh, Vietnam. The project will supply clean electricity to the VinFast electric vehicle manufacturing plant, the VinES battery manufacturing facility and the VG battery manufacturing joint venture. The project marks VinEnergo’s first operational renewable energy installation under the Direct Power Purchase Agreement (DPPA) mechanism. It is designed to support the electricity requirements of major industrial facilities while reducing dependence on conventional grid power. The initial beneficiaries include Future Production, Investment and Development Joint Stock Company, which owns and operates the VinFast electric car and motorcycle manufacturing plant in Ha Tinh, and VinES Ha Tinh Energy Solutions Joint Stock Company, the operator of the VinES battery manufacturing facility. The rooftop solar installation will also supply electricity to the VG joint venture battery factory within the same electric vehicle and battery manufacturing complex. According to company estimates, the integrated solar and storage system is expected to generate approximately 39 million kWh of clean electricity during its first year of operation. The project is projected to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by more than 25,000 tonnes annually, equivalent to the estimated annual carbon absorption of over 1.13 million trees. The transition to renewable electricity is also expected to ease pressure on the regional power grid, improve energy self-sufficiency for participating factories and deliver annual cost savings of nearly VND 3.5 billion. The successful commissioning and initial stable supply to the three industrial facilities provide a foundation for VinEnergo to expand its green energy activities in subsequent phases. The company aims to develop an integrated energy model combining renewable generation, large-scale battery storage, electricity distribution and retail infrastructure to support growing industrial demand in the Vung Ang Economic Zone. Nguyen Huong Giang, Deputy General Director of VinEnergo, said the project represents an important step towards developing a comprehensive energy ecosystem covering renewable generation, storage, DPPA mechanisms and electricity distribution. She highlighted the company’s focus on applying Vietnamese-developed products, manufacturing capabilities and technology to address the energy requirements of industrial customers. Beyond this project, VinEnergo is providing BESS solutions for several major projects of Hanoi Power Corporation and Northern Power Corporation, with a combined capacity exceeding 1.1 GWh. Internationally, the company has announced a renewable energy project portfolio totalling 10 GW and is implementing its first projects in Asia and Europe. VinEnergo aims to expand its project portfolio to 100 GW within the next three years, positioning itself among the world’s leading renewable energy companies. artigo.texto: DE SOTO, Kan. — KSHB 41 reporter Elyse Schoenig covers Johnson County. She also focuses on issues surrounding the cost of healthcare, saving for retirement and personal debt. Share your story idea with Elyse. — The data center debate has become one of the top issues nationwide, and it's playing a role in this year's Kansas governor race. The De Soto, Kansas, community knows this topic all too well. In De Soto, two data center projects are moving forward. Johnson County voter Abby Baker lives in De Soto. She said she's fighting to keep her community informed and that the issue of data centers influenced how she voted. "I would hope that the next governor would have more safeguards in place for all of Kansas," Baker said. "It is becoming a household issue, right? Every single place is having the same issue of getting these hyperscale data centers in these small communities, and they're wanting them out." NBC News reported that pro-data center super PAC Building the Future is spending more than $1.5 million to support Sen. Ty Masterson, the Republican candidate in the Kansas governor race. Sen. Cindy Holscher, his Democratic opponent, told NBC News she would "keep fighting for guardrails on data centers." Masterson and Holscher both voted last year for a bill to give data center developers sales tax exemptions. Holscher has changed her position on the legislation, now advocating for a statewide moratorium. Masterson opposes moratoriums. Park University professor Matt Harris told KSHB 41 last week the data center issue is becoming more top of mind for voters. "It's particularly an issue we see where people have really strong opinions where there have been proposed data centers, and so in those areas I think it's going to become a bigger political issue, particularly at the local level," Harris said. It's important to note there are no clearly defined party lines on the issue. "It doesn't really matter if you're red or blue or somewhere in between. It really is just a matter of, it's affecting us," Baker said. Baker said, for her, this issue is bigger than politics. "It's exactly like affordable housing or schools or anything else. It's just one of those new issues that I think, unfortunately, is going to be around for a while," Baker said. artigo.texto: CATL Extends Battery Lead to 39.1% as Dongfeng Deal Widens Charging and Swap Reach Published on 11/02/2026 at 16:01 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL shares climbed 3.1% on Monday, riding a broader rally in Hong Kong-listed lithium battery names after SNE Research published fresh installation data. A separate report put the gain at 3.4%. Either way, the advance came with a sector-wide tailwind — but the company also carried an argument of its own. Global installations of electric-vehicle batteries reached 994.5 GWh between January and September 2026, up 19.7% year on year, according to SNE Research. September alone accounted for 145.1 GWh, a worldwide record for a single month. CATL's slice of that market keeps widening. The company installed 389.2 GWh over the nine-month stretch, a 24.9% increase that outpaced the overall market and lifted its share to 39.1%. That compares with 38.3% for January through August, leaving CATL with the industry's largest market share. The distinction matters: a growing market is a sector story, while above-market growth is a company-specific one. Volume Strength, Earnings Drag The top line tells a different story than the bottom line. Revenue for the third quarter of 2026 came in at RMB 165.22 billion, up 58.6% from a year earlier. Net profit attributable to shareholders reached RMB 21.25 billion — a gain of just 14.5%. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? That gap between revenue and profit growth is the number to watch. Reuters reported on October 21 that earnings momentum had slowed amid tougher competition in batteries and cooling growth in Chinese car sales. Market leadership is intact; the question is how efficiently CATL converts volume into profit. Dongfeng Deal Covers Charging, Swapping and Overseas Push Dongfeng Motor said Friday it had signed an agreement to deepen cooperation with CATL. The pact spans ultra-fast charging, battery swapping, overseas markets and joint brand marketing — pairing technical collaboration with shared commercial promotion. The tie-up builds on CATL's existing swapping infrastructure. On October 20 the company unveiled its Tianxing II battery platform for heavy trucks and said it would expand its Qiji swap network to 900 stations in China by the end of the year, with 2,000 targeted by 2027. Project Pipeline Fills Out Other developments rounded out the week. On Friday, CATL-affiliated Yichun Times New Energy Mining received environmental approval for the Zhenkouli–Jianxiawo lithium mining project — a permitting milestone rather than evidence of active extraction. A day earlier, CATL presented its TENER+ energy storage system, with nine megawatt-hours of capacity, at All-Energy Australia, and signed letters of intent with Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group and the University of New South Wales. Those agreements open the door to cooperation; they do not constitute binding sales orders. CATL at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. On the technology front, CATL said Tuesday that trial small-series production of sulfide solid-state batteries remains on schedule for 2027 — a future plan, not a completed manufacturing step. The bull case rests on the installation figures: CATL is not merely keeping pace with a rising market, it is gaining ground on it. The project news adds color to that picture but does not substitute for proof on the earnings line. What remains to be demonstrated is how convincingly the company turns market strength into profit growth. Ad CATL Stock: New Analysis - 2 November Fresh CATL information released. What's the impact for investors? Our latest independent report examines recent figures and market trends.

For global investors, Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) contractors, project developers, and asset owners, Sigenergy’s Tier 1 status offers strong assurance of long-term operational stability and technical performance, facilitating smoother project financing and risk mitigation across the energy value chain. The Tier 1 status validates Sigenergy’s rapid worldwide growth, fueled by continuous R&D investment and its visionary "AI in All" strategy. By integrating artificial intelligence into its flexible, modular product architecture, Sigenergy delivers highly reliable, innovative energy storage solutions tailored for diverse applications, ranging from Commercial & Industrial (C&I) projects to complex, utility-scale power plants. This milestone reinforces Sigenergy’s commitment to empowering a broader spectrum of global customers, asset owners, and partners with scalable efficiency, robust safety, and long-term project value. artigo.texto: Com quase 2 GW de projetos solares sob contratos assinados na Colômbia , a Sungrow identifica uma tendência entre alguns desenvolvedores: construir usinas fotovoltaicas preparadas para incorporar sistemas de armazenamento de energia (BESS) dois ou três anos depois , adiando assim parte do investimento inicial. Durante a Future Energy Summit (FES) Colômbia 2026 , Héctor Núñez , diretor comercial da Sungrow para o norte da América Latina, explicou que essa estratégia já está sendo aplicada por meio de inversores centrais com conexões de corrente contínua (CC), em um mercado onde a evolução dos mecanismos de contratação e remuneração para armazenamento pode influenciar as decisões de investimento. “Você não precisa comprar uma bateria no primeiro dia, pode instalá-la dois ou três anos depois, porque o sistema já estará pronto para acomodar esse armazenamento”, disse ele. Essa modalidade é especialmente relevante para aplicações de arbitragem de energia e deslocamento temporal da geração, que permitem que a eletricidade produzida durante as horas de radiação solar seja armazenada e usada posteriormente. Do ponto de vista financeiro, preparar uma usina para integrar sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) não significa financiar o armazenamento desde o início . A decisão de incorporar baterias pode estar sujeita à evolução das receitas esperadas, aos custos dos equipamentos e às condições de conexão à rede. A alternativa não elimina as avaliações técnicas necessárias para uma futura expansão, mas permite antecipar alguns dos requisitos de integração entre a central fotovoltaica e o sistema de armazenamento. Essa discussão ganha relevância após a Colômbia ter incorporado o armazenamento de energia em seu mecanismo de aquisição de energia limpa. Em julho de 2026, o Ministério de Minas e Energia anunciou a adjudicação de 995 MW de geração de energia solar e quase 100 MW de armazenamento em baterias , no âmbito de um processo de aquisição de energia limpa. O concurso público representou um avanço para as instalações híbridas, ao incorporar baterias em contratos de longo prazo, uma condição que pode facilitar a avaliação financeira deste tipo de projeto. “Acredito que isso será o catalisador para que todos os projetos daqui para frente considerem o armazenamento de energia”, afirmou Núñez. No entanto, considerar baterias no projeto de uma usina de energia não implica necessariamente em instalá-las desde o início. Desenvolver configurações preparadas para integração posterior permite que diversas opções comerciais permaneçam em aberto. Neste ponto, a Sungrow identifica duas modalidades tecnológicas: o acoplamento CA , que integra as baterias através de conexões de corrente alternada, e o acoplamento CC , que permite que elas sejam interligadas através de uma arquitetura de corrente contínua. A escolha depende das características de cada projeto, dos equipamentos existentes e dos serviços a serem prestados. Em particular, o acoplamento CA pode oferecer maior flexibilidade para determinadas aplicações na rede elétrica, enquanto as configurações CC podem ser interessantes para deslocar a geração fotovoltaica para outros horários do dia. Seguir leyendo A possibilidade de adiar o armazenamento torna-se especialmente importante quando a receita esperada provém principalmente da venda de energia, sem uma remuneração adicional suficientemente definida para outros benefícios da bateria. O valor econômico das baterias além da arbitragem A Colômbia avançou em junho de 2026 com a Resolução CREG 101 113 , que estabelece regras para a integração de sistemas de armazenamento de baterias no Sistema Interligado Nacional, tanto associados à geração quanto por meio de instalações independentes. As regulamentações abrangem os aspectos técnicos, operacionais e comerciais dessas tecnologias. No entanto, o debate no setor também gira em torno das condições econômicas que permitirão às empresas aproveitar seus diversos serviços. “Por que não remunerar ou estabelecer uma taxa para esses serviços complementares, que certamente ajudariam a amortizar esses projetos de armazenamento?”, questionou o representante da Sungrow. Ao contrário da arbitragem, que depende das diferenças no valor da energia entre diferentes momentos, os serviços auxiliares permitem o uso de baterias para funções como regulação de frequência e suporte à estabilidade do sistema . O reconhecimento econômico desses benefícios pode modificar a estrutura de receitas de um projeto e, portanto, influenciar a decisão de instalar armazenamento desde o início ou incorporá-lo posteriormente. Em paralelo, Núñez destacou as possibilidades de desenvolver sistemas BESS autônomos , independentes de usinas de energia renovável, para lidar com restrições em nós críticos da rede elétrica. “Existem redes críticas que já estão sobrecarregadas, e não queremos sofrer com cortes de energia amanhã. Por que não considerar um sistema de armazenamento para regular a frequência e outras variáveis nesses nós críticos?”, disse ele. A proposta amplia o escopo do armazenamento para além da sua integração com parques solares e abre a discussão sobre mecanismos contratuais específicos para atender às necessidades do sistema elétrico. Olhando para o futuro, em 2027, a Sungrow prevê um aumento na atividade fotovoltaica na Colômbia, após um ano de 2026 que, segundo a empresa, registrou resultados comerciais positivos no fornecimento de inversores. Embora tenha evitado definir um número para a nova capacidade até 2030, Núñez considerou que o mercado poderia incorporar vários gigawatts adicionais de energia solar acompanhados de baterias. Nesse cenário, o momento da incorporação do armazenamento torna-se uma decisão econômica e tecnológica relevante : instalá-lo juntamente com a planta para aproveitar suas características desde o início, ou preparar a infraestrutura para incorporá-lo quando as condições contratuais e de remuneração o justificarem.

For the A-shares, Morgan Stanley kept its "Overweight" rating but removed the stock from its list of preferred picks, while lowering the target to RMB 335 from RMB 500. UOB Kay Hian took a different tack. The brokerage retained its buy recommendation on both share classes, pointing to a quarterly profit that came in below expectations. It nevertheless set a markedly lower valuation mark for the A-shares, reducing its target to RMB 343 from RMB 585. The buy call remains in place for that share class as well. A Quarter That Grew, Just Not Fast Enough The downgrades followed CATL's third-quarter 2026 results, released on October 20, which showed a net profit attributable to shareholders of RMB 21.246 billion. That represented year-on-year growth of 14.54%. Reuters highlighted the deceleration in earnings growth, pointing to fierce competition and slowing growth in Chinese car sales. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? Charging, Swapping and a Sodium-Ion Bet On the operational front, CATL has been unusually busy. On Thursday in Wuhan, the company and Dongfeng Motor signed a strategic cooperation agreement covering ultrafast charging and battery-swapping technology and systems, as well as vehicle energy supply, overseas markets and brand marketing, according to Dongfeng. That deal came two days after CATL's October 22 strategic agreement with the BAIC Group, which spans vehicle development, battery supplies, the build-out of a swapping network and battery services. The partners are targeting one million vehicles compatible with the swapping technology. Heavy trucks are getting attention too. CATL unveiled its Tianxing II battery platform on October 20, and Reuters reports the company plans to have 900 battery-swapping stations for trucks operating in China by the end of the year, rising to 2,000 by 2027.
