artigo.texto: Data-center fury is a campaign dud See more of our coverage in your search results. Tales of data centers’ impact on this election may have been greatly exaggerated. For months, prominent outlets ran headlines like “Data centers have become political napalm. Election Day will show how far it’s spread,” “Data centers are galvanizing the midterms” and “How data centres became the sleeper issue that could decide the US midterms.” But all that outrage likely will not amount to much. In polls nationwide and in states where data centers have supposedly been a hot topic, such as Texas and Ohio, the issue consistently ranks among the least important to voters. In a CNN Texas poll last month, just 3% named the issue as their top concern; in Ohio, only 2% did. The polling — and guidance from political strategists — suggest that the media coverage and activist frenzy surrounding data centers simply isn’t moving the needle. It is a dramatic shift from earlier this year, when politicians across both parties raced to distance themselves from the industry. Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott ordered a pause on new environmental permits for data centers, while Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro removed them from his state’s fast-track permitting program. In Ohio, Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown attacked Republican Sen. Jon Husted for helping bring data centers into the state, while Husted introduced legislation aimed at protecting residents from higher electricity bills. Likewise, in Texas, Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico pushed for tougher restrictions on data-center development. But now? That has largely been forgotten, strategists say. “Candidates who made a data-center moratorium a pillar of their campaigns didn’t get much traction… centering on data centers is going to distract Democrats from the core issues that we know voters are deciding on,” said one Democratic strategist. “Candidates in these ‘data center’ races are primarily putting their ad money into messaging around the economy, corruption and healthcare.” “This is an issue that people are not voting on — nobody’s closing on data centers,” said one longtime Republican strategist who worked on Trump’s 2024 campaign. “For most voters, it’s an imaginary issue. It’s something that they’re just being told about, but it’s not something that is tangibly affecting their lives. The Republicans strategist notes that he advised candidates to stop discussing it and focus on issues that the majority of voters care about. That so much attention was paid to an issue voters actually care little about gives greater credence to the idea that foreign adversaries may have played a role in fomenting data-center anxieties. A Bitcoin Policy Institute report covered by The Post in July claimed that a China-linked network associated with far-left donor Neville Roy Singham Singham and the Party for Socialism and Liberation had inserted itself into local data-center fights across 14 states. The report credited those efforts with helping stall or block at least $23.6 billion in proposed investment through rallies, petitions, door-knocking and packed public hearings. Other data points also suggest foreign interference was a factor — like the fact OpenAI said it had banned accounts likely originating in China that used ChatGPT to generate anti-data-center comments and images. X identified roughly 200 accounts within a much larger Chinese bot network posting content aimed at influencing the American debate over AI and energy policy. To be sure, many Americans still resist these centers in their communities. Some experts caution that politicians have simply kicked the can down the road — and that the fight over data centers could return once the midterms are over. “23% of proposals for new data centers were suspended in competitive congressional districts… versus 13% nationwide,” Paul Renshaw said, based on data that his fact-checking outlet PressAudit compiled. But even he says this isn’t going to be an issue that has to last. In fact, simply rebranding could help dramatically. “People are surprisingly pliable and willing to change their minds… All of the data tells me that people just want a better deal, and they have the power to negotiate for it.” Still others are skeptical that data centers will return as a potent political target — and think the backlash could fade as communities begin to see the benefits. “It was always a fabricated issue… Once they start seeing the effects of [data centers] in their schools and in their local infrastructure, perception is going to change,” said, referring to the tax revenue and jobs that projects could bring. Maybe the answer is to build and bet on the future. If data centers haven’t moved the needle with voters as a threat, perhaps they will as a benefit.

artigo.texto: Among the nearly 100 pages of risk factors outlined in Anthropic PBC’s landmark initial public offering are the catastrophic threats to humanity that have grabbed headlines. However, it also flagged a more immediate concern that could derail business: mounting backlash against data centers. Public controversy and regulatory scrutiny over the environmental impact, land and water use as well as consumption of limited power resources threaten to delay or prevent data-center development, Anthropic said in the prospectus. That would raise costs and limit its ability to scale, develop and deploy artificial intelligence (AI) models, it says. The company is right to worry. Hatred toward data centers has united people across the political spectrum and around the globe. Warning that the technology could create existential risks probably does not inspire anyone to want to give the AI boom a physical address in their backyards. Illustration: Yusha Opposition to the build-out has surfaced in Australia, the UK and even rural China. Now, it is starting to fester in pockets of Japan, just as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is pushing massive investment. Meanwhile, Anthropic is reportedly in final talks with NTT Data Group to build one of the country’s biggest data centers near Osaka. Yet while anxiety around the technology runs high globally, the Japanese are unusually sanguine about it — robots are seen here more as friendly helpers such as Doraemon than The Terminator. For a smaller, relatively insular economy facing acute labor shortages and demographic pressures, the upsides could be enormous. Many of AI’s strengths neatly address Japan’s acute gaps: translation in a country that has been flooded with foreign tourists, software engineering in a tech industry historically stronger in hardware than coding, boosting efficiency for small and medium-size manufacturers, and easing administrative burdens for the growing cohort of elder caregivers. The list goes on. For now, Japan’s opposition is scattered and local, hardly close to the organized political movement we are seeing in the US. However, there was little excuse anywhere to be so caught off guard. I have been tracking the AI backlash for a while, and the industry’s implicit threat that this might kill us all or take your job has never been an effective way to greet new neighbors. Outside of the Silicon Valley bubble, data centers as the physical manifestation of an abstract tech revolution have become easy targets. It is more than noise, eyesore or water use. It is about having a say. This is partly why the US revolt goes far beyond NIMBYism. Nearly three-quarters of Americans oppose having a data center in their community, while two-thirds are against new ones anywhere. It is already having a material impact: In the first half of this year alone, at least 106 projects, representing about US$198 billion in investment, were blocked or delayed, the Data Center Watch said. It offers lessons for Tokyo to not assume these are just isolated groups of Luddites. Japan has the most favorable environment for data center development among the OECD markets in the Asia-Pacific region, given its established digital infrastructure sector, BloombergNEF assessed. It already has some 2 gigawatts of operating IT capacity, second in the region only to China. Local opposition is a lurking threat, but the more immediate constraint is power. These facilities guzzle enormous amounts of energy to run servers and cooling, and Japan has never been energy rich. Power demand from new data centers and chip fabs is expected to rise from less than 1 percent of the country’s electricity consumption this year to nearly 7 percent by 2035, SMBC Nikko analysts have said. Addressing this challenge could help catalyze a broader shift toward clean energy. The government, for its part, seems aware of the problem. Takaichi has pledged a “sufficient and stable supply of electricity” to meet the growing demands from data centers, doubling down on an earlier promise to “take all possible measures” to do so. The policy direction is right, if ambitious, but increasing investments in green energy would help Japan build resilience in the future, not just power these facilities. Currently, most data center capacity is concentrated in the Greater Tokyo region and Osaka. Mindful of risks in the event of earthquakes or other unexpected shocks, officials have identified potential future sites in Hokkaido, Kyushu and elsewhere. Spreading infrastructure beyond crowded urban areas would also reduce some of the nuisance complaints that have fueled opposition elsewhere. Japan was initially slow to adopt AI, but usage has finally surged. That delay could become a second-mover advantage that the country cannot afford to squander as investors start questioning the payoff from the expensive, hype-fueled AI infrastructure spree. The country has long excelled at developing infrastructure that works for people, from trains that run on time to urban design that fosters community. That could be a major advantage. If Tokyo can construct data centers without neighbors bringing out the pitchforks, it could define what comes next. Catherine Thorbecke is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asia tech. Previously she was a tech reporter at CNN and ABC News. artigo.texto: Dear Editor, As a parent and a teacher, I urge local leaders to demand accountability for data centers. Right now, big polluters are profiting while our families foot the bill. Data centers take up acres of much-needed land that could otherwise be used for affordable housing, education or agriculture. We need our rural landscapes to keep protecting wildlife and providing clean air and water. READ MORE The rush to power data centers is driving new fossil fuel development, threatening climate progress and bringing more toxic pollution to communities. Instead, we could be powering our lives with clean energy that protects our wallets, our climate and our health. The progress we have made in the last 20 years in restricting emissions and reducing pollution will be reversed, especially if data centers are gas powered. This shouldn’t be a difficult choice. Let’s hold data centers accountable with common-sense guardrails now. Anne D’Olivo Manchester, Vt.

artigo.texto: A Chinese green tech company has recently made history with the launch of the world’s first commercially deployed, fully integrated 800-volt direct current (DC) power system at a massive artificial intelligence (AI) data center. Shanghai’s Envision Energy announced the technology on Monday, November 2. It is currently powering live computer workloads at the company’s Galaxy AI data center campus in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, China. The platform combines solid-state transformers, battery energy storage, as well as smart controls to deliver electricity from the grid to computing equipment. As per company representatives, it could cut energy loses, lower infrastructure costs, and support more powerful AI servers within the same space. Kevin Huang, Envision Energy’s senior VP, pointed to the technology’s potential. “AI data centers need power systems that coordinate renewable energy, energy storage, and the grid to meet computing demand,” Huang explained. Powering AI servers As AI data centers expand, they require more electricity to run. Reports show that global data center power demand could surge by 160 percent by 2030. Moreover, research suggests data centers alone could require as much as 68 gigawatts (GW) of capacity worldwide by 2027, roughly equivalent to California’s power grid. More from Energy See All But delivering that power efficiently remains a massive challenge. Traditional data center power systems utilize multiple conversion stages to deliver electricity from the grid to servers. These stages require additional equipment, cables, and space. To address these challenge, Envision came up with a new system that can convert electricity directly from a 10-kilovolt (kV) medium-voltage input to an 800-volt DC power system. It reduces the need for extra equipment and copper cables, leaving more room for computer hardware. To maintain a stable electricity supply, the firm integrated solid-state transformers with battery energy storage. The batteries can also respond to sudden changes in power demand within seconds and provide backup power for several minutes. At the same time, Envision’s Dubhe Controller, coordinates both the transformers and the batteries through its Dubhe Energy Foundation Model. As a result, the system can respond to rapid changes in electricity demand within milliseconds. Targeting more power Envision’s Galaxy AI data center campus began operations in August 2026. It has a planned capacity of three gigawatts (GW). Once fully developed, the facility is expected to support up to one million AI accelerators operating simultaneously. Huang said the system uses renewable energy to power AI workloads. “This is a critical step in turning power-compute coordination from a strategic vision into an operational reality,” he concluded in a press release. In the future, the company aims to source more than 80 percent of the campus’s electricity through direct renewable energy connections. The power architecture could serve as a reference for other data centers as the industry moves toward 800-volt DC infrastructure. “Already operating commercially ahead of wider industry adoption, the system provides a reference for the industry’s transition to 800V DC,” the firm stated. It also aims to expand the technology via its Mission Gobi initiative. It targets five GW of green AI data center capacity across desert regions worldwide by 2030.

artigo.texto: A Google energy executive has told reporters that data centers in orbit can cost up to 100 times more than the same capacity on the ground, according to a report from The Information. We could not open the original paywalled story, so the executive’s name, the exact wording and the method behind the 100x figure remain unconfirmed in this article. What we can verify is the surrounding picture: Google’s own researchers, outside engineers and rival space firms all agree that orbital computing costs more than terrestrial computing today, and they disagree mainly on how much more. The timing matters. Google launched its first Project Suncatcher test satellite on Oct. 1, 2026, and the spacecraft started answering prompts within weeks. We covered that milestone when the first orbital TPU replied with a haiku. Now the company’s own energy leadership is putting a hard price warning on the idea, just as investors weigh a record wave of earthbound data center spending. This analysis lays out what is known about the claim, how it compares with other published estimates, why launch economics dominate the math, and what the number means for cloud buyers who plan capacity over the next five years. It also offers five predictions and a short FAQ. Throughout, we attribute figures to the outlet that published them and label our own arithmetic as arithmetic. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Google’s Energy Chief Reportedly Said About Space Data Centers The headline claim is simple. An energy chief at Google said space data centers can cost up to 100 times more than data centers on Earth, and The Information carried the story. The phrase “up to” matters. It signals a ceiling for the worst case rather than a central estimate, and it likely reflects a spread of scenarios that depend on launch price, satellite lifetime and how much compute each satellite carries. We searched for the underlying text and found no public version of it. Searches for the 100x phrase surfaced only unrelated uses of the number, such as one startup’s plan to give its second spacecraft 100 times the power generation of its first. That absence does not make the claim false. Paywalled scoops often circulate for days before other outlets match the details. It does mean readers should treat the multiplier as reported rather than independently confirmed. One more caution applies. A cost multiplier on its own says little without a baseline. A 100x premium over a cheap grid-connected hall in Iowa is a different statement from a 100x premium over a 2030 gigawatt campus with its own nuclear supply. Until the original report’s assumptions surface, the safest reading is directional: Google’s energy side sees orbital compute as far more expensive than the ground option for now. How 100x Compares With Other Published Estimates The 100x figure sits at the extreme end of a wide range. IEEE Spectrum estimated that designing, building and launching a one-gigawatt orbital data center would cost more than $50 billion, based on a network of about 4,300 satellites and including five years of operating costs. The same analysis put a comparable terrestrial facility at roughly $16 billion. That is a premium of about three times, not one hundred. Skeptics quoted in 2026 coverage land in the same neighborhood. A roundup of the sector reported that critics calculate orbital compute at roughly three times the cost per watt of ground equivalents. Proponents argue the opposite direction. Starcloud, a startup that already flew an Nvidia H100 in orbit, claims unit economics near $0.05 per kilowatt-hour that would make orbital capacity competitive with terrestrial power by the early 2030s. Elon Musk has said space-based solar data centers could beat ground ones within two to three years, a timeline that CNBC’s June 2026 analysis called disputed. Read together, the table shows a spread of two orders of magnitude, from parity to 100x. The spread exists because each party picks a different launch price, hardware life and workload. That makes the 100x figure less a rebuttal of Google’s own research than a different slice of the same model, run with pessimistic inputs. Why Launch Cost Drives the Gap Nearly every serious analysis starts with price per kilogram to low Earth orbit. Google’s researchers argued that orbital computing approaches parity with ground data centers on a cost-per-kilowatt basis once launch falls to about $200 per kilogram. Coverage of the original Suncatcher research put today’s Falcon Heavy price near $1,500 per kilogram, and projected a drop toward $200 by around 2035. Other published ranges run from about $1,000 to $2,900 per kilogram depending on vehicle and customer, and one 2026 sector roundup cited about $2,700 per kilogram for Falcon 9. Simple division shows how sensitive the result is. At $2,700 per kilogram, launch costs run 13.5 times the $200 target. At $1,500 they run 7.5 times. Launch is only one line item, because hardened chips, solar arrays, radiators, inter-satellite links and replacement flights add cost on top. A pessimistic stack of those items is how an analyst could reach a very high multiple. Back-of-envelope arithmetic (ours, not a forecast) Launch price vs. Google's $200/kg parity target $2,700 / $200 = 13.5x $1,500 / $200 = 7.5x Capacity cost for a 1 GW site, using IEEE Spectrum's terrestrial baseline $16B x 3 = $48B (close to IEEE Spectrum's "over $50B") $16B x 100 = $1.6T (what a literal 100x would imply) The $1.6 trillion line is the useful sanity check. No credible developer plans a gigawatt of orbital capacity at that price, so a literal 100x would describe a scenario nobody intends to build. It is a warning about what happens if launch prices stay flat and satellites fail early, not a quote for a project. Launch supply is the second constraint. Quilty Space analysts have warned the industry may fall about 150 launches short

artigo.texto: A lawsuit seeking to reverse the Sangamon County Board’s April 7 approval of zoning to allow for construction of a data center could hinge on the court’s interpretation of the word “shall” within the county’s data center code. Circuit Judge Adam Giganti, at the conclusion of an Oct. 30 hearing on motions to dismiss the suit, said he’s “going to take the matter under advisement and will render a decision as soon as possible.” The July 6 lawsuit was originally filed against Sangamon County and the County Board by residents who live approximately a mile or less from the site. They are seeking to overturn the county’s approval of the project, claiming procedural violations and unchecked environmental concerns. The Sangamon County Board approved a conditional use permit on April 7 that would allow a data center to be constructed on 280 acres of farmland by a vote of 17-10, with one board member abstaining. Amongst other things such as lack of a noise study and pollution concerns, the suit claims the approved zoning petition had insufficient documentation as required by the County Code’s own language stating “(t)he petition for a conditional permitted use for a data center shall include… letters from the serving utility companies indicating the availability and adequacy of utility services.” The County Board approved the zoning petition despite the electricity utility letter submitted referencing a different data center project altogether and the water utility letter stating it was still reviewing CyrusOne’s application. The County Board’s lawyers argue that the Board was “conditionally approving the (conditional use) permit contingent on future submission of these materials.” The Rural Electric Convenience Cooperative will-serve electricity letter, dated Aug. 26, 2025, makes no mention of CyrusOne but it does say the electric co-op will provide electricity to a different, substantially smaller project called the Diamond Core Data Center. The Jan. 29 Apple Creek Water Cooperative letter included in the zoning petition states the water utility is still reviewing CyrusOne’s application. READ PREVIOUS ILLINOIS TIMES COVERAGE OF THE LAWSUIT HERE: Data center lawsuit could be tossed out County Board defends data center approval in court Residents sue Sangamon County, CyrusOne Illinois Times called and emailed both utility companies and Sean Middleton, president and CEO of RECC – who has been publicly supportive of the project – over the past three weeks asking if either company could provide updated will-serve utility letters for the CyrusOne data center project but neither responded to numerous requests. Apple Creek Water Cooperative referred Illinois Times to its attorney from Rammelkamp Bradney but multiple voicemails left for Bradley Wilson were not returned. In court, the county’s lawyers from Champaign law firm Webber & Thies argued the plaintiffs’ “artful pleading” is because the residents are simply upset with the outcome of April’s vote. The lawyers say the county had plenty of reason for approving the data center through the potential for economic incentives, so the lawsuit should be terminated. “The County Board here or the legislature or whatever legislative body it is has policy power. They have the right to legislate. They are making decisions. They are the people’s representatives. The ordinary citizen’s remedy – if they disagree with that decision – is political,” said attorney Daniel Thies during the Oct. 30 hearing. “We don’t want ordinary citizens who have lost in the political process to be able then to hold out the legislators. “The county’s legislative body can decide that it’s going to value economic development more than the potential for a little bit of pollution. That is a prerogative of the people’s representatives through their elected body,” Thies said. The county’s own staff report shows about $71 million of projected property tax revenue would go to three taxing bodies based in Macoupin County, with six Sangamon-based taxing districts expected to split roughly $27 million over a 20-year period, if all assessments go according to plan. Sangamon County itself could expect to see just over $445,000 for 20 years in annual tax revenue, though some large data centers in northern Illinois and other parts of the country have later appealed for property tax reductions. Meanwhile, no state or local sales tax will apply to any of the anticipated $500 million investment since CyrusOne secured a tax break before Gov. JB Pritzker’s executive order to pause a state program providing deals to developers went into effect. As for property value concerns, Thies said the existence of a data center could lead to nearby property value increases with the potential for neighboring data center developments. “There was testimony of a real estate appraiser who studied this question and determined that the surrounding property values, in fact, would not be depressed and very well could rise as they have adjacent other data centers that have been built around the country,” he said. Chloe Russell, a Plainfield lawyer representing members of the Caruthers family, who have farmed land in southwest Sangamon County for close to two centuries, and Cathy Bettis, owner of Joette Kennel, argued Oct. 30 the complaint is not contending issues with the county’s reasoning but “it pleads the county’s violations” of “mandatory petition elements. “On the utility letters, both defendants point to the conditions in the approval order requiring updated and definitive will-serve letters before a building permit is issued. Those conditions prove our point. If the letters had been adequate, no condition would have been needed,” she said, before pointing out how each will-serve letter does not comply with the county’s own code. “The ordinance says the petition ‘shall include,’ before the board acts. artigo.texto: Company leverages expanding residential solar platform and long-duration energy storage capabilities to capitalize on rising demand for reliable, cost-effective power NEW PORT RICHEY, Fla., Nov. 02, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Zeo Energy Corp. (Nasdaq: ZEO) ("Zeo,” "Zeo Energy,” or the "Company”), a provider of residential solar and commercial long-duration energy storage ("LDES”) solutions, today outlined its strategy to drive growth across its two complementary business segments, leveraging continued momentum in residential solar and an expanding pipeline of commercial energy storage opportunities supporting data centers and other energy-intensive applications. Zeo's growth strategy builds on its vertically integrated residential solar platform, which generated 9.2% year-over-year revenue growth during the first half of 2026 despite broader industry headwinds, alongside its commercial energy storage business. Together, these businesses position Zeo to address increasing demand for affordable, reliable and flexible energy solutions across residential and commercial markets. "We see significant opportunities to create value across both sides of our business,” said Tim Bridgewater, Chairman and CEO of Zeo Energy. "Our residential solar platform continues to demonstrate its resilience in a challenging market, supported by a differentiated sales model and disciplined operating approach. At the same time, our commercial energy storage business is positioning us to address growing demand for dependable power solutions, particularly as data center development places increasing pressure on traditional grid infrastructure.” Residential Solar: Driving Growth Through a Differentiated Operating Model Zeo's residential solar business generated $29.4 million in revenue during the first six months of 2026, with second-quarter revenue increasing 23% sequentially. The Company achieved this growth despite a challenging industry environment characterized by elevated financing costs and reduced residential solar activity. The Company's vertically integrated operating model encompasses customer acquisition, system design, permitting, installation and ongoing service, providing greater control over the customer experience and operational execution. Zeo's differentiated direct-sales organization, supported by investments in technology and AI-enabled customer relationship management tools, is designed to improve productivity and enhance operating efficiency. Zeo maintains a disciplined regional growth strategy, concentrating its residential solar operations in select markets, including Virginia, Ohio, Illinois and Pennsylvania, alongside its established presence in Florida. The Company believes this targeted approach enables it to leverage existing infrastructure, optimize customer acquisition costs and expand its presence in attractive markets. The residential solar market also presents a significant long-term growth opportunity. With approximately 8% penetration among an estimated 95 million U.S. homes, compared with approximately 15%-25% penetration in certain international markets, the Company believes substantial runway remains for domestic adoption. Rising utility rates, growing interest in energy independence and the continued development of residential financing solutions are expected to support demand over time. Commercial Energy Storage: Addressing Growing Data Center Power Demand Through its commercial division, Zeo is developing an energy storage business focused on long-duration solutions for data centers, utilities and other commercial and industrial customers. The Company's commercial strategy emphasizes behind-the-meter power infrastructure designed to deliver reliable, continuous electricity while incorporating renewable energy generation and storage technologies. Zeo is particularly focused on opportunities involving smaller and midsized data centers with power requirements of approximately 20 to 50 megawatts, where flexible energy infrastructure can help address grid capacity constraints and accelerate access to power. Zeo's commercial engineering team is evaluating a range of LDES technologies, including molten salt, compressed carbon dioxide and alternative battery chemistries, with an emphasis on applications requiring approximately 10 to 14 hours of energy storage duration. The Company is currently pursuing approximately six commercial projects at various stages of development, reflecting growing demand for distributed power infrastructure and long-duration energy storage solutions. Among these opportunities is Zeo's previously announced non-binding memorandum of understanding with Creekstone Energy to explore the development of approximately 280 megawatts of energy generation and storage capacity for a planned data center campus in Millard County, Utah. The proposed development would incorporate solar photovoltaic generation and storage as part of a subsequent phase of the project's behind-the-meter power infrastructure. Zeo is also evaluating additional opportunities in Utah and other markets where data center expansion is creating demand for reliable, scalable power solutions. Multiple Growth Drivers Supported by a Strengthened Balance Sheet Zeo is pursuing a multifaceted growth strategy designed to capitalize on opportunities across its residential and commercial businesses while maintaining financial discipline. In residential solar, the Company is focused on expanding its sales organization, increasing productivity in existing markets and introducing complementary offerings, including roofing and HVAC services. These additional services are intended to leverage Zeo's established customer relationships and infrastructure to generate incremental revenue opportunities. The Company also continues to evaluate selective acquisition opportunities that could expand its geographic reach, enhance operating capabilities or provide access to complementary commercial energy projects. artigo.texto: Brookfield is targeting a massive artificial intelligence data center in the north of England, as Europe scrambles to develop infrastructure to support the rollout of AI amid high energy and land costs. Energy company Drax Group said Tuesday it has signed an agreement with Brookfield and the asset manager's neocloud platform Radiant to jointly develop an AI data center on the Drax Power Station estate in North Yorkshire. London-listed shares of Drax were up 8.8% in early morning trading. The project is initially targeting up to 100 megawatts of capacity to be operational from the first quarter of 2028, with an additional 500 MW of capacity to be brought online between 2028 and 2031. It is then looking to secure more than 1 gigawatt of capacity at the site by an unspecified date. Brookfield estimates total investment, including semiconductors, could exceed £20 billion ($26.8 billion), with an initial £2.5 billion investment in phase 1. "This is a unique opportunity for the UK's AI ecosystem to build at scale," Radiant CEO Mahdi Yahya said in a statement. "By designing, building and operating from the UK, it will give British researchers, startups and enterprises access to frontier compute at home." The first phase of Brookfield's project in North Yorkshire will use power from the grid and target commercial customers from early 2028. The initial phase is subject to planning, regulatory and network approvals from the government and relevant agencies, alongside securing a tenant for the project, Drax said in a statement said. The company added that final investment decisions are yet to be made. Europe's AI data center push While the U.S. has surged ahead on developing the huge data centers needed to power AI, Europe has been slower to break ground on the facilities. The U.K. in particular has struggled with high energy costs and challenges with long waiting times for businesses to connect to the grid. In October, it was reported that Microsoft had pulled out of a deal to anchor an Nscale data center just outside London, amid delays connecting to the country's power grid. An Nscale spokesperson told CNBC at the time that it remained "committed" to the project and was "exploring alternative power sources for the site." Unlike the U.K., the Nordics benefit from abundant power and available land. Countries in the region, like Finland, have seen major commitments to develop AI data centers this year. In September, Google said it would invest at least 13 billion euros ($15.1 billion) into AI infrastructure in the country, marking the tech giant's largest single investment in Europe.

artigo.texto: *This content was translated by AI.View Original As the Chinese government imposes a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries while including sodium-ion batteries in the scope of tax incentives, major battery companies such as HiNa Battery are accelerating efforts to build large-scale production systems aimed at the commercial electric vehicle market. Through an announcement issued by China’s Ministry of Finance, General Administration of Customs, and State Taxation Administration, a 2% consumption tax will be levied on specific lithium-ion batteries starting September 1 this year, with plans to raise the rate to 4% in the future. In contrast, sodium-ion batteries, all-solid-state batteries, and fuel cells are exempt from the consumption tax until December 31, 2028, provided they meet national standards. Such tax benefits serve as policy support to offset the narrowing price competitiveness of sodium batteries due to falling lithium prices. Against this policy backdrop, HiNa Battery signed an agreement to build a sodium-ion battery production base with an annual capacity of 10 GWh in Jiangxia District, Wuhan City. As the first phase, a 3 GWh facility will be constructed first, with construction set to begin in early 2027 and initial production to commence within that year. In addition, HiNa Battery is partnering with Qingli Special Vehicle Group to develop sodium-battery-based special-purpose sanitation vehicles, including street sweepers and food waste collection trucks. Sodium-ion batteries are noted for their excellent low-temperature performance as a key strength. Tests on large commercial vehicles demonstrated that they maintain over 90% of available capacity even in extreme environments at minus 40 degrees Celsius. However, challenges remain, including limits in energy density and the manufacturing process for hard-carbon anode materials, so initial adoption is expected to be active primarily among large commercial vehicles and special-purpose vehicles rather than passenger cars. *This content was translated by AI.View Original

artigo.texto: They all spiked: Construction of data centers and power plants; orders for equipment at US manufacturers; and inflation in construction. By Wolf Richter for WOLF STREET. Data center construction spending spiked by another 8.6% in September from August, and by 90% year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $96 billion, according to construction data from the Census Bureau today. Since the beginning of 2021, the annual rate of construction spending on data centers has spiked by 950%. The AI data center construction boom is continuing along a near-exponential curve. Nothing that needs to be funded can grow on an exponential curve for long. But the inflection point imposed by capital constraints hasn’t come yet. The big 12 AI companies are still raising massive amounts of money, more than they’re spending, and have already accumulated an unused war chest of $1.1 trillion in cash and cash equivalents, much of which they can spend even if tanking market make further fund raises too difficult (my analysis). Not even local resistance on the ground by people, municipalities, and state governments have managed to slow the overall growth of data centers though they have delayed or stalled one or the other project. Data centers, their demand on power, their effect on electricity prices, and related issues have entered midterm election rhetoric, but that issue will fade in a couple of days. Construction is the cheap part of data centers. These amounts only reflect the construction costs of the buildings, the improvements around the buildings, and the equipment integrated into the buildings, such as HVAC systems. Not included is the expensive part of a data center: The servers and racks, electronic and optical equipment to connect the servers to the internet, the electrical equipment to supply the servers with power, including in many cases onsite power generators. The construction spending trend – though only a slice of total investments in data centers – is a good indicator about future demand for equipment needed to turn an empty building into an operating data center. Construction spending on power plants and distribution infrastructure rose by 0.9% in September from August and by 11.1% year-over-year to an annual rate of $192 billion. Since the beginning of 2021, the spending rate has increased by 63%. Power plant construction spending includes the costs of the power generation equipment. Factory construction spending has been roughly stable over the past three months at an annual rate of $170 billion, and that was up by 128% from the beginning of 2021. But it has fallen off the construction boom levels a few years ago. This is still a massive amount of factory construction spending, 76% higher than data center spending. And it indicates that expansion of the US manufacturing capacity continues at a breakneck pace. Equipping a modern factory, including semiconductor plants, is by far more expensive than the costs of construction of that factory. Once the factories are built and equipped and production starts, their real contribution to the economy and employment begins and continues for decades. Building a factory is not a one-time shot but a long-term contribution to US production. It’s not the construction spending that matters to the economy, but the future production that will come from these new factories. Shockwaves of demand for US manufacturers. Demand for the equipment that is needed for data centers, power plants, and factories has sent a shockwave of demand through the industrial economy. Orders received by manufacturers in the US of “core capital goods” (durable goods without defense and aircraft) spiked by 10.4% year-over-year in September, to $88 billion, according to separate data from the Census Bureau in October. This category includes manufacturers of factory equipment, construction machinery, computers and electronics, electrical equipment, fabricated metal products, farm implements, appliances, heavy-duty trucks, railroad rolling stock, ships, etc. Orders for machinery spiked by 16.1% year-over-year, to $46.0 billion. This has data centers, power plants, and factories written all over it. Industries in Machinery Manufacturing (North American Industry Classification System, NAICS, code 333) includes manufacturers of: - Engine, Turbine, and Power Transmission Equipment - Ventilation, Heating, Air-Conditioning, and Commercial Refrigeration Equipment - Machinery for Construction, Agriculture, and Mining - Industrial Machinery - Commercial and Service Industry Machinery - Metalworking Machinery - Other General-Purpose Machinery. Orders for computer and electronic products spiked by 16.6% year-over-year to $31 billion. This includes orders for semiconductors at US-located semiconductor fabs. Industries in computer and electronic products manufacturing (NAICS 334) include manufacturers of: - Computer and Peripheral Equipment - Semiconductor and Other Electronic Components - Communications Equipment - Audio and Video Equipment - Navigational, Measuring, Electromedical, and Control Instruments - Magnetic and Optical Media. Construction hit by the second wave of inflation. The Producer Price Index (PPI) for construction materials spiked by 11.0% year-over-year in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics in October. This includes steel mill products, concrete, lumber, gypsum, etc. For an analysis of overall PPI inflation, see: Businesses Slammed by 6.3% PPI Inflation, Worst since 2022, Much Worse than Consumer-Facing Inflation The PPI for nonresidential construction services spiked by 14.0% year-over-year. This includes trade services, transportation, warehousing, architectural engineering, and legal services. artigo.texto: SpaceX's AI division, SpaceXAI, lost its bid to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit, which is proceeding in federal court in Mississippi, according to a judge's opinion released late Friday. The lawsuit claims that the AI division of CEO Elon Musk's aerospace and defense tech conglomerate violated the Clean Air Act with its use of gas-fired combustion turbines to power its massive AI data centers in Greater Memphis. The Colossus data centers and a power plant that SpaceXAI is also building in Southaven, Mississippi, have faced community backlash for years. The Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice filed the suit on behalf of the NAACP in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi in April 2026. The suit alleges that between August and December 2025, xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech, installed and operated 27 gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, "without an air permit or regard for the health and safety of people living nearby." (SpaceXAI is owned and operated by SpaceX, which has rebranded it as SpaceXAI or SpaceXSI.) The turbines emit smog-forming pollutants and particulate matter that can increase health risks and cause an unpleasant odor, among other unwanted impacts, according to the suit. Lawyers for SpaceXAI argued in their motion to dismiss, filed in June, that the NAACP suit should be tossed because the company's use of the turbines, which it characterized as "mobile," was exempt from permitting requirements. They also argued that NAACP didn't have a right to sue under the federal Clean Air Act, and suits by such community groups were unconstitutional. The judge presiding over the case rejected those arguments, writing: "Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not 'mobile sources' under Mississippi's SIP, and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs' claims will proceed." The decision comes about two weeks after the same court rejected a Department of Justice's request to end the case against Musk's company. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

artigo.texto: The Westbrook City Council voted unanimously Monday night to prohibit standalone data centers . The city updated its land use ordinance to remove the use of data centers from the Rock Row Contract Zone. However, it still allows data centers as an accessory use, like server rooms and IT rooms for hospitals and other large organizations. Previously, the Rock Row Contract Zone was the only place data centers were permitted, and the city’s ordinances didn’t include any additional standards for data centers beyond a usual site plan review. Mayor David Morse said he supported the ordinance amendment and noted substantial concerns about data centers, such as electricity and water demands, noise and infrastructure burdens. “First and foremost our resources and infrastructure need to support the people who live here, our existing businesses, and the housing and economic opportunities our community needs,” Morse said. “Resource-consuming data centers are simply not a good fit for Westbrook.” In June, the Westbrook City Council passed a 180-day data center moratorium on data centers, though the city hadn’t received any applications to build such a facility like some of its neighbors had. During the moratorium, the planning board was tasked with reviewing the city’s ordinances and providing a recommendation. It recommended only permitting data centers as an accessory use and updating the city’s definition of a data center. Westbrook now defines data centers as “one or more buildings or spaces on a property that house networked computer systems and associated equipment, such as servers, network hardware, data storage, power generation or cooling systems, to process and manage data.” Cities and towns across the state have passed temporary moratoriums, and in a handful of others, voters will decide on their ballots Tuesday to temporarily or permanently ban data centers.

artigo.texto: Texas Is Becoming A Hotspot For AI Data Centers, And It's Not Just About Cheap Land The Lone Star State, already home to hundreds of AI data centers, is set to open hundreds more in the coming years. Texas currently has over 300 operational data centers and around 250 under-construction or planned ones, for a total of 561 facilities, many of which are concentrated in the Dallas-Fort Worth area. Land availability and cost are certainly important factors, but there are other reasons that explain why Texas is such a desirable market for data center investors. According to commercial real estate and investment firm CBRE, as of April 2026, 78% of investors viewed Dallas-Fort Worth as the "most attractive market" for data center development thanks to power availability and cost, fiber Internet availability, and lower natural disaster risk than other parts of the country. Much of the state, including major cities, has a deregulated energy market that allows homes and businesses to choose their supplier rather than having to rely on a local utility company. It's a system that's intended to provide options to consumers and promote competition, but, in practice, often leads to higher costs. Texas is also known for its lax, business-friendly regulations and has tried to make itself more appealing to data center investors with a state sales tax exemption for data centers. While announcing a $40 billion Google investment intended to boost the state's AI infrastructure, Governor Greg Abbott called Texas "the epicenter of AI development," framing the deal as a job-creating opportunity. While the state might appear an ideal frontier for the AI data center boom, these facilities are facing increasing amounts of backlash from ordinary Texans. Data centers are increasingly unpopular By now, you're probably aware of the multitude of issues that make data centers controversial, such as resource consumption that drives up utility prices (especially in places where resources are already strained) and creating pollution that contributes to climate change. AI data centers have also driven a memory chip shortage that has led to skyrocketing consumer tech prices and come with unexpected consequences like threats to zoo animals and livestock. That's why increasing numbers of people are pushing back against proposed data centers and calling for more regulation on existing ones. Opinions on data centers and their impact are becoming increasingly negative, and elected officials on the local and state level are starting to take note. In July, New York became the first state to put a one-year moratorium on new data centers as the state develops regulations to make them less disruptive and destructive. As of this writing, 16 states have introduced legislation targeting new projects, though several have already failed. Even Gov. Abbott, currently locked in an unexpectedly close gubernatorial race, has changed his tune. In August, the governor mandated a comprehensive audit for all proposed data centers, and in September, he halted all data center permits until the audit is completed. These executive orders are essentially a moratorium on all projects in Texas, which is a major shift in under a year and reflects the public's growing distaste for data centers and their proponents. What other states are seeing data center booms? It's worth mentioning that counting data centers is difficult, as there's no universal definition for what a data center even is. On top of that, they're measured differently; some only count operating data centers, while others go by power consumption or size. Before the moratorium, Texas was on track to become the state with the most data centers by the end of the decade, but it may remain in second place for longer to Virginia. According to the U.S. Data Center Map, which measures active, under-construction, and planned facilities, Virginia has 591 data centers to Texas' 561. In a distant third is California with 343 data centers, followed by Ohio (238) and Georgia (232). The gap between Virginia and Texas could widen depending on how long the audit takes. In the previously mentioned CBRE survey, 72% of investors viewed Northern Virginia as an appealing market for data centers. That said, Virginia is also tightening regulation in response to public outcry. In September, Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced comprehensive data center accountability standards, and a newly introduced state Senate bill that would put a moratorium on new approvals already has bipartisan support. As for power consumption, it's true that everything is bigger in Texas. The state's data centers have a reported power total of 103.7 GW, 10.5 GW of which comes from operational facilities. Virginia is second at 40.6 GW total and 9 GW active. Pennsylvania comes next at 23.4 GW total, though just 328.6 MW of that's from operational data centers. Only counting active ones, Georgia comes in third at 2.5 GW.

artigo.texto: A Melbourne-developed battery that can power a home or be taken on the road is moving towards local production, backed by $6.77 million in funding support from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA). Clutch Industries will establish and operate a scalable manufacturing line in Victoria for its portable PowerNet battery—a modular4 kWh battery made using solid-state battery cells. Related article: Western Australia to lead nation in plug-in solar and batteries The solid-state battery architecture delivers a safer, lighter, and a more compact energy storage system. PowerNet units can be combined to form a household energy storage system or used individually to power caravans, 4WDs, boats and other off-grid applications. Clutch Industries CEO Brad Davis said, “Clutch Industries has a long history of Australian manufacturing, and through our Density battery business, we’re building on that experience to develop next generation energy storage solutions right here in Australia. ARENA’s support will help us take the next major step in scaling up local battery manufacturing. “Our vision for Density goes well beyond a single product. We’re unlocking product innovation, using breakthroughs in battery technology to create solutions that were previously impractical or simply not possible. “With Density products already available through major Australian retailers, we’re excited to continue expanding the brand, growing our manufacturing capabilities and bringing Australian-developed battery technology to more consumers.” The project is expected to help move the technology from product development into scalable Australian manufacturing. Testing will also provide practical evidence about the battery’s real-world performance. Related article: Solar sharing tech wins Good Design Award of the Year The project is being supported through ARENA’s Battery Breakthrough Initiative.

artigo.texto: As a lifetime organizer, my colleagues and I have proven the cliché — “you can’t fight City Hall” — wrong. Whether that City Hall was in New York, Jersey City, Chicago, Baltimore, Philadelphia, D.C., or a dozen other places, we repeatedly won, often over the initial opposition or indifference of mayors and governors. But City Hall is no longer the primary locus of power. Today it is in the unprecedented concentration of money and influence represented by a handful of tech companies based in Silicon Valley. Their dominant role, decades in the making, through Republican and Democratic administrations, has now peaked. So is it time for a new cliché — “you can’t fight Big Tech?” That’s certainly what the tech industry would like people to say. And their wholly owned subsidiary, called the Trump administration, parrots and promotes this line. But, once again, I would take a breath and look at the facts. Here’s one: in 2026, approximately $260 billion in data center construction was stopped in its tracks, according to a study done by Heatmap. For a while, it looked as if projects propelled by trillions in investment dollars, unlimited demand from AI companies, local municipalities desperate for tax revenues, and unions eager for work were unstoppable. But the momentum has already slowed. And the pace of the rejection of new centers has increased because of good, solid local organizing. Everything about this situation is familiar to me. As an organizer with a Metro Industrial Areas Foundation affiliate in Jersey City, Interfaith Community Organization, I was part of an effort that exposed the presence of toxic hexavalent chromium in Jersey City. A team of leaders — the Rev. Willard Ashley, Fr. Geoff Curtiss, the late Myrtle Smith, along with Metro IAF organizers Joe Morris and Stephen Roberson — patiently documented the damage done in Jersey City. Honeywell and PPG each had left tons of toxic chromate waste in the soil and drinking water of Jersey City. Untold numbers of workers and residents had contracted cancer and respiratory conditions. The kids who used the playing fields developed sores on their arms and legs. Fishermen ate fish that sickened them. The state, even under the so-called environmentalist Gov. Jim Florio, either showed no interest or actively cooperated with the polluting companies. The revolving door between state environmental officials and company executives spun constantly. In the long run, none of that worked. Our team sued Honeywell. And a federal court ordered Honeywell to spend $400 million to clean the 100-acre Bayfront site — with the company removing more material, 1.5 million tons, than was taken from the World Trade Center site. A second company, PPG, then settled for $600 million, and is finishing the clean-up of its 100-acre site. The data center cowboys use the same playbook. Avoid accountability. Sign non-disclosure agreements with municipalities. Provide no reasonable estimate of environmental dangers, of increases in water and energy costs, of health risks. Run your diesel generators with impunity, as one Virginia data center just did, forcing residents to flee. New York’ governor, Kathy Hochul and N.J. Gov. Mikie Sherrill have shown that they understand the games played by these companies and are demanding accountability. What the chromium story shows is that endless money and wired relationships only go so far. Nothing is inevitable if elected leaders and organized residents take the initiative and stop data centers in their tracks. It would be far better to halt and properly regulate these centers now, before they inflict the kind of damage the residents and workers of Jersey City endured, than after more harm is done to our kids and grandkids. Gecan is a senior advisor at Metro Industrial Areas Foundation and the author of “Going Public.”

artigo.texto: Nvidia pode garantir dívida bilionária de data center de IA Fabricante de chips estuda ser fiadora de empréstimos da Nscale para construção de campus de IA na Virgínia Ocidental, num sinal de como o setor força limites para manter a expansão. A Nvidia está negociando um papel incomum para uma fabricante de chips: o de fiadora bilionária. A empresa discute garantir parte do financiamento de dívida que a Nscale, provedora de nuvem especializada em inteligência artificial, precisa para erguer um megacampus de data centers na Virgínia Ocidental. O projeto tem como principal cliente a Anthropic, dona do chatbot Claude, que assinou um contrato de 44,6 bilhões de dólares apenas para o primeiro prédio do complexo. O arranjo, conhecido como garantia de valor residual, funcionaria assim: se a Nscale deixar de pagar os custos de construção, a Nvidia assumiria temporariamente a instalação, buscando um comprador e um novo inquilino. Não é um investimento direto. É, na prática, colocar o nome e o balanço da maior empresa de semicondutores do mundo como rede de segurança de um projeto alheio. Por que a Nvidia está disposta a ser fiadora A resposta curta é demanda. O campus da Virgínia Ocidental deve usar os chips de próxima geração Vera Rubin da Nvidia. Há ainda negociações para um segundo prédio, avaliado em cerca de 45 bilhões de dólares. Manter a Nscale de pé significa manter um canal de escoamento para centenas de milhares de GPUs de última geração. A Anthropic é uma das maiores compradoras de poder computacional do planeta. Como analisamos na cobertura do setor de IA, empresas desse porte distribuem seus gastos de infraestrutura entre vários fornecedores de chips. Para a Nvidia, garantir que o projeto da Nscale saia do papel é, indiretamente, garantir que a Anthropic continue dependente de sua arquitetura. A Nvidia já investiu cerca de 170 bilhões de dólares em aportes e linhas de crédito para neoclouds e grandes clientes. Em setembro, comprometeu 1 bilhão de dólares em financiamento conversível à própria Nscale. A diferença agora é o nível de comprometimento: até então, o apoio da fabricante cobria aluguéis e compra de chips, não obras de construção civil. O problema estrutural das neoclouds Neoclouds são provedoras de computação em nuvem focadas em IA que não contam com um negócio gerador de caixa robusto por trás. Diferente de Amazon (AWS), Microsoft (Azure) ou Google Cloud, que financiam seus data centers com receitas de operações diversificadas, empresas como Nscale, CoreWeave e Nebius dependem quase inteiramente de captação externa. O mercado já sinalizou desconforto com esse modelo. Ações da CoreWeave, Nebius e IREN acumularam quedas superiores a 30% ao longo de outubro. A própria Nscale busca abrir capital com valuation de até 35 bilhões de dólares, mas os números operacionais são modestos: em agosto, a empresa tinha cerca de 25 mil chips avançados em operação, uma fração dos quase 500 mil que planeja implantar. Os obstáculos não são apenas financeiros. O campus na Virgínia Ocidental enfrentou problemas ambientais, com escoamento do canteiro de obras inundando residências vizinhas mais de uma vez. A certificação estadual só saiu em setembro, após meses de negociação. E neste mês, a Microsoft desistiu de um projeto da Nscale na Inglaterra depois que a conexão à rede elétrica foi empurrada para a década de 2030. Anthropic também enfrenta seus próprios desafios Do outro lado da mesa, a Anthropic não está em posição confortável. A empresa protocolou pedido de IPO, mas a Blackstone alertou investidores de que a companhia pode receber uma classificação de crédito abaixo do grau de investimento após a abertura de capital. Uma nota “junk” elevaria os custos de captação e poderia obrigar a Anthropic a continuar dependendo de parceiros financeiramente mais sólidos para lastrear suas dívidas. Esse contexto explica por que a Nvidia se dispõe a ir tão longe. Se a Anthropic tiver dificuldade para financiar sua própria expansão, ela precisa de parceiros de infraestrutura que consigam levantar capital. Se esses parceiros também não conseguem, a cadeia inteira emperra. E quem mais perde com um freio na construção de data centers é justamente quem vende os chips que vão dentro deles. Como discutimos na análise sobre o papel da Nvidia no ecossistema de IA, a empresa vem assumindo uma função que vai muito além de fabricar semicondutores. Ela atua como banco, fiadora e investidora estratégica de toda uma cadeia produtiva. É um modelo sem precedente claro na indústria de tecnologia. O que isso significa para o mercado de IA O movimento revela uma tensão estrutural no boom de inteligência artificial. Há apetite quase ilimitado por capacidade computacional, mas o financiamento dessa infraestrutura depende de modelos cada vez mais criativos e arriscados. Quando o maior fabricante de chips precisa co-assinar empréstimos de construção civil para garantir que seus produtos tenham onde ser instalados, o ecossistema está operando nos limites do viável. Para investidores, o sinal é duplo. Por um lado, confirma que a demanda por chips de IA permanece forte o suficiente para justificar compromissos bilionários. Por outro, mostra que o elo mais frágil da cadeia não é a tecnologia, mas a infraestrutura física e seu financiamento. Como acompanhamos na editoria de finanças, setores que dependem de alavancagem pesada em ambientes de juros elevados tendem a sofrer correções abruptas quando a confiança dos credores oscila. A decisão final da Nvidia sobre a garantia ainda não foi formalizada. Mas o simples fato de a negociação existir já diz muito sobre o estágio em que o ciclo de investimento em IA se encontra: a fase em que construir é tão difícil quanto inventar. Este conteúdo é informativo e educacional e não constitui recomendação de investimento. Rentabilidade passada não é garantia de resultados futuros.

artigo.texto: De acordo com os novos regulamentos, o Presidente do Comitê Popular Provincial tem autoridade para aprovar o registro de projetos, a alteração do registro de projetos, mudanças nos componentes participantes, o cancelamento do registro de projetos e a emissão de créditos de carbono no âmbito do mecanismo nacional de troca e compensação de créditos de carbono. É importante destacar que as organizações e agências participantes do projeto, dentro do escopo especificado, podem submeter suas candidaturas diretamente, via correio, no Centro de Atendimento da Administração Pública Provincial, ou online, através do Portal Nacional de Serviços Públicos e do aplicativo nacional de identificação. Em determinados casos de cadastro no Sistema Nacional de Cadastro, o Presidente do Comitê Popular da província receptora é responsável por conceder a abertura da conta e enviar as informações ao órgão ou organização competente, no prazo de 5 dias úteis a partir da data de recebimento da solicitação; em caso de recusa, o motivo deve ser claramente justificado. O decreto também especifica os procedimentos e prazos para o processamento de pedidos de projetos de geração de créditos de carbono. Especificamente, o prazo para notificar a validade do pedido é de 3 dias úteis; o prazo para divulgar o pedido e consultar a opinião pública é de 22 dias úteis. Para projetos implementados em várias províncias, o registro exige o consenso das localidades relevantes. Após a conclusão das etapas de consulta, avaliação e análise, conforme prescrito, o Presidente do Comitê Popular da província que receber a solicitação decidirá sobre a aprovação do registro do projeto e sua publicação no Sistema Nacional de Registro. Para procedimentos relacionados à alteração de participantes do projeto, o tempo de processamento não deverá exceder 7 dias úteis a partir da data de recebimento da solicitação; o procedimento para cancelamento do registro do projeto deverá ser concluído em um prazo não superior a 22 dias úteis. Com relação à emissão de créditos de carbono, o Decreto estipula claramente os documentos necessários, a responsabilidade pela obtenção de pareceres dos órgãos competentes e o prazo de processamento. No prazo de 10 dias úteis a partir da data de recebimento dos pareceres dos órgãos e organizações competentes, o Presidente do Comitê Popular da província que recebeu a solicitação deverá decidir sobre a emissão dos créditos de carbono e publicá-los no Sistema Nacional de Registro; caso o crédito não seja emitido, os motivos deverão ser claramente justificados. Para projetos de carbono florestal, os procedimentos de registro, ajuste, cancelamento de registro e emissão de créditos são realizados de acordo com o Decreto Governamental nº 180/2026/ND-CP, de 21 de maio de 2026, que regulamenta os serviços de sequestro e armazenamento de carbono florestal. O Decreto nº 396/2026/ND-CP entra em vigor a partir de 12 de dezembro de 2026.

artigo.texto: A single large AI data center can use as much electricity as tens of thousands of homes, and residents in a growing number of communities worry about what that could mean for their utility bills. That concern has carried over from public hearings into tomorrow’s midterm elections. Recent polls show majorities of Democrats and independents, along with a sizable share of Republicans, oppose new data centers in their areas. That leaves candidates in both parties answering questions about projects once courted by state and local leaders. Supporters say the facilities bring jobs, tax revenue and an advantage in AI development. Further, a new poll from ABC News, the Washington Post and Ipsos found that a majority of Americans (57%) believe AI is bad for society, with many more pointing to its dangers than the potential benefits the tech could bring. An even larger number of those polled (66%) are opposed to the construction of new data centers in the US, and more (72%) would be opposed if it were in their community. More from CNET Opposition to AI crosses party lines. The technology has faced a surge in public disapproval this year, putting political candidates on blast and potentially affecting outcomes in key races, political and polling experts told CNET. Ambivalence about AI also feeds into negativity toward data centers, which have, in a short time, become a rare bipartisan issue everyone’s talking about, according to Christopher Lee, partner and senior political strategist for Foresight Strategic Advisors. Lee, who has closely followed election trends in southwestern states such as Nevada and Arizona, said the issue of data centers — massive AI server and compute farms that consume vast electricity and water resources — is going to “hammer” some candidates, especially those who weren’t transparent with constituents in the past about the cost to communities. If a politician voted for the construction of a data center earlier this year, their “political career is going to run into a stone wall,” he said. Reading the room The ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos survey asked a wide range of questions about how Americans will vote in the midterms and what they think of the political parties. Alongside the economy, immigration and the war against Iran, the AI rollout is a critical issue. As noted by CNET reporter Katelyn Chedraoui, AI regulation and data center construction have been the subject of controversy, protests and increased legal action in communities. The poll confirmed as much: 67% of respondents felt the government isn’t doing enough to regulate AI, with risks including widespread job losses, psychological dependency, economic inequality and even human extinction. Fears and negativity toward AI also extend to the election process itself, with AI election interference among Americans’ top 10 fears for 2026. A national PR campaign funded by tech leaders and supported by the Trump administration, meant to tout the alleged benefits of data centers, such as job creation and technological advancements, doesn’t seem to be having the intended effect. Some politicians, especially those running for congressional seats, seem to be better at reading the room. According to Lindsey Cormack, an associate professor of political science at Stevens Institute of Technology and co-host of the podcast Government That Doesn’t Suck, many candidates are paying close attention to how they communicate about AI developments, with a particular focus on the problems they present rather than the benefits they provide. “It’s difficult to persuade people with promises of economic development when they’re worried about their electricity bills or water supply,” she said. Cormack, creator of the congressional newsletter archive DCinbox, has tracked a sharp rise in lawmakers linking data centers to consumer energy costs. In an email to CNET, she noted that between January and September 2025, just 5% of Republican newsletters discussing data centers mentioned electricity bills or ratepayers (4 of 76). Over the same period in 2026, that figure surged to 54% (97 of 180). Democrats showed a similar focus, with 40% of their data center newsletters (71 of 176) raising the issue in 2026. The midterms won’t be the end of the battle. AI and data centers are “going to be an issue in 2028 and 2030 and way beyond that,” Lee said.

Nov 2, 2026 New Mexico Community Center Gains Solar Resilience A building that began as a one-room schoolhouse has grown over the decades into a lifeline for a New Mexico community far from city infrastructure, and a recent solar installation has added resilience to the site. According to Solar Power World, the structure now houses the Ojo Sarco Community Center, which was founded in the early 20th century in an unincorporated community of about 300 people roughly 43 miles northeast of Santa Fe. Carol Miller, a grant writer and board member for the center, described the community as lacking political voice and having lost resources over the years, including its post office. She said residents must commute for nearly everything, with a round trip for basic amenities taking about 40 minutes. The community center has sought to fill those gaps with services including a twice-monthly food bank, summer meal programs for children, safety classes and resident outings such as a night at the opera. The center also recently met all the qualifications to become a state library. PPC Solar, also known as Paradise Power Company, of Taos, built a 7.5-kW solar project paired with 10.6-kWh of LFP energy storage at the center at no cost to the community. The contractor donates a solar array to a regional nonprofit each year, and the Ojo Sarco Community Center was awarded the project after three years of applying. CEO Daniel Weinman said his father founded Paradise Power Company in the 1970s and that the company has installed solar in off-the-grid communities since its start. He said the annual nonprofit donation program has run for more than a decade and has served farming organizations and land conservation groups, among others, with the aim of finding the right fit and making a good impact. For this project, he said resiliency was the best way to do that. Solar Power World spoke with PPC Solar and center organizers about the project's effect since it was built in fall 2025. Larry Miller, project manager and board member, called it a transformative project for the small community and said the solar panels are now part of the center's history and are pointed out to visitors. Carol Miller said the installation has lowered electric costs, which matters for a shoestring operation. She said internet remains available even when the power is out, that children attending library programs are solar oriented, and that the company and its staff have had ripple effects throughout the broader community. Preston Bastardo, who works in sales and design at PPC Solar, said mounting the array on the roof presented challenges that required exploring the attic to land things where needed. He said the building has two large areas and that installation of the batteries faced restrictions, but a mechanical closet was suitable for them. For backup circuits, the project used a partial facility backup with a critical loads panel next to the main panel, and he said everything went smoothly. Weinman traced the effort to the company's roots, noting that in 1972 there was no technology supporting solar and that his father developed his own controls and safety protections, found used panels and batteries, and brought power to places without it. He said his own home started with kerosene lanterns and did not have electricity until a solar power system was installed, which he described as life changing. He said building on that legacy and offering systems to communities that need them adds to it and is profound, and that the company wants to continue participating however it can. Carol Miller said the community is very old and proud of it. Having worked with local businesses and its electrical cooperative, she said owning its power makes the community an exception rather than the rule, and that any technology shared equally in a low-income community has ripple effects beyond what some imagined years ago. artigo.texto: BOTETOURT CO., Va. – Botetourt County, its Board of Supervisors, its Economic Development Authority and a shell company owned by Google are facing a lawsuit over a planned 312-acre Google data center project. The 72-page lawsuit, obtained by 10 News, was filed by a Botetourt County resident who alleges the county violated the Virginia Freedom of Information Act (VFOIA) when it adopted key agreements related to the project without adequately disclosing the actions to the public. The lawsuit argues VFOIA requires local governments to identify the subject matter being discussed during closed meetings. It alleges the Board of Supervisors failed to properly do so before discussing and adopting the Performance Agreement Resolution and the Performance Agreement (two key contacts for the project). The lawsuit asks the Botetourt County Circuit Court to declare the two actions null and void, prevent the Board of Supervisors from taking further action on the performance agreement and related resolution and take back any action take on the Performance Agreement after June 24, 2025. This would include rescinding the expedited permits issued to Google and Google’s eligibility to participate in the Botetourt County Third Party Inspection Program. It would also require the board to follow VFOIA when adopting similar resolutions. Botetourt County officials released the following statement in response to the lawsuit: “As this matter involves pending litigation, Botetourt County will not comment on the specific allegations or discuss legal matters. The County respects the legal process and remains committed to providing accurate and appropriate information to the public as the matter moves forward.”
