artigo.texto: TL;DR: A Proposta 45, medida de votação na Califórnia que promete acelerar a construção de infraestrutura considerada "essencial", pode abrir uma brecha para que desenvolvedores de data centers evitem a fiscalização pública, segundo alertas de ativistas ambientais. O que aconteceu A iniciativa de votação, conhecida como Proposta 45, foi apresentada como uma solução para agilizar a aprovação de projetos de infraestrutura considerados críticos, incluindo data centers, redes de energia e instalações de telecomunicações. O texto da proposta permite que esses empreendimentos sejam classificados como "essenciais", o que reduz a necessidade de avaliações ambientais detalhadas e de audiências públicas. Organizações de defesa ambiental apontam que a redação vaga da medida pode ser explorada por empresas de tecnologia para construir ou expandir data centers sem a devida transparência. A preocupação central é que, ao serem enquadrados como infraestrutura essencial, esses projetos escapariam de processos de licenciamento que normalmente exigem estudos de impacto ambiental, consultas à comunidade e divulgação de documentos técnicos. Até o momento, a proposta está em fase de campanha, com defensores argumentando que a rapidez na implantação de data centers é vital para a competitividade econômica da Califórnia, enquanto críticos temem que a falta de controle comprometa a qualidade do ar, o consumo de água e a gestão de resíduos eletrônicos. Como chegamos aqui A Califórnia tem sido um dos principais polos de tecnologia dos Estados Unidos, abrigando gigantes como Google, Amazon e Meta, que mantêm enormes fazendas de servidores para atender à demanda global de serviços em nuvem. Nos últimos anos, a pressão por maior capacidade de processamento levou a um aumento significativo na construção de data centers, especialmente em áreas com energia renovável abundante. Entretanto, a expansão acelerada trouxe desafios ambientais. Data centers consomem grandes quantidades de energia elétrica e água para refrigeração, além de gerar calor e ruído. Em resposta, a agência estadual de proteção ambiental (California Environmental Protection Agency) tem exigido avaliações de impacto cada vez mais rigorosas, o que, segundo alguns setores da indústria, retarda projetos e aumenta custos. Foi nesse contexto que a Proposta 45 surgiu, impulsionada por lobby de grandes corporações de tecnologia e grupos de interesse que defendem a desburocratização. A proposta foi incluída na cédula de votação como parte de um pacote de reformas voltadas para a modernização da infraestrutura estadual. Entretanto, organizações não‑governamentais, como a Sierra Club California, alertam que a definição de "infraestrutura essencial" está muito ampla e pode ser interpretada de forma a incluir projetos que, embora tecnicamente críticos, ainda geram impactos ambientais significativos. Elas pedem que a redação da medida seja revisada para garantir que avaliações ambientais não sejam suprimidas. O que vem depois Se aprovada, a Proposta 45 entrará em vigor imediatamente, permitindo que desenvolvedores de data centers solicitem autorizações simplificadas. Isso pode acelerar a construção de novos centros ou a expansão dos existentes, reduzindo o tempo de aprovação de meses para semanas. Por outro lado, a falta de auditoria pública pode dificultar a participação da sociedade civil em decisões que afetam a qualidade de vida nas comunidades vizinhas. A ausência de estudos de impacto pode ocultar riscos como: - Consumo excessivo de água em regiões já vulneráveis à escassez; - Emissão de gases de efeito estufa decorrente de fontes de energia não renováveis; - Poluição sonora e térmica que afeta residências e áreas naturais; - Descarte inadequado de componentes eletrônicos e resíduos de refrigerantes. Os críticos também apontam que a medida pode criar um precedente perigoso para outras categorias de projetos, como usinas de energia ou instalações de mineração, que poderiam ser classificadas como essenciais e, assim, escapar de processos de licenciamento. O futuro da Proposta 45 dependerá da campanha de informação nas próximas semanas. Grupos ambientalistas planejam intensificar a divulgação de documentos que demonstram os potenciais impactos, enquanto representantes da indústria de tecnologia prometem que a medida trará benefícios econômicos e de competitividade global. Para ficar no radar Para os leitores brasileiros interessados em tecnologia e sustentabilidade, a discussão em torno da Proposta 45 oferece alguns pontos de atenção: - Impacto nos serviços de nuvem. Caso a medida seja aprovada, a Califórnia pode acelerar a expansão de data centers, o que pode influenciar preços e disponibilidade de serviços de cloud computing usados por empresas brasileiras. - Precedente regulatório. Uma brecha legislativa nos EUA pode inspirar debates semelhantes em outras regiões, inclusive no Brasil, onde a regulação ambiental de data centers ainda está em fase de consolidação. - Consciência ambiental. O caso destaca a importância de equilibrar desenvolvimento tecnológico com responsabilidade ambiental – um tema que vem ganhando força em conferências como a Campus Party Brasil. Fique atento às próximas edições dos principais jornais californianos e aos comunicados das organizações ambientais. A decisão final será conhecida após a votação, prevista para o próximo ciclo eleitoral estadual. Independentemente do resultado, a Proposta 45 evidencia um dilema recorrente: como conciliar a necessidade de infraestrutura digital avançada com a preservação dos recursos naturais e a transparência pública? O debate está apenas começando, e o desfecho poderá moldar o futuro dos data centers não só nos EUA, mas também em mercados emergentes que buscam atrair investimentos em tecnologia.

artigo.texto: Exelon utilities could spend $3 billion to $7 billion building 1.5 GW to 3.5 GW of regulated energy storage, not including a $1 billion, 500-MW project already proposed for New Jersey, company officials said Friday during an earnings call. “With regulated storage, we have certainty that projects get built, and control over when and how they're deployed,” Robert Kleczynski, Exelon’s CFO, said during the call. “We view utility-owned storage as one option alongside competitive development, not a replacement for it.” Customers would benefit from the projects through lower capacity prices and the flow-through of investment tax credits, which would ease the assets’ effect on electricity rates, he said. Three states where Exelon utilities operate — New Jersey, Maryland and Delaware — allow them to own energy storage facilities to bolster grid resiliency, Kleczynski noted. Atlantic City Electric’s 500-MW project, developed with Invenergy, would be the largest battery installation in the PJM Interconnection and is expected to provide more than $700 million in net benefits to customers, he said. Exelon expects the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities to make a decision on the proposal late in the first quarter next year, according to Kleczynski. PJM isn’t moving fast enough to add generation onto its system, which is the biggest issue facing consumers in the grid operator’s Mid-Atlantic and Midwest footprint, according to Calvin Butler, Exelon president and CEO. Two key PJM initiatives — its backstop capacity procurement plan and its Interim Resource Adequacy Service proposal — have been delayed by only partial approvals by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. “Neither proposal would have solved the reliability and affordability challenges facing our customers, but both represented important steps forward,” Butler said. However, adding energy storage and transmission can help address the issue, according to Butler. Exelon’s current capital expenditure plan calls for investing $16.3 billion on transmission through 2029, and the Chicago-based company sees opportunity for $12 billion to $17 billion in transmission spending beyond that plan, including on infrastructure for large loads. Exelon’s “high-probability” large load additions remained flat at 11 GW — with 9 GW in Commonwealth Edison’s service area in northern Illinois and 2 GW in the Mid-Atlantic region, the company said. Its future pipeline slipped to 23 GW — 14 GW with ComEd and 9 GW in the Mid-Atlantic — from 25 GW last quarter. On the financial front, Exelon’s third-quarter income fell to $729 million, down from $875 million in the same period last year, partly due to higher writeoffs related to a rate case, and higher storm and interest expenses. Third-quarter revenue jumped to $7.3 billion from $6.7 billion in the year-ago period. Not including one-time factors, third-quarter adjusted income increased to 87 cents/share from 86 cents/share in the third quarter in 2025. In a note, Jefferies equity analyst on Friday said the earnings results and the potential spending on storage and transmission, in addition to Exelon’s $41.7 billion capital expenditure plan, were “favorable.” However, the analysts warned that regulatory uncertainty in 2027 dampens the outlook and may offset any incremental earnings from new capital expenditures. Exelon has close to 11 million customers through its six utility subsidiaries — Atlantic City Electric, Baltimore Gas and Electric, ComEd, Delmarva Power & Light, PECO Energy Co. and Potomac Electric Power Co.

artigo.texto: Investing.com -- NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) has instructed its data center partners to reduce their exposure to Chinese customers, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday, citing five people with knowledge of the matter. The chipmaker now requires cloud computing clients to sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies, the FT reported. The company previously had no such restrictions in place. The instructions have been delivered verbally through Nvidia's sales force and regional teams rather than through written documents, the FT report said. The move creates additional obstacles for Chinese technology companies seeking to pursue artificial intelligence development. Many Chinese firms have relied on leasing advanced computing capacity through overseas cloud computing arrangements for AI tasks, including model training. The restrictions come as Washington continues efforts to limit Chinese access to advanced U.S. chips through cloud computing deals. Nvidia chips were seen being smuggled to China in recent years, despite the U.S. imposing strict restrictions on any sales to China since at least 2022. Several high-ranked employees at server maker Super Micro, which assembles Nvidia-based servers, were charged with smuggling about $2.5 billion worth of Nvidia AI servers to China earlier this year. artigo.texto: Lithium-ion batteries have become the backbone of electric vehicles and energy storage. But a rival chemistry built around one of the world’s most abundant elements is now becoming more and more viable. Sodium-ion batteries are entering commercial production, with major manufacturers betting they could make energy storage cheaper, more resilient, and less dependent on lithium. In February 2026, China’s CATL and automaker Changan unveiled what they described as the world’s first mass-production passenger vehicle equipped with sodium-ion batteries, with sales planned for the middle of the year. In April, CATL also signed a major agreement to supply 60 gigawatt-hours of sodium-ion batteries to energy storage company Beijing HyperStrong Technology over three years. These developments suggest sodium-ion technology is approaching a new stage. But it still faces a fundamental challenge. Lithium-ion batteries have a considerable head start in energy density, cost, and manufacturing scale. Sodium is abundant, but that doesn’t automatically make better batteries Both technologies work on the same basic principle. During charging and discharging, ions move between a positive electrode (cathode) and a negative electrode (anode), with an electrolyte allowing them to travel between the two. The main difference is the element carrying the charge. Lithium-ion batteries use lithium, while sodium-ion batteries use sodium, which is widely available in seawater and common salts. That abundance could reduce dependence on lithium mining and price fluctuations. Sodium-ion cells can also use aluminum current collectors on both electrodes, potentially reducing their reliance on copper. Some designs avoid lithium, cobalt, and graphite altogether. More from Energy See All However, sodium-ion batteries are not automatically free of critical minerals. Certain commercial cathode chemistries still use materials such as nickel and manganese, while their hard-carbon anodes require specialized manufacturing. The supply chain for these components is also much less mature. The International Energy Agency (IEA) notes that sodium-ion battery production remains heavily concentrated in China, despite the potential for more geographically diverse raw-material supplies. Lithium-ion still has the energy-density advantage For electric vehicles, one of the most important measures is energy density. It measures how much energy a battery can store relative to its weight or volume. Here, lithium-ion remains ahead. According to the IEA’s 2026 assessment, the latest sodium-ion cells can reach around 175 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg). By comparison, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells can reach approximately 205 Wh/kg, while nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries can reach around 265 Wh/kg. A less energy-dense battery needs to be larger or heavier to store the same amount of energy. In a vehicle, this can mean less driving range or less space for passengers and cargo. The IEA estimates that an average SUV equipped with sodium-ion batteries could achieve up to 350 kilometers (217 miles) of range, compared with approximately 400-600 kilometers (249–373 miles) for lithium-ion vehicles under average weather conditions. Sodium-ion batteries do have an important advantage in colder environments. The latest cells can retain around 90 percent of their nominal capacity at temperatures as low as -40°C (-40°F), outperforming conventional lithium-ion chemistries, particularly LFP. This could make them useful in cold-weather vehicles and equipment. The competition is shifting toward specific applications Sodium-ion’s strongest near-term opportunity may not be replacing the battery in every electric car. Instead, it could find a place in smaller vehicles, two- and three-wheelers, urban delivery fleets, and stationary energy storage, where weight and volume are sometimes less restrictive. The grid-storage market is particularly interesting. Batteries used to store electricity from solar and wind installations do not need to fit inside a vehicle or maximize driving range. Cost, safety, durability, and reliable performance can matter more than energy density. CATL’s 60 GWh agreement with HyperStrong reflects this opportunity, while its TENER sodium-ion storage system, unveiled in June 2026, points to growing interest in commercial-scale stationary applications. Still, the economics are not settled. Lithium-ion manufacturing has benefited from decades of investment and enormous production volumes. In particular, LFP batteries have become highly cost-competitive, making it difficult for sodium-ion to win simply because sodium is cheaper and more abundant. The IEA says global sodium-ion production in 2025 was less than 1 percent of lithium-ion output. Even announced projects for 2030 represent only a fraction of planned lithium-ion manufacturing capacity. A second battery chemistry, not necessarily a replacement The arrival of sodium-ion batteries is important, but it does not mean lithium-ion is about to lose its dominant position. Lithium-based cells continue to improve, while sodium-ion manufacturers still need to scale production, refine materials, and demonstrate consistent performance. The more likely outcome is a battery industry with multiple chemistries serving different needs. Lithium-ion will remain attractive where range, weight and energy density are priorities. Sodium-ion could become increasingly useful where cold-weather performance, material availability and supply-chain diversification carry greater value. Right now, sodium-ion’s biggest achievement may be giving battery manufacturers another option. And in an industry increasingly shaped by the demand for electric vehicles and grid storage, having more than one viable chemistry could prove just as important as developing a better battery.

artigo.texto: Real estate titans are eagerly watching the upcoming Texas gubernatorial race in anticipation of potential changes to the state's policy on data center development. The asset class dominated discussion on the real estate panel at the Bloomberg Invest conference at the Joule Hotel in Downtown Dallas on Tuesday. When the moderator (former TRDer Joe Lovinger) asked if anything could stymie Texas' growth story, Crow Holdings' Michael Hyun pointed to data center regulation: "If there is a significant slowdown in that development, it affects so many areas of the Texas economy." It's something of a double-edged sword for someone like Hyun, who also noted that the frenzy has drawn real estate's finite resources to the buzzy asset class. "You're competing for many of the same contractors to develop your site and guess who can pay more?" he asked. Still, he characterized a crackdown on data center development as "economic suicide." In the lead up to the midterm elections, Gov. Greg Abbott, facing a viable challenger in Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa, veered from his typical pro-business stance and responded to community outrage over data development. He directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to halt approvals for data center projects and ordered the Public Utility Commission of Texas to audit pending projects. Even so, at least $9 million or 13 percent of the money he's raised since July 2025 came from data center developers or entities tied to data center development, the Texas Tribune reported. Hinojosa has characterized Abbott's actions as temporary moves in service of attracting voters. She says she supports strict legislative guardrails for data center development to protect water supply and grid capacity and curb tax breaks. Laura Hines-Pierce, the co-CEO of Houston-based Hines, was also on the Bloomberg Invest panel. She said the issue isn't as binary as being for or against data centers. According to Hines-Pierce, part of the gray area is in the domain of developer responsibility. "Data centers don't need to be a Star Wars ship that landed in the middle of a community," Hines-Pearce said. DFW tops real estate markets to watch list … again North Texas topped the list of markets to watch for the third consecutive year in a report from the Urban Land Institute and PricewaterhouseCoopers. The report points to robust industrial development — including data centers — as well as corporate relocations and the rise of Y'all Street.

artigo.texto: Everyone treats Contemporary Amperex Technology, better known as CATL, as just a massive electric vehicle battery supplier. That assumption misses the entire trajectory of where the company is actually heading. As EV sales growth normalizes globally, the world's largest battery maker isn't just sitting back to wait for the next automotive boom. They are aggressively restructuring their business model around two pillars: high-capacity energy storage systems (BESS) and standardized battery swapping networks like their Choco-Swap system. If you want to understand how the next wave of the energy transition works, you have to look past standard passenger car cells. CATL is turning batteries from simple automotive components into fluid financial assets and grid-balancing machinery. The Energy Storage Shift Nobody Talks About While media headlines obsess over monthly EV delivery numbers, CATL's utility-scale energy storage business has quietly exploded. Power grids everywhere are straining under the weight of intermittent renewable generation like wind and solar. You cannot run a modern grid on sunshine and good intentions without massive stationary storage backing it up. CATL didn't just stumble into this market. Their TENER energy storage platform, which offers large-scale capacity with zero degradation over the initial years of operation, has completely changed what utility providers expect from hardware. Look at the massive supply deals they've locked inâsuch as multi-gigawatt-hour agreements with global integrators and partners like HyperStrong and international energy giants. The economics here are entirely different from passenger cars. Energy storage buyers care about lifecycle costs, thermal safety, and footprint efficiency. By pushing standardized lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry into massive utility containers and even pivoting automotive manufacturing linesâsuch as adapting facilities originally slated for EV cells toward stationary storage productsâCATL is insulating itself against cyclical slowdowns in consumer car sales. When consumer auto demand dips, grid infrastructure spending picks up the slack. Cracking the Code on Battery Swapping For years, skeptics dismissed battery swapping as an expensive, fragmented niche dominated only by stubborn pioneers like Nio. The hurdles were obvious: every car maker built different vehicle architectures, proprietary pack sizes, and distinct mounting points. Standardization seemed impossible. Then CATL introduced Choco-Swap, introducing standardized 20# and 25# modular battery blocks designed to fit multiple vehicle types. Instead of forcing a single car brand to own the entire ecosystem, CATL acts as an independent banker of energy. Here is why this model actually works in practice: - Fleet operators can swap a depleted pack in minutes, eliminating range anxiety and severe vehicle downtime. - Drivers can subscribe to modular blocks based on their actual mileage needs rather than paying upfront for a massive, expensive solid pack they rarely fully utilize. - The physical battery blocks inside the swap stations double as decentralized energy storage units, feeding power back into the grid during peak demand hours. Building thousands of swap stations requires serious capital. But CATL isn't treating these stations as mere fueling stops. They are physical nodes in a distributed virtual power plant. The Financialization of Energy What makes CATL genuinely formidable is how they manage risk. Through their battery asset management framework, they track real-time health data across millions of active cells using cloud diagnostics. This data allows them to evaluate credit, price flexible subscription plans, and offer precise buy-back guarantees based on residual battery health. When a battery is no longer fit for high-performance passenger vehicle driving, it gets pulled from the rotation and redeployed into a stationary energy storage container for grid backup. Finally, it heads to recycling facilities to recover critical lithium, cobalt, and nickel. It's a closed-loop financial and physical ecosystem. Competitors who only sell raw hardware are fighting a margin race to the bottom. CATL is building a recurring revenue model that stretches across the entire lifecycle of a mineral. Geopolitical Realities and Supply Chain Control You cannot talk about CATL without addressing the heavy friction of global trade politics. Western markets are throwing up tariffs, domestic content requirements, and strict regulatory walls to keep Chinese clean-tech dominance at bay. Yet, CATL keeps finding operational workarounds. Instead of direct exports, they rely on technology licensing agreements, localized joint ventures, and massive vertical integration projectsâsuch as their multi-billion-dollar investments in raw material extraction and processing hubs in Indonesia. By locking down the supply chain from nickel mining all the way to grid-scale software management, they maintain cost advantages that Western manufacturers struggle to match. The strategy is pragmatic. If you cannot easily export finished packs into a specific market due to trade rules, you license the tech, supply the core components, or pivot local production lines toward stationary storage, which often faces different regulatory classifications than passenger automotive batteries. What Comes Next CATL's next phase of growth won't be defined by how many passenger cars roll off assembly lines with their logos on the pack. It will be determined by how deeply they embed themselves into the fabric of global energy infrastructure. By scaling modular battery swapping for urban mobility and blanketing utility grids with high-performance storage blocks, they are transforming from a simple manufacturer into an essential energy utility. If you're betting against them because car sales wobble for a few quarters, you're missing the entire board.

artigo.texto: Massive AI Data Center Sparks Backlash Despite Clean Energy Promises As more governments put increasing pressure on tech companies to develop more sustainable data centres, to ensure they do not place a further burden on the grid, several tech firms are investing in developing new energy capacity and incorporating other innovative ideas into their facility development. This has led Google to suggest that the development of its new U.S. data centre in Minnesota, and associated energy development, will have a positive benefit on the region's transmission network. Google has proposed an agreement with Xcel Energy to support significant wind, solar and battery storage development alongside its new 780-MW Project Skyway data centre. The tech giant plans to finance Xcel's addition of 1.4 GW of wind, 200 MW of solar power and 300 MW of battery storage to the grid. While the combined capacity of these projects exceeds the data centre's projected electricity demand, wind and solar generation fluctuate depending on weather conditions, and battery storage does not generate additional electricity. Xcel Energy says the new energy resources will serve the wider grid, benefiting other customers as well as the data centre. Google plans to cover the associated costs under the proposed agreement, including payments for capacity it does not fully use. The aim is to get the residents of Pine Island, Minnesota, on board with its development plans, particularly as 71 per cent of Americans surveyed in a Gallup poll earlier this year opposed the construction of a data centre in their local area. Developing such a significant renewable energy project will also help Google meet its target of operating entirely on carbon-free energy by 2030. The proposed agreement includes minimum demand charges and exit fees, meaning that Google will be required to finance the development of the infrastructure even if the demand for AI decreases. Under the proposed agreement, Google would pay minimum monthly charges based on at least 75 per cent of its contracted capacity, even if its electricity consumption falls below that level. If the company terminates the agreement early, it could face exit fees equivalent to as much as eight years of minimum demand charges. Amanda Rome, executive vice president and chief customer officer at Xcel Energy, explained, "Nobody wants to have a big buildout and then have nowhere for that power to go and nobody to pay for that power… That's where these protections come in." The Clean Energy Accelerator Charge (CEAC) agreement model uses the same structure as the Clean Transition Tariff (CTT) Google developed with NV Energy. It is currently pending approval from the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission. In its statement about the agreement, Google's Head of Energy Market Innovation, Briana Kobor, said, "Google's partnership with Xcel Energy reimagines how data centres can be served, enabling us to be a catalyst for electricity innovation and helping to ensure our growth supports a cleaner, more affordable energy future for the communities we call home." The rapid rollout of data centres in the United States is driving up the country's electricity demand to unprecedented levels. The U.S. DOE Office of Science national laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, estimates that data centres could account for 11.8 per cent of total U.S. electricity by 2030. Meanwhile, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) projects that electricity consumed by data centre servers could reach between 446 billion and 818 billion kilowatt-hours (BkWh) annually by 2050, accounting for between 22 per cent and 33 per cent of commercial building electricity consumption. This is driving demand for new clean energy capacity to ensure that data centres are not powered by fossil fuels – although several companies still depend on gas-powered plants. As utilities respond to the growing power demand by rapidly building out the grid, which costs billions of dollars to do, they are ultimately expecting the demand for AI data centres to continue. However, if the demand for AI wanes or the government decides to regulate the sector more strictly, electricity demand could fall, potentially leaving consumers to foot the bill for infrastructure upgrades. In addition, the use of clean power in data centre operations is not the only sustainability concern. In October last year, the Minnesota Centre for Environmental Advocacy filed a lawsuit against the city of Pine Island, claiming that the environmental study for the development was vague, initially omitted Google as the end user, and failed to disclose impacts on energy, water, noise, and generators. The initial Alternative Urban Area Review (AUAR) indicated that the new data centre would use approximately 55.7 million gallons of water per year, thereby increasing the city's total water consumption by approximately 50 per cent. Meanwhile, environmental groups have voiced concerns about the lack of comprehensive groundwater impact analysis. Meanwhile, opponents have questioned whether wastewater discharges may potentially run into the Zumbro River. In a Pine Island survey conducted between 1st and 31st August, 75.8 per cent of participants are against the construction of Project Skyway. While Google has made bold promises to upgrade the grid through clean energy projects, residents and environmental groups have broader concerns about consumer protections and the projects' environmental impact. So, while Google may be attempting to develop a more "sustainable" data centre, it is failing to win over local residents, who remain concerned about the long-term implications of building a giant AI data centre. artigo.texto: Pitt County to hold hearing on data center moratorium GREENVILLE, Pitt County — Pitt County commissioners will hold a public hearing on a proposed moratorium on new data centers. The hearing is scheduled for Monday, Nov. 16, at or after 6 p.m. in the Eugene James Auditorium at the County Administration Building, 1717 W. Fifth St. in Greenville. The proposed moratorium would temporarily pause construction, development and permitting for data centers in Pitt County. The length of the pause would be determined at the hearing. County officials say the moratorium would give them time to study potential impacts on utilities, energy use, the environment, public safety and zoning. They also want to consider additional land-use rules for data centers. Residents can share comments at the hearing. Written comments may be emailed to Kimberly.Hines@pittcountync.gov or mailed to the Pitt County Clerk to the Board.

artigo.texto: Development of All-Solid-State Batteries for Next-Generation Vehicles To achieve carbon neutrality and expand the possibilities of electrified mobility, Honda took on the challenge of developing all-solid-state batteries for automotive applications that combine high energy density with low cost. While building a pilot production line designed for mass production, Honda also developed battery cell specifications and established its own all-solid-state cell design compatible with a low-cost manufacturing process. To safely harness the extremely challenging lithium-metal anode, the team established the required âelectrochemical reaction,â âcell structure,â and âmanufacturing processâ technologies, achieving a high level of balance across capacity, mass producibility, durability, and safety. These achievements, which can extend EV driving range, create more cabin space, and reduce vehicle weight, earned the Presidentâs Award as a key technology expected to strengthen product competitiveness in the electrification era. - BACKSTORY - Interview From No Blueprint to a Battery We Can Manufacture. â Hondaâs All-Solid-State Lithium-Metal Battery: Taking More Than a Decade of Research Toward Mass Production â Interview participants: Maeyama, Kamaya, Usui, Kagei, Noji, Taniuchi, Toyoshima, Sasano, Watanabe, Taguchi, Nakajima, Tanaka Extend driving range. Create more cabin space. Make the vehicle lighter. An all-solid-state lithium-metal battery could dramatically change the value of BEVs. Honda has continued R&D to harness a high-energy-density lithium-metal anode and make it viable for future vehicles. No one, however, had a blueprint for how to get there. Good materials alone do not make a battery. Nor can a single working small cell be installed in a vehicle. Dozens of electrodes of consistent quality must be stacked, produced quickly and reliably, proven safe, and ultimately turned into a technology that can be mass-produced as an industrial product. Some members had spent years researching all-solid-state batteries at Honda. Others joined from entirely different fields, including engines, chassis, and machining. Engineers with diverse expertiseâmaterials, design, prototyping, production engineering, evaluationâcame together around one ambitious goal. The development of this all-solid-state lithium-metal battery earned the Presidentâs Award. Tracing the path behind it reveals a team that kept creating its own answers precisely because no one else had them. More Than a Decade of Knowledge, Turned into Development Speed. â All-Solid-State Battery Research That Began with Only a Handful of People Around 2013, the Honda research effort that would evolve into todayâs all-solid-state battery program was still a small team of just a few people. Maeyama and Kamaya, who had been involved since those early days, started by setting up the experimental environment itself. How should the battery be made? How should the materials be evaluated? How should the results be analyzed? With little experimental equipment, they hand-built tiny prototypes resembling coin cells and tested methods one by one. âWhether the result was good or bad, we didnât know why. Thatâs where we started.â Maeyama recalls those days. Today, all-solid-state batteries are widely known as a next-generation battery technology. Back then, however, their value wasn't widely understood, even within the company. Kamaya remembers explaining battery data and still being asked, âWhy are we working on solid-state batteries?â Still, they kept going. What kept Maeyama going was the sense that, little by little, they were unquestionably moving forward. âResults were hard to come by, but we knew more about something no one else in the world understood than anyone else did at that moment. Looking back six months or a year, there were always more things we could do. I think thatâs what kept us going.â For Kamaya, the colleagues pursuing the same research mattered just as much. To turn the all-solid-state battery into something real. Because colleagues were working toward the same goal, they could keep at the research for years. That time would later prove enormously valuable. When someone proposed, âLetâs try this approachâ to a new problem, a long-serving member could immediately respond, âWe tried that before. Hereâs what happened.â Instead of repeating the same tests, they could move directly to the next approach no one had tried. The knowledge accumulated over more than a decade was more than a research history. It had become a technology in itselfâone that accelerated todayâs development. Turning a Difficult Material into Value for the Vehicle. â Mastering Lithium Metal One defining feature of Hondaâs all-solid-state battery is the use of lithium metal for the negative electrode. The aim was straightforward. Store more energy in a smaller battery. With the same packaging space, extend driving range. With the same driving range, make the battery smaller, freeing up cabin space and reducing vehicle weight. This is the customer value Honda expects from its all-solid-state lithium-metal battery. But lithium metal is difficult to handle. As the battery charges and discharges, its shape changes as it expands and contracts. Lithium does not always deposit in the intended way. Kamaya likens the difference from a graphite anode to having âassigned seats.â In graphite, lithium ions can settle at defined sites. Lithium metal has no assigned seats. It can deposit freely, changing shape and potentially affecting durability and safety. That is why controlling lithium metal is such a major challenge. One technology that helps turn this âwild horseâ into something viable for a vehicle is the restraint and cushioning technology developed by Usui. artigo.texto: Shares in Gresham House Energy Storage (GRID) jumped over 6% today after the £540m battery fund unexpectedly put itself up for sale, whilst at the same time saying it would continue to “pursue” its growth plan. Just six weeks after formally rejecting a call from activist investor PrimeStone Capital to sell up and claiming a strong first half showed the potential of its recovery programme, the investment trust’s board u-turned and cited shareholder feedback it could not ignore. Announcing that the company’s financial advisers had been instructed to launch a formal sale process (FSP), chair John Leggate said: “The decision by the board to launch a formal sale process has been taken after careful consideration of a wide range of feedback from our shareholders and has not been taken lightly. It comes against a backdrop in which the board and the manager continue to execute the company’s growth plan which has been reflected in the continued growth in the company’s earnings and a 15.8% uplift in its net asset value during the first six months of the year. “Despite no change in the board’s confidence in the company’s ability to deliver on the growth plan, we recognise some shareholders’ increased desire to accelerate value delivery which has caused the board to commence an FSP process whilst continuing to pursue the growth plan.” GRID shares leaped 6.4% to 101p, a 23% discount to NAV per share of 131.3p at 30 June. Our view Richard Williams, senior analyst at QuotedData, said: “The decision to launch a formal sale process follows growing shareholder pressure to accelerate value realisation, with the 15.8% increase in NAV during the first half of 2026 not being adequately reflected in the share price. The timing is interesting given the substantial value that could still be unlocked through the development pipeline, with three projects totalling 777MW targeting final investment decisions next year that have the potential to generate further meaningful NAV uplifts. This creates something of a dilemma: a sale could provide shareholders with a quicker route to realising value, but potentially at the expense of the considerable upside the board believes remains in the portfolio. Running the sale process alongside the Growth Plan is therefore a pragmatic approach, allowing potential buyers to assess that future value while preserving the option of continuing independently. Much will depend on whether prospective bidders are prepared to recognise the value of GRID’s development pipeline rather than simply its existing operational assets.”

artigo.texto: TerraVolt Holdings, Inc., an infrastructure developer specializing in powered land solutions for data centers, has executed option agreements to purchase 1,077 acres of land outside the town of Declo in Cassia County, Idaho, on which it intends to develop a behind-the-meter digital infrastructure campus. The company said in a press release that the property was zoned for multiple use and was situated near long-haul fiber routes and the Williams Northwest Pipeline. The campus will have an initial 240 MW of dedicated on-site power generation, backed by TerraVolt’s previously announced firm natural gas supply agreement of 55,000 MMBtu per day. “These option agreements secure site control, allowing our team to advance land use plans, environmental due diligence, power plant, electrical distribution, and water treatment system designs, and county and state permitting,” said Joel Stone, TerraVolt Holding Chairman and Chief Executive Officer. “By pairing a strategic, expansive land parcel directly with firm gas supply and pipeline access, we are addressing the single largest bottleneck in the digital economy: the multi-year wait for large-load grid interconnections.” With on-site, islanded power generation, the proposed campus will avoid utility interconnection delays. In states like Texas, data center developments that require grid interconnection face lengthy delays, with w.media reporting in September that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas was tracking 438 GW of large load requests, 89 percent of which were for data centers. TerraVolt said the behind-the-meter deployment will reduce the time-to-power schedule for hyperscale and neocloud deployments and protect existing ratepayers from grid strain or rate increases. TerraVolt plans to sell shovel-ready building sites to data center operators, providing power, fiber, potable and fire-protection water, wastewater treatment, and other site services under long-term infrastructure services agreements.TerraVolt also intends to require low water usage for any data center developments on the property, making it a condition of sale for each site. “We look forward to working closely with Cassia County officials and the local community to deliver responsible, long-term industrial tax base growth without impacting local power rates or the agricultural water the region depends on. That is why every building on this campus will be required to use cooling technologies with low water usage,” said Stone. According to Data Center Map, there are currently 25 data centers under development or operational in Idaho. The state is also home to Meta’s Kuna Data Center, a more than US$ 1.2 billion investment, which became operational on September 3, 2026.

artigo.texto: Por que Data Centers são importantes? E quais os problemas? Guia do Adulto Premium te explica as polêmicas em torno das estruturas que sustentam a inteligência artificial. Crédito: Larissa Burchard/Estadão Gerando resumo Com comunidades em todos os Estados Unidos rejeitando data centers, cresce a pressão política para limitar sua construção. Mas, a milhares de quilômetros de distância, o maior país da América do Sul já é um dos principais mercados de IA e está facilitando sua expansão. Os brasileiros enviam 215 milhões de mensagens ao ChatGPT por dia, segundo a OpenAI, o que torna o país o terceiro maior mercado do criador do chatbot em número de usuários semanais, atrás dos Estados Unidos e da Índia. O Google disse que planeja dobrar sua infraestrutura de nuvem no país até 2030 em resposta à crescente demanda ,e chegou a assinar um acordo de patrocínio com a Confederação Brasileira de Futebol em março para integrar o Gemini às seleções nacionais masculinas, femininas e de base. Outras gigantes da tecnologia também estão investindo. A Amazon Web Services gastou mais de US$ 3,8 bilhões em infraestrutura de data centers no País desde 2011 e se comprometeu a investir outro US$ 1,8 bilhão até 2034, enquanto a Microsoft destinou US$ 2,7 bilhões à infraestrutura de nuvem e IA ao longo de três anos. A demanda local, e não a transferência de operações de empresas americanas para o exterior, impulsionou grande parte do crescimento dos data centers na América Latina. Mas Carlos Barrera, CEO da Atlas Renewable Energy, acredita que isso pode mudar. “De fato, vemos a região como uma válvula de escape atraente para algumas das restrições de capacidade que vocês estão vendo agora nos Estados Unidos”, disse. Com uma população de quase 215 milhões de pessoas distribuídas por uma área maior do que a dos 48 Estados contíguos dos Estados Unidos, o Brasil faz sentido como um país a ser cortejado pelas empresas de hiperescala. Sua oferta de eletricidade também é um grande atrativo e custa menos da metade do que nos Estados Unidos. Segundo um relatório do Ministério de Minas e Energia, o País gera quase 87% de sua eletricidade a partir de fontes renováveis, e o rápido crescimento da energia eólica e solar também levou a um excedente. “A reação negativa nos Estados Unidos não está tanto expulsando as empresas de hiperescala do país, mas direcionando-as para onde a energia estiver disponível primeiro”, disse à Fortune James Mercer, diretor da Metro Colo Advisory, empresa de consultoria em data centers. Leia também - Executivo do setor de chips compara corrida de IA a cassinos e impacta ações tech pelo mundo - IA muda o mapa da Bolsa: software perde espaço e impulsiona chips, energia e data centers Mas a eletricidade barata do Brasil também pode ficar mais cara. Barrera disse que o Brasil precisará de mais linhas de transmissão para conectar grandes data centers à rede elétrica, e que autoridades do governo estão divididas sobre a possibilidade de as contas de luz aumentarem ou não. Outro obstáculo ao crescimento da IA no Brasil é o sistema tributário. Os altos impostos federais de importação tornavam mais caro construir grandes data centers no País em comparação com outros países da região. Para resolver isso, o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva sancionou uma lei em 15 de setembro que reduz os impostos sobre equipamentos de data centers que atendam certos requisitos. Isso contrasta com propostas de alguns parlamentares americanos para taxar o consumo de eletricidade e a produção dos data centers. “Se o Brasil quisesse ser um ator relevante no setor de data centers, precisava fazer essa mudança na legislação tributária”, disse à Fortune Christopher Torto, CEO da Ascenty, a maior provedora de serviços de data centers e conectividade da América Latina. Soberania de dados O governo Lula espera que a isenção fiscal, ao trazer mais capacidade computacional para o País, ajude as empresas brasileiras a desenvolver produtos de IA e a depender menos de serviços estrangeiros. Atualmente, 60% dos dados digitais brasileiros são processados no exterior, segundo o Ministério do Desenvolvimento brasileiro. De acordo com a legislação, chamada Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter), as empresas devem oferecer pelo menos 10% de seus serviços computacionais elegíveis a clientes brasileiros e investir 2% do valor dos equipamentos beneficiados pela isenção fiscal em pesquisa e desenvolvimento no Brasil. “O objetivo é melhorar a soberania de dados do Brasil, para que não dependamos tanto de serviços estrangeiros, especialmente nesse momento com Trump”, disse à Fortune Ana Carolina de Assis Nunes, antropóloga brasileira e pesquisadora de data centers no instituto de políticas públicas sem fins lucrativos Data & Society. Nunes destacou que o Brasil quer depender menos da tecnologia estrangeira, mas está concedendo incentivos fiscais às mesmas empresas que dominam o setor. Torto admitiu que é improvável que o Brasil desenvolva seu próprio Google ou Microsoft. Ainda assim, ter data centers locais no país poderia melhorar a latência e manter mais dados no território nacional. “Não se trata apenas dos modelos ou dos próprios data centers; tudo o que gira em torno deles será, de fato, o maior investimento no longo prazo”, disse ele. Potencial de reação negativa Embora o Brasil não tenha visto a mesma escala de reação negativa aos data centers que os Estados Unidos, alguma resistência surgiu. Dias antes de o Redata se tornar lei, procuradores federais brasileiros recorreram à Justiça contra um projeto de data center ligado ao TikTok. Eles queriam um estudo de impacto ambiental e uma consulta ao povo indígena Anacé antes de o data center entrar em operação. Nunes disse que a oposição aos data centers no Brasil não é tão politicamente unida quanto nos Estados Unidos, onde eles têm recebido críticas tanto da esquerda quanto da direita. artigo.texto: Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76. When New York became the first state in the country to enact a moratorium on data center development, Adrienne Yocina was excited. For the past two years, the mom of three has been organizing in western Genesee County to stop a 600-megawatt data center from coming to a site close to the Tonawanda Seneca Nation’s reservation and a federal wildlife refuge. But almost four months after the one-year moratorium began, Yocina tells me that she’s “getting nervous.” She’s worried that Democratic governor Kathy Hochul won’t sign a stronger bill to impose a stricter moratorium, and is concerned that the state Department of Environmental Conservation is not adequately involved in the process of evaluating data centers in New York. “I feel like she’s just trying to shut us up,” she says of Hochul. Data centers are at the center of midterm races across the country, with politicians of both parties making promises to enact regulations or moratoriums on development. After next week comes the tough part: Newly elected officials must either break their word or follow through on those promises as they weigh large infrastructure projects coming to their states and residents who say they’ll reject data centers no matter what. How will those compromises go—and will they appease voters? New York’s moratorium, and the continued opposition from some groups, may offer clues. In July, just two months after dismissing the idea of a data center moratorium, Hochul signed the nation’s first executive order to put a pause on development. Her order was a compromise. Just weeks prior, the state legislature had passed an omnibus bill that would have implemented a one-year moratorium throughout New York. The bill contained several provisions that made it more aggressive than Hochul’s moratorium, including stricter limits on the size of data centers and a mandate that the Department of Environmental Conservation conduct a thorough environmental impact review of data center operations. Rather than sign the bill, Hochul issued her own order. (The governor has until the end of the year to sign that bill, and her office says they are still looking at it.) One of the bill’s State Senate sponsors, Democrat Kristen Gonzalez, has been publicly supportive of Hochul’s moratorium. The governor’s office, Gonzalez says, proactively reached out to her after her bill passed to help design the moratorium for more immediate relief for New Yorkers. Gonzalez went on a data center tour of New York at the end of the summer, talking to residents around the state about their concerns. She told me that the people she talked to overwhelmingly wanted Hochul to go further and implement more aggressive measures to protect communities from data centers. “There are local communities statewide that are living near existing data centers, dealing with significant air pollution and noise pollution, who are struggling with rising utility bills and rising water bills,” she told me. “We see the moratorium as a first step, but it can’t be the last.” Hochul has a comfortable lead over Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman ahead of Tuesday’s election—something that may have been helped by the moratorium’s passing. In a recent Quinnipiac poll of New York voters, 53 percent of respondents said they trusted Hochul to do a better job in handling AI and data centers, compared to just 31 percent trusting Blakeman. Blakeman, who has voiced support for data centers, called Hochul’s moratorium “crazy” when it was passed in July. His campaign didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. Hochul has also touted her tough-on-data-center bona fides on the campaign trail. Early last month, she hosted a roundtable discussion on data centers with agricultural, environmental, and business leaders at a farm in the Hudson Valley. There, she told reporters that she wanted to work with the state legislature to implement more aggressive protections, including banning tax breaks for data centers. At the event, Hochul was flanked by Gonzalez and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, one of Washington’s most prominent data center critics. I asked Hochul at the event how she anticipates handling continued opposition after her moratorium ends. How does New York balance economic development with community opposition if some people don’t want data centers in their backyards under any circumstances, even with the assurances from the state that Hochul’s office is working to create? The purpose of her pause, she said, was that communities should be able to choose. “This is democracy in action,” she said. “If you want it, it should come with all kinds of guardrails and restraints, but if you don’t want it, it doesn’t come.” More New Yorkers may end up choosing the latter option. A Siena poll from September found that 63 percent of New Yorkers would oppose data centers being built in their area even after Hochul’s moratorium expires. (It’s even higher for New York Democrats, with 75 percent saying they’d remain opposed to data center development post-moratorium.) Many newly elected (or reelected) governors will face a similar dynamic: At least 20 gubernatorial candidates have promised a data center moratorium or pause, according to research compiled by government relations company MultiState. Even more have promised to regulate the industry more tightly. Formerly data-center-friendly incumbents like Texas’s Greg Abbott and Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro have also made pledges to be stricter on their development. artigo.texto: Westbrook City Council unanimously approves ban on standalone data centers The new land-use rules allow smaller data operations that support other businesses while removing data centers as a permitted use at Rock Row Westbrook City Council unanimously approves ban on standalone data centers The new land-use rules allow smaller data operations that support other businesses while removing data centers as a permitted use at Rock Row The Westbrook City Council unanimously approved an ordinance Monday night prohibiting standalone data centers in the city. The ordinance allows data centers only as an accessory use, so smaller operations, like server rooms, can continue to support other businesses. The changes also remove data centers as a permitted use in the Rock Row Contract Zone, previously the only area in Westbrook where they were allowed. The vote comes after a 180-day moratorium on new data center projects adopted by the City Council in June. During that time, the Planning Board reviewed the city's existing regulations and considered concerns raised over water usage, energy demands, noise and economic development. The Planning Board unanimously recommended the ordinance following a public hearing on Oct. 6. The City Council held its first reading of the ordinance on October 19 before taking it up for a second and final reading Monday.

artigo.texto: It appears that BYD Malaysia is gearing up to launch the 2026 refresh of the Denza D9 electric MPV in our market soon. This is based on a new teaser recently published across Denza Malaysia’s social media channels. While the teaser is light on details, the refreshed 2026 Denza D9 is expected to carry major upgrades in charging capability, performance, and equipment. 2026 Denza D9 Malaysia: 2nd-Gen BYD Blade Battery with Flash Charging support? One of the headline upgrades expected on the 2026 Denza D9 is support for BYD’s Flash Charging technology. This aligns with BYD Malaysia’s ongoing rollout of BYD Flash Chargers at key Denza centres, including Balakong, KL North, and Glenmarie. Regional momentum points in the same direction: BYD last month introduced the Flash Charging-capable D9 in Indonesia—where the brand is marketed as Danza due to an ongoing local trademark dispute. On the other hand, the Hong Kong market has recently received the D9 Duo featuring not only Flash Charging capability but also CCS2 and GB/T ports. With Flash Charging enabled, the updated D9 can juice up from 10% to 70% in just 5 minutes, while a 10% to 97% top-up takes approximately 9 minutes. To support these speeds, the refreshed model adopts BYD’s 2nd-generation Blade Battery. In Indonesia, the battery pack on the Danza D9 grows to 115.03kWh—a noticeable bump over the 103.36kWh 1st-gen pack fitted to the initial Denza D9 launched in Malaysia in early 2025. That extra capacity extends range considerably: Indonesia’s 2026 Danza D9 FWD claims up to 730km (NEDC), compared to the 600km (NEDC) rated for the existing Malaysian-spec Denza D9 FWD. 2026 Denza D9 Malaysia: More punch and tech additions We are also expecting a healthy bump in performance output as well. The 2026 Danza D9 FWD in Indonesia delivers 340kW (456hp) and 365Nm of torque, far outpacing the 230kW (308hp) and 360Nm produced by Malaysia’s current front-drive model. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s D9 Duo AWD boasts a combined output of 410kW (550hp) and 445Nm. By comparison, the existing AWD variant in Malaysia puts out 275kW (369hp), though it holds a slight edge on peak torque at 470Nm. Other equipment likely bound for our 2026 update includes BYD’s DiSus-C dual-valve intelligent damping suspension, a 16-speaker Devialet audio system, a Child Presence Detection (CPD) sensor, and power-adjustment switches for the third-row seating.

artigo.texto: Southeast ConstructionTech is having a moment, and data centers are the reason. Hypepotamus ran a story under the headline “Data centers, regional growth fuels SE ConstructionTech” that describes a sector gaining momentum after major acquisitions and funding announcements. The piece cites a CBRE report showing Atlanta led North America in data-center capacity under construction during the first half of 2026. That single data point carries more weight than it first appears. Capacity under construction is a leading indicator. It tells you where concrete, steel, electricians, schedulers and software licenses will flow over the next two years. For a region full of general contractors, it also tells software vendors where the buyers are. This analysis walks through what the reporting confirms, what it leaves out, and what it means for cloud buyers, contractors and startup investors. It also sets the story against the wider spending cycle covered in our look at how long the AI capex boom can last. Where the available sources give no figure, we say so instead of guessing. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What the Hypepotamus Report Actually Confirms Start with the hard facts, because the available excerpt is short on numbers. Hypepotamus describes the Southeast construction-technology sector as gaining momentum following major acquisitions and funding announcements. It ties that momentum to data-center construction and to broader regional growth. The story names five companies as potential customers for ConstructionTech products: Pulte Group, Holder Construction, Brasfield & Gorrie, Innventure and Cardinal Infrastructure Group. That list spans homebuilding, commercial general contracting and infrastructure work, which matters. It suggests the demand is not confined to one project type. What the excerpt does not provide is equally clear. It gives no acquisition amounts, no funding totals, no product names, no named individuals, no project specifications, no prices and no on-record quotations. We treat all of those as unconfirmed. Any article that fills those gaps with precise figures is guessing, and readers should discount it accordingly. The practical takeaway is simple. The direction of travel is documented. The size of the money is not. Anyone building a business case on this story needs to pull the underlying deal announcements before putting a number in a slide deck. Atlanta Leads North America in Data-Center Construction The headline claim is the CBRE finding. According to the report cited by Hypepotamus, Atlanta led North America in data-center capacity under construction in the first half of 2026. For a metro that many readers associate with logistics and film production rather than hyperscale computing, that is a notable ranking. The story does not supply the megawatt totals, and we will not invent them. What we can say is that leading the continent in active construction puts Atlanta in front of the other large markets that have historically dominated data-center headlines. The ranking reflects pipeline, not completed capacity. Why “Under Construction” Beats “Operating” as a Signal Operating inventory shows what the market built in the past. Capacity under construction shows what developers, utilities and lenders committed to in the recent past and are now paying to deliver. It is a better read on where demand for labor and tooling lands next. A ConstructionTech vendor selling scheduling, document control or field reporting software cares about active sites. Software seats follow crews. A market with a large number of live data-center builds creates a dense cluster of potential customers inside a few hours of driving, which cuts sales costs and speeds up reference selling. The Five Named Customers and What They Signal Hypepotamus lists five organizations as potential customers. The table below summarizes what the story confirms about each. We deliberately avoid adding revenue, headcount or project counts, since the excerpt gives none. The key phrase is potential customer. The story does not say any of these firms signed a contract, rolled out a product or invested in a startup. Readers should not infer purchases from a list of prospects. It is a map of who could buy, not a record of who did. Still, the mix tells a story. A residential builder, large commercial contractors, an innovation-driven company and an infrastructure group all sit on the same prospect list. Vendors that once targeted only commercial general contractors now see a wider addressable market across the region. Why Data Centers Pull ConstructionTech Along Data-center projects are unusually demanding to build. They stack electrical, mechanical and cooling systems into schedules that developers want finished fast, because idle capacity earns nothing and tenants often sign leases well before completion. Every week of delay costs real money. That pressure rewards tools that tighten coordination. Contractors on these jobs juggle long-lead equipment, dozens of trades and heavy documentation. Software that flags a late delivery, a missing submittal or a schedule slip earlier has a direct dollar value. It is the kind of pitch a project executive understands in one meeting. Hypepotamus frames the regional story as a combination of data-center demand and broader growth. We read that as a flywheel. Big builds attract specialist contractors. Specialist contractors attract vendors. Vendors attract investors and acquirers, which funds more product. Each turn makes the next one easier. artigo.texto: A German startup has given old e-scooter batteries a second life by using them to develop a high-performance, affordable, and sustainable 70-kilowatt-hour (kWh) energy storage system for industrial use. The technology was designed by EDENenergy, a Freiburg-based cleantech startup and spin-off of the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (ISE). It relies on modular units and advanced power electronics to connect used batteries into one larger energy storage system. Florian Bierwirth, EDENenergy CEO and co-founder highlighted the importance of repurposing old batteries. “It allows different storage units to be connected and enables communication with various modules without having to disassemble the batteries,” he said. According to the team, the batteries can retain over 90 percent of their original capacity, which makes them suitable for reuse in industrial energy storage. They could also enable businesses to store excess solar power while reducing battery waste. Old batteries reused Reports indicate that about one million batteries from e-bikes and e-scooters are prematurely discarded in Germany each year. However, many of them still have enough capacity to remain useful for several more years. Reusing these batteries has been difficult because they come in different designs, cell types, and battery management systems. To address this, former Fraunhofer ISE researchers developed power electronics that can connect different batteries without dismantling them. More from Energy See All The startup initially focused on batteries from large e-scooter fleet operators to ensure a consistent supply of compatible units. Its first industrial storage system combines 112 used e-scooter batteries, each tested before installation. While the team initially expected the batteries to retain around 80 percent of their original capacity, tests on the first 350 units revealed that some retained well over 90 percent. The firm delivered its first storage system to a customer last month. “In mid-October, we delivered the first storage system to a customer, which was an important milestone for our young company,” Bierwirth highlighted. “With this storage size, we initially aim to target medium-sized companies in the region that have a photovoltaic system but do not yet have a storage solution.” Keeping storage capacity EDENenergy said that the technology is also modular. This means that individual batteries can be replaced without shutting down the entire system. According to the company, municipal utilities could use it to reduce peak electricity demand, increase solar power consumption, or trade electricity. The startup will also remotely monitor the batteries to check their condition and determine when individual modules need to be replaced. Once a battery reaches the end of its useful life, it is removed and sent to recycling partners. Moreover, the system could maintain its full 70 kWh capacity even after 10 years. By comparison, conventional battery storage manufacturers typically guarantee around 80 percent of the original capacity after a decade. At the same time, the batteries could last longer in stationary applications as they experience fewer vibrations and temperature fluctuations. “In stationary storage systems, where – unlike in their first life – they are exposed to fewer vibrations or temperature fluctuations, these batteries can continue to perform well for several more years,” the company concluded in a press statement. Moving forward, the team plans to expand its industrial storage systems to 300 kWh.

artigo.texto: Compartilhar Primeiro Data Center Verde do RN é inaugurado pelo Sebrae-RN O Rio Grande do Norte passa a contar com seu primeiro Data Center Verde. Inaugurado na noite desta quinta-feira (29), o Data Center Sebrae Senador Fernando Bezerra está instalado na sede do Sebrae-RN, em Natal, e será responsável pelo armazenamento e processamento de dados de 12 unidades estaduais do Sistema Sebrae, localizadas nas regiões Nordeste, Norte e Sudeste. A estrutura amplia a capacidade tecnológica da instituição e reforça as estratégias de segurança da informação e transformação digital dos pequenos negócios. Com investimento de R$ 76 milhões, provenientes do Sebrae Nacional e das unidades estaduais participantes, o equipamento conta com capacidade inicial de armazenamento de 2 petabytes, com possibilidade de expansão futura. Um dos diferenciais da estrutura é o sistema de energia solar instalado especificamente para atender à demanda do data center, com baterias de lítio para armazenamento de energia, reforçando a proposta de aliar infraestrutura tecnológica e eficiência energética. Além do Rio Grande do Norte, serão atendidos os estados do Acre, Amapá, Amazonas, Espírito Santo, Maranhão, Pará, Paraíba, Piauí, Roraima, Sergipe e Tocantins. O Data Center Senador Fernando Bezerra é o segundo do Sistema Sebrae no país. O primeiro foi inaugurado em 2024, no Distrito Federal. Durante a cerimônia de inauguração e descerramento da placa do Data Center Sebrae Senador Fernando Bezerra, representantes do Sebrae Nacional e das unidades estaduais participantes destacaram a importância da estrutura para a segurança da informação, a inovação e o fortalecimento dos pequenos negócios. Tecnologia e novas oportunidades Representando o Sebrae Nacional, o gerente da Unidade de Tecnologia da Informação, Diego Ramos, destacou a importância da inauguração para a instituição e para o desenvolvimento tecnológico do Rio Grande do Norte. Segundo ele, o projeto vai além do investimento em infraestrutura e poderá contribuir para a criação de oportunidades de negócios e o fortalecimento de um ecossistema de inovação no estado. “Esse lançamento marca não somente a história do Sebrae-RN, mas também a do estado. É o primeiro data center verde do Rio Grande do Norte, e isso traz não apenas tecnologia, mas oportunidades de novos negócios”, afirmou. Almeida ressaltou ainda que o equipamento integra a estratégia de criação da Nuvem Sebrae, iniciativa que prevê a interligação de data centers de diferentes estados para ampliar a capacidade tecnológica da instituição e qualificar o atendimento às micro e pequenas empresas diante dos avanços da transformação digital e da inteligência artificial. “Daqui a alguns anos, não vamos estar mais discutindo qual é a capacidade desse data center, mas, sim, a quantidade de histórias e de momentos importantes que ele deixou para tantos micro e pequenos empresários desse Brasil”, concluiu. O vice-presidente da Associação Brasileira dos Sebraes Estaduais (Abase) e diretor-superintendente do Sebrae Paraíba, Luis Alberto Gonçalves de Amorim, também destacou a relevância da iniciativa para acompanhar as transformações tecnológicas e preparar a instituição para os desafios futuros. “A evolução tecnológica exige atualização constante, planejamento e cooperação entre as unidades estaduais. A implantação do equipamento demonstra a importância de unir esforços e investir em soluções capazes de responder às novas demandas da sociedade e dos pequenos negócios”, pontuou. Integração para fortalecer os pequenos negócios O diretor-superintendente do Sebrae-RN, Zeca Melo, enfatizou a importância da integração entre as unidades estaduais e do apoio do Conselho Deliberativo para viabilizar projetos estratégicos da instituição. Ele também reconheceu o trabalho das equipes de Tecnologia da Informação envolvidas na implantação do equipamento. Ao destacar a dimensão do público potencialmente beneficiado, Zeca Melo ressaltou que os 12 estados participantes reúnem milhões de pequenos negócios, o que reforça a importância da atuação conjunta para ampliar a capacidade de atendimento do Sebrae. “Esses 12 estados representam quase 3 milhões de pequenos negócios. A implantação desse data center fortalece a estrutura tecnológica do Sebrae e amplia nossa capacidade de atender aos pequenos negócios, contribuindo para o desenvolvimento e a modernização da instituição em todo o país”, afirmou. Homenagem a Fernando Bezerra A solenidade também marcou a homenagem ao senador Fernando Bezerra, que dá nome ao equipamento. Engenheiro, empresário, ex-presidente da Confederação Nacional da Indústria (CNI), senador da República e ministro, ele teve atuação importante na trajetória do Sebrae-RN. Na década de 1990, foi o primeiro presidente do Conselho Deliberativo Estadual da instituição e contribuiu para viabilizar a aquisição do imóvel onde funciona a atual sede, em Natal. Durante a cerimônia, Fernando Bezerra destacou a contribuição do Sebrae para o desenvolvimento econômico do Brasil e do Rio Grande do Norte. Ele também defendeu maior aproximação entre o poder público, a instituição e as entidades empresariais para impulsionar o crescimento do estado. “O Rio Grande do Norte, se ouvisse mais o Sebrae, estaria muito melhor. A força do desenvolvimento se faz com a iniciativa privada e com iniciativas como a do Sebrae aqui no Rio Grande do Norte”, afirmou. Após o descerramento da placa, os convidados participaram de uma visita guiada às instalações do Data Center Sebrae Senador Fernando Bezerra, que passa a integrar a infraestrutura tecnológica do Sistema Sebrae no país.

artigo.texto: National nonresidential construction spending increased 0.6% in September, mainly on the strength of data center development, according to an Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) analysis of data published on Monday by the U.S. Census Bureau. “Nonresidential construction spending grew for the sixth consecutive month in September,” said ABC Chief Economist Anirban Basu on Monday. “As has been the case for several months, data centers accounted for virtually all of that increase. Excluding data centers and the closely related power category, nonresidential spending actually fell in September.” Basu said spending on data center category construction jumped 8.6% in September and has grown at an annualized rate of 217% since May. “Given the recent rise in treasury yields and ongoing materials price escalation, momentum will remain narrowly concentrated in artificial intelligence-related segments over the next several months,” said Basu. “While contractors remain busy in the aggregate, according to ABC’s Construction Backlog Indicator, current market dynamics will continue to favor larger contractors who are far more likely to be involved in data center and power projects.” Meanwhile, residential construction spending declined -5.4% for the month of September and is down -8.8% compared to September of 2025, according to the ABC. On a monthly basis, construction spending increased in half of the 16 nonresidential subcategories, including manufacturing which was up +0.1% between August and September 2026 but still down –17% compared to September 2025. Nonresidential construction spending declined in these sectors during the month of September: Education (-0.1%); Commercial (-0.2%); Healthcare (-0.3%); Highway and Street (-0.4%); Public Safety (-0.6%); Amusement and Recreation (-1.2%) Conservation and Development (-4.5%).

artigo.texto: AI Models & Platforms Envision Deploys SST-Based 800V DC Power at Ulanqab AI Data Center Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google Envision said on Nov. 2, 2026, that an integrated 800-volt direct-current (800V DC) power system is now powering live computing workloads at its Galaxy AI data center campus in Ulanqab, China, a deployment the company described in its announcement as the world’s first commercial use of such a system in a large-scale AI data center. The announcement says the system delivers power end to end, from medium-voltage AC input to the server rack, and that it is already operating commercially ahead of wider industry adoption, providing a reference for AI data centers moving to 800V DC power infrastructure. Solid-State Transformers and Real-Time Coordination The newly deployed system integrates three hardware layers: solid-state transformers (SST), battery energy storage (BESS), and equipment that adjusts direct-current voltage for computing hardware. Coordinating them is Envision’s Dubhe Controller, which runs with the company’s Dubhe Energy Foundation Model and adjusts the transformers and batteries in real time so that power supply tracks computing demand, including abrupt swings in load. According to Envision, the deployment is built around three capabilities: stable SST conversion directly from 10-kilovolt medium voltage to an 800V DC bus across operating conditions; battery storage that provides both second-scale power support and minute-scale backup; and millisecond-level coordination between SST and storage that absorbs GPU load fluctuations locally. Envision said the 800V DC architecture simplifies AI data center power systems, citing higher power conversion and watt-to-bit efficiency, a more compact equipment footprint, and reduced cabling and copper requirements. Those advantages, the company said, can lower infrastructure costs and support higher computing density within the same space. Rising Power Demand Per Rack The announcement frames the deployment against a specific operational problem: as AI computing demand accelerates, operators must deliver more power to each rack within constrained space while keeping supply stable as computing loads swing sharply from moment to moment. “AI data centers need power systems that coordinate renewable energy, energy storage, and the grid to meet computing demand,” said Kevin Huang, Senior Vice President of Envision Energy and President of Energy Storage and AIDC Power Systems. Huang said the live system demonstrates an end-to-end architecture connecting renewable supply with computing demand, calling it a critical step in moving power-compute coordination from strategic vision to day-to-day operating practice. Galaxy Campus and Mission Gobi The Galaxy campus, in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, began operations in August 2026, when Envision commissioned the site on Aug. 6 anchored by a 120,000-square-meter AI supercomputing facility, according to the company’s commissioning announcement at the time. That record described the campus as designed to scale to over 2GW of capacity; the Nov. 2 release states a planned capacity of 3GW and says the campus is designed to support up to one million AI accelerators operating in parallel at full build-out, with more than 80% of its power planned to come from direct renewable electricity connections. Envision’s Galaxy campus page markets the site as a net-zero AI data center, advertising long-term fixed electricity pricing at 20% below grid rates under a 10-year price lock, bundled electricity and green certificates, and a 60% green power direct-supply ratio. Envision said it aims to scale the approach through Mission Gobi, an initiative unveiled at VivaTech in Paris in June 2026 with Galaxy as its first flagship project. Mission Gobi targets 5GW of green AI data center capacity in desert regions worldwide by 2030, and the company presents it as a replicable blueprint, arguing that developing even 1% of global desert and Gobi regions could support computing capacity at terawatt scale at highly competitive cost.
