artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Canary Live Bay Area By Canary Media A new report from Georgetown and Duke researchers looks at the advantages of using batteries to meet data center demand — and offers some advice for states. Developers and utilities are building tons of gas generation to power the data center boom. It’s an expansion that could cost them and the rest of us dearly, both in terms of climate change and money that may end up wasted if computing demand fails to materialize. But there’s a cleaner, cheaper, and faster-to-deploy alternative: batteries. That’s the conclusion of a new report from researchers at Georgetown and Duke universities, which lays out the ways states can push utilities and tech firms to opt for energy storage over fossil fuels whenever possible. Fossil fuel power — whether in the form of giant utility-scale plants or generators installed behind the meter at data centers — has become the go-to for many in the AI industry. That’s because gas generation offers round-the-clock power in a single package. Overall, U.S. utilities are planning more than 60 gigawatts of new gas plants to serve data center demand, and around 90 GW of behind-the-meter gas generators for data centers have been proposed nationwide. “At the moment, there’s a lot of inertia and status quo pressure for much of the behind-the-meter resources being natural gas,” said Ian Hitchcock, report co-author and senior program coordinator at the Duke Initiative for Science and Society. Moving ahead with those gas power plans does more than spell climate disaster. If data center proposals fall through or shut down early, other utility customers could be on the hook for the cost of overbuilding gas. That’s called “stranded asset” risk — and states have only begun to tackle it, even amid mounting fears that the AI sector is a bubble about to pop. Batteries “can act as a hedge against that risk,” last week’s report explains. Batteries are much cheaper than round-the-clock gas generation in situations where hours of stored energy can solve near-term needs. They’re also inherently modular and flexible in ways that gas power plants are not, which allows planners to increase or cut back on deployment if data center demand shifts sharply. Plus, batteries can help avoid the need for costly grid buildouts that would otherwise be used to serve increasing electricity demand, and can act as shock absorbers to cushion the grid against data centers’ massive and fast-changing computing loads. While lithium-ion batteries can’t provide round-the-clock power, they can meet large portions of data center electricity needs, said Jackson Ewing, director of energy and climate policy at Duke University’s Nicholas Institute of Energy, Environment & Sustainability. And unlike more future-forward solutions — such as advanced geothermal, next-generation nuclear, and novel long-duration energy storage technologies — “batteries are already showing serious momentum in terms of their deployment trajectory.” In fact, utilities and data center developers are increasingly embracing batteries, even as they pursue gas. A new forecast from BloombergNEF sees U.S. energy storage deployment surpassing 11,000 gigawatt-hours by 2036, a 30% increase from its 10-year forecast from just six months ago. Data center demand is pushing much of that growth. So, what can state decision-makers do to further encourage data centers to opt for batteries? States that directly regulate utility investments can craft “bring your own new clean energy” tariff structures. These regulations can set minimum requirements for data centers to procure or pay for enough carbon-free generation and energy storage to cover some or all of their electricity needs. Certain jurisdictions are already moving ahead with this approach; Google, for example, has signed onto such tariffs with regulators in Nevada and Minnesota. Things get more complicated in states with “restructured” energy markets. In these places, regulators have limited authority over the independent power producers that build big generation and battery projects and sell power into wholesale electricity markets. Still, the report highlights several ways that these states can encourage battery development to serve data centers, including via state energy storage mandates like those launched in Illinois, Maryland and New Jersey, and engaging in state energy planning in conjunction with regional grid operators. “There is not a jurisdiction that has no potential action items if they’re serious about trying to deploy this,” Hitchcock said. Jeff St. John is chief reporter and policy specialist at Canary Media. He covers innovative grid technologies, rooftop solar and batteries, clean hydrogen, EV charging, and more. artigo.texto: Cloud Revenue Hits $168B as AI Capacity Expands Cloud infrastructure revenue reached $168 billion in the third quarter as providers brought higher-priced AI capacity online, reinforcing demand for new data centers even as power constraints slow delivery. Cloud providers are bringing data center capacity online for higher-priced AI services as enterprise cloud infrastructure spending accelerates, reinforcing demand for construction even as power constraints complicate delivery. Worldwide spending on cloud infrastructure services reached $168 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up 55% from a year earlier, according to a Synergy Research Group report. The market has doubled in eight quarters, and AI-specific services now account for roughly one-third of total revenue. John Dinsdale, chief analyst at Synergy, told Data Center Knowledge that three factors are driving the surge: additional capacity coming online, higher pricing, and a continued shift toward more expensive AI services. “A lot of the additional capacity that is coming online is specifically targeting more valuable, higher-priced AI services,” he said. That shift in pricing and service mix helps explain how cloud revenue can grow faster than the data center capacity supporting it. JLL’s August midyear report illustrated the construction demand behind that expansion. Hyperscalers accounted for 59% of North American data center tenant demand, while 28 GW of owner-occupied capacity was under construction, according to JLL. Neoclouds – specialized cloud providers offering GPU-as-a-Service to enterprise customers – represented another 11% of demand, while AI companies accounted for 7%, broadening the customer base competing for facilities. The buildout is expected to continue. Global data center capital spending is projected to exceed $3 trillion by 2030 as hyperscalers, sovereign AI programs, and specialized cloud providers expand their infrastructure to support growing AI workloads, according to an August report from Dell’Oro Group. AI Changes the Cloud Customer Mix The cloud market’s expansion is also reshaping which companies need infrastructure and how they compete. Amazon retained the largest share of worldwide cloud infrastructure revenue at 26%, followed by Microsoft at 19%, and Google at 16%, Synergy reported. “AI has totally transformed the cloud market in terms of service capabilities, customer demand, and growth opportunities,” Dinsdale said. Microsoft and Google grew faster than Amazon, while Oracle and neocloud providers, including CoreWeave, Crusoe, and Nebius, were among the fastest-growing companies outside the top three. Synergy said neocloud expansion is eroding the market shares of some established providers. For data center operators, that changing mix raises questions about tenant durability and contract stability, particularly if some fast-growing providers consolidate. Dinsdale said he expects the underlying infrastructure to retain value even if an individual neocloud’s prospects change. Construction Demand Persists Despite Power and Tenant Risks CBRE’s August report on North American data center trends found 7,481 MW under construction across eight primary markets in the first half of 2026, up 24.8% from a year earlier. More than 80% was preleased, up from 74.3% a year earlier. Power constraints continued to extend completion schedules, leaving customers competing for capacity that has yet to be delivered. Those commitments mean operators evaluating expansion must weigh construction schedules and tenant stability alongside cloud revenue growth. Dinsdale said he expects data centers, installed equipment, and existing customer contracts to find new owners if neocloud providers consolidate or fail. That suggests consolidation would redistribute infrastructure rather than leave large amounts of it unused, though the financial outcome would vary significantly by asset. “Whatever happens to a neocloud company and its prospects for carrying on as an independent entity, there will be valuable assets that will not go to waste,” he said. “Valuations will vary greatly, but I don’t imagine too many stranded assets being trashed.”

BYD October EV sales reach a record 300,000+ The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026. BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark. To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates. October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year. BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units. According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America. Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year. artigo.texto: CIL Selects Neopulse for 80 MW/320 MWh BESS Project Neopulse Energy will provide technical oversight for CIL's 80 MW/320 MWh BESS project in Odisha. November 03, 2026. By EI News Network Coal India Ltd. (CIL) has appointed Neopulse Energy Pvt. Ltd. as the Owner’s Engineer for its proposed 80 MW/320 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Odisha. The company will provide technical advisory and engineering oversight during the selection of the engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractor and subsequent project execution. As part of the pre-award responsibilities, Neopulse Energy will assist CIL in preparing technical specifications, defining equipment requirements and evaluating technical bids submitted by prospective EPC contractors. Following the award of the EPC contract, Neopulse Energy will review the contractor’s engineering designs, vendor documentation and quality plans. Its scope will also cover technical supervision of equipment manufacturing, construction activities, testing and commissioning. The 80 MW/320 MWh installation will have a four-hour storage duration. The project is expected to provide grid flexibility and support the integration of renewable energy into the electricity network. Battery storage systems can help manage variations in solar and wind power generation and improve the reliability of electricity supply. The appointment places Neopulse Energy in an advisory and technical oversight role, with responsibilities extending from the EPC tendering process through project commissioning. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Marketing Bago’s carbon market initiative at COP31 By Aliyu Umar Aliyu As global climate diplomacy shifts from promises to practical implementation, Niger State has an opportunity to position its emerging carbon market initiative as a vehicle for investment, job creation and sustainable development. For Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago, popularly known as the Farmer Governor, the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), scheduled for November 9–20, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, offers a strategic platform to advance the state’s green economy vision. The conference will bring together governments, investors, climate finance institutions, development partners and environmental experts to discuss practical responses to climate change. For Niger State, however, participation should go beyond showcasing its environmental ambitions. The priority should be to secure credible partnerships, develop investment-ready projects and establish a clear pathway for converting its natural resources into measurable climate and economic benefits. Governor Bago’s vision presents an opportunity to connect climate action with Niger State’s agricultural strength, forest resources, renewable energy potential and waste-management needs. If properly developed, these assets could support projects that reduce greenhouse gas emissions while creating employment, improving energy access and strengthening rural livelihoods. Niger State’s participation at COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in November 2024 provided an earlier opportunity to promote its green economy agenda, including sustainable agriculture, renewable energy and forest conservation. COP31 should build on that engagement by moving from international advocacy towards practical project development and investment mobilisation. From Green Economy Vision to Carbon Market Investment Carbon markets provide a potential mechanism for financing projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. Under recognised crediting systems, a carbon credit generally represents one metric tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent reduced or removed, subject to the applicable methodology and verification requirements. For Niger State, opportunities could include methane capture at landfills, climate-smart rice cultivation, solar mini-grids and forest restoration. These initiatives could attract investors while supporting the state’s wider development objectives. However, natural resources alone do not guarantee carbon revenue. Projects must demonstrate credible emissions reductions, additionality, appropriate monitoring and independent verification. They must also comply with relevant national regulations and international carbon market requirements. This is particularly important as Niger State seeks to position itself as a pioneer in subnational carbon market development in Nigeria. The ambition to become the country’s first subnational government to open its carbon market to investment, and to advance towards international carbon-credit sales, could be significant. The proposed Niger State Carbon Market Office could play a central role by coordinating project identification, technical assessments, investor engagement, regulatory compliance and stakeholder participation. Its effectiveness will depend on a clear mandate, adequate expertise, transparent procedures and coordination with the relevant federal authorities. International cooperation could accelerate this process. In correspondence to the Niger State team concerning a post-feasibility mission action plan, myclimate’s Article 6 Bilateral Cooperation Team disclosed that a draft memorandum of understanding (MoU) on project development and carbon market activities was undergoing internal legal review, with the intention of finalising it before COP31. The correspondence, signed on behalf of the team by Nsikan-George Emana, Senior Project Manager for Bilateral Cooperation at myclimate, proposed November 12, 2026, for a strategic meeting with the Niger State Government, during which the parties hope to sign the agreement. The proposed engagement offers an opportunity to establish a framework for technical cooperation, project development and potential international market participation. Nevertheless, the MoU remains prospective until formally concluded, and its existence should not be mistaken for evidence that investment has already been secured or carbon credits sold. Niger State should approach the meeting with clearly defined priorities, including project timelines, financing arrangements, responsibilities, community safeguards and measurable implementation targets. Article 6 and the International Opportunity The proposed partnership is particularly relevant to Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which provides frameworks for international cooperation in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. At COP29 in November 2024, countries made significant progress on the rules governing international carbon trading and the UN-supervised carbon crediting mechanism. Under Article 6.2, countries can cooperate through internationally transferred mitigation outcomes, subject to applicable accounting and authorisation requirements. Article 6.4 provides a UN-supervised crediting mechanism, while Article 6.8 addresses non-market approaches. For Niger State, these frameworks could create opportunities to develop projects that attract international finance and contribute to Nigeria’s climate commitments. However, the state must work within Nigeria’s national climate governance arrangements. International transfers under Article 6 cannot be treated as an exclusively state-level transaction where national authorisation and accounting are required. Potential projects should therefore be developed with appropriate technical, legal and financial support. artigo.texto: A operadora de telecomunicações russa Rostelecom está iniciando a construção de data centers subterrâneos. A primeira instalação deverá ser construída em parceria com a Norilsk Nickel. Essas instalações são consideradas as mais seguras, pois possuem três níveis de segurança. O primeiro nível envolve a criação de um sistema de backup para armazenar cópias de dados que possam ser necessárias caso a infraestrutura principal falhe. O segundo nível envolve a criação de locais geograficamente distribuídos para armazenar poder computacional e serviços. Isso permitirá que a infraestrutura seja distribuída em vez de concentrada em um único local. O terceiro nível envolve a criação de centros de dados subterrâneos, levando em consideração os piores cenários de ameaça. Estão sendo propostas instalações de data centers subterrâneos em minas de carvão abandonadas. Além de garantir a segurança de instalações estratégicas, essa medida também visa apoiar a indústria carbonífera da Rússia. Anteriormente, o presidente da Rostelecom, Mikhail Oseevsky, afirmou no Fórum SOC que o mercado russo de data centers está passando por mudanças devido a diversos fatores, incluindo o fato de os data centers estarem se tornando alvos em conflitos. As mudanças que ele descreveu incluem data centers domésticos consumindo menos energia, distribuídos por vários locais e, possivelmente, até mesmo a transição para energia nuclear. Segundo Oseevsky, dois "fatores" — a segurança física dos centros e a disponibilidade de eletricidade — estão atualmente "mudando drasticamente o paradigma". Ele acredita que esses fatores irão alterar o modelo de construção de centros de dados e sua localização. Especialistas já haviam levantado a ideia de instalar data centers no subsolo. Eles observaram que a construção precisaria levar em consideração as condições locais e uma série de riscos potenciais. Esses riscos incluem não apenas a ameaça de ataques com mísseis ou drones, mas também fenômenos naturais como terremotos ou inundações. Em outubro de 2026, os centros de dados da Yandex e do Sberbank foram danificados por ataques de drones, e a restauração dos serviços online nesses centros ainda está em andamento. Segundo cálculos de especialistas, a construção de uma instalação subterrânea pode ser cerca de 30 a 40% mais cara do que uma instalação comparável construída acima do solo. A estrutura de custos de um centro de dados subterrâneo também é diferente: os custos de refrigeração podem ser reduzidos, mas custos adicionais são incorridos, incluindo suporte e impermeabilização para as estruturas, ventilação da mina e monitoramento de gases, sistemas subterrâneos de supressão e evacuação de incêndio, equipamentos de elevação, cabeamento de energia e fibra óptica a partir do solo e canais de comunicação de backup. O custo também depende se a instalação será construída do zero ou se uma estrutura subterrânea existente será reformada.

artigo.texto: China is giving sodium-ion batteries a temporary tax advantage over conventional lithium-ion technology as manufacturers look to bring the alternative chemistry into commercial electric vehicles. One of the country’s leading sodium-ion battery developers, Hina Battery, is planning a 10 GWh production base in Wuhan and has partnered with a vehicle manufacturer to develop electric sanitation trucks. The expansion comes as China introduces a consumption tax on specified lithium-ion batteries while exempting qualifying sodium-ion batteries through 2028. The policy could improve the economics of sodium-ion production, although falling lithium prices have narrowed the cost gap between the two chemistries. The technology is also attracting attention for its performance in extreme cold. FAW Jiefang reported that one of its electric heavy trucks equipped with a sodium-ion battery retained more than 90% of its usable capacity during testing at minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Creating a tax advantage for sodium-ion batteries China’s Ministry of Finance, General Administration of Customs and State Taxation Administration issued Announcement No. 20 (2026) on July 16, revising consumption tax rules for several battery categories. From September 1, 2026, specified lithium-ion batteries became subject to a 2% consumption tax. The rate is scheduled to rise to 4% on September 1, 2027. Qualifying sodium-ion batteries, solid-state batteries and fuel cells are exempt from the tax through December 31, 2028, provided they meet applicable national standards. More from Transportation See All The exemption gives sodium-ion manufacturers a temporary fiscal advantage, but it does not automatically make their products cheaper to produce. Battery-grade lithium carbonate averaged approximately $13,500, per metric ton on October 28. Meanwhile, square lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells for electric vehicles averaged about 5.7 US cents, per watt-hour on October 22. Sodium is more widely distributed geographically than lithium, potentially offering manufacturers a more diversified raw-material supply. However, the downstream sodium-ion supply chain remains concentrated in China, particularly in cell manufacturing, cathode materials and hard-carbon production. Hina targets commercial vehicle production in Wuhan Hina Battery signed an agreement with Wuhan’s Jiangxia District on October 14 to establish a sodium-ion battery production base with planned annual capacity of 10 GWh, with the first phase expected to provide 3 GWh of capacity. Construction is scheduled to begin in early 2027, with initial production targeted before the end of that year. The project was announced during the fourth National Sodium Battery Symposium, showcasing China’s effort to move sodium-ion technology beyond laboratory development and into larger-scale manufacturing. Hina has also signed a separate agreement with Chengli Special Automobile Group to develop sodium-ion-powered sanitation vehicles. The planned lineup includes refuse collection trucks, hook-lift vehicles, dust-suppression trucks and food-waste collection vehicles. Sodium-ion batteries have several potential advantages over lithium-ion alternatives, including access to more widely available raw materials and the possibility of better performance in low temperatures. Their main limitation remains lower energy density, which can translate into heavier or larger battery packs for the same amount of stored energy.

artigo.texto: Share This Article The Connecticut-based company behind a data center planned in Arkansas sued local officials in federal court Thursday over regulations targeting projects like it, claiming the county didn’t have the authority to enact such limits and that the state’s open meetings law was circumvented. The 38-page lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court of Eastern Arkansas, accused Pulaski County of enacting regulations targeting AVAIO Digital’s planned data center that infringe on the federal government’s authority to regulate interstate electrical transmission and commerce. AVAIO asked the court for an injunction preventing the regulations from being applied to its project, monetary damages and for the disclosure of public records it said had been withheld from them. It marks the second lawsuit filed in federal court this year connected to data center projects that have appeared in the state over the last two years. Entergy Arkansas unsuccessfully sued the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, one of its reporters and a local resident in September over the publication of details of the utility’s power agreement for Google’s West Memphis data center that the resident obtained through a public records request. The regulations AVAIO is contesting went into effect earlier this week after the quorum court overrode Democratic Judge Barry Hyde’s veto of them, and were drafted in response to community anger over AVAIO’s project located just off 145th Street. The regulations create uncertainty and threaten AVAIO’s “existing business, financial, and investment arrangements,” the company wrote in the complaint. The lawsuit also accused Democratic nominee for county judge, Wendell Griffen, of having “unlawful control over the Pulaski County Quorum Court,” pointing to his role authoring and advocating for the regulations. Griffen told the Arkansas Advocate that the lawsuit was expected, and said it was the county’s “constitutional power” to regulate data centers within its boundaries. A spokesperson for Pulaski County did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday evening. The company said Griffen and several members of the quorum court engaged in polling and deliberations that violated the Arkansas Freedom of Information Act. The lawsuit also named Democratic Justice of the Peace Julie Blackwood, who was the lead legislative sponsor of the regulations. Griffen also disputed AVAIO’s characterizations of his communications with quorum court members. “If they contend that a private citizen exercising his First Amendment right to approach members of the legislative body of the county about a matter of public interest is unlawful authority, then they need to reread the First Amendment to the Constitution of the United States,” Griffen said. The ordinance “is without effect because it is an obstacle to the full exercise of the federal government’s authorities under the Federal Power Act to regulate the transmission of electricity,” AVAIO wrote in its complaint. The alleged polling, the company said, also makes the passed ordinance invalid. Judge Lee Rudofsky, who oversaw Entergy’s lawsuit against the Democrat-Gazette, is the assigned judge on the case. Arkansas Advocate is part of States Newsroom, a network of news bureaus supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity. Arkansas Advocate maintains editorial independence. This article was published with permission from the Arkansas Advocate. Contact Editor Andrew DeMillo for questions: [email protected]. Follow Arkansas Advocate on Facebook and Twitter.

artigo.texto: Storing electricity at the scale of several gigawatt-hours is becoming a reality for power grids around the world. From a solar-powered development in Abu Dhabi to battery installations across Saudi Arabia, these projects are designed to store electricity and supply it when it is needed. The following list includes individual facilities, multi-site programs, and phased developments, with capacities reflecting their published scope. Some are already operating, others remain under development, and Moss Landing illustrates why historical capacity must be distinguished from what a facility can deliver today. 1. Masdar–EWEC round-the-clock project, UAE -19 GWh Abu Dhabi’s Masdar–EWEC development combines a 5.2-gigawatt solar plant with 19 gigawatt-hours of battery storage. The project is designed to deliver 1 gigawatt of renewable electricity around the clock, extending solar power delivery beyond daylight hours. Masdar laid the foundation for the project in October 2025, with operations targeted for 2027. Its design includes grid-forming technology, black-start capability, and forecasting and dispatch systems to coordinate electricity generation, storage, and delivery. 2. SEC–BYD battery storage program, Saudi Arabia – 12.5 GWh BYD announced a 12.5-gigawatt-hour energy storage contract with Saudi Electricity Company in February 2025. The agreement covers multiple grid-scale projects and brings BYD’s combined Saudi cooperation with the utility to 15.1 gigawatt-hours, including an earlier 2.6-gigawatt-hour delivery. More from Energy See All MEED identifies the program as five facilities with a combined power rating of 2.5 gigawatts, built with Alfanar as the engineering, procurement, and construction contractor. Equipment supplier NR Electric reported that SEC’s five-region, 2.5-gigawatt storage project completed its grid-connected charging and discharging tests on May 27, 2026, marking commissioning. 3. Oasis de Atacama, Chile – 14.1 GWh (overall platform) Grenergy’s Oasis de Atacama is a phased solar and battery storage development in Chile. Although earlier plans set its storage capacity at about 11 gigawatt-hours, the company’s September 2026 announcement raised the overall platform a capacity to 14.1 gigawatt-hours. That figure reflects the wider development, with individual phases coming online separately. Grenergy confirmed in September 2026 that Gabriela, the fourth phase, was operational with 272 megawatts of solar generation and 1,100 megawatt-hours of battery storage. 4. Najran, Khamis Mushait, and Madaya storage program, Saudi Arabia – 7.8 GWh Saudi Arabia’s 7.8-gigawatt-hour storage deployment spans three sites at Najran, Khamis Mushait, and Madaya. Sungrow supplied more than 1,500 PowerTitan 2.0 systems and announced grid connection completion in December 2025. The equipment integrates batteries, power conversion systems, medium-voltage transformers, and switching equipment into preassembled units. Sungrow says factory testing and preassembly reduced on-site installation work, while a local service team supported installation, commissioning, and grid connection. 5. Envision Jingyi Chagan Hada, China – 4 GWh The Envision Jingyi Chagan Hada Energy Storage Power Station in Inner Mongolia has a reported capacity of 4 gigawatt-hours. It connected to the grid in late December 2025, forming part of Envision’s wider 12.8-gigawatt-hour regional storage cluster. According to the Sustainable Markets Initiative’s project showcase, the station passed the grid’s three-charge, three-discharge verification in a single attempt. Its control system combines forecasting, dispatch, and electricity-market trading, coordinating how stored energy is managed and sold. 6. Edwards & Sanborn, USA – 3.287 GWh California’s Edwards & Sanborn project combines solar generation with 3.287 gigawatt-hours of battery storage. Developer Terra-Gen and contractor Mortenson announced substantial completion of the Kern County development in January 2024. The installation spans more than 4,600 acres, with part of the project on Edwards Air Force Base. Mortenson identifies LG Chem, Samsung, and BYD as battery suppliers, while the project serves customers including California utilities, the city of San Jose, and Starbucks. 7. Moss Landing, USA – 3 GWh (historical installed capacity) Vistra’s Moss Landing Energy Storage Facility reached 750 megawatts and 3,000 megawatt-hours of installed capacity after its third expansion entered commercial operation in June 2023. That expansion added 350 megawatts and 1,400 megawatt-hours, establishing the California site as a major early example of multi-gigawatt-hour battery storage. Its historical capacity requires qualification following the January 2025 fire at the 300-megawatt facility. EPA confirms that the affected building has had no active battery storage operations since that incident, while Vistra subsequently decided not to return the separate 100-megawatt facility to service. 8. Collie Battery, Australia – 2.24 GWh Neoen’s Collie Battery in Western Australia has a combined capacity of 560 megawatts and 2,240 megawatt-hours. The development comprises a 219-megawatt first stage and a 341-megawatt second stage; the company’s October 2025 update said both are operational. The service addresses electricity reliability risks associated with coal-plant retirements, growing rooftop solar generation, and demand on Western Australia’s South-West Interconnected System. 9. Bisha BESS, Saudi Arabia – 2 GWh The Bisha battery storage facility in Saudi Arabia’s Aseer province is rated at 500 megawatts and 2,000 megawatt-hours. Contractor Alfanar describes the delivered installation as a four-hour system that stores electricity during low-demand periods for redistribution when demand rises. Bisha has also demonstrated a capability needed after a major grid outage: black start, or restoring power without relying on an already energized network. NR Electric reported a successful black-start test

artigo.texto: MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- On October 28, HiTHIUM, a leading global energy storage technology company, showcased its ∞Power 6.9MWh 8-hour long-duration battery energy storage system (BESS) at All Energy Australia in Melbourne, alongside its grid compliance capabilities, localized service network and energy storage solutions for C&I and residential applications. Long-duration energy storage is increasingly important for grid flexibility and supply reliability in Australia. The federal government supports dispatchable clean energy projects through the Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS), while New South Wales continues to advance dedicated LDES tenders, creating new opportunities for storage projects of eight hours or longer. At the exhibition, HiTHIUM showcased its ∞Power 6.9MWh 8-hour-native BESS. Australia's high-price events are lengthening, with 4-hour-plus events accounting for over 70% of scarcity revenue in 2025 and shifting storage value toward firm supply duration. CSIRO GenCost analysis shows that two 4-hour systems delivering the same 8-hour output would cost about 23% more than a purpose-built 8-hour system, which offers greater value potential during price peaks. Integrated into a standard 20-foot container, ∞Power 6.9MWh BESS offers up to 96% round-trip efficiency, a 25-year design life, and compatibility with PCS and EMS products from major global suppliers. Compared with a 4-hour configuration, it reduces land use by 15% and can lower LCOS through system optimization. Developed in line with NFPA, IEC and AS standards, the system also delivers a high level of safety. To address Australia's grid connection requirements, HiTHIUM presented its Grid Compliance Simulation and Verification Platform, supporting projects through grid connection, from R0 assessment and R1 capability assessment to commissioning and R2 model validation. By combining grid-code interpretation, plant-level modelling, automated simulation, hardware-in-the-loop testing and site measurement validation, the platform helps identify potential compliance risks earlier and reduce late-stage rework. HiTHIUM continues to strengthen its localized service capabilities in Australia. The company has established a localized service network across Australia, covering spare-parts warehousing, training, operations and maintenance (O&M), and compliant battery recycling, with nationwide service coverage. At the exhibition, HiTHIUM signed strategic cooperation agreements with Raystech, Ingeteam and other Australian partners to further strengthen its local workforce, spare-parts infrastructure and safety capabilities. The company also announced that its Brisbane service center is scheduled to open by mid-2027, further expanding its regional service network and bringing efficient, reliable support closer to Australian customers. HiTHIUM also showcased its ∞Power 1022kWh liquid-cooled C&I energy storage cabinet, which combines its proprietary ∞Cell 1175Ah LDES cells with an integrated design for applications including peak shaving and solar self-consumption. For residential applications, the company presented the HeroEE 16 and ARKVOLT F8S series, supporting flexible deployment and integration with solar, heat pumps and EV charging. Through its 8-hour LDES technology, grid compliance expertise and expanding local service network, HiTHIUM is strengthening its ability to support Australian energy storage projects from development and grid connection through long-term operation. These efforts reflect HiTHIUM's commitment to supporting Australia's evolving energy storage needs with integrated solutions and sustained local support.

artigo.texto: Nidec is selling its fan-motor heritage to the data center market, and the pitch now has a video attached. Data Center Frontier lists a video titled “Nidec Brings Decades of Experience to Today’s Data Center Technology Needs.” The confirmed point from that listing is narrow but useful: Nidec is applying thermal-solution design technologies, developed through its fan-motor expertise, to liquid-cooling product development. The story lands in a market that keeps spending. We covered the money side in AI Capex Tops $740B as Markets Doubt the Boom, and the hardware that soaks up those budgets includes cooling loops and backup generators as much as chips. Nidec sits on both of those lines. This analysis separates what Nidec and Data Center Frontier have actually put on the record from what remains open. The fact base is small. No on-record speaker quote was identified in the available results, so this piece paraphrases company statements and names the source each time. Where a number is missing, we say so rather than fill the gap. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Data Center Frontier Published About Nidec The headline is a video title, not a press release. That distinction matters. A video listing on a trade site tells you the vendor has a story it wants told to data center operators, and it tells you which message Nidec chose to lead with: decades of experience. The confirmed content is the link between fan motors and liquid cooling. Nidec built its thermal know-how around moving air with small, efficient motors. It now applies the design thinking behind that work to liquid-cooling products. The listing gives no product price, no launch date, no customer name and no performance claim, and we treat all of those as unconfirmed. Beyond the video, Nidec’s own product pages fill in the portfolio. They list two coolant distribution unit (CDU) formats, In-Rack and In-Row, and they state a shipment count for the In-Rack unit. Nidec Power, a separate arm of the group, describes its generator line for data center backup and prime power. Taken together, the sources describe a vendor that wants to be a one-stop supplier for both heat removal and electrical resilience. The takeaway: this is a positioning story backed by a few hard figures. The figures are worth examining, because they are the only parts a buyer can test. Nidec Data Center Cooling: From Fan Motors to Liquid Loops Nidec is best known as a motor maker. Its corporate site organizes the catalog by application, and the product search by application shows how wide that catalog runs. Fan motors are one thread in it. They are also the thread Data Center Frontier highlights, because fans were the first tool data centers used to throw heat away. Air cooling and liquid cooling look like different trades, yet they share engineering problems. Both need reliable rotating parts. Both need tight control of flow. Both punish designs that waste energy on the pump or fan itself. A company that has spent years tuning fan motors for low noise and steady airflow has real knowledge to carry over, and that is the argument Nidec makes. The argument has limits. A fan moves air through a chassis. A CDU moves coolant between the facility loop and the server loop, with pumps, heat exchangers, filtration and controls in the mix. The motor know-how transfers, but the system design is new ground. Nidec has to prove that the transfer works at the scale operators now demand. Why does this matter to the cloud sector? Cloud operators plan capacity in racks and megawatts. Whatever limits rack density limits how much compute a given building can host. Cooling hardware therefore shapes the cloud cost curve more than most readers assume, even though it rarely makes headlines. The CDU Lineup: In-Rack and In-Row Nidec lists two liquid-cooling products on its product pages: the Coolant Distribution Unit (In-Rack) and the Coolant Distribution Unit (In-Row). The names describe where the unit sits relative to the servers it serves. In-Rack CDU An In-Rack unit lives inside the rack envelope. The appeal is proximity. Short coolant runs keep plumbing simple, and operators can add cooling rack by rack as they add compute. The tradeoff is space. Every slot the cooling unit occupies is a slot the IT gear cannot use, so operators weigh footprint against flexibility. Nidec states that more than 13 kpcs of these In-Rack CDUs have shipped globally. That is the one volume number on the record, and we return to it below. In-Row CDU An In-Row unit sits at the end of, or between, rack rows and serves several racks from one point. The case for it is economy of scale. One larger unit can feed a group of racks, which can cut the number of separate pieces to buy, install and maintain. The case against is concentration. A single unit that serves many racks becomes a bigger failure domain unless the design adds redundancy. Nidec lists the In-Row product alongside the In-Rack one, but the sources available for this report give no shipment figure for it. We do not infer one. 13 kpcs Shipped: Reading the CDU Volume Figure Nidec states that over 13 kpcs In-Rack CDUs have been shipped globally. The abbreviation means thousands of pieces, so the claim reads as more than 13,000 units. Shipment counts of this kind serve as proof of maturity. They tell a buyer the product has left the lab and survived real installations. Still, a shipped count answers only one question. It does not say how many units run in production today, how many sit in warehouses, or how many served pilots. It does not break out customers, regions or rack types. It also covers a period the company does not define in the material we reviewed. Treat it as a floor on credibility, not a performance score. Compare that with how chip vendors report. artigo.texto: BYD has reached an important milestone in India, with its Sealion 7 electric SUV recording over 5,000 customer deliveries since February 2025. The milestone comes as the company continues to expand the SUV’s range with new variants and special editions. The Sealion 7 is currently offered in four versions, including the Dynamic, Premium, Performance and the recently launched Festive Edition. The SUV uses BYD’s Blade Battery technology and Cell-to-Body architecture. It also gets an ocean-inspired exterior design, a panoramic glass roof and a rotating touchscreen inside the cabin. BYD Sealion 7: Battery and Performance The Sealion 7 is available with two battery pack options, depending on the variant. The Premium and Performance versions get an 82.56kWh battery pack, while the Dynamic uses a smaller 71.8kWh unit. Here are the key specifications of the electric SUV: The dual-motor Performance variant produces 390kW of power and 690Nm of torque. It can accelerate from 0 to 100km/h in 4.5 seconds. The Premium version gets the larger battery and has a claimed NEDC range of 567km. Both versions come with a panoramic glass roof and a 15.6-inch rotating touchscreen infotainment system. Dynamic Variant Added in August 2026 BYD introduced the Sealion 7 Dynamic in August 2026 at an introductory price of Rs 41.90 lakh (ex-showroom). This version gets a 71.8kWh Blade Battery with a claimed NEDC range of 520km. Despite being the entry-level version, it retains some of the familiar equipment found in the higher variants. - 71.8kWh Blade Battery - Claimed range of 520km - Panoramic glass roof - 15.6-inch rotating touchscreen Sealion 7 Festive Edition Limited to 150 Units In October 2026, BYD launched the Sealion 7 Festive Edition at Rs 50.60 lakh (ex-showroom). Production is limited to 150 units, and the special version is based on the Premium variant. It gets a Tan and Black cabin theme with quilted Nappa leather upholstery. Other additions include an electric sunshade for the panoramic glass roof and a head-up display. The Festive Edition also forms part of BYD India’s ‘Celebrate Your Dreams with BYD’ festive campaign. BYD’s Statement on the Milestone Commenting on the achievement, Rajeev Chauhan, Head of Electric Passenger Vehicle Business at BYD India, said that the Sealion 7 has been one of the company’s strongest-performing models in the country. He also spoke about the growing interest in electric SUVs that offer performance, technology and premium comfort. The company plans to build on the response by improving the ownership experience and expanding its product range for Indian customers. BYD’s Next India Launch: Denza D9 BYD is also preparing to introduce its luxury Denza brand in India on November 13, 2026. The D9 luxury MPV is expected to be among its first offerings in the country. The international-spec electric version gets a 103kWh battery and a front-mounted electric motor producing 313bhp and 360Nm. It has a claimed WLTP range of up to 520km. The D9 gets a three-row cabin with second-row captain seats offering electric adjustment, heating, ventilation and massage functions. It also features premium upholstery, multi-zone climate control and a large touchscreen infotainment system. Its expected price in India is around Rs 90 lakh.

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Envision implanta energia de corrente contínua de 800 V baseada em transformadores de estado sólido em centro de dados de IA em Ulanqab Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Em 2 de novembro de 2026, a Envision anunciou que um sistema integrado de energia de corrente contínua de 800 volts (800 V CC) já está alimentando cargas de computação em operação em seu campus de centros de dados de IA Galaxy, em Ulanqab, na China. A empresa descreveu seu anúncio como o primeiro uso comercial desse tipo de sistema em um centro de dados de IA de grande escala no mundo. O sistema fornece energia de ponta a ponta, desde a entrada de corrente alternada de média tensão até o rack de servidores, e já está em operação comercial antes de uma adoção mais ampla pelo setor. Com isso, serve de referência para centros de dados de IA que estão migrando para uma infraestrutura de energia de 800 V CC. Transformadores de estado sólido e coordenação em tempo real O sistema recém-implantado integra três camadas de hardware: transformadores de estado sólido (SST), armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) e equipamentos que ajustam a tensão de corrente contínua para o hardware de computação. A coordenação fica a cargo do Dubhe Controller, da Envision, que opera com o modelo de base de energia Dubhe da empresa e ajusta os transformadores e as baterias em tempo real para que o fornecimento de energia acompanhe a demanda de computação, inclusive diante de mudanças abruptas na carga. A implantação se baseia em três capacidades: conversão estável por SST, diretamente de média tensão de 10 quilovolts para um barramento de 800 V CC em diferentes condições operacionais; armazenamento em baterias que oferece tanto suporte de energia na escala de segundos quanto reserva na escala de minutos; e coordenação, no nível de milissegundos, entre os SST e o armazenamento, que absorve localmente as flutuações de carga das GPUs. A Envision afirmou que a arquitetura de 800 V CC simplifica os sistemas de energia para centros de dados de IA, citando maior eficiência de conversão de energia e de watts em bits, uma área ocupada pelos equipamentos mais compacta e menor necessidade de cabeamento e cobre. Essas vantagens podem reduzir os custos de infraestrutura e permitir maior densidade de computação no mesmo espaço. Aumento da demanda de energia por rack O anúncio situa a implantação diante de um problema operacional específico: à medida que a demanda por computação de IA acelera, os operadores precisam fornecer mais energia a cada rack em um espaço limitado, mantendo a estabilidade do fornecimento mesmo quando as cargas de computação variam bruscamente de um momento para o outro. “Os centros de dados de IA precisam de sistemas de energia que coordenem as fontes renováveis, o armazenamento de energia e a rede elétrica para atender à demanda de computação”, afirmou Kevin Huang, vice-presidente sênior da Envision Energy e presidente das áreas de armazenamento de energia e sistemas de energia para centros de dados de IA. Huang disse que o sistema em operação demonstra uma arquitetura de ponta a ponta que conecta o fornecimento de energia renovável à demanda de computação e a classificou como uma etapa decisiva para transformar a coordenação entre energia e computação de uma visão estratégica em prática operacional cotidiana. Campus Galaxy e Mission Gobi O campus Galaxy, em Ulanqab, na Mongólia Interior, iniciou suas operações em agosto de 2026, quando a Envision comissionou o local, em 6 de agosto, tendo como estrutura central uma instalação de supercomputação de IA de 120.000 metros quadrados, segundo o anúncio de comissionamento da empresa na época. Esse registro descrevia o campus como projetado para atingir mais de 2 GW de capacidade; o comunicado de 2 de novembro informa uma capacidade planejada de 3 GW e afirma que o campus foi projetado para dar suporte a até um milhão de aceleradores de IA operando em paralelo quando estiver totalmente construído, com mais de 80% da energia planejada proveniente de conexões diretas de eletricidade renovável. A página do campus Galaxy da Envision apresenta o local como um centro de dados de IA com emissões líquidas zero e anuncia preços fixos de eletricidade de longo prazo, 20% abaixo das tarifas da rede elétrica, com contrato de preço fixo por 10 anos, eletricidade e certificados verdes incluídos em pacote e uma proporção de 60% de fornecimento direto de energia verde. A Envision pretende ampliar essa abordagem por meio da Mission Gobi, uma iniciativa apresentada na VivaTech, em Paris, em junho de 2026, que tem o campus Galaxy como seu primeiro projeto emblemático. A Mission Gobi tem como meta alcançar 5 GW de capacidade de centros de dados de IA verdes em regiões desérticas do mundo até 2030. A empresa a apresenta como um modelo replicável e argumenta que o desenvolvimento de apenas 1% das regiões desérticas e de Gobi do mundo poderia viabilizar capacidade de computação na escala de terawatts a um custo altamente competitivo.

artigo.texto: Indonesia’s SM+ Data Centers and LG Sinar Mas, together with Korea Investment Real Asset Management (KIRA), have today opened a 21-megawatt (MW) AI-ready data center in Jakarta, the firms’ joint press release said. The facility, known as SMX01, is ready for service with customer onboarding and stabilizing operations being priorities now. The colocation facility has attracted interest from prospective global, regional, and domestic customers. Located in Jakarta’s central business district, SMX01 is designed to accommodate conventional enterprise workloads and higher-density AI computing, with flexibility for modular expansion as demand increases. The facility is owned and managed by SM+ Data Centers, with KIRA as the investment partner and LG Sinar Mas, a joint venture between South Korea’s LG CNS and Sinar Mas-backed SM+, in charge of its design, construction, and technical operations. “Computing requirements are becoming more varied. Some still run conventional systems, while others are beginning to need significantly higher performance capacity for AI. That is why we built SMX01 so it can expand alongside the market and our customers’ needs,” said Herson Suindah, President Director and Group CEO of SM+ Holdings. “SMX01 reaching Ready for Service is an important investment milestone because it turns long-term capital into operating digital infrastructure that can support Indonesia’s next phase of digital growth. We see strong fundamentals in the market, and we are pleased to continue working with SM+ Data Centers and LG Sinar Mas as the facility moves from development into operations,” said Yong Sik Kim, CEO of KIRA. “A data center’s readiness for AI cannot be measured by rack numbers alone. Power, cooling, and structural load capacity must be planned together from the outset. This is the approach we have brought from our experience building and operating data centers in Korea and globally,” said Donghyup Han, CEO of LG Sinar Mas. SM+ owns and manages 31 data centers across 25 Indonesian cities, including 30 edge data centers, with nearly 45 MW of combined IT load capacity in operations.

The Tier 1 status validates Sigenergy’s rapid worldwide growth, fueled by continuous R&D investment and its visionary "AI in All" strategy. By integrating artificial intelligence into its flexible, modular product architecture, Sigenergy delivers highly reliable, innovative energy storage solutions tailored for diverse applications, ranging from Commercial & Industrial (C&I) projects to complex, utility-scale power plants. artigo.texto: Econergy Ltd, a leading European renewable energy independent power producer (IPP), has acquired a portfolio of four UK battery energy storage systems (BESS) projects totalling 106 MW. Under the agreement, Econergy has acquired 100% of the shares in the holding company of the four assets, giving it full ownership and control. The acquired 106 MW portfolio is expected to generate approximately £4.7 million in EBITDA in 2027 before undergoing proposed augmentation. The acquisition adds revenue-generating assets to Econergy’s UK portfolio, with scope to build on their value through planned upgrades to long-duration storage. All four standalone BESS assets are in commercial operation, and each site is currently operating as a one-hour battery, with potential to upgrade to three-hour storage. Increasing the duration allows the assets to store more energy and dispatch electricity over a longer period, giving them greater flexibility to respond to changing power prices and market conditions. This could also create additional opportunities to shift electricity from periods of high renewable generation to times when demand is higher, helping to increase the value generated by the assets. The additional 106 MW increases Econergy’s operational UK BESS capacity from 90 MW to 196 MW, taking the company from two to six assets connected to the grid. With a 1.6 GW UK storage pipeline under development, the acquisition builds on Econergy’s wider strategy to diversify its European portfolio across technologies and markets. Storage now accounts for approximately 45% of its total port-folio and 40% of its advanced portfolio. Alongside these four projects, Econergy's operating UK BESS portfolio today comprises West Melton (50 MW/100 MWh, operating since 2024) and Dalmarnock (40 MW/120 MWh, connected to the grid on 1 October 2026). Across Europe, Econergy has a BESS portfolio of 5.9 GW, with 3.3 GW expected to be connected, under construction or pre-construction by 2028. Eyal Podhorzer, CEO and Director, Econergy, said: “We’re pleased to be purchasing these four projects, which represent a business opportunity with clear up-side. The addition of 106 MW of operational storage capacity and the potential to augment the assets to three-hour duration gives us a pathway to build on the portfolio and develop its longer-term value. Alongside our existing assets, and those in development, these projects strengthen our foothold in the UK and a growing platform for further expansion. “This acquisition reflects the way we are evolving our portfolio in response to the changing dynamics of European power markets. The UK has strong storage fundamentals, and its scale and market structure make it an important part of our wider energy storage strategy.” For more news and technical articles from the global renewable industry, read the latest issue of Energy Global magazine. artigo.texto: O alcance da medida atinge setores estratégicos da economia nacional, como ferro, aço, alumínio, cimento, fertilizantes e hidrogênio. Por Ana Paula Oriola De Raeffray e Louis Henri Frederic De Raeffray A precificação de carbono deixou definitivamente o campo dos discursos ambientais para se consolidar como variável bruta de comércio exterior, competitividade e acesso ao mercado europeu. Com a entrada em sua fase definitiva, o Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) da União Europeia impõe uma nova realidade: o teor de emissões incorporado aos bens exportados determina, agora, o seu custo efetivo de entrada no bloco. O alcance da medida atinge diretamente setores estratégicos da economia nacional, como ferro, aço, alumínio, cimento, fertilizantes e hidrogênio. Para além do valor nominal dos certificados vinculados ao mercado europeu (EU ETS), o ponto cego para o exportador brasileiro reside na assimetria de mensuração. Duas toneladas de aço fisicamente idênticas enfrentarão condições econômicas totalmente distintas na aduana europeia, a depender do volume de emissões do processo produtivo, das metodologias de comprovação e do aproveitamento do preço de carbono pago no país de origem. É justamente nesse gargalo que o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), instituído pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, ganha dimensão comercial crítica. A consulta pública lançada pelo Ministério da Fazenda em julho de 2026 — introduzindo gradualmente as regras de Monitoramento, Relato e Verificação (MRV) para indústrias de base — expôs a urgência desse alinhamento. A legislação europeia permite deduzir do encargo do CBAM os valores efetivamente quitados no Brasil, mas essa compensação exige equivalência metodológica e validação documental aceitas em Bruxelas. Sem a célere garantia de interoperabilidade entre as métricas brasileiras e as exigências europeias, o risco de dupla oneração econômica torna-se iminente. A indústria nacional corre o perigo real de arcar com o custo doméstico de carbono sem conseguir abatê-lo nas exportações para a Europa, perdendo margem e competitividade perante players globais. A gravidade do tema já extrapolou a esfera regulatória interna e atingiu o contencioso comercial internacional. Não por acaso, em setembro de 2026, o Órgão de Solução de Controvérsias da Organização Mundial do Comércio (OMC) acolheu a criação de um painel para analisar a conformidade do CBAM e do EU ETS. A presença do Brasil como terceiro interessado — ao lado de potências como China, Índia, Estados Unidos e Japão — ratifica que a suposta neutralidade comercial do mecanismo europeu é alvo de forte questionamento global. Para a indústria de transformação no Brasil, a discussão deixou de ser conceitual e passou a ser estritamente operacional. Não basta acompanhar a cotação das licenças de carbono; exige-se mapear precursores, mensurar emissões incorporadas com rigor auditável e transmitir dados incontestáveis aos importadores. O debate migrou da sustentabilidade isolada para a mesa da diretoria financeira, do compliance e do planejamento de vendas. Paralelamente, o avanço do CBAM reconfigura a segurança jurídica da contratação internacional. Cláusulas de fornecimento antes restritas a alíquotas aduaneiras e Incoterms exigem, a partir de agora, regramento explícito sobre a alocação do risco tributário do carbono, deveres de transparência nas emissões e garantias de auditoria. A capacidade de estruturar contratos juridicamente blindados contra contenciosos internacionais — seja em arbitragens de comércio exterior ou perante cortes estrangeiras — tornou-se pilar tão decisivo quanto a eficiência operacional da fábrica. O Brasil encontra-se diante de um divisor de águas. O país detém uma das matrizes energéticas mais limpas do planeta, mas arrisca perder mercados globais por falhas de integração institucional. Não cabe ao Estado ou ao setor produtivo adotar uma postura passiva. É fundamental acelerar a regulamentação do SBCE com foco na diplomacia comercial, enquanto as lideranças empresariais devem encarar a contabilidade de carbono como investimento prioritário em inteligência de mercado. Em suma, o carbono passou a compor o preço final do produto ao lado do frete, do câmbio e das tarifas alfandegárias. Para os exportadores brasileiros, a adaptação soberana e rigorosa a essas exigências não representa um debate para o futuro: é a condição imediata para a sobrevivência comercial no cenário global. (Ana Paula Oriola De Raeffray é doutora em Direito pela Pontifícia Universidade Católica de São Paulo (PUC-SP) e Louis Henri Frederic De Raeffray é consultor do escritório Raeffray Brugioni Advogados) PARTICIPAÇÃO DO LEITOR Participe desta discussão Compartilhe sua opinião sobre este assunto. artigo.texto: Via a brief news release on Oct. 26, Anthropic said that it had filed a registration statement on Form S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) regarding its upcoming initial public offering (IPO). There's not much detail on the release, but the prospectus with the SEC shows that the San Francisco-based company that developed the AI chatbot Claude sees a five-year power bottleneck. The company is moving from a cloud-only, fixed-time compute model to a hybrid setup that includes directly leased chips hosted in data center facilities. In the prospectus, Anthropic discusses launching a new initiative, "Anthropic Direct," to build its own dedicated data centers rather than relying entirely on third-party cloud providers. The company expects this move to lower its long-term costs. Partner companies will buy the land, secure power, build the facilities, and run the daily operations. Anthropic will then lease the computing power directly from those partners. Last month, Anthropic began signing these agreements, committing to $125.2 billion in lease payments over five years, before interest. Anthropic is likely to use behind-the-meter power generation for its data centers to accelerate its development. How Bloom Energy could benefit Bloom Energy (BE -8.61%) provides an alternative to drawing power from a centralized electrical grid through on-site solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) technology. The energy company's SOFCs provide continuous low-emission electrical power. Instead of waiting for a power grid to ramp up to power an Anthropic data center, Anthropic can use Bloom Energy's modular generators to bring data centers online sooner. It isn't far-fetched that Anthropic would turn to Bloom because several of Anthropic cloud-based partners already use Bloom for power needs. Amazon (AMZN -1.41%), through Amazon Web Services, is a major cloud partner for Anthropic. AWS works closely with American Electric Power (AEP +0.67%), which deploys Bloom Energy fuel cells across multiple data center campuses. Specialized cloud provider CoreWeave (CRWV -9.66%), which works with Anthropic, has a partnership to use Bloom Energy power cells at a data center. Bloom is already seeing strong growth The company's financial strength and growing stability are two other reasons Anthropic would turn to it rather than another power provider. Bloom Energy posted record numbers in the third quarter. It reported revenue of $1.26 billion, up 138% year over year. That allowed the company to raise full-year revenue guidance to between $4.4 billion and $4.6 billion, up 122% at the midpoint. BE Bloom Energy NYSE · As of 5:00 PM ET 10/30/26 It's not just revenue that's growing. The company reported earnings per share (EPS) of $0.78, up from an EPS loss of $0.10 in the same period a year ago. Bloom points to a yearly non-GAAP (generally accepted accounting principles) EPS range of $3.10 to $3.40, compared to $0.76 in 2025. Bloom has an edge over Oklo Another possibility for Anthropic is to use small modular reactors (SMRs) from Oklo (OKLO -5.82%) to provide behind-the-meter power to its data centers. However, Bloom's SOFCs are already operating at scale. Its systems can be made, delivered, and put into use within months to a year, providing a quick power solution for new data centers. Oklo's SMRs are promising, but its first commercial reactor is not scheduled to come online until 2027 or later, with large-scale multi-gigawatt rollouts pushed out toward 2030 and beyond. On top of that, the regulatory climate for Bloom's power cells is much easier than for any type of nuclear reactor.

artigo.texto: Kingston data center: City leaders approve special use permit KINGSTON, Ga. - Kingston city officials cleared the path Monday night for a massive 350,000-square-foot data center despite fierce community opposition. What we know: Kingston leaders approved a special use permit paving the way for the facility to be built on 560 acres along State Road 293 near Law Road. Thor Equities, a New York City-based developer, expects the campus to generate at least $2 million every year for municipal coffers and deliver 50 or more high-paying jobs. Mayor Michael McFarland called the vote a major financial turning point for local government. "We've been in dire straits as far as financial, and this is kind of a little blessing for us to help us get this city turned around and try to stand on our own," McFarland said. What we don't know: Project timelines and construction start dates for the site remain unannounced by municipal leaders and developer representatives. Local perspective: Furious neighbors packed the meeting room, warning the data center would permanently shatter rural peace. Opponents raised urgent alarms over surging water consumption, power grid strain, noise, pollution and wildlife habitat destruction. Longtime property owners worry their quality of life will vanish forever under industrial development. "I've lived here for 25 years, I love this town. When they leave, it's the lasting footprint we'll have to deal with," resident Cooper Thompson said. RELATED: Bartow County data center: Neighbors raise water, land concerns What they're saying: Frustrated community members described intense personal grief following the council's decision. "I'm just very disappointed, very heart broken," resident Mary Ann Townsend said. Other neighbors stressed the irreversible ecological threats facing local land. "Most people don't want to pay attention to all the species we're losing," resident Paul Muir said. Townsend emphasized that the facility will forever alter views and property lines for generations of local families. "Our grandchildren, as well as us, are going to be looking at this thing every time we come out of our yards. The folks that have lived in that area that have lived there for 50 years or longer have been done an injustice," Townsend said. What's next: Neighbors say their fight against the industrial campus is far from finished. A group of residents has already consulted legal counsel and plans to file a lawsuit attempting to block the data center from breaking ground. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from FOX 5 Atlanta's Denise Dillon, who reported live from Kingston, gathered statements from residents, city officials and Thor Equities representatives, and covered the municipal permit vote.

artigo.texto: Healthy early voter turnout in Mason County attributed to data centers MASON COUNTY, W.Va. (WCHS) — Two data center projects in Mason County, including what could be one of the largest in the world, and an impacted levy extension are driving what some are calling healthy voter turnout there. "Men and women fought for your right to [vote] and it's almost a slap in the face [not to vote] to those patriots that really gave, sacrificed their lives and fortunes for you and I to have the freedom we have and it's really important that we be civic-minded to participate in the process," Mason County Clerk Diana Cromley said. It's the busiest time in the busiest month of the year for Mason County staff, who are spread across the county making sure all the preparations are in place for the thousands of expected voters on Election Day. "People say, 'Oh, I think the election fairy just shows up on Election Day,'" Cromley said. "There's a lot that happens behind the scenes. We touch and test every machine before it goes out of here so we've got over 100 machines that we're touching, making sure that it will give a vote to you and a vote to this person. We check the whole shebang." Nearly 175 poll workers will be at the polls as early as 5 a.m. Tuesday getting 30 precincts ready. "We have a big county," Cromley said. "I don't know if you're familiar with our county but we have two rivers that stretch it. You drive from one end of our county to the other, it's going to take you probably an hour and a half." Cromley said she doesn't want people to accidentally drive an hour away to the wrong precinct and said to call them if a registration card isn't in hand. "Voters who show up and they're at the wrong place and I always advise poll workers – don't send them around the county," she said. "Just call our office and we can tell you what precinct they need to vote at. It makes voters very agitated and upset if you send them all over the county – 'Drive here, I'm not in that book, I'm not in that book.' All of those are because they've moved and they haven't changed their address." Of Mason County's 15,668 registered voters, 2,062 have already cast a ballot. Cromley said the healthy turnout is driven by two planned data centers by Nscale and Starwood Digital Ventures, as well as a levy extension referendum tied to those data centers. The levy could mean tens of millions of dollars for public schools. Opponents of the referendum say a "no" vote could mean money back in the hands of taxpayers. Those for it say a "no" vote also means that data centers would keep their money rather than giving it to local schools. There are four local races. Three of them are contested, including the race for Mason County Commission and the race for West Virginia House of Delegates Districts 17 and 18. The polls are open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. Tuesday in Mason County across 30 precincts.

artigo.texto: Malaysia-based renewable energy firm Northern Solar Holdings Berhad has secured a total of 189 megawatts (MW) for two data center projects in Malaysia, the firm said in two separate exchange filings yesterday. Its wholly-owned subsidiary Northern Solar Assets Sdn. Bhd. had accepted the two letters of award (LOA) to supply the data centers with solar energy under the corporate renewable energy supply scheme (CRESS). Both LOAs include a battery energy storage system (BESS) as well. The first LOA was awarded by a Malaysian property investment and data center infrastructure developer in respect of 100MWac solar capacity coupled with a BESS for a data center with an annual electricity requirement of 262.8 million kilowatt-hours (kWh). The second, awarded by a Malaysian subsidiary of a Singapore-based data center operator, provides 89MWac solar coupled with a BESS for a data center with annual electricity requirement of 233.89 million kWh. The commencement date of both projects has not been finalised and Northern Solar will update once definitive agreements are signed. Both data centers will have a combined annual electricity requirement of almost 500 million kWh. The total value of both projects was not disclosed. In October, Northern Solar had secured a RM34 million contract to develop a 9.5MW large-scale solar photovoltaic plant.

artigo.texto: As the global race to secure electric vehicle (EV) supply chains intensifies, Morocco is positioning itself as a manufacturing hub linking Europe’s automotive market with Asia’s battery industry. Morocco’s emergence as a battery manufacturing hub could create new opportunities for lithium miners, developers, and explorers as the country positions itself to supply Europe’s EV market. Chinese companies are investing US$6 billion ($8.5 billion) in Morocco’s battery supply chain, as previously reported. The investment targets battery cell and cathode material production as manufacturers seek to diversify their operations amid changing trade dynamics between China and the European Union (EU). With the EU imposing additional duties on Chinese-made EVs, manufacturers are looking at production locations that offer access to international markets while reducing exposure to trade restrictions. An established automotive industry Morocco’s push into battery manufacturing builds on an established automotive export industry. The country is Africa’s largest vehicle manufacturing and export hub, generating MAD 93.7 billion ($13.5 billion) in exports by mid-2026. The country is now gaining a greater share of the EV supply chain through the latest investment by Chinese companies. The investment also signals the growing opportunities for the broader mining sector, as the expansion of battery manufacturing capacity increases the importance of securing reliable supplies of lithium for the energy transition. For lithium producers, the Morocco investment could provide an additional source of demand as battery manufacturing capacity expands beyond established production centres in China. However, the lithium sourcing arrangements for the planned facilities have not been disclosed, leaving uncertainty over which producers could benefit and how much additional demand the projects could generate. Developers: Global Lithium For developers and explorers, the expansion of battery manufacturing offers a potential opportunity for projects seeking a place in the evolving global supply chain. As Morocco expands its downstream manufacturing capacity, projects that can show competitive production costs, reliable supply, and a clear pathway to production could position themselves to attract potential customers and strategic partners. Global Lithium Resources (ASX:GL1) is focused on derisking its Manna Lithium Project in Western Australia, ahead of a final investment decision expected by the end of 2026. Manna boasts a 51.6 million tonne (Mt) mineral resource base, which is considered the third-largest in the Kalgoorlie lithium province. An optimised Definitive Feasibility Study (DFS) for the project has been completed, confirming Manna has a long mine life and is an economically robust lithium asset. Developers such as Global Lithium are demonstrating their projects’ economic viability, particularly as new production capacity enters the market. Explorers: Venari Minerals Meanwhile, for explorers, the latest investment in Morocco presents a potential longer-term demand signal rather than an immediate commercial opportunity. Increased battery manufacturing capacity could support the investment case for new lithium discoveries. However, explorers will still need to establish commercially viable resources before they can benefit from any additional demand. For example, Venari Minerals (ASX:VMS) is advancing its Red Mountain Lithium Project in Nevada, US, which hosts a resource of 500Mt @ 0.61% lithium carbonate equivalent. The company recently announced it is seeking US Department of War (DoW) funding for Red Mountain. This follows its admission to the US Defense Industrial Base Consortium. Membership provides access to DoW grant opportunities and a network of defence contractors to support domestic strategic mineral supply chains. It also enables faster collaboration between government, industry, academia, and non-traditional suppliers. Venari has advanced metallurgical test work at the project, with Scoping Study-level leachability results showing that the lithium is highly leachable. Beneficiation test work also revealed that mineralisation has ‘excellent’ characteristics for removing gangue minerals while retaining valuable lithium-bearing clays and reducing acid consumption. The extent to which Morocco’s expansion translates into opportunities for explorers depends on various factors. These include whether manufacturers seek to secure future supply through partnerships, project investments, or offtake agreements. Morocco’s ambitions could create another source of demand for lithium across the supply chain. However, the impact on individual companies will depend on the scale of additional consumption, the origin of raw materials, and how quickly Morocco’s planned battery manufacturing capacity moves into production.
