artigo.texto: RECUPERAÇÃO Um projeto de instalação de centros de dados no fundo do mar pode comprometer o habitat de aproximadamente 300 baleias belugas na Enseada de Cook, no Alasca, nos Estados Unidos. A proposta prevê a instalação de mais de 300 turbinas de maré em uma região essencial à sobrevivência da população, considerada criticamente ameaçada de extinção. O funcionamento dos equipamentos causa ruídos contínuos e alterações na temperatura da água, com consequências para orientação, alimentação e reprodução dos animais. Apresentada pela empresa DeepGreen Holdings LLC, a iniciativa prevê 66 módulos de centros de dados subaquáticos em uma área de aproximadamente 1.650 acres. A região abriga uma das menores populações de belugas do mundo, estimada em 331 indivíduos, segundo o Centro de Mamíferos Marinhos dos Estados Unidos. As baleias dependem intensamente da ecolocalização para encontrar alimento, identificar obstáculos, comunicar-se e navegar. Na Enseada de Cook, o derretimento das geleiras deixa a água turva, reduzindo a visibilidade e tornando esse sistema sensorial ainda mais importante para a sobrevivência dos animais. O funcionamento dos centros de dados pode interferir diretamente nessa capacidade. Bombas, ventiladores e turbinas produzem ruídos persistentes, especialmente em baixas frequências, que se propagam pela água e podem comprometer a percepção dos sons utilizados pelas baleias. A construção das estruturas também representa uma fonte de perturbação. A cravação de estacas no fundo do mar, por exemplo, produz ruídos intensos. “Bombas, ventiladores e, principalmente, conjuntos de turbinas produzem um som contínuo de baixa frequência, e a cravação de estacas durante a construção é ainda mais barulhenta”, explicou Vishal Misra, professor e cientista da computação da Universidade Columbia, à revista Scientific American. Para animais que dependem da ecolocalização para realizar atividades essenciais, a introdução de fontes permanentes de ruído em seu habitat pode representar uma ameaça significativa. A interferência acústica pode dificultar a localização de presas, a comunicação entre indivíduos e os deslocamentos necessários à sobrevivência. O aquecimento da água ameaça a alimentação Os impactos potenciais não se restringem à poluição sonora. A transferência de calor dos servidores para a água do mar pode modificar as condições ambientais da região e afetar outras espécies das quais as belugas dependem para se alimentar. Entre elas está o salmão, importante componente da alimentação das baleias. Esses peixes necessitam de temperaturas adequadas para o desenvolvimento dos ovos, a manutenção do metabolismo e a migração. Alterações térmicas podem comprometer essas etapas e modificar a disponibilidade de alimento no ambiente. A eventual redução dos recursos alimentares acrescentaria outra pressão sobre uma população que já enfrenta dificuldades para sobreviver. Para as belugas da Enseada de Cook, a degradação do habitat significa perder condições necessárias para encontrar alimento, reproduzir-se e manter seus grupos. Outro projeto ameaça habitat de baleias no Maine A DeepGreen também propôs uma instalação subaquática no estado do Maine, onde pretende ocupar 27 acres e utilizar até 50 turbinas de maré nas proximidades de áreas de alimentação da baleia-franca-do-atlântico-norte. A espécie possui menos de 400 indivíduos, segundo estimativas citadas pelo Centro de Mamíferos Marinhos. O aquecimento das águas no início da década de 2010 contribuiu para que essas baleias abandonassem áreas de alimentação que utilizavam anteriormente. A instalação de equipamentos capazes de produzir ruído e liberar calor nas proximidades de regiões importantes para a alimentação pode acrescentar pressões a uma espécie cuja sobrevivência já está ameaçada. As duas propostas integram uma iniciativa que busca aproveitar a energia das marés para alimentar centros de processamento de dados. A água do mar também seria utilizada para dissipar o calor produzido pelos servidores, reduzindo a necessidade de grandes volumes de água doce empregados na refrigeração de instalações terrestres. O projeto está inserido na expansão da infraestrutura computacional, impulsionada também pelo crescimento da inteligência artificial. A demanda por processamento exige instalações cada vez maiores e amplia a pressão sobre os recursos naturais utilizados para sustentar essas operações. Moradores e organizações contestam as instalações As propostas enfrentam resistência nos dois estados. No Maine, a cidade de Eastport aprovou por unanimidade, em agosto, uma moratória sobre o projeto da DeepGreen. No fim de setembro, o município também solicitou à Comissão Federal de Regulamentação de Energia dos Estados Unidos (FERC) que rejeitasse a instalação. Inicialmente, a agência considerou insuficientes os pedidos apresentados para o Alasca e o Maine, apontando falta de informações técnicas e ausência de identificação adequada das comunidades indígenas historicamente ligadas às áreas dos projetos. Posteriormente, as propostas foram reapresentadas e aceitas para análise. A aceitação dos pedidos, entretanto, não representa autorização para iniciar as obras. Celeste Miller, representante da FERC, esclareceu à Scientific American que uma licença preliminar não permite qualquer tipo de construção. Organizações ligadas à conservação da vida marinha e à pesca também apresentaram objeções. artigo.texto: With maritime transport now included in the UK Emissions Trading Scheme, ship managers need to understand how the new requirements sit alongside the EU ETS, what this means for SHIPMAN agreements and where potential debt and liability exposures may arise. Since 1st July 2026, maritime transport has been included in the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS). Ship managers must now deal with a second emissions trading scheme to consider alongside the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). The schemes use separate allowances and have different geographical scopes, but the work involved will be familiar to managers already dealing with the EU ETS. Both schemes require emissions to be monitored, reported and verified, followed by the surrender of allowances. The EU ETS covers voyages between EU and EEA ports, part of voyages between EU and non-EU ports, and emissions in EU ports. The UK ETS initially covers domestic UK voyages and emissions in UK ports. Managers will therefore need to identify the emissions falling under each scheme and ensure the correct allowances are surrendered. Does this mean SHIPMAN must be amended again? In most cases, no. The BIMCO ETS clause in SHIPMAN 2024 was not drafted solely for the EU ETS. An Emission Scheme is defined to include the EU ETS and any similar system imposed by an applicable lawful authority. The wording allows the clause to apply to similar schemes introduced elsewhere, including in the UK, the US or China. Where the BIMCO clause has been used without amendments which narrow its scope, the UK ETS should already be covered. Managers should, however, check any bespoke wording. A clause which refers only to the EU ETS or EU Allowances may not extend to the UK scheme. For managers, a more immediate concern may be whether the owner provides the allowances. Where the manager is the responsible entity under SHIPMAN, the owner must provide the allowances needed for compliance. If the owner fails to transfer them, or the manager purchases allowances and is not reimbursed, a substantial debt may arise. ITIC’s new ship managers’ debt collection cover is relevant in this situation. ITIC can fund approved costs incurred in pursuing unpaid management fees and debts relating to emissions liabilities, including EU ETS and FuelEU liabilities. The cover does not insure the credit risk or pay the cost of the allowances. It covers the costs of recovering money due to the manager. In many cases, an initial approach from ITIC may be sufficient to obtain payment. Where it is not, further recovery action can be considered, such as the appointment of lawyers. A manager may also face a claim arising from an error in carrying out its responsibilities. For example, the manager could submit inaccurate emissions data, allocate emissions to the wrong scheme, fail to report within the required period or surrender the incorrect number of allowances. If an error causes the owner a loss and results in a claim against the manager, ITIC’s professional indemnity cover may respond, subject to terms and conditions of the cover. The distinction between these two exposures is clear. If the owner has failed to pay an amount due, it is a debt recovery issue. If the manager has made an error which causes a loss, it may result in a professional indemnity claim. For managers using the BIMCO ETS clause in SHIPMAN 2024, the arrival of the UK ETS should not in itself mean revisiting the contract. The priority is to check that the clause has not been narrowed through bespoke amendments and that responsibility for providing allowances and reimbursing costs is clear. If the owner does not pay, ITIC may be able to assist with the cost of recovery.

artigo.texto: Wildfires in Indonesia have ignited a structural challenge within the voluntary carbon market: the validity of credits derived from forest conservation projects when the underlying asset is destroyed by fire. This is not a speculative risk but an operational mechanism failure that directly impacts the integrity of carbon offset claims. The core issue lies in the divergence between the theoretical reduction of emissions-preventing deforestation-and the physical reality of carbon release when peatlands and vegetation burn. The carbon credit mechanism operates on a specific physical premise: one credit represents one tonne of greenhouse gases either reduced or removed. In the context of forest projects, this value is generated by preserving the carbon stored in trees and soil. Unlike renewable energy projects that displace fossil fuel consumption, forest projects carry a unique operational risk: the carbon asset is biologically active and subject to environmental reversal. When a fire occurs, the carbon previously locked in the biomass and peat is released back into the atmosphere, potentially negating the emissions savings that the project was credited for delivering. The verification of this loss is a multi-stage operational process. It does not rely on visual confirmation alone, such as satellite imagery of burn scars, which can be misleading in peatland areas where fires smoulder underground. Instead, independent verifiers must conduct scientific field measurements to quantify the exact volume of underground peat and biomass consumed. As Bjorn Fonden, Asia-Pacific director at the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA), noted, the assessment question is not whether trees remain standing, but whether the project prevented emissions that would otherwise have occurred. If the verified loss reverses previously issued credits, the project may generate fewer new credits in subsequent years, and the specific loss must be compensated to preserve the integrity of the market. The primary operational safeguard against this risk is the buffer pool mechanism. Under this system, a mandatory percentage of credits generated by forest projects-typically around 5 per cent, depending on the project type and risk profile-is withheld from sale and placed into a shared reserve. This reserve acts as a financial and operational insurance policy. When a verified reversal event occurs, credits from the buffer pool are cancelled to offset the loss, ensuring that the total amount of credits in circulation remains accurate. This system is designed to be cross-subsidised; credits from projects in lower-risk regions can cover losses in higher-risk areas, provided the total reserve is sufficient. Ben Rattenbury from carbon ratings firm Sylvera explained that the adequacy of this volume is determined by the crediting standards, which set the rules for how much must be set aside based on historical risk data. However, a significant operational constraint is emerging due to climate change. The buffer pool system was calibrated based on historical fire patterns. As extreme weather events become more frequent and severe, the frequency of large-scale fire events may exceed the rate at which credits are added to the reserve. If multiple large forests burn within a short period, the carbon released could outpace the credits available in the buffer pool, creating a systemic shortfall. This creates a structural mismatch between the pace of environmental degradation and the financial buffering capacity of the market. Some standards are updating their risk calculations to account for these extreme conditions, but the challenge of keeping reserve levels sufficient in the face of accelerating climate risks remains unresolved. Despite these risks, the market has continued to function. Data from carbon market database Allied Offsets indicates that 1,056 new buyers from the Asia-Pacific region entered the market last year. In Singapore, where carbon trading is a significant economic activity, the impact on market depth has been limited. Oi-Yee Choo, CEO of Singapore-based carbon exchange Climate Impact X, stated that trading activity involving Indonesian credits on their platform has remained stable, with no significant shift in demand. This stability suggests that market participants continue to value the offset mechanism, likely because the credit revenue itself serves a critical operational function in fire prevention. The revenue from carbon credits is not merely a financial gain; it is an operational resource for asset maintenance. Funds from these projects are directed toward forest patrols, firefighting teams, early-warning systems, and the maintenance of water levels in peatlands. In peatland areas, preventing the soil from drying out is a critical operational step, as dried peat becomes highly flammable and vulnerable to long-smouldering fires. Zhang Yiwen, co-founder of carbon removal startup CarbonSynk, emphasized that effective projects require due diligence, including the use of satellite images and historical data to identify high-risk zones, and active engagement with local communities to address human activities that contribute to fire risk. The sustainability of the carbon credit market in regions like Indonesia now depends on this operational feedback loop: whether the revenue generated by credits can sufficiently fund the physical measures-patrols, water management, and firefighting-needed to prevent the very events that invalidate the credits. The system is no longer just about protecting a forest for today; it is about ensuring the financial and operational mechanisms can withstand the fires of tomorrow. artigo.texto: Three Kansas communities to decide on data center bans this election WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH) - Data centers are a big talking point in this midterm election. In Kansas, three communities will decide whether to allow them to built in their cities. El Dorado, Emporia and Ottawa all have data center questions on their ballot. El Dorado In El Dorado, citizens will vote on whether to prohibit “high-impact data centers” with an electrical capacity over 10 megawatts. A ‘yes’ vote supports prohibiting high-impact data centers and battery energy storage systems for 10 years. A ‘no’ vote opposes prohibiting high-impact data centers and battery energy storage systems for 10 years. ‘Protect the Heartland,’ the group opposing data centers in El Dorado, successfully placed the issue on the ballot, saying that residents felt this was their last option. “We felt that we had no other choice but to petition our government for an ordinance,” said Danica Dickson, who opposes data centers. “The ordinance does not ban all data centers. It only bans data centers with a capacity of 10 megawatts and above.” Those who support bringing a data center to El Dorado, like the ‘El Dorado Forward’ organization, say that they believe the city has enough safeguards in place to host one. “We are an economic development-friendly group, not necessarily a data center-friendly group,” said Samuel McVay with El Dorado Forward. “We do believe there are good projects, and we want to regulate the bad ones. We believe our city has systems in place to do that.” The vote serves as a binding mandate, so El Dorado gets to choose between total prohibition or entering the data center market under local government regulation. Related Story: Citizen group wins court fight over El Dorado data center petition Emporia Meanwhile, Emporia is also considering a proposal to ban data centers for several years. The ordinance, if passed, would ban high-impact data centers, including those with a peak electrical load of 10 megawatts or facilities that consume more than 10,000 gallons of water per day. A ‘yes’ vote supports prohibiting high-impact data center construction in the city. A ‘no’ vote opposes prohibiting high-impact data center construction in the city. 12 News asked both supporters and opponents what they think about the fact that three Kansas cities have data center measures on the ballot this election. Opponents say it reflects a lack of trust in local government. “It tells me governments are not representing people at this time,” said Jay Vehige, an opponent. “If they were, we would not have had to go through the petition process. But it also tells me that democracy in Kansas is alive and well.” Supporters of the data center in Emporia, like the spokesperson for Flint Hills Digital Campus, say that the election is about more than data centers and it could affect future development projects. “Residents are not being asked to approve or reject a specific data center development. They are being asked to vote on a proposed prohibition of high-impact data centers for a decade, a decision that could have implications well beyond any single project,” the spokesperson said. “Our vision is simple: The next great chapter of American innovation should not be limited by geography, and communities like Emporia deserve the opportunity to help write it.” Related Content: - Petition protesting Emporia data center deemed invalid - Teacher arrested, carried out of Emporia City Commission meeting - Emporia City Commission hosting special meeting to discuss data center ballot ruling Ottawa In Ottawa, voters are deciding whether they will implement a ban on any utility-intensive data centers. A ‘yes’ vote would adopt the ban, and a ‘no’ vote would reject the ban. The proposal does not include a specified expiration date, differing from El Dorado’s proposed ban of 10 years. Community reaction Regardless of the outcome, both sides say they hope the community can unite again after the elections. “This issue has united people on both sides of the aisle,” Dickson said. “Hopefully the temperature cools down and we can all talk again and remember that we are neighbors,” McVay said. artigo.texto: Data centers are deeply unpopular. But what if we called them something else? Axios reports that OpenAI is preparing a “PR blitz” for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, too. The company’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028,” when he expects AI to be “the issue” in the presidential election. So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development of AI “speed limits”; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards — and yes, rebranding data centers as “AI compute campuses.” Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they will no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments) as “good and healthy.” “Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects,” he said.

artigo.texto: CATL Wins Exclusive Battery Deal for Blue Vector Skyla V30 Aircraft In this article (8) CATL has signed strategic and product agreements with Hangzhou-based Blue Vector Intelligent Technology to serve as the exclusive battery partner for its commercial passenger aircraft. Announced by the battery maker on Monday, the tie-up focuses on the Skyla V30, an all-electric tiltrotor model that has secured more than 100 pre-sales orders since its global debut in July. Under the agreement, CATL will develop custom aviation batteries for the six-seat aircraft. The companies did not disclose financial terms, battery specifications or a delivery schedule. Validating the Skyla V30 Platform Engineering work on the airframe is already moving beyond initial digital design. Blue Vector rolled out its first full-scale technology demonstrator, designated A/C01, on August 31 in Harbin in northeastern China. The demonstrator airframe has entered a testing sequence covering systems integration, ground trials and tilt-transition flights. Those trials will test the transition between vertical lift and horizontal forward flight, which forms the core technical challenge for tiltrotor electric craft designed for intercity transit. Commercial demand is building ahead of type certification. Blue Vector booked pre-sales commitments for 60 V30 aircraft at the Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou on September 24. Singapore-based aviation operator Moon Aero accounted for 30 of those aircraft, representing the platform’s first overseas pre-sales customer. That booking brought total advance orders past 100 units as the company conducts airworthiness validation with Chinese civil aviation regulators. Capital Structure and Production Targets Development work relies on fresh venture backing secured over the past two quarters. Blue Vector closed a funding round of more than 100 million yuan ($14.9 million) on June 30, led jointly by Shenzhen Capital Group and an unnamed industrial dollar fund. That transaction marked the company’s fifth capital injection in roughly six months. Across that period, the startup collected more than 400 million yuan to finance aircraft development, prototype construction and test flights. Securing an exclusive battery partnership before airworthiness certification freezes the aircraft’s internal layout. For aircraft manufacturers, battery weight, thermal management and energy density dictate maximum payload and cabin configuration. Swapping pack suppliers later in the certification pipeline resets regulatory approvals, locking airframe designers into their chosen cell platform. For CATL, the deal locks in a captive customer across passenger transit routes in eastern China and regional hubs like Singapore. Operating intercity routes between regional cities demands high cycle life and rapid charging turnaround times at terminal pads, creating recurring replacement demand for specialized aviation-grade cells. Building Out Electric Aviation Across China The Blue Vector contract expands CATL’s ongoing effort to position its battery systems across the electric vertical takeoff and landing sector. In August 2024, the battery maker agreed to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in Shanghai-based aircraft manufacturer Autoflight to co-develop aviation packs. That collaboration extended into terminal infrastructure late last year. In November 2025, Autoflight and CATL revealed a floating vertiport vessel that integrates passenger landing pads, battery storage and high-power charging systems onto a marine barge, providing water-based terminal access for coastal cities. Blue Vector must now clear tilt-transition flight trials in Harbin and advance formal airworthiness certification for the Skyla V30 before delivering the first production units to Moon Aero and domestic operators. Questions & Answers Q. What is the current development status of the Skyla V30 aircraft? Blue Vector rolled out its full-scale technology demonstrator, designated A/C01, on 31 August in Harbin. The demonstrator has entered testing for systems integration, ground trials and tilt-transition flights between vertical lift and horizontal forward flight ahead of type certification with Chinese regulators. Q. Who has placed pre-orders for the aircraft so far? Blue Vector has secured more than 100 advance orders, including a commitment for 60 units booked in Hangzhou on 24 September. Singapore-based operator Moon Aero agreed to take 30 of those aircraft, becoming the platform's first overseas customer alongside domestic buyers. Q. Why was the battery partnership finalised before regulatory certification? Battery weight, energy density and thermal management determine an aircraft's maximum payload and internal layout. Agreeing on a supplier early avoids costly redesigns, as changing battery packs later in the certification pipeline resets regulatory approvals and disrupts airworthiness validation. Q. How is Blue Vector financing the aircraft's development and testing? The startup gathered more than 400 million yuan across five capital injections in roughly six months. This included a funding round of over 100 million yuan on 30 June, led by Shenzhen Capital Group and an industrial dollar fund, to finance development and test flights. artigo.texto: The American Water Works Association (AWWA), an international, nonprofit scientific and educational society, has released a report outlining how water utilities can assess the potential effects of proposed data center developments on water supplies, infrastructure and wastewater systems. The report titled Cooling the Cloud: Considerations for Water Utilities Evaluating Data Center Development, was developed with Carollo Engineers. It examines the resource, technological, financial and contractual issues utilities should consider before approving or supporting data center projects. These include water supply reliability, infrastructure capacity, wastewater impacts, environmental considerations and the recovery of costs associated with development. According to a press release, the report builds on AWWA’s 2025 publication, Cooling the Cloud: Water Utilities in a Data-Driven World, which examined the relationship between data center development, water utilities and local communities. “Water utilities are foundational to local economic development and industrial growth, making their early involvement in community planning essential for major development projects,” said David LaFrance, CEO, AWWA. “Each community will ultimately consider many factors and viewpoints as it assesses data center proposals, AWWA looks forward to working with our many members to share additional insights on data center development and support informed decision-making.” The report outlines a project-by-project approach, urging utilities to first assess data centers’ cooling technologies, projected average and peak water consumption, wastewater needs and potential future expansion. These factors should be weighed against available water supplies, infrastructure capacity, reuse opportunities and environmental impacts before utilities commit resources. It also calls on utilities to establish clear agreements with developers covering infrastructure investments, project costs and each party’s responsibilities as developments evolve. The aim is to prevent existing customers from bearing additional financial burdens. The report further emphasizes early public engagement, with utilities encouraged to disclose projected water demand, system capacity, potential rate impacts and unresolved concerns. Community benefit agreements are also suggested as a way to improve transparency and ensure accountability. It is noteworthy that the AWWA report does not take a position for or against data center development, but is intended to help utilities evaluate proposals based on their individual circumstances.

artigo.texto: KITCHENER, ON, Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Recurrent Energy, a subsidiary of Canadian Solar Inc. ("Canadian Solar") (NASDAQ: CSIQ) and a leading global developer, owner, and operator of solar and energy storage assets, today announced the sale of two standalone BESS projects in France to BW ESS, a global energy storage owner-operator. The portfolio comprises two projects: Baixas, located in the Pyrénées-Orientales department, with a capacity of 100 MW / 400 MWh, and Coquainvilliers, located in Calvados, with a capacity of 100 MW / 400 MWh. Both projects benefit from advanced transmission-level grid connection positions and have been developed around strong grid fundamentals, including very limited expected network constraints. Together, they will provide 200 MW / 800 MWh of flexible capacity to the French electricity system. Recurrent Energy originated and developed both projects, including securing the land, advancing grid connection, and managing permitting and local stakeholder engagement. BW ESS will acquire the projects, marking the first transaction between the two companies and BW ESS' entry into the French energy market. Recurrent Energy will continue to lead the projects through the remaining development phase, drawing on its local market knowledge, technical capabilities, and experience in delivering renewable energy and storage projects. Once the remaining development milestones have been achieved, BW ESS will lead the delivery of the assets through construction and into commercial operation. BW ESS intends to own and operate the assets over the long term. Erik Strømsø, CEO and Co-Founder of BW ESS, commented: "We are excited to work with Recurrent Energy through the next phase and to apply BW ESS' long-term owner-operator expertise as we bring these assets into construction and operation. Entering France is a significant milestone for BW ESS and a natural next step in the expansion of our global energy storage platform. These acquisitions give us an immediate 200 MW / 800 MWh platform in the country and provide a strong foundation for building a sizeable French portfolio. France has a strong nuclear base, but it also has a growing need for flexibility as weather-sensitive demand and an evolving generation mix create more variable system conditions. Batteries can complement France's nuclear backbone by adding the rapid-response flexibility needed to balance the system, absorb surplus power, and make low-carbon generation available when it is most valuable." Dylan Marx, CEO of Recurrent Energy, said: "This transaction with BW ESS showcases our ability to create value through the delivery of high-quality BESS projects, while remaining closely involved in their development through to commercial operation. It is a strong testament to the BESS platform we have built in France and our ability to continue scaling it. Once operational, the projects will provide flexible storage capacity to support grid stability, balance supply and demand, and facilitate the further integration of renewable energy into the French electricity system." artigo.texto: Landover data center project faces new hurdle PRINCE GEORGES COUNTY, Md. (7News) — A proposed data center campus at the former Landover Mall site in Prince George’s County could face a major hurdle after county leaders changed the rules governing data center development. The County Council recently approved legislation closing a loophole in a 2021 law that allowed the Brightseat Park proposal to move forward without another round of council approval. Under the new law, the proposed development must now return before the County Council for additional approval, potentially putting the project in jeopardy as opposition among nearby residents continues to grow. The property, located along Brightseat Road in Landover, has been waiting for redevelopment for more than two decades. Landover Mall opened in 1972 but closed in 2002. The mall was eventually demolished, and its last major store, Sears, closed in 2014. Developers have been pursuing plans for a massive data center campus at the site for the past couple of years. But opponents say the project should not be allowed to move forward under older permitting standards, particularly as Prince George’s County considers tighter restrictions on data center development. “Residents have made it very clear that they do not want the Landover Data center and this development should not be allowed to proceed with building using old permitting standards. But instead should be required to follow any new building standards that are put in place, if and when a moratorium is lifted,” said Beth Landry of the Chesapeake Climate Action Network. SEE ALSO | Amazon is backing out of planned data center project at former GW campus The council’s latest action comes roughly three months after county leaders extended a moratorium on new data center development across Prince George’s County. Council Member Shayla Adams-Stafford has indicated that the new approval requirement could make it extremely difficult for the Brightseat Park proposal to move forward, given the growing opposition. The legislation also signals a tougher approach to future data center proposals, with developers facing additional council oversight, more detailed site review and greater opportunities for public input. The project is not officially dead, but its path forward has become considerably more complicated.

artigo.texto: Headlines report falling battery prices, LFPs dominating stationary storage, and sodium-ion edging into utility tenders. These market swings point to the chemistry likely to dominate the global storage race and what it could mean for grid operators, end users and investors. Battery cell manufacturing overcapacity and fierce competition drove lithium-ion (Li-ion) prices down over the past decade, and they continue to fall. In its 2025 Lithium-Ion Battery Price Survey, BloombergNEF puts the average global battery pack price at $108/kWh in 2025, down 8% from 2024. Stationary storage packs fell further, to around $70/kWh, down 45% year-on-year, while China’s average pack price dropped to $84/kWh. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) drove much of that price decline. The IEA reports that LFP packs were more than 40% cheaper per kWh than nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) packs in 2025. Part of that gap reflects LFP’s grip on stationary storage, where it accounted for more than 90% of global installations that year. However, while batteries keep getting cheaper to manufacture, the risks from commodity prices, supply-chain constraints and overcapacity cycles can sharply reverse the trend in the short term. artigo.texto: Zefiro Part-Funds Isometric Carbon Protocol for Orphaned Well Plugging Zefiro Methane helped fund and shape Isometric's orphaned well protocol, open for public consultation until November 14, 2026. It would allow the company to resume originating credits. Zefiro Methane Corp., a North American environmental services company specializing in methane abatement and the plugging of orphaned and end-of-life oil and gas wells, says it has supported the upcoming launch of a carbon credit methodology for plugging orphaned wells in the United States and Canada. The Orphaned Well Plugging (OWP) Protocol, developed by the carbon registry Isometric, is nearing completion. Once finalized, it would allow Zefiro to originate carbon credits again from the type of plugging work it performs today, according to the company. In a neighboring area of decarbonization, Cupola and SWCorp Malaysia team up to test low-carbon recycling. Zefiro says these credits would come on top of record fiscal 2026 revenue of $42.5 million. A protocol in consultation until November 14 Isometric released the draft OWP Protocol on October 15, 2026, opening a 30-day public consultation that ends on November 14, 2026. The text sets out requirements for projects that permanently plug leaking orphaned wells to stop methane from escaping into the atmosphere. Credits are based on a direct, on-site measurement of each well's methane leak before plugging. That measurement is projected over a 20-year crediting period using a conservative decline rate. A permanence check takes place 12 to 18 months after plugging, and a portion of credits is withheld until the well is confirmed sealed. To be eligible, a project must show that the well is orphaned, that no public program has scheduled it for plugging and that it would not have been plugged without carbon finance. Zefiro's role as an external contributor The protocol was developed by Isometric's Science Team and reviewed by members of its Science Network, which includes more than 500 academic experts. Zefiro was one of three orphaned well project developers that part-funded its development, and it provided expertise drawn from its field operations and carbon market experience. Isometric notes in its announcement that funding does not influence a protocol's requirements. Credits are issued only where an independent, accredited auditor has confirmed that a project is compliant. Zefiro's input came from Sam Jennings, Director of Carbon Operations, and Tina Reine, Chief Commercial Officer. Mr. Jennings, a second-generation petroleum landman, has two decades of experience at Shell, ConocoPhillips, Marathon and Devon. Ms. Reine, who leads Zefiro's activities in the voluntary carbon markets, has worked in environmental markets since 2007 and holds an MBA from Columbia Business School. Isometric and a growing market London-based Isometric began in carbon removal before expanding into industrial emissions, energy, fuels and materials. Its customers include Microsoft, Boeing, JPMorgan Chase and Anglo American. By its own figures, it serves more than 200 projects worldwide and has been contracted to certify more than 16 million tonnes. In September 2026, Intercontinental Exchange, parent company of the New York Stock Exchange, joined its $50 million Series A financing, and the two companies plan to combine Isometric's certification technology with ICE's market infrastructure and data capabilities. According to MSCI, capital committed to carbon credits hit a record $22 billion in 2025, and the market could be worth between $60 billion and $270 billion by 2050. Zefiro says it completed the first sale of carbon offsets originated under the American Carbon Registry's orphaned well methodology. Mr. Jennings said a framework combining scientific rigor with the practical requirements of financing could help attract the investment needed to plug more leaking orphaned wells. artigo.texto: Nearly 15 years worth of hard-won pollution reduction efforts are set to be undone in the United States, as a wave of data centers powered by gas plants enters construction. That’s according to a new analysis by the Sierra Club, first reported by Bloomberg, which notes that the US energy grid is expected to belch out 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030, assuming the country’s currently-planned AI developments enter operation as scheduled. That’s a massive rise compared to even 2025 — itself a near-record year for US carbon emissions. If the AI industry and its data center developers get their way, the analysis found, emissions will likely skyrocket by 42 percent over the five-year period, an expected increase of 618 million tons compared to 2025. “The numbers continue to sort of boggle our minds,” the Sierra Club’s principal advisor for climate and energy Jeremy Fisher told Bloomberg. Due to major bottlenecks in the electrical grid, many data center developers have opted for on- or near-site power plants, which are overwhelmingly fueled by noxious fossil fuels. Projects like Elon Musk’s 1.2 gigawatt data center near Memphis are already choking out residents with fleets of methane generators, which legal experts say flaunt all kinds of local permitting and federal environmental regulations. Still, for anybody banking on having clean air to breathe, there is some hope. The number of data center projects at risk of cancellation is rising precipitously as time goes on — driven by grass roots organizing and increasing financial pressures. So if you’re one of the many activists mounting opposition to data centers in your community, just know that the benefits of a cancelled hyperscale facility extend far beyond your backyard. artigo.texto: Liquid Cooling Retrofits: Hard, but Sometimes Worth It Liquid cooling retrofits can boost density and efficiency, but cost, downtime, and infrastructure limits mean they make sense only in select cases. There is little question that liquid cooling is becoming an increasingly attractive way to manage rising heat loads inside data centers, especially as operators deploy denser racks and more AI infrastructure. In many scenarios, liquid cooling can improve thermal efficiency and reduce dependence on large volumes of airflow. It can also help operators curb water use in designs that would otherwise rely heavily on evaporative cooling. The challenge, however, is that most existing data centers were not designed with liquid cooling in mind. Retrofitting an older facility to support liquid cooling can be technically feasible, but it is rarely simple. Here’s a look at why retrofits are difficult – and when the investment may still make sense. Why Liquid Cooling Retrofits Are Difficult From a logistical standpoint, installing liquid cooling is relatively easy when building a new data center. Designers can account for piping, rack loads, redundancy, heat rejection, and maintenance access from the start. It is much harder when an operator wants to retrofit an existing facility, whether to replace or supplement a traditional air-based cooling design. In that case, several challenges tend to stand in the way. Space Constraints Complicate Piping Liquid cooling systems require supply and return lines to run close to servers and other heat-generating IT equipment. In many existing server rooms, however, available space is already constrained, and much of it is occupied by networking and power cabling. Addressing that problem may require repositioning racks, reworking cable pathways, or creating new routes for coolant distribution. In some cases, operators may even need to expand white space or make other physical changes to the facility. All of that is possible, but it can be expensive and disruptive. Heavier Racks Can Strain Raised Floors The structural components of liquid cooling systems, combined with coolant itself and higher-density compute hardware, can significantly increase rack weight. In AI-heavy environments, fully loaded racks can exceed 3,000 pounds. The added weight is especially challenging in facilities with raised floors. Raised-floor designs are common in older data centers because they support airflow management for conventional air cooling. But they may not be able to support heavier liquid-cooled racks without reinforcement or redesign. That can mean extensive structural work before a retrofit can move forward. Downtime Is Hard to Avoid Even for operators willing to make the investments needed to support a retrofit, downtime is often a major concern. Structural modifications, mechanical upgrades, and rack-level changes can take months, especially if servers must be moved or workloads shifted elsewhere during the transition. Even when no major building work is required, some disruption is likely as systems move from an existing cooling model to a liquid-assisted design. That might be manageable for organizations with spare capacity in other facilities or the ability to burst into the cloud, but it is a much harder proposition for sites supporting mission-critical workloads. Mechanical Systems May Need Major Upgrades Adding liquid cooling requires supporting infrastructure to remove heat from the building, which may entail changes to pumps, heat exchangers, water loops, or dry-cooling equipment. Older facilities may not have enough capacity in their mechanical plant to support those changes. Even when they do, integrating new liquid cooling equipment with legacy systems can be complex. Operators must also consider factors such as leak detection, water quality, redundancy, and maintenance procedures. Liquid Cooling Adds Operational Complexity A retrofit can also create ongoing operational challenges. Liquid cooling introduces new equipment, maintenance needs, and failure scenarios that require staff training and updated procedures. When a Liquid Cooling Retrofit Is Worth It Given the cost, complexity, and disruption involved, many operators will conclude that a full liquid cooling retrofit is not the right move for their facilities. Still, there are cases where the economics and the operational logic are compelling. One is a partial deployment. Instead of replacing an entire cooling architecture, an operator may add liquid cooling only for the highest-density racks while leaving the broader air-cooling system in place. That reduces structural changes and the risks of downtime. It is also the approach many colocation providers have taken as they add support for liquid-cooled deployments without converting entire facilities. Another scenario is the single-tenant data center, where one organization directly captures the long-term efficiency and capacity benefits. In those cases, it is often easier to justify the capital expense because the operator and the beneficiary are the same. Retrofits can also make more sense in regions facing water constraints or regulatory pressure around resource consumption. Where water availability is limited or sustainability targets are becoming harder to meet, the case for moving at least some workloads to liquid cooling can grow stronger. Finally, a retrofit may be attractive when the alternative is building new capacity from scratch. If an operator needs to support denser server hardware but does not want to add another facility, liquid cooling may provide a way to increase compute capacity within an existing footprint. In that scenario, retrofitting may be less expensive than expanding the data center portfolio. Retrofitting an existing data center for liquid cooling is difficult, and in many cases the costs will outweigh the benefits. But not always. artigo.texto: OpenAI doesn't want to call them "data centers" anymore. Instead, the ChatGPT maker plans to propose a new, more chic name for the behemoth factories that power your chatbot queries. That new name is "compute campuses," an OpenAI spokesperson confirmed to Business Insider on Sunday. "Compute campuses better describes the scale and role of the infrastructure we're building for AI," the spokesperson said. "These are long-term investments in computing, energy infrastructure and skilled work." Though much has been said about the less-than-stellar reputations of AI data centers (a recent Pew Research poll found that 54% of Americans say AI data centers are bad for the environment), efforts to ameliorate that view have mostly failed. Data centers are now a major issue for voters in the midterms. While major data center builders like Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft have pledged millions of dollars to the communities and schools surrounding their centers, OpenAI is betting that a complete rebrand will also help turn around public opinion. "We want the communities hosting that infrastructure to help shape it and share in the opportunities it creates," the OpenAI spokesperson said. Time will tell, however, if the "compute campus" lingo catches on. Axios earlier reported that OpenAI was also preparing for a blue wave in Tuesday's midterm elections, which could result in a more regulatory-minded government.

artigo.texto: O Brasil deu mais um passo na construção de seu mercado regulado de carbono. A publicação, em 29 de outubro, das primeiras regras para a implementação das obrigações de mensuração, relato e verificação de emissões inaugura etapa importante desse processo. O Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões, criado em 2024, insere o País num movimento internacional de precificação das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. É um instrumento que pode contribuir para o cumprimento dos compromissos climáticos ao valorizar ativos naturais, com efeitos sobre investimentos, custos de produção e competitividade. A nova portaria estabelece um cronograma para que setores passem a mensurar e reportar suas emissões. O País entra, portanto, em uma fase de aprendizado e construção das metodologias que sustentarão o sistema. O processo de regulamentação é marcado por uma interlocução entre poder público e setor produtivo que merece reconhecimento. Aliado ao rigor técnico e à prudência, o diálogo é fundamental para assegurar regras equilibradas que considerem as particularidades da economia brasileira, proporcionem segurança jurídica e estimulem investimentos. O desafio é construir um marco regulatório que concilie integridade ambiental e desenvolvimento econômico, evitando distorções que não se traduzam em benefícios ambientais. Temos uma estrutura produtiva muito particular, com elevada participação de fontes renováveis em segmentos que fizeram investimentos expressivos em eficiência e redução de emissões. Reconhecer essas características e evitar importar modelos concebidos para realidades diferentes é fundamental. Esse cuidado é especialmente relevante quando se olha para setores que já incorporam fontes renováveis, ativos biológicos e ciclos longos de investimento. É o caso da indústria de árvores cultivadas na produção de celulose, em que a dimensão florestal e a industrial são partes indissociáveis de uma mesma cadeia. O setor cultiva 10,7 milhões de hectares de florestas plantadas para fins produtivos e conserva milhões de hectares de vegetação nativa. Todos os dias, planta 2,2 milhões de árvores para fins comerciais. Ao crescerem, elas retiram carbono da atmosfera e o armazenam em sua biomassa. Ao mesmo tempo, fornecem matéria-prima renovável para produtos presentes no cotidiano de bilhões de pessoas e sustentam uma indústria que utiliza 92% de fontes renováveis de energia e investe continuamente na eficiência de seus processos. Uma regulamentação tecnicamente consistente precisa enxergar o ciclo produtivo em sua integralidade, estimular novos avanços e não penalizar quem já investiu. O Brasil tem enorme potencial para retirar CO2 da atmosfera a partir de suas florestas – plantadas ou naturais. A lei que criou o mercado de carbono já prevê o reconhecimento dessas remoções. Agora é fundamental que a regulamentação transforme essa previsão em mecanismos concretos, capazes de valorizar a contribuição das florestas e estimular novos investimentos, gerar empregos e fortalecer nossa competitividade no mercado internacional. Há ainda uma oportunidade que ultrapassa nossas fronteiras. O Acordo de Paris criou mecanismos de transferência internacional de resultados comprovados de redução ou remoção de emissões, os ITMOs (na sigla em inglês). Esse mecanismo pode abrir portas para o financiamento internacional de projetos que contribuam para o enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas, como aqueles ligados à restauração florestal. As regras nacionais para essas operações, ainda em discussão, devem garantir segurança jurídica, transparência e integridade ambiental, criando condições para a atração de investimentos. A discussão ganha mais relevância às vésperas da COP-31, que será realizada de 9 a 20 de novembro, em Antália, na Turquia. A conferência ocorrerá num mundo marcado por guerras, tensões geopolíticas, crise energética e disputas econômicas, no qual a agenda da sustentabilidade perde espaço. Após anos de negociação, as conferências entram no terreno da implementação: como financiar, medir e viabilizar, na economia real, as transformações acordadas. O encontro terá entre seus desafios avançar nas regras para geração de créditos de carbono, conciliando a credibilidade dos créditos às regras viáveis para projetos que exigem investimento e planejamento de longo prazo, como o plantio de florestas. Para o Brasil, essa pauta precisa ser tratada também como agenda de desenvolvimento. Não cabe tratá-la nem com entusiasmo acrítico nem como ameaça ao setor produtivo. É preciso assegurar que o mercado de carbono cumpra seu papel de promover a descarbonização, ao mesmo tempo em que estimule investimentos, valorize iniciativas já desenvolvidas e fortaleça a competitividade. Temos vantagens naturais importantes, uma matriz energética renovável, experiência científica acumulada e setores econômicos que avançaram na agenda de descarbonização. Mas vantagem comparativa não se transforma automaticamente em vantagem econômica. Isso depende de ambiente de negócios, infraestrutura, tecnologia, segurança jurídica e boas escolhas regulatórias.

artigo.texto: Gia Lai reduz as emissões de CO₂ em 10,2 milhões de toneladas anualmente a partir de energia renovável. Gia Lai possui 85 usinas de energia renovável, que contribuem para uma redução de aproximadamente 10 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ anualmente, mas apenas 29 usinas estão atualmente vendendo créditos de carbono. Em 31 de outubro, o Comitê Popular da província de Gia Lai anunciou a aprovação do plano geral para o desenvolvimento do mercado de créditos de carbono. Isso identifica a energia renovável como uma das áreas com grande potencial para reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa e gerar créditos de carbono. FOTO: TRANG ANH De acordo com o plano, Gia Lai possui atualmente 85 projetos de energia renovável em operação, gerando eletricidade com capacidade total de 4.167 MW. Até 2025, essas usinas produzirão e fornecerão aproximadamente 15.479 milhões de kWh à rede elétrica nacional, contribuindo para uma redução nas emissões de gases de efeito estufa de cerca de 10,2 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ por ano. Você também pode gostar No entanto, a exploração de créditos de carbono neste setor ainda não atingiu todo o seu potencial. Um levantamento mostra que apenas 29 das 85 centrais elétricas da província, com uma capacidade total de 1.264 MW, implementaram e comercializaram créditos de carbono, o que equivale a aproximadamente 30,33% da capacidade total de energia renovável em operação. O plano identifica Gia Lai como uma província com muitas vantagens naturais para a expansão de projetos de energia limpa. De acordo com o plano aprovado, até 2030, a província deverá contar com 45 projetos de energia eólica, com capacidade total de 3.285 MW, produzindo aproximadamente 9,92 milhões de MWh/ano. O setor de energia solar deverá ter 24 projetos, com capacidade total de 1.530 MW, produzindo aproximadamente 2,5 milhões de MWh/ano. Em relação à energia hidrelétrica, a província planeja ter 47 projetos com capacidade total de 578 MW, produzindo aproximadamente 1,7 milhão de MWh/ano. Além disso, subprodutos agrícolas como café, cana-de-açúcar, mandioca, casca de arroz, palha e subprodutos florestais oferecem oportunidades para o desenvolvimento de dois projetos de energia de biomassa com capacidade de 52 MW. O setor de valorização energética de resíduos também prevê três projetos com capacidade total de 45 MW. Você também pode gostar Além da energia, Gia Lai também possui uma vantagem significativa em recursos florestais, com mais de 1,03 milhão de hectares de floresta e área florestal plantada, dos quais mais de 692.000 hectares são floresta natural. Este é um recurso importante para o desenvolvimento de projetos de proteção florestal, reduzindo as emissões provenientes do desmatamento e da degradação florestal. Na zona costeira, a província possui aproximadamente 99,5 hectares de manguezais, 152,35 hectares de recifes de coral e 200 hectares de pradarias marinhas, o que abre potencial para o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono verde. No setor pecuário, a província conta atualmente com cerca de 56.180 instalações de biodigestores, que processam aproximadamente 1.000 toneladas de esterco por dia. A recuperação de metano a partir de dejetos animais e a utilização do biogás para geração de energia elétrica também contribuem para a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. O projeto visa estabelecer gradualmente um mercado transparente de créditos de carbono, em consonância com o roteiro nacional, criando recursos financeiros adicionais para a proteção ambiental, a transição verde e o desenvolvimento econômico sustentável.

artigo.texto: Judge says xAI must face NAACP lawsuit on data center pollution The legal battle revolves around the AI company’s operations in southern Memphis. A federal judge's latest ruling has denied xAI's request to dismiss a lawsuit that alleges its data center campus in Memphis, Tennessee is running turbines without proper permits and violating the Clean Air Act. The decision, from US District Judge Debra M. Brown, allows the lawsuit, which was filed by the NAACP, to move forward. The organization filed its legal action against xAI in April, accusing the company that's now known as SpaceXSI of using unpermitted methane gas turbines to power data centers in the Memphis area. Despite the ongoing lawsuit that also claimed it's violating the Clear Air Act, Elon Musk's company continued to add more gas turbines to another AI data center site in the nearby Southhaven, Mississippi community. In response, xAI requested to dismiss the NAACP lawsuit and even received support from the Justice Department, which claimed that the company's operations are a crucial part of US military operations. xAI said the lawsuit should be dismissed, claiming that its turbines were exempt from permitting requirements since they were mobile. Judge Brown wrote in her decision that the power plant where all the turbines were providing power to xAI's data center wasn't mobile and therefore not exempt from the permitting process. The lawsuit comes at a time when AI companies are ramping up the construction of data centers to fuel their AI needs, while neighbors are becoming increasingly averse to these buildouts.

artigo.texto: Ohio: O Estado concentra o maior número de iniciativas eleitorais relacionadas a data centers: 21. Ohio já é um dos principais mercados para desenvolvedores desse tipo de empreendimento. Atualmente, 154 data centers estão em operação, outros 27 estão em construção e 57 estão em fase de planejamento. - Treze municípios terão propostas de proibição de data centers nas urnas: Conneaut, Defiance, Granville, Grove City, Hubbard, Monroeville, Oregon, Pataskala, Piqua, Sunbury, Trenton, Upper Sandusky e Urbana. Algumas dessas iniciativas, porém, restringem apenas instalações classificadas como de “alto impacto” ou empreendimentos que consumam mais de 25 megawatts de energia. - Os distritos rurais de Monroe e Sprigg votarão sobre a adoção de novas regras de zoneamento destinadas a preservar o “caráter rural e agrícola” dessas regiões. Na prática, as medidas impediriam a construção de data centers. As duas pequenas comunidades do sul de Ohio estão entre as possíveis localidades para grandes empreendimentos, incluindo um terreno de aproximadamente 4,05 milhões de metros quadrados que está sendo avaliado para receber um data center da Amazon Web Services. - A cidade de Wilmington votará quatro propostas relacionadas ao zoneamento de quatro terrenos específicos, que permitiriam o avanço de um projeto de data center. A votação ocorre depois que a Suprema Corte de Ohio manteve a decisão do conselho eleitoral do condado de bloquear um referendo que estabeleceria restrições mais abrangentes. - Além disso, os eleitores de Ashville decidirão se querem impedir a construção de um data center cujas obras já começaram. Já os moradores do vilarejo de Perry votarão uma resolução que exigiria que os desenvolvedores oferecessem garantias financeiras ao município e respeitassem limites de ruído nas instalações para ter acesso a incentivos fiscais. - Illinois: Seis municípios do Estado votarão propostas destinadas a orientar seus governos locais sobre a aprovação ou construção de novos data centers: Chouteau, Granite City, Joliet, Morgan, Nameoki e Venice. - Enquanto isso, os eleitores de Bloomington decidirão se aprovam uma moratória integral sobre futuros empreendimentos desse tipo. No início deste ano, a cidade e o município vizinho de Normal estabeleceram uma suspensão de seis meses para instalações com consumo superior a 5 megawatts de energia. - Wisconsin: Os eleitores de Janesville decidirão se futuros projetos com investimentos superiores a US$ 450 milhões (aproximadamente R$ 2,3 bilhões) em uma antiga fábrica de autopeças deverão receber aprovação da maioria da população. Na prática, a votação determinará se o terreno poderá ser utilizado para a construção de um data center. - A proposta se refere especificamente à área de uma antiga fábrica da General Motors, que encerrou suas atividades em 2008, durante a crise da indústria automobilística, deixando um terreno contaminado após o fechamento. - Janesville enfrenta dificuldades para dar uma nova destinação à propriedade desde então. Recentemente, a cidade passou a avaliar a possibilidade de construir um data center no local, proposta que provocou forte reação contrária da população. - Governos locais de outras cidades de Wisconsin também estabeleceram moratórias temporárias para data centers ao longo do ano, incluindo Madison, em janeiro, e Milwaukee, em outubro. - Kansas: As cidades de El Dorado e Emporia votarão sobre a proibição de data centers classificados como de “alto impacto”. Já Ottawa decidirá sobre uma restrição a instalações de “alto consumo de serviços públicos”, definição que abrange empreendimentos com demanda superior a 25 megawatts de energia. - Maine: Quatro municípios do Estado votarão propostas de moratória à construção de data centers, embora a maioria tenha prazo determinado. Peru e Wells decidirão sobre suspensões de 180 dias, enquanto Wiscasset votará uma proibição de seis meses para novos empreendimentos e projetos de expansão de instalações existentes. - A cidade de North Berwick, por sua vez, votará uma proposta própria para proibir data centers com área superior a 2.323 metros quadrados. - Cidades maiores do Maine, incluindo Bangor, já adotaram moratórias locais. Além disso, a Assembleia Legislativa do Estado aprovou uma suspensão válida para todo o território estadual no início deste ano. A medida, porém, foi vetada pela governadora Janet Mills em abril. Esta lista foi elaborada com base em dados de organizações sem fins lucrativos que monitoram iniciativas eleitorais, incluindo o levantamento da Ballotpedia sobre propostas relacionadas a data centers, além de estatísticas sobre consumo de energia e projetos planejados do U.S. Data Center Map. Em quais outros lugares haverá votação sobre data centers? Na Califórnia, a cidade de Alhambra, no condado de Los Angeles, votará uma proposta para proibir data centers. Se aprovada, será a segunda cidade do Estado a adotar esse tipo de restrição por meio de votação popular. Em junho, os eleitores de Monterey Park aprovaram uma moratória. Em Edgewater, na Flórida, a Câmara Municipal já aprovou uma moratória para data centers em setembro. Agora, a medida será submetida aos eleitores para inclusão na carta municipal, documento que estabelece as regras de funcionamento do governo local. Em Nevada, os eleitores de Boulder City decidirão se novos data centers poderão ser construídos em uma área específica que já abriga projetos de geração de energia solar. Em Nova Jersey, os moradores de Downe Township votarão para indicar se apoiam a construção de data centers na pequena comunidade localizada no sul do Estado. A proposta, no entanto, não prevê uma votação sobre a proibição desses empreendimentos. Já os eleitores de Harwood, em Dakota do Norte, decidirão se empreendimentos industriais, incluindo data centers, deverão passar por uma análise adicional e, pelo menos, uma audiência pública antes de serem aprovados. artigo.texto: Warrick Co. holds public meeting on data center zoning ordinance Officials say the proposed ordinance would not rezone any property or approve a data center project WARRICK CO., Ind. (WFIE) - The Warrick County Area Plan Commission held the special forum at Friedman Park Event Center to take public comment on a proposed data center ordinance. Many people in the audience voiced frustration with the draft. First responders: “We still have not had a seat at the table” Christopher Stephens of the Boonville Fire Department was the first speaker. He said fire chiefs across the county have asked to be involved and have not been heard. “We still have not had a seat at the table. There’s been very minimal e-mail communication back and forth, but the requests that have been made multiple times by multiple fire chiefs in the county have apparently fallen on deaf ears,” said Stephens. Residents call for more information Yvon Lauren, a Warrick County resident, told the commission the county should learn more before it passes any ordinance. “I think that we have to make an effort to learn more about it before we pass any kind of ordinance in this county. I have several homes here. I have a large family here and I plan to retire here, stay here. And I really think it’s time we take this very seriously,” said Lauren. Critics say the draft is too vague and that officials still don’t know enough about data centers. “There is some point going to be a glut of data centers” Jim Mauror, also a Warrick County resident, questioned whether the county needs more data centers at all. “There is some point going to be a glut of data centers. We cannot build them continuously and at some point the data centers won’t even be necessary,” said Mauror. Many people at the forum oppose data centers in any form and asked what the benefits would be. Some said there are enough of them already. What the ordinance would do The draft ordinance would create a floating Data Center Overlay District, known as DC-O. Under the proposal, a data center could be built only on land zoned for heavy industrial use (M-2) that also has DC-O zoning. Getting DC-O zoning would require a site-specific rezoning approved by the Board of Commissioners. The ordinance also defines what counts as a data center and lists requirements they would have to follow. Those include: - Operational sound of no more than 55 decibels (dBA) at a neighboring home or residential zoning boundary. - Data center buildings set back at least 300 feet from homes or other residential zoning. - Intensive outdoor equipment, such as generators, transformers and battery storage, set back at least 500 feet. - A landscaped buffer of at least 100 feet near residential property. The draft also asks developers to provide fire and emergency medical services information in their applications. That includes responder training needs and any added staffing or service demands the project would create. Officials say the ordinance does not approve any data center and does not rezone any property. Connection to Project Alloy The forum follows the announcement of “Project Alloy.” It is a proposed data center on roughly 700 acres of Alcoa-owned land near the company’s river-side complex. County officials have said the ordinance is not written around any single project. It is meant to set standards for any data center proposed in the county. What’s next The Warrick County Board of Commissioners will consider the ordinance at a meeting on Nov. 9 at 4 p.m. at Friedman Park Event Center, the same venue as Monday’s forum. artigo.texto: Construindo um centro de dados de tráfego: Evite investimentos fragmentados e duplicados. (Chinhphu.vn) - Na tarde de 31 de outubro, o Ministério da Segurança Pública realizou uma conferência para divulgar e implementar o Projeto "Construção de um Centro de Dados para gerenciamento, monitoramento, tratamento de infrações e operação de tráfego no período de 2026 a 2030, com uma visão para 2050". O membro do Politburo e Vice-Primeiro-Ministro Permanente , Pham Gia Tuc , e o General Luong Tam Quang, membro do Politburo e Ministro da Segurança Pública, copresidiram a conferência. Entre os participantes estavam representantes de ministérios e agências centrais, províncias e cidades, e das forças de segurança pública do povo. Adote uma gestão de tráfego proativa e orientada por dados. Em seu discurso de abertura na conferência, o Ministro da Segurança Pública , Luong Tam Quang, enfatizou que a implementação do Projeto é um passo fundamental para concretizar as políticas do Partido em relação à garantia da segurança humana e à construção de uma sociedade disciplinada, segura, civilizada e harmoniosamente desenvolvida. O Comitê do Partido e o Governo identificaram a implementação do Projeto como uma tarefa importante, urgente e estrategicamente significativa, visando reformar fundamentalmente o método de gestão estatal no setor de transportes, passando de um modelo focado principalmente na detecção e tratamento de infrações para uma gestão proativa e orientada por dados. Segundo o Ministro Luong Tam Quang, o sistema de centros de dados de transporte deve ter uma arquitetura geral unificada, padrões de dados e uma plataforma de aplicação comum em todo o país; promovendo, ao mesmo tempo, o papel proativo das localidades na organização e operação de acordo com a estrutura hierárquica, garantindo conectividade perfeita entre os dois níveis de centros. Todos os sistemas e projetos de componentes devem aderir à arquitetura comum, evitando resolutamente investimentos fragmentados, sobrepostos e isolados que carecem de interoperabilidade. O processo de implementação deve garantir a segurança e a proteção dos dados, colocando as pessoas no centro. A aplicação da inteligência artificial ( IA ) deve ser transparente, rastreável e sujeita a controle humano. A eficácia do projeto deve ser medida pela sua capacidade de compreender a situação, gerir o tráfego, prevenir e lidar com infrações, reduzir acidentes e congestionamentos e melhorar a qualidade do serviço para cidadãos e empresas. Ao apresentar seu relatório na Conferência, o Tenente-General Nguyen Ngoc Lam, Vice-Ministro da Segurança Pública, afirmou que, de acordo com o Projeto aprovado pelo Primeiro-Ministro na Decisão nº 456/QD-TTg, de 20 de março de 2026, o sistema está organizado segundo um modelo de dois níveis, compreendendo um centro de nível nacional operado pelo Departamento de Polícia de Trânsito e 34 centros de nível provincial operados pelos Departamentos de Polícia de Trânsito das províncias e cidades, de acordo com a estrutura hierárquica. Esses centros estão interligados, compartilhando dados de forma bidirecional, com o objetivo de agregar, analisar e prever as condições de tráfego, bem como comandar e gerenciar o tráfego em nível nacional e local. O sistema visa integrar dados sobre veículos, condutores, acidentes de trânsito, processamento de infrações, infraestrutura e câmeras de vigilância, aplicando inteligência artificial para auxiliar na detecção de anomalias, identificação de riscos, alerta de incidentes e coordenação do gerenciamento de situações de trânsito. A verificação e as decisões sobre o tratamento de infrações continuarão sendo tomadas por autoridades competentes, em conformidade com a lei. O projeto também visa desenvolver serviços públicos online, fornecendo informações sobre as condições do trânsito, alertando sobre congestionamentos e acidentes, auxiliando as pessoas na escolha de rotas adequadas, reduzindo o tempo e os custos de viagem e simplificando os procedimentos administrativos. Você também pode gostar Líderes de ministérios e setores discursando - Foto: chinhphu.vn/Phuong Nguyen Padronizar as normas técnicas e garantir os recursos necessários para a sua implementação. Para conectar os centros locais de monitoramento e controle de tráfego ao centro nacional, o sistema precisa ser construído sobre uma base unificada em termos de padrões técnicos, arquitetura de conexão e compartilhamento de dados. Ao mesmo tempo, a integração de equipamentos existentes, condições de infraestrutura e capacidades de alocação de recursos em nível local apresenta requisitos diferentes durante a implementação do projeto. O Major-General Do Thanh Binh, Diretor do Departamento de Polícia de Trânsito, afirmou que a unidade está desenvolvendo um plano abrangente referente à arquitetura tecnológica, software de gestão, infraestrutura de rede de transmissão, sistemas de servidores e segurança da informação; simultaneamente, padronizando os dados de entrada e identificando produtos operacionais para atender à gestão, comando, controle e prestação de serviços públicos. O sistema está sendo construído para atender aos requisitos de conexão e compartilhamento de dados entre os níveis nacional e local, satisfazendo as necessidades de armazenamento, processamento e operação estável de informações. Em seu discurso na conferência, um representante do Ministério da Ciência e Tecnologia propôs a coordenação com o Ministério da Segurança Pública e outros ministérios e agências para revisar e aprimorar o sistema de normas e regulamentos técnicos, com foco na arquitetura de conectividade, protocolos de troca, formatos de dados compartilhados e qualidade e segurança dos dados. artigo.texto: Data centers were once hailed as the pinnacle of technological innovation, the engines of economic growth, and a determinant of competitive edge. In 2026, however, their high costs, rising electricity demands, and alarming environmental implications have put them at the forefront of national attention. As their name suggests, data centers are buildings that house, run, and cool computers. They can be as small as a room with a single computer or as large as a labyrinth lined with hundreds of thousands of servers. The largest in the United States, Meta’s Prineville data center, covers a vast 4.6 million square feet in the middle of a remote, high-desert region of Oregon. Meta doesn’t disclose just how many servers are inside the facility, but it is estimated that the number is in the hundreds of thousands. While there are already a whopping 3,582 data centers in the United States, the explosive use of AI has triggered an aggressive spike in demand being felt across the country. Current demand is expected to triple by 2030. While these data centers seemingly pop up out of nowhere, the inputs required to run them cannot be underestimated. While reportedly renewable-based, the Prineville data center alone consumes nearly 1.4 million megawatt-hours of electricity annually. In 2023, annual data center energy use in the United States sat at roughly 176 million megawatt-hours. That’s enough electricity to power 16.8 million homes for a year. That is enough electricity to power every home in California and Florida … together … for a year. In addition to electricity, data centers require substantial amounts of water to prevent servers from overheating. In 2014, U.S. data centers “drank” about 5.6 billion gallons of water. In 2023, they consumed 17.4 billion gallons. That’s enough water for one billion showers, three for each American. At first glance, “data center” gives off the notion of being modern and green. After some light research, however, you can find that they account for 0.5 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions. Half a percentage point seems nearly negligible, but 0.5% translates to 212 million metric tons of CO2, more than what is produced annually by a medium-sized industrialized country like the Netherlands. The Sierra Club, one of the oldest environmental protection organizations in the United States, published a report finding that by 2030, U.S. data centers will be outputting a carbon footprint as large as the entirety of Mexico’s, threatening to set progress on greenhouse gas emissions back by 15 years. While these findings would point to reconsidering the current data center approval process, the White House, prioritizing economic growth, has accelerated approval. A 2025 executive order directs federal agencies to fast-track environmental reviews, open up federal lands, and commit other federal resources to these projects. Unsurprisingly, many Americans would disagree with a data center free-for-all. Fifty-four percent of Americans view data centers as being bad for the environment. More tellingly, Gallup finds that seven in 10 Americans oppose data center construction in their communities. Americans oppose data center development when it comes to their doorstep. While data centers’ rising electricity demands, strong thirst, and behemoth carbon footprint hold their own weight, voters are voicing more concerns about data centers. From higher energy prices in areas in close proximity to data centers and noise pollution concerns to driving up the price of rural farmland and backlash over contaminated wastewater, Americans are tired of being forced to deal with the environmental and fiscal costs of an industry whose benefits are concentrated among big tech investors. Thus, data centers are becoming a hot-button issue in the 2026 midterms, situated among campaign issues such as the “economy,” “immigration,” and “crime.” While there are not clean-cut partisan trends regarding data centers, state-office candidates typically fall into one of two camps: regulation or moratorium. The more conservative approach, moratorium, focuses on a temporary pause or cap on data center development. In Massachusetts, for example, Governor Maura Healey has issued a data center moratorium requiring data center developers to receive local approval. Generally speaking, moratoriums commonly allow state governments to assess options, discuss with community groups, and ultimately make an informed decision. The more growth-oriented approach—regulation—emphasizes the economic competitiveness side of the equation but establishes guardrail regulations that data center developers must satisfy. Both camps acknowledge the various impacts of data centers but address them differently. While data centers have become a major flashpoint in gubernatorial and local elected office positions, they also manifest themselves through ballot measures, questions voters answer at the polls. There are 49 ballot measures regarding data centers this midterm cycle, and voters in 13 states will have the opportunity to influence their state’s data center policy. Measures consist of yes/no questions pertaining to approval, zoning, and prohibition. See if you will have the opportunity to vote directly on data centers here. While artificial intelligence and data centers undeniably bolster the United States’ competitive edge, their infrastructure is not free. There are environmental, financial, and social costs that have become increasingly difficult to ignore. For Boston College, students must consider the entire equation regarding data centers. That means balancing environmental impacts, energy affordability, and AI ambitions. While asking ChatGPT or Claude a question may not have a direct financial cost, it ultimately comes at an environmental cost that some bear more than others.
