artigo.texto: Estherville city council advances data center rules to public hearing ESTHERVILLE, Iowa — A proposed data center in Estherville is moving forward to a public hearing following discussions by city leaders over health and noise concerns. The Estherville City Council agreed to send the Planning and Zoning Commission’s draft rules to a public hearing on Nov. 16. City leaders revealed they are in discussions with two developers, though only one data center would be considered for the community. During the meeting, council members discussed potential noise and low-frequency impacts near an elementary school. Council Member at Large David Hovinga cited his own research on health risks, casting the lone vote against advancing the measure and urging Planning and Zoning to strengthen protections first. “There are issues of sickness, issues of cardiovascular health, mental health issues, low frequency issues, that can’t be mitigated by sound dampening walls and things like that,” Hovinga said. “If the technology is at a place where they can fix those things, then that’s wonderful. But, I would need to see that before I would be comfortable moving forward with a data center in Estherville.” Public input and informational meeting Following the public hearing, the ordinance can still be sent back to the Planning and Zoning Commission for revisions. City officials emphasized the importance of community feedback as the proposal moves forward. “I would encourage everyone to come out to share their thoughts with the other council members,” a council member said during the meeting. “I think all of us want to hear from the public. All of us want to know what the community and citizens of Estherville think about this proposed data center.” Residents will have multiple opportunities to learn more and provide input on the proposal: - On Thursday, Nov. 12, Path-One Data Centers will host an informational meeting at the American Legion in Estherville, where community members can ask questions about small-scale data centers. - On Monday, Nov. 16, at 5 p.m., the Estherville City Council will hold its first official public hearing regarding the potential project. The location for that meeting has not yet been announced. Want to get the latest news and weather from Siouxland’s News Source? artigo.texto: Households could get energy boost as Octopus explores new home batteries The collaboration will be between the energy provider and CATL and Ampace - Bookmark - CommentsGo to comments Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Join today Already a member? Log in Homeowners could be given a boost with their energy bills, with Octopus Energy teaming up with manufacturers to develop a new generation of home battery storage options. Battery storage typically works by allowing units to siphon in power and store it, chemically or by other means, when the cost of energy is low. Later, when usage price increases, that energy can be reintroduced to the home system to avoid using the higher-billed energy. In theory, as well as lowering bills, it can also reduce strain on the wider grid at key demand times once widely adopted. The ability to integrate home storage batteries with solar panels, for example, can give a home its own source of low-cost energy beyond just when the panels are functioning - like after dark - and the battery’s management system should be able to maximise the efficiency of the home’s energy use overall. Octopus already have plans to release the “Nook”: two battery storage options for bigger or smaller amounts, each of which can store between 2 and 10 kWh of energy. The latter is a little over a medium-sized house’s daily energy use, according to Ofgem figures. Now, through their agreement with zero-carbon new energy technology firm CATL and lithium-ion battery tech firm Ampace, Octopus Energy will look to develop new ranges of cutting-edge options, as they seek to increase the lifecycle of such systems and produce far more affordable home batteries. At its most efficient, a home battery system should be able to offload power back to the grid too, to help further cut household energy bills. As well as the Nook battery options, Octopus already offer other green energy solutions including heat pumps and EV chargers. Jason Zhu, president of energy storage at Ampace said: “The future of energy is not just about generating or storing more power, but about making energy smarter, more connected, and more accessible.” The advance of battery technology and intelligent energy management could “fundamentally reshape how energy is delivered and consumed,” he added. Greg Jackson, CEO of Octopus Energy Group, agreed that the partnership “will transform home energy storage.” “Together, we're building next-generation batteries where hardware and software work in complete harmony to slash energy bills and speed up the green energy transition,” he added. Raymond Ye, president of residential energy storage systems at Ampace, added: “Europe’s energy transition is creating growing demand for smarter and more flexible home energy solutions; with this partnership we see great potential to accelerate innovation and deliver greater value to the market.” Join our commenting forum Join thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their replies Comments

artigo.texto: Novo calendário alcança fornecedores de materiais, energia e combustíveis e prevê entrada do transporte rodoviário; veja os possíveis efeitos para o setor César Tizo - novembro 1, 2026 A produção de materiais usados nos carros, a cadeia de combustíveis e a operação de frotas estão entre as frentes alcançadas pelo novo calendário do mercado regulado de carbono no Brasil. Para o setor automotivo, a mudança começa pelos fornecedores: atividades como produção de aço, alumínio e vidro integram a primeira etapa de preparação, em 2027. O transporte rodoviário de passageiros e cargas terá seu primeiro ano até 2031. O cronograma foi definido pela Portaria SEMC/MF nº 3.199, publicada em 29 de outubro de 2026. A norma organiza a entrada gradual dos setores nas obrigações de mensuração, relato e verificação de emissões de gases de efeito estufa, conhecidas pela sigla MRV. Refino de petróleo e setor elétrico entram na segunda etapa, com preparação até 2029. A relação com o mercado de veículos ocorre tanto nos insumos industriais quanto nos serviços de transporte. O enquadramento dos operadores ainda depende de regulamentação específica: a portaria não inclui automaticamente todas as montadoras, fabricantes de autopeças, concessionárias ou transportadoras, nem permite calcular um aumento no preço dos carros. O cronograma alcança atividades presentes na cadeia de fornecimento de materiais para veículos, como siderurgia integrada, produção de alumínio e fabricação de vidro plano e de segurança. Também inclui determinados produtos químicos, entre eles eteno e negro de carbono, além da produção de petróleo e gás natural. O efeito direto das obrigações recairá sobre os operadores das fontes e instalações que forem efetivamente reguladas. Para as montadoras e fabricantes de componentes que compram esses materiais, o interesse está em acompanhar como seus fornecedores passarão a medir e apresentar as emissões associadas às atividades abrangidas. Como consequência possível, informações de emissões poderão ganhar peso nas decisões de compra de materiais e na avaliação de fornecedores. Essa é uma perspectiva para a cadeia industrial, e não uma exigência de seleção de fornecedores criada pela portaria. O ato não determina a substituição de aço por alumínio ou a adoção de um material específico nos carros. A distinção entre atividades industriais também importa. Usinas siderúrgicas integradas estão na etapa com início em 2027; as semi-integradas integram a fase seguinte, com primeiro ano até 2029. Portanto, nem mesmo todos os produtores de um material entram simultaneamente. A produção de petróleo e gás natural aparece na primeira etapa, enquanto o refino de petróleo fica na segunda. O setor elétrico também integra essa segunda fase, que contempla geração, transmissão e distribuição de energia. São atividades ligadas ao abastecimento dos veículos a combustão e à infraestrutura que atende os elétricos. O objeto da norma é organizar os dados de emissões dessas operações. Ela não altera a composição da gasolina ou do diesel nem estabelece uma nova tarifa de recarga. A repercussão econômica para cada cadeia dependerá das regras finais de cobertura, das metodologias e, posteriormente, do funcionamento do mercado de emissões. Para quem acompanha a descarbonização automotiva, a mudança reforça a importância de observar também a fabricação dos materiais e o fornecimento de energia e combustíveis. Entretanto, o cronograma do SBCE, por si só, não produz uma comparação completa de emissões entre um carro elétrico, um híbrido e um modelo a combustão. O transporte rodoviário de passageiros e de cargas integra a terceira etapa, junto dos transportes ferroviário e aquaviário. O primeiro ano dessa fase deverá começar até 2031. Essa referência marca a preparação do monitoramento, e não a entrega imediata de um inventário verificado por todas as empresas de transporte. Para uma transportadora ou operadora de ônibus, o ponto central será saber quais fontes móveis e operações estarão abrangidas e como suas emissões deverão ser mensuradas. A portaria prevê regulamentação específica para definir fontes, instalações e atividades reguladas, considerando as particularidades de cada setor. O número de caminhões ou ônibus da frota não determina, sozinho, o enquadramento. Também será necessário observar os patamares de emissões previstos em lei e as metodologias aplicáveis. A presença de um código da Classificação Nacional de Atividades Econômicas (CNAE) no anexo não submete automaticamente todas as atividades daquele código às obrigações. Outro detalhe relevante para empresas com operações diversificadas é que o anexo considera a atividade regulada exercida na instalação ou pelo conjunto de fontes móveis, mesmo quando corresponda a um CNAE secundário. Assim, olhar apenas a atividade principal do estabelecimento pode ser insuficiente. Ainda não há base para atribuir um valor de aumento a carros, combustíveis ou fretes em função dessa portaria. O calendário de monitoramento é uma etapa distinta das futuras regras de limitação e conciliação de emissões. Segundo o Ministério da Fazenda, a fase inicial não impõe limites de emissão ou custos de aquisição de cotas. O Plano Nacional de Alocação tem início previsto para 2030, com distribuição gratuita de cotas na largada. Essa previsão geral não antecipa a entrada de todos os setores, que segue escalonada. Como análise dos possíveis efeitos para o setor automotivo, as decisões futuras poderão influenciar investimentos em processos industriais, eficiência operacional e tecnologias de redução de emissões. A intensidade desses efeitos, os custos de adaptação e eventual repasse aos compradores dependerão do desenho final das regras e das respostas das empresas. Para o motorista particular, a portaria não cria cobrança pelo uso do automóvel nem uma obrigação individual de comprar créditos de carbono. artigo.texto: The European Investment Bank (EIB) will provide a loan of up to $90 million, guaranteed by the EU through the European Fund for Sustainable Development Plus (EFSD+), to finance the first phase of the Dandara solar photovoltaic (PV) and battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Egypt. Located in Qena Governorate, Phase 1 comprises a 569 MWp solar PV plant and an associated 100 MWh BESS. Dandara Solar Power S.A.E., a project company owned by Norwegian renewable energy developer Scatec ASA and acting as the lead developer, will develop, construct, operate, and maintain the project. The facility will supply renewable electricity to Misr Aluminium Company (EgyptAlum), under a long-term power purchase agreement (PPA). EgyptAlum’s payment obligations are supported by a guarantee from Egypt’s Ministry of Finance. The project is expected to generate around 1,500 GWh of electricity during its first year of operation. The EIB financing, provided through its development arm EIB Global, is backed by the EU, and will be arranged alongside the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and African Development Bank (AfDB) funds. Construction is expected to begin soon, with commercial operations scheduled to commence in April 2028.

artigo.texto: Daikin has introduced a new Coolant Distribution Unit (CDU) designed for high-density AI data center applications, with orders scheduled to open on November 1, 2027. The unit transfers thermal energy between the Facility Water System (FWS) and Technology Cooling System (TCS), supporting temperature management in environments with high thermal loads. The CDU range offers cooling capacities from 400 kW (approximately 1.36 million BTU/h) to 2.5 MW (approximately 8.53 million BTU/h) per unit. Up to ten CDUs can operate in parallel under centralized temperature and pressure control. Daikin also offers preassembled skid solutions integrating multiple units for larger installations, with configurations suitable for new projects and retrofits. For operational reliability, the CDU incorporates redundant pumps, duplicated temperature and pressure sensors, integrated leak detection and advanced alarm management. The hydraulic circuit uses AISI 316L stainless steel with grooved mechanical couplings instead of welded joints. Front-side service access and sliding rails for pump removal are designed to simplify maintenance and component replacement. Daikin’s proprietary controller coordinates multiple CDUs and adjusts TCS operating parameters using variable-speed pumps and flow, pressure and temperature measurements. A modulating valve with an equal-percentage control characteristic and high-speed actuator regulates heat transfer between the FWS and TCS circuits to control TCS outlet temperature. Alongside the CDU launch, Daikin is expanding its Intelligent Data Center Manager (iDCM) platform beyond chilled water plant control to cover equipment within the data hall. The platform supports centralized monitoring of CDUs, CRAHs, AHUs and Fan Wall systems, including real-time temperatures, equipment status and alarms. It also provides diagnostic functions and integration with existing Building Management Systems (BMS).

artigo.texto: A proposed Senate bill could generate $55 billion in transmission charges from data centers over 10 years if it becomes law. It would require large computing facilities to pay more for access to the electricity grid and the infrastructure needed to serve them. For data center developers, the proposal could raise the cost of grid-connected projects, influence where new campuses are built and change the economics of behind-the-meter generation. It could also make firm transmission service more expensive relative to arrangements in which operators accept power curtailments during grid stress. Developers could face greater pressure to demonstrate load flexibility. But shifting more costs to data centers addresses only part of the ratepayer problem. Utilities also need assurance that the large loads driving infrastructure investments will materialize, arrive on schedule and consume the electricity developers have promised. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to revise its transmission-pricing policy. Under the proposal, utilities would charge data centers for both their share of existing transmission infrastructure and incremental costs associated with serving their loads. Grid Strategies, a consulting firm that specializes in the power sector, estimated in a recently published white paper that the pricing changes would generate approximately $5.5 billion annually in transmission charges, compared with roughly $2 billion that data centers currently pay. The analysis projected a $35 billion increase over current arrangements across the decade. The projected $55 billion includes $35 billion in embedded transmission costs and $20 billion in incremental costs. Both categories support the grid, but the additional revenue could enable transmission construction that otherwise might not happen, said Rob Gramlich, president of Grid Strategies. PJM and MISO account for most projected charges Grid Strategies estimated that data centers in PJM's and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator's (MISO's) regions would account for approximately 82% of the projected $5.53 billion in annual charges. The analysis assigned about $2.31 billion in annual charges to PJM and $2.25 billion to MISO. It projects 13.4 gigawatts of new data center capacity in PJM and 16.7 GW in MISO. PJM's higher charges, despite its smaller projected pipeline, reflect the region's higher transmission rates, Gramlich said. Grid Strategies based its incremental transmission cost estimates largely on MISO data. The analysis includes 163 approved transmission projects representing approximately $11.4 billion in investment to connect 43.5 GW of large loads. Researchers calculated an average incremental cost per megawatt and applied it across the regions they studied. Grid Strategies estimated the projected revenue could support nearly 10,000 miles of new 765-kilovolt transmission lines over 10 years. That construction would depend on when and where data centers connect to the grid. The analysis excluded Texas' ERCOT market, where FERC doesn't traditionally regulate transmission service. Grid connections likely to remain attractive Higher transmission charges could make locations with available electrical capacity and predictable power-delivery timelines more attractive. Developers could also turn to behind-the-meter generation to reduce their reliance on utility-supplied electricity. Gramlich said he doesn't expect most data centers to abandon grid connections. Reliable power from an entirely off-grid system generally costs more and presents greater operational challenges, he said. He expects behind-the-meter generation to supplement utility service rather than replace it, potentially reducing the incremental transmission charges associated with a project. The $55 billion estimate assumes new data centers take firm transmission service. Developers that operate entirely off grid wouldn't generate those charges. Gramlich said that scenario is unlikely because data centers still derive substantial value from grid connections. Behind-the-meter generation also brings its own costs and dependencies, including fuel supplies, equipment, permitting and maintenance. Developers may reduce their transmission exposure while taking on other operational and financial risks, said Neil Osnato of Persistence Analytics Group. Utilities need proof demand will materialize Higher transmission charges won't prevent utilities from building infrastructure for data center projects that developers later delay, downsize or abandon. Before committing billions of dollars, utilities should require binding capacity commitments, financial security tied to their actual exposure and contractual protections against early termination, Osnato said. Developers should specify reserved megawatts, expected load ramps, enforceable milestones and consequences for delays or downsizing. Deposits and collateral should cover the costs a utility could fail to recover if a project falls through. Depending on the development, financial backing could include letters of credit, cash collateral or parent-company guarantees. Minimum-billing commitments and early-termination provisions can also protect other customers when actual consumption falls below projections, or a developer abandons a project. Utilities should tie major spending decisions to verified milestones, including site control, permits, financing commitments and executed power arrangements. A material change in a project's load forecast, commissioning schedule or financing should trigger a fresh review of the utility's exposure and remaining construction commitments. Some existing utility tariffs and agreements already contain versions of these protections, Osnato said. artigo.texto: Diante do desafio gigantesco de construir cada vez mais data centers, os EUA estão criando o "Tesla das escavadeiras" Os Estados Unidos estão em uma corrida para erguer centros de dados para os próximos anos, mas precisam de trabalhadores; Uma startup chamada Bedrock Robotics conta com escavadeiras equipadas com IA física para suprir a demanda por mão de obra A startup norte-americana Bedrock Robotics captou US$ 600 milhões em uma rodada Série C com apoio de investidores como a Nvidia. Fundada em 2024, a empresa desenvolve inteligência artificial para operar maquinários pesados de construção de forma autônoma. O aporte visa expandir essa tecnologia para mais veículos e fortalecer suas operações e equipe executiva, buscando suprir a crescente demanda por infraestrutura e data centers em meio aos desafios de escassez de mão de obra. Escavar um terreno para uma rodovia, uma fábrica ou um data center parece um trabalho seguro para um ser humano, já que ainda se depende de uma pessoa no comando do equipamento. No entanto, uma startup de São Francisco quer mudar as regras do jogo: ela pretende colocar uma inteligência artificial no comando desse maquinário pesado. A empresa chama-se Bedrock Robotics, acaba de captar 600 milhões de dólares (cerca de R$ 3,2 bilhões) e sua proposta surge como resposta para um mundo com a pirâmide demográfica invertida. Em resumo No dia 26 de outubro, a Bedrock anunciou uma rodada de financiamento Série C de 600 milhões de dólares. Fundada em 2024 como uma empresa de maquinário de construção autônomo, ela conta com investidores como Valor Equity, 8VC e — como não poderia deixar de ser — a Nvidia. O investimento não veio diretamente da Nvidia, mas sim por meio de seu braço de capital de risco; ainda assim, era previsível que a Nvidia aportasse recursos em uma empresa de IA aplicada ao mundo físico que apresenta um potencial considerável. A ideia da companhia é utilizar o montante captado para expandir sua tecnologia a mais máquinas, fortalecendo tanto o trabalho em campo quanto a estrutura comercial e operacional. Parte desse capital foi destinada à contratação de uma vice-presidente de operações — com passagens anteriores pela Amazon e pela Uber — e de um executivo que liderou a área jurídica da divisão de condução autônoma da Uber. artigo.texto: AI’s Expansion Hits the Limits of Local Power Power shortages and local opposition are delaying data center projects, making AI expansion harder, costlier, and more dependent on scarce grid access. Grid connection delays and local resistance are extending development timelines as operators race to add AI-related capacity, though analysts differ on whether those constraints are already limiting AI development. Data center projects are taking longer to reach construction as developers struggle to secure electricity connections and local approval, complicating expansion plans intended to meet growing AI demand. Projects that broke ground between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026 waited an average of just over two years after being announced, according to GlobalData. That compares with about 18 months for projects that started construction between early 2020 and mid-2025. Martina Raveni, senior analyst on GlobalData’s Strategic Intelligence team, told Data Center Knowledge that grid access and public opposition are the two biggest constraints. “The grid is the hardest to fix because it is structural: new grid infrastructure takes five to 15 years to build, while a data center takes one to three,” she said. GlobalData forecasts annual data center electricity consumption will rise from 590 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 1,520 TWh in 2030. Meeting that demand will require developers to address power, permitting, and construction bottlenecks that investment alone cannot quickly overcome. Grid Access Determines What Can Move Forward A project’s other development challenges can become secondary when there is no available electricity connection. Luis Fernandes, IDC senior research manager for cloud and data centers within enterprise infrastructure, told Data Center Knowledge that discussions with developers, designers, and large operators consistently point to grid access as the dominant obstacle. “It is by a long shot the biggest cause for delay in projects, to the point that we haven't seen delays in projects for any other reason, given that the lack of grid connection halts the entire exercise,” Fernandes said. Raveni said developers in Europe’s main data center hubs can wait up to a decade for a connection. Skilled labor shortages add another constraint, with insufficient electricians and other trades pushing some delivery schedules back by around a year. Delays are expected to be more common than cancellations, with Fernandes suggesting some stalled projects could change hands as other operators seek opportunities to acquire and complete them. “Speed in construction [comes at] a premium, and a paused construction site is still bleeding cash,” he said. Raveni cautioned that it remains too early to quantify eventual cancellations, although projects in grid-constrained locations or facing strong local opposition are particularly exposed. Community Pushback Makes Timelines Harder to Predict Community resistance can disrupt projects even when developers have customers and funding. Concerns about electricity bills, water consumption, noise, and land use can affect permitting and construction schedules. Ya-Han Brownlee-Chen, DP World’s vice president of data center strategy in the Americas, told Data Center Knowledge that local acceptance is becoming one of the sector’s most significant barriers to development. “There's a growing tension between the demand for AI infrastructure and communities' willingness to accommodate the physical facilities required to support it,” she said. That tension complicates site selection and makes construction timelines harder to predict. Brownlee-Chen also pointed to rising costs for land, equipment, and other resources, with owners seeking premiums for sites that could accommodate data centers. Those pressures can affect whether a delayed project remains financially viable. She said outcomes will depend on developers’ ability to resolve local objections, obtain infrastructure, and execute within a workable schedule, rather than on demand alone. On-Site Power Can Reduce Delays but Add New Risks Developers seeking alternatives to delayed grid connections can face additional environmental and permitting challenges. Raveni said on-site gas generation can bridge a power gap, but redundancy requirements may necessitate generating capacity substantially greater than the data center’s normal needs. Air pollution and water concerns can then intensify the same local resistance developers are trying to resolve. “The real risk is that a temporary fix becomes permanent and pushes emissions up just as grids are decarbonizing,” she explained. Power and cooling decisions also need to account for their combined demands on local resources. Joe Johnston, executive vice president and president of applied water at Xylem, said the infrastructure challenges need to be addressed together. “Some of the biggest barriers to data center growth are tied to physical infrastructure, particularly power availability, water resources, and cooling capacity,” Johnston told Data Center Knowledge. Johnston called for more efficient and resilient water and cooling infrastructure to support expansion while reducing pressure on community resources. GlobalData, for example, identified closed-loop cooling, water stewardship, and diversified power supplies among operators’ responses, although it describes progress as uneven. The Effect on AI Remains Unclear Longer development schedules raise questions about when infrastructure constraints will limit AI deployment, beyond increasing the cost of new capacity. Raveni said access restrictions are already emerging, citing cloud providers rationing capacity, customers needing to reserve further ahead, and usage caps affecting large AI companies. Fernandes, however, offered a more measured conclusion. “In terms of compute capacity, there is no hard evidence that we can point to [showing] that being a limitation to AI development,” he said. artigo.texto: The Scoop Wall Street is finding out just how expensive things can get in a matter of months. For a look at how much investorsâ jitters are reshaping AI-related debt financing, look to QTS, an investment-grade Blackstone-backed data center operator, that just six months ago was weighing a deal to borrow $800 million at a rate of 1.7 percentage points over Treasurys. That deal never went through. And now, that same debt is being shopped to investors at 2.2 to 2.50 points above comparable Treasury yields for a nearly identical offering, according to people familiar with the matter. Both offerings involve the same company, same blue-chip Wall Street backing, and the same collateral â just for a lot more money. Blackstone declined to comment.Â As debt jitters spread and borrowing gets more expensive, itâs a lesson in just how much sentiment has shifted in such a short amount of time. Know More On Friday, the Financial Times reported that Blackstone told investors it no longer expected Anthropic to get an investment-grade credit rating immediately after its IPO, a reversal of previous guidance about the frontier lab, which is raising billions of dollars to finance its AI buildout. And investment-grade SpaceXâs $40 billion debt launch saw its pricing widen out â reaching an expected 8.75% yield for the riskier portion of its recent debt deal, up from where pricing was discussed just a week earlier, Semafor reported.

artigo.texto: By Terry Murry on Monday, November 2nd, 2026 in Columbia Basin News Columbia Basin Top Stories HERMISTON – Gov. Tina Kotek’s moratorium on permits for data centers is scheduled to end on July 1, 2027. That impacts data centers in the process of opening in Umatilla, but it doesn’t impact Hermiston. However, if the moratorium becomes permanent. Hermiston and Umatilla County will be hit hard. “If an actual moratorium were to take place, we estimate just from data centers operating in Hermiston itself, it would probably end up costing taxpayers in Umatilla County somewhere in the range of a half billion dollars of lost potential revenue over the next 20 years,” Hermiston Assistant City Manager Mark Morgan said. The city of Umatilla has declared an emergency and is in talks with representatives in the governor’s office. Umatilla County is holding a special meeting at 9 a.m. Wednesday to decide about hiring a Portland law firm. The firm, Tonkon Torp LLP, specializes in business law. The agenda does not state specifically it is about the data center moratorium, but both Umatilla and Hermiston officials have said they have support from Umatilla County. “We agree with the city of Umatilla and Umatilla County that the actions taken by the governor are illegal,” Morgan said. “We’ve met with governor’s representatives and we’re working in concert with the city of Umatilla and Umatilla County to examine all of our legal remedies.” The legal contract mentioned in the Umatilla County agenda stated the help from the law firm is not to exceed $250,000. The special meeting is at 9 a.m. Wednesday in Room 130 of the Umatilla County Courthouse in Pendleton. Editor’s note: Morgan made his comments on the KUMA Coffee Break on Nov. 2 and talks about other issues in Hermiston. The podcast is available at Nov. 2 | Hermiston Asst. artigo.texto: O Google ligou um chip de inteligência artificial em órbita, enviou uma instrução do solo e recebeu de volta um haicai. Sundar Pichai, presidente-executivo da empresa, anunciou o resultado em 30 de outubro de 2026, segundo o site francês Numerama. A máquina é uma TPU Trillium, o mesmo tipo de processador que o Google instala em seus data centers, e estava a bordo de um satélite do projeto Suncatcher. A resposta saiu do modelo aberto Gemma, rodando na própria placa, em cinco, sete e cinco sílabas no original. O feito é modesto em computação e grande em sinal. O Google ensaia tirar do chão a conta de energia que a inteligência artificial passou a cobrar. O que subiu em 1º de outubro O satélite partiu em 1º de outubro de 2026 numa missão de carona da SpaceX, a Transporter-18, que decolou da base de Vandenberg, na Califórnia. Batizado de MVP, o produto mínimo viável do projeto foi construído com a Planet, operadora de satélites de observação da Terra. O equipamento tem o tamanho de uma geladeira, carrega quatro TPUs Trillium e cerca de um quilowatt de painéis solares. O voo queria saber se chips desenhados para salas climatizadas sobrevivem à vibração do lançamento, ao vácuo, aos extremos de temperatura e à radiação. A resposta veio com sotaque de propaganda. “Bola azul abaixo, os dados correm em graça silenciosa, a luz das estrelas alimenta meu núcleo” (no original em inglês divulgado por Sundar Pichai: “Blue marble below, Data streams in silent grace, Starlight feeds my core”), escreveu o modelo. A conta de energia saiu do chão A ideia do Suncatcher foi revelada em novembro de 2025 e nasceu de um diagnóstico que o setor repete. A inteligência artificial já esbarra menos nos processadores e mais na eletricidade, no resfriamento e no terreno disponível. A Agência Internacional de Energia calculou em abril de 2025 que os data centers consumiram cerca de 415 terawatts-hora em 2024, perto de 1,5% da eletricidade do mundo. A projeção da agência, no relatório sobre energia e inteligência artificial, é mais que o dobro até 2030. No Google, a fatura aparece nos próprios relatórios ambientais. As emissões da empresa cresceram cerca de metade desde 2019, quando ela prometeu zerá-las até 2030, e a companhia atribui boa parte do avanço à expansão da IA. A aposta do Suncatcher é geométrica. Numa órbita heliossíncrona chamada amanhecer-entardecer, a cerca de 650 quilômetros de altitude, o satélite acompanha permanentemente a fronteira entre o dia e a noite, e o Google afirma que ali os painéis rendem até oito vezes mais que no solo. O laser de 2027 e o tamanho real da aposta O estudo técnico do Project Suncatcher publicado pelo Google Research em novembro de 2025 descreve o desenho completo. Grupos de 81 satélites voando a algumas centenas de metros uns dos outros, ligados por laser, com 1,6 terabit por segundo medido em bancada. Num acelerador de partículas, as TPUs Trillium não apresentaram falha dura até 15 krad de dose de prótons, bem acima do previsto para uma missão de cinco anos. O exame decisivo ficou para 2027, quando dois satélites terão de trocar dados por laser em formação cerrada. A concorrência já mostrou que o caminho tem chão. A Starcloud, apoiada pela Nvidia, rodou o Gemma num processador H100 em órbita em dezembro de 2025 e chegou a treinar o nanoGPT, rede aberta criada por Andrej Karpathy, sobre a obra completa de Shakespeare. Pichai disse em entrevista à Fox News em dezembro de 2025 que, dentro de uma década, construir data centers no espaço pareceria mais normal. A pergunta que o anúncio deixa aberta não é técnica. Energia solar captada em órbita e convertida em gigawatts de computação privada transforma uma faixa do espaço próximo em infraestrutura de uma empresa só. O Tratado do Espaço Sideral de 1967, assinado pelo Brasil, proíbe que qualquer país se aproprie de áreas do espaço, mas não define como se reparte o uso comercial de uma órbita. Posições orbitais e faixas de radiofrequência passam pela União Internacional de Telecomunicações, e as conexões por laser não seguem a mesma coordenação. A órbita baixa já é um condomínio disputado. A constelação Starlink, da SpaceX, soma milhares de satélites e é operada pela mesma empresa que levou o equipamento do Google ao espaço, o que deixa o projeto dependente de um concorrente direto. No Brasil, a pressão chega pelo chão. O país atraiu data centers por ter uma das matrizes elétricas mais renováveis entre as grandes economias, e cada novo galpão de servidores disputa energia, água para resfriamento e território com as redes locais e com os usos já instalados. O movimento do Google não reduz essa disputa. Se der certo, ele sobe a demanda e deixa intacta a pergunta sobre quem paga a conta energética aqui embaixo. O teste de formação cerrada em 2027 decide se o Suncatcher vira infraestrutura. Até lá, o haicai prova apenas que um chip de data center acordou no vácuo e respondeu. Se o laser falhar, terá sido o que sempre foi, um poema muito curto.

artigo.texto: Segundo a mídia chinesa , um projeto de armazenamento de energia em ar liquefeito (LAES) de 60 megawatts (MW) no noroeste da China foi oficialmente conectado à rede elétrica e começou a gerar eletricidade. Isso é considerado um avanço significativo na engenharia e comercialização da tecnologia LAES. Localizado em Golmud, província de Qinghai, no noroeste da China, o projeto foi investido e construído pelo China Green Development Investment Group (CGDG). Segundo a empresa, trata-se atualmente da maior instalação de LAES (energia eletroquímica de ar frio) do mundo . O projeto representa um marco significativo nos esforços da China para desenvolver tecnologias de armazenamento de energia que apoiem seu sistema elétrico em meio à crescente proporção de energia renovável. Segundo a China Green Development Investment Corporation, a instalação tem uma capacidade instalada total de 60 MW e deverá absorver aproximadamente 600.000 quilowatts-hora (kWh) de energia limpa por dia. O projeto deverá gerar cerca de 180 milhões de kWh de eletricidade anualmente, o suficiente para atender às necessidades anuais de eletricidade de aproximadamente 30.000 residências. O projeto de armazenamento de energia por ar liquefeito (LEA, na sigla em inglês) é uma tecnologia emergente de armazenamento de energia a longo prazo. Essa tecnologia utiliza eletricidade para comprimir e resfriar o ar até que ele se transforme em estado líquido durante períodos de baixa demanda de eletricidade. Quando há necessidade de eletricidade, o ar liquefeito é aquecido e expandido para acionar uma turbina, gerando assim eletricidade. Essa tecnologia é considerada superior ao armazenamento de baterias tradicional em termos de escala, tempo de armazenamento e vida útil. O Grupo de Investimento em Desenvolvimento Verde da China afirmou que o projeto Golmud utiliza um processo de liquefação criogênica com congelamento profundo a -194 graus Celsius. Os equipamentos utilizados no projeto são totalmente nacionais, com 100% de seus componentes fabricados na China. O grupo também afirmou que o projeto aplica tecnologias para as quais detém direitos de propriedade intelectual independentes. Segundo a China Green Development Investment Corporation, este projeto é atualmente líder mundial em capacidade e volume de armazenamento no campo de projetos de armazenamento de energia em ar liquefeito. Espera-se que este projeto apoie a absorção de energia renovável, reduza a carga de pico (corte de pico) para usinas termelétricas e utilize a energia de resfriamento do gás natural liquefeito (GNL). Especialistas acreditam que a operação do projeto representa mais um passo em frente para a China na construção de um novo tipo de sistema de energia, no qual a energia renovável desempenha um papel de liderança no fornecimento. Este projeto preencheu muitas lacunas nas aplicações de engenharia em larga escala de projetos de armazenamento de energia em ar liquefeito em todo o mundo, ao mesmo tempo que forneceu um modelo escalável para aplicações de tecnologia de armazenamento de longo prazo em larga escala, contribuindo para a formação de uma cadeia industrial completa – um passo significativo em direção às metas duplas de carbono da China. Segundo um relatório da Administração Nacional de Energia da China, até o final de 2025, a capacidade instalada de novos sistemas de armazenamento de energia no país atingirá 136 gigawatts (GW), um aumento de 84% em relação ao ano anterior e 40 vezes a capacidade no final de 2020.

artigo.texto: Data centers impulsionam o crescimento dos gastos com construção não residencial nos EUA Os gastos com construção não residencial nos EUA subiram na comparação mensal em 8 das 16 subcategorias, segundo a Associated Builders and Contractors. Os gastos privados com construção não residencial aumentaram 1,1% em setembro, enquanto os gastos públicos com construção não residencial recuaram 0,1%. O economista-chefe da ABC, Anirban Basu, afirmou que os gastos com construção não residencial cresceram pelo sexto mês consecutivo em setembro. Ele observou que os data centers responderam por quase todo o ganho e que, excluindo os data centers e a categoria de energia, estreitamente relacionada, os gastos não residenciais caíram no mês. Basu descreveu o ritmo de expansão dos data centers como cada vez mais difícil de contextualizar. Os gastos nessa categoria subiram mais 8,6% em setembro e cresceram a uma taxa anualizada de 217% desde maio. Para os próximos meses, Basu disse que o impulso permanecerá estreitamente concentrado nos segmentos ligados à inteligência artificial, citando os recentes aumentos no rendimento dos títulos do Tesouro e a escalada contínua dos preços de materiais. Ele acrescentou que, embora os empreiteiros sigam ocupados no agregado, segundo o Indicador de Carteira de Obras da ABC, as condições atuais de mercado continuarão a favorecer os empreiteiros de maior porte, que têm probabilidade muito maior de estar envolvidos em projetos de data centers e de energia.

artigo.texto: The nationwide crunch for power — mostly driven by massive data centers — is so severe, even the board members of a local utility company are weighing the benefits of a temporary pause on their development. Members of Salt River Project’s district board consulted utility staff Monday about their options for curtailing new data center interconnection agreements, amid concerns that residential customers may end up subsidizing the AI data center boom’s growing energy bill. Data centers’ forecasted energy demands are unprecedented. In an exchange between two SRP board members and the utility’s chief legal executive, Michael O’Connor, it was revealed that more than half of SRP’s planned capacity could go directly to new data centers. “I’ve heard these figures in separate presentations,” said Krista O’Brien, a director-at-large, “that we’re planning to grow by 4,700 megawatts by 2035, and then I’ve also heard that 3,000 of those megawatts are data centers.” SRP’s chief legal executive Michael O’Connor said that estimation seemed plausible. Another board member responded, saying those figures match what they heard at a September Power Committee meeting. That added capacity will add millions in new infrastructure, operations and maintenance costs for SRP. Ken Clark, who represents SRP’s sixth division, says that’s a concern, because the utility has dealt with relatively flat energy growth for the last 20 years. “I find it very hard to believe that we are not shifting costs to other customer classes just by the fact that we have to build new plants that we would not otherwise have had to build, right?” said Clark. But O’Connor says it’s unlikely SRP can pass a data center moratorium, because state law says the utility must serve any eligible customer. That law is provided as a check on SRP’s legal monopoly on much of the Phoenix metro, including parts of Mesa, Tempe and Chandler. “You have this service territory,” O’Connor said. “No one else can come in and serve here. In exchange, you actually have to serve those people coming in.” O’Connor says exceptions can be made if there are safety concerns, to which director at-large Kathy L. Mohr-Almeida asked, “there’s reports that data centers — you know, it’s likely that artificial intelligence has a 10% to 25% opportunity to eliminate humanity. Is that not something that is a safety concern?” O’Connor said he didn’t disagree that reports like that exist, but he says, SRP has a specific role it must fulfill within state law. “And as you’re going to see, because we have exclusive service territory and an obligation to serve, some of those questions are really left for the legislature, or the communities themselves — not SRP,” O’Connor said. John Tucker, SRP’s director of financial strategy, addressed concerns from Kennedy and other board members that SRP is shifting the costs of serving new data centers onto other customers. Tucker explained two new tariffs board members approved for large energy customers last year. He says SRP collects the estimated costs associated with meeting 80% of a data center’s peak energy demand up front, an industry-leading level for developer collateral. Collaterals are collected by utility companies in large energy agreements, usually at much lower rates, to ensure operational costs can still be met if the business shuts down and the utility loses that customer. Tucker says SRP also collects collateral on data centers’ associated transmission costs. “We’ve been sending out some very large bills to some of these data centers in terms of the infrastructure costs,” Tucker said. “These are nine-figure bills that we’re sending to people.” Between these two cost streams, Tucker says data centers are paying more than it costs the utility to serve them. There was little public discussion on the impact to SRP’s water supplies before leaders went into executive session on the item. - An Arizona Court of Appeals panel still won’t let Arizona Public Service levy an extra fee on customers who have solar panels on their homes. - Outside groups from across the political spectrum have poured nearly $2 million into Arizona’s Corporation Commission race, which will decide which two candidates secure seats on the state’s top utility regulator next year. - AI data centers in the Phoenix area use relatively little water on site, but they use lots of electricity, which takes a lot of water to generate. - The agency, which delivers water to the Phoenix and Tucson areas, joins Nevada and Arizona in its legal claims against the harms of water cutbacks from the shrinking river. - Amid ongoing rate cases for two of the state’s largest electric providers, Arizona’s top utility regulators have spent time embroiled in an internal employment dispute that has spilled into public view.

artigo.texto: Localizado em Golmud, província de Qinghai, no noroeste da China, o projeto foi investido e construído pelo China Green Development Investment Group (CGDG). Segundo a empresa, trata-se atualmente da maior instalação de LAES (energia eletroquímica de ar frio) do mundo . A China alcança um avanço significativo no armazenamento de energia utilizando ar liquefeito. Segundo a mídia chinesa, um projeto de armazenamento de energia em ar liquefeito (LAES) de 60 megawatts (MW) no noroeste da China foi oficialmente conectado à rede elétrica e começou a gerar eletricidade. Isso é considerado um avanço significativo na engenharia e comercialização da tecnologia LAES. O projeto representa um marco significativo nos esforços da China para desenvolver tecnologias de armazenamento de energia que apoiem seu sistema elétrico em meio à crescente proporção de energia renovável. Segundo a CGDG, a instalação tem uma capacidade instalada total de 60 MW, com previsão de absorver aproximadamente 600.000 kWh de energia limpa por dia. Espera-se que o projeto gere cerca de 180 milhões de kWh de eletricidade anualmente, o suficiente para atender às necessidades de consumo anual de aproximadamente 30.000 residências. O LAES é uma tecnologia emergente de armazenamento de energia a longo prazo. Ele utiliza eletricidade para comprimir e resfriar o ar até que ele se liquefique durante períodos de baixa demanda de eletricidade. Quando a eletricidade é necessária, o ar liquefeito é aquecido e expandido para acionar uma turbina, gerando assim eletricidade. Essa tecnologia é considerada superior ao armazenamento de energia em baterias tradicionais em termos de escala, tempo de armazenamento e vida útil. A CGDG afirmou que o projeto Golmud utiliza um processo de liquefação criogênica a -194 graus Celsius. Os equipamentos utilizados no projeto são totalmente nacionais, com 100% de seus componentes fabricados na China. A empresa também afirmou que o projeto aplica tecnologias para as quais detém direitos de propriedade intelectual independentes. Segundo a CGDG, este projeto é atualmente líder mundial em capacidade e volume de armazenamento no setor de armazenamento de energia de baixa agregação (LAES). Espera-se que o projeto apoie a absorção de energia renovável, alivie a demanda de pico das usinas termelétricas e utilize a energia de resfriamento do gás natural liquefeito (GNL). Especialistas acreditam que a operação do projeto representa um avanço significativo para a China na construção de um novo tipo de sistema de energia, onde a energia renovável desempenha um papel fundamental no fornecimento. Este projeto preenche muitas lacunas em aplicações de armazenamento de energia de longa duração em larga escala globalmente e fornece um modelo escalável para aplicações de tecnologia de armazenamento de energia de longo prazo em larga escala, contribuindo para a formação de uma cadeia industrial completa – um passo crucial para alcançar as metas de carbono da China. Segundo um relatório da Administração Nacional de Energia da China, até o final de 2025, a capacidade instalada de novos sistemas de armazenamento de energia no país atingirá 136 gigawatts (GW), um aumento de 84% em relação ao ano anterior e 40 vezes maior do que no final de 2020.

artigo.texto: Marvell Technology's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday. "You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here." Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release. Marvell shares slumped 13% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank nearly 19%. But both stocks have been huge winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with Marvell more than doubling in the past year, prior to Monday's sell-off, and Lumentum quadrupling over that stretch. Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models. "We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said. Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028. Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending. This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology. Marvell's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies. In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers. "This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them." Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone. CORRECTION: This story has been updated to reflect that Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston described the deal as an 'enormous' opportunity. A previous version of this story incorrectly cited the Marvell CEO.

(TSXV: ETL) (FSE: OW3) (OTCQX: EEMMF), “E3”, “E3 Lithium” or the “Company,” a leader in Canadian lithium development has entered into a collaborative research agreement (the “Project”) between E3, the National Research Council of Canada (“NRC”), and major South Korean battery manufacturer POSCO through its subsidiary POSCO AMERICA CORPORATION (“POSCO”), among other input contributors, whereby E3 will be the exclusive lithium carbonate provider to the Project to support the development of a “made in Canada” lithium-manganese-rich (LMR) cathode. E3 Lithium is receiving CA$98,798 in funding from the NRC’s Critical Battery Materials Initiative, for this Project. E3’s lithium carbonate contributions will support the Project in producing lithium-manganese-rich (LMR) cathode active materials (CAM) from Canadian feedstocks. E3, along with Manganese X Energy Corp. and NiVolt Technologies Inc., will produce the necessary chemical precursors, while the NRC will carry out downstream synthesis into cathode material and testing in coin cells. POSCO will provide industrial validation of the CAM material, according to their internal benchmark metrics. POSCO is one of the world’s leading battery materials producers, with integrated capabilities targeting one million tonnes of cathode capacity by 2030, currently supplying major global automakers and battery manufacturers. “E3 Lithium is working alongside a group of Canadian peers developing cathode for the future of North American batteries," said Chris Doornbos, President and CEO of E3 Lithium. artigo.texto: It is the largest BESS by storage capacity (MWh) in Europe and a significant step forward in the delivery of infrastructure supporting the UK’s transition to a cleaner, more resilient energy system. Located adjacent to National Grid’s Hams Hall substation, the project will help balance variable electricity demand and intermittent renewable generation, supporting greater integration of renewable energy while strengthening grid resilience and energy security. The project reached commercial operation just 20 days after energisation. From commissioning and testing to operational readiness, BW ESS worked closely with partners including Sungrow, Energy-IO, National Grid and NESO. Achieving this milestone safely and efficiently reflects the engineering expertise, rigorous preparation and close coordination behind Hams Hall, as well as the technical capability and commitment of everyone involved. Hams Hall’s capacity will increase to 400 MW/1,424 MWh following completion of its second phase. At full capacity, the project will be capable of supporting the electricity needs of around 1.3 million homes for up to 3.5 hours, which is approximately equivalent to the number of households across Greater Manchester. “The start of commercial operations at Hams Hall is a landmark moment for BW ESS and a significant addition to Europe’s energy infrastructure” said Erik Strømsø, CEO and Co-Founder of BW ESS. “The project was built and commissioned on budget and ahead of schedule, which is a remarkable achievement for a system of this scale and complexity and a testament to the dedication and expertise of our team, and the commitment and collaboration of our partners.” Long-term revenues for the project are underpinned by a 10-year floor and optimisation agreement with EDF and financing was recently secured from lenders OCBC, Rabobank and Societe Generale. Hams Hall forms part of BW ESS’ 2.6 GWh Ardenham portfolio, co-owned with leading energy and decarbonisation investor AIP Management. Its entry into commercial operations expands BW ESS’ operating presence in the UK, alongside the 331 MWh Bramley BESS in Hampshire. artigo.texto: Blackstone, one of the largest private equity firms in the world, officially changed the name of its dedicated energy investment fund to include the phrase “energy transition” in 2022, having already ceased investing in oil and gas production five years earlier. The pivot toward a new energy future has not diminished interest in the fund. In mid-October, Blackstone announced that the fund pulled in $8.7 billion in investor money this year, reportedly turning away an additional $3 billion to stay under its maximum investment cap. Blackstone’s is one of several energy transition funds at private equity firms that have consistently grown over the past decade. That growth has continued even as general climate-oriented investment has fallen over the last few years. Colloquially, “energy transition” refers to the shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy that is necessary to limit the worst impacts of climate change. But on Wall Street, the term can mean something a bit different. Some transition funds — including Blackstone’s — see opportunities for profit in natural gas, data centers, and rising electricity costs. “I know a lot of the investors out there do consider gas a transition fuel,” said Ryan Loughead, a senior associate and former climate solutions analyst for BloombergNEF, an energy research firm. Private equity funds take new investor money every few years, and then use it to buy existing companies, maximize their profits, and then sell them, returning the money from the sale to investors. Unlike publicly traded companies, whose stocks are available for anyone to buy, private equity firms typically only take investments from large organizations, like pension funds, or very wealthy individuals, and they have faced criticism for prioritizing returns at the expense of workers and the environment. The transition to renewable energy has been a booming business for private equity firms. “Transition funds” in private equity have raked in $178 billion between 2021 and the beginning of 2026, triple the amount raised by comparable funds dedicated to fossil fuels and general energy, according to Loughead’s research. They’ve maintained their popularity even as other forms of climate-related investments have flagged in the United States, with climate-related venture capital on track to suffer its worst year this decade. (While private equity funds buy out established companies, venture capital funds make smaller investments in startups.) These shifts have coincided with changes in federal policy, as well as the overall economy. The Biden administration’s signature climate law once spurred innovation in new technologies, but Republicans in Congress repealed most of that legislation last year. Meanwhile, the tech industry’s data center buildout is creating surging demand for electricity and drawing trillions of dollars from investors. In the financial industry, the energy transition has grown into a sophisticated economic trend with established players and markets, said Dan Cohn, an energy finance analyst with the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a think tank focused on the energy transition. Private equity funds don’t typically demonstrate investor interest in a budding industry so much as a view that the industry is becoming economically important. “Investors are sensing oncoming scarcity [of electricity] and are positioning themselves accordingly,” Cohn said. “That speaks to both the moment of rising electricity demand, but also the maturity of clean energy technologies.” But while these funds seek to capitalize on high demand for electricity, they don’t all show a clear commitment to reducing emissions. Blackstone’s fund is explicit in its view that methane gas, a fossil fuel, is an essential component of the energy transition. The fund no longer invests in oil and gas fields, but it does invest in natural gas plants. When Blackstone rebranded the fund in 2022, the fund’s director, David Foley, explained why natural gas plants were still on the table. “A lot of the capital invested in the energy transition is going into simple renewable power generation assets like solar and wind,” he told an industry publication. “While this is important, just adding renewables to the grid doesn’t necessarily mean you can shut down and remove existing sources of power, such as coal and gas.” This year, the fund announced investments in six companies, including a natural gas plant operator and a data center cooling technology company, alongside a company focused on renewable energy development and some transmission and grid technology companies. Blackstone did not reply to a request for comment. Meanwhile, the private equity firm Brookfield governs its transition funds partly through an explicit commitment to decarbonization and emissions reductions. The company has said it can invest in natural gas in cases where it replaces dirtier fossil fuels, but Brookfield has also drawn criticism for describing gas expansion as part of the energy transition. Similar funds in Europe, like Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ Energy Transition Fund, are far more focused on clean energy sources like green hydrogen, with little emphasis on natural gas. “‘Energy transition’ is a flexible term,” Cohn said. “And I’m unsurprised to see either the gas or electrical equipment and data center-related companies in some of these funds. That is perfectly consistent with how I know some investors think about the energy transition.” BlackRock, another private equity giant unrelated to Blackstone, explicitly defines “transition” investing as something different from “sustainable” investing: “not all sustainable strategies are transition, and not all transition strategies are sustainable,” its website reads. That partial overlap could complicate investors’ claims about how sustainable their portfolios are. artigo.texto: Recently, the groundbreaking ceremony for the industrialisation base project of hydrogen energy application for new-type power and energy storage battery systems in plateau and extreme cold conditions was held in the Changchun Economic and Technological Development Zone, marking the project’s entry into the substantive construction phase. This project is a key demonstration initiative within the regional new energy layout, focused on addressing the practical challenges of deploying energy storage and hydrogen technologies in extreme cold environments. Total floor area: 31,523 m². Yuedong Steel Structure is responsible for the general construction contracting. The project is located in the Changchun Economic and Technological Development Zone.Total floor area: 31,523.12 m².The plan includes the construction of Plant 1, Plant 2, and auxiliary guardhouse facilities. The project has a clear positioning, specifically targeting special operating conditions such as plateaus and extreme cold, to advance the industrialisation of ESS battery systems and hydrogen-related technologies. Such scenarios have long been plagued by equipment performance degradation and operational stability challenges caused by low temperatures, representing an area where China’s new energy industry has yet to achieve a breakthrough. Jilin Province Yuedong Steel Structure Group Co., Ltd. is undertaking the general construction contracting for this project, responsible for the overall implementation of civil works and supporting facilities. On the day of the groundbreaking, representatives from the construction, design, supervision, and contracting parties attended the event to witness the project’s commencement period. Building a technology transfer platform for cold-region applications and addressing supply gaps in new energy equipment Industrial projects in extreme cold regions impose higher requirements on construction techniques, material selection, and scheduling. The project team will advance each construction period in accordance with regulatory standards, with particular attention to structural details, pipeline reservations, and equipment foundations suited to extreme cold conditions, striving to deliver a safe, stable, quality-compliant engineering platform with demonstrative impact. Northeast China and extensive plateau regions across the country are rich in wind and solar power resources, but low temperatures constrain the large-scale deployment of energy storage and hydrogen equipment. Many energy storage and hydrogen products perform well under normal temperature conditions, yet their reliability and service life are significantly affected after prolonged exposure to low temperatures. Once this industrialisation base is completed, it will establish a corresponding technology transfer platform, facilitating the transition of energy storage and hydrogen technologies adapted to extreme cold conditions from the laboratory to mass production. After the base becomes operational, it will be capable of undertaking trial production, pilot testing, and batch manufacturing of related products, thereby addressing the supply gap in new energy equipment for cold regions. Leveraging Changchun’s industrial supporting advantages, the base can also integrate with provincial wind and solar power development and hydrogen demonstration application projects, forming a closed loop encompassing technology R&D, equipment manufacturing, and scenario validation. The maturation of energy storage and hydrogen technologies for cold regions can also extend outward, providing product support for new energy projects in other plateau and extreme cold areas across China.

artigo.texto: O primeiro teste de inteligência artificial do Google em órbita terminou de um jeito inesperado: com um poema enviado do espaço para a Terra. A empresa anunciou em 30 de outubro de 2026 que o satélite experimental do Project Suncatcher executou o modelo Gemma 4 em um de seus chips de IA e transmitiu a resposta para uma estação terrestre. É um passo importante para a ideia de construir data centers no espaço, alimentados por energia solar. Mas há uma diferença entre a demonstração e essa ambição: por enquanto, o Google tem um protótipo que realiza tarefas curtas de processamento, não um serviço comercial capaz de substituir os enormes centros de dados em funcionamento na Terra. O que a inteligência artificial do Google escreveu no espaço? Depois de semanas verificando os sistemas do satélite, os engenheiros enviaram uma instrução da Terra pedindo ao Gemma 4 que produzisse um haicai, forma curta de poema de origem japonesa, sobre estar no espaço. O texto foi gerado pelo computador a bordo e recebido durante a passagem da nave pela região de Svalbard, na Noruega. Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨ O poema descreve a Terra como uma esfera azul abaixo do satélite, imagina fluxos de dados em silêncio e associa a luz das estrelas à energia que alimenta o computador. A resposta pode parecer simples, mas é a prova de que o equipamento recebeu uma instrução, executou um modelo de linguagem em órbita e devolveu o resultado. O Google chama esse resultado de seu primeiro marco de “Hello World”, expressão usada em programação para indicar que um sistema conseguiu realizar uma operação inicial. Segundo a empresa, foi a primeira resposta de IA obtida a partir de uma TPU de classe data center em órbita. Isso não equivale a dizer que foi a primeira IA da história a funcionar no espaço. Depois do haicai, os pesquisadores fizeram novos testes com poemas de outro formato e solicitações sobre o estado dos equipamentos do satélite. A confirmação foi publicada no blog oficial do Google em 30 de outubro. Como funciona o satélite do Project Suncatcher? O protótipo foi desenvolvido em parceria com a Planet Labs e lançado em 1º de outubro de 2026 a bordo de um foguete Falcon 9, da SpaceX, na missão Transporter-18. O equipamento leva quatro TPUs, sigla para Tensor Processing Units, os processadores especializados que o Google também utiliza para acelerar modelos de inteligência artificial em seus servidores terrestres. O modelo usado no teste foi o Gemma 4, da família de modelos abertos do Google DeepMind. Ele não deve ser confundido com o Gemini, serviço de IA oferecido aos usuários. A demonstração foi de inferência: o sistema utilizou um modelo já preparado para produzir uma resposta, em vez de treinar um novo modelo do zero. Segundo informações publicadas pelo TechCrunch, o satélite gera até cerca de 1 kW de potência elétrica, mas dispõe de energia e capacidade de dissipar calor suficientes para acionar apenas uma TPU por vez, durante aproximadamente 20 minutos. Portanto, ter quatro chips a bordo não significa que todos possam trabalhar simultaneamente. Essa restrição explica parte da complexidade da missão. Um computador potente produz calor mesmo no espaço, e o vácuo não permite resfriá-lo por circulação de ar como acontece na Terra. O calor precisa ser conduzido para superfícies capazes de irradiá-lo. A nave também está sujeita à radiação espacial, que pode alterar informações armazenadas e comprometer os cálculos. Por que o Google quer construir data centers no espaço? A ideia do Project Suncatcher é investigar se conjuntos de satélites, abastecidos por painéis solares e conectados entre si, poderão executar trabalhos de IA em grande escala. Em determinadas órbitas, o acesso frequente à luz solar poderia oferecer uma fonte de energia atraente para uma indústria que precisa de cada vez mais eletricidade. O desafio é transformar essa vantagem potencial em uma infraestrutura confiável. Não basta colocar chips em órbita. Será necessário demonstrar resfriamento eficiente, resistência a anos de radiação, comunicação rápida entre satélites, manutenção viável e custos de lançamento competitivos. Isso também ajuda a entender o debate sobre os gastos bilionários da indústria com servidores e aceleradores de IA. O Overdrive já explicou por que os investimentos em inteligência artificial levantam preocupações financeiras. Levar parte desse processamento ao espaço seria uma aposta ainda mais longa, não uma solução imediata para o preço da computação. Qual é o próximo passo do Google? Com a primeira resposta recebida, a equipe continuará avaliando como as TPUs se comportam sob estresse térmico e exposição à radiação em condições reais de voo. Esses resultados são fundamentais para descobrir se componentes utilizados em data centers podem operar de forma confiável fora da Terra. O próximo objetivo anunciado é colocar dois satélites interconectados em órbita em 2027. A missão deverá explorar a comunicação por enlaces ópticos, que utilizam luz para transmitir dados entre naves. Essa conexão é essencial para a proposta de fazer diversos computadores espaciais trabalharem de maneira coordenada. Até lá, o poema é um resultado técnico, não a inauguração de uma nuvem de IA espacial para consumidores. Para quem quer experimentar modelos semelhantes sem depender integralmente da nuvem, o Overdrive reúne opções de inteligência artificial que podem rodar no computador e um guia para executar IA local sem internet. Perguntas rápidas O Google já tem um data center funcionando no espaço? O Google tem um protótipo em órbita que executou uma tarefa de inteligência artificial e enviou o resultado à Terra. Ainda não existe, nessa missão, um data center comercial operando continuamente como os servidores terrestres. Qual IA escreveu o poema enviado pelo satélite? artigo.texto: The Petersburg Borough Assembly will discuss a temporary moratorium on permits for data centers this afternoon. They’ll also discuss moving training materials for the fire department and vote on a tentative collective bargaining agreement with the borough employees’ union. The proposed data center moratorium would last through September 2027. It would prevent the borough from issuing permits to new data centers, or expansions to data centers that would exceed Petersburg’s grid capacity, rely on generators, or use uncontained cooling systems. While there are currently no data centers in Petersburg, they have been a topic of regular discussion at assembly meetings. A local developer has shown interest in building one in town. During the moratorium, the borough would study the impacts of data centers and look into regulation options. Petersburg isn’t the only community looking into regulating data centers. Sitka’s Planning Commission has recommended banning data centers in their community. This ordinance is in its first reading. If approved, it will need to be considered two more times to become law. Also today, the borough assembly will discuss the steps and costs required to move fire department training materials to the fire hall. The department’s training materials used to be housed at Scow Bay, but upcoming site work for a major harbor project now requires their equipment to be removed and relocated. Additionally, the assembly will decide whether or not to approve a tentative agreement between the borough and the employees’ union, the Petersburg Municipal Employees Association. The last agreement between the borough and the union expired at the end of June. The union has not yet voted on the proposal. In addition to approving the tentative agreement, the assembly will take a final vote on budget changes to fund cost-of-living adjustments and longevity pay increases included in the proposal. At the previous assembly meeting, Molly Taiber, a negotiator for the union, requested the borough delay approving budget adjustments until the union could vote. You can find the full Borough Assembly agenda here. The assembly meets at noon, and KFSK will broadcast that meeting live.
