artigo.texto: A sprawling data center and energy complex proposal east of Casper is not dead, according to the property owner, despite Prometheus Hyperscale pulling out of the project last Wednesday. Falls Ranch, a limited partnership owned by Texas billionaire Russell Gordy, announced last week that “work will continue without delay.” “The work by the community and local leaders has helped lay the foundation for a project with the potential to position Natrona County as a leader in the growing data center industry, building on Wyoming’s energy resources, skilled workforce and experience supporting major industrial development, and should not be wasted,” Falls Ranch stated in a press release after Prometheus’ announcement. Though it was not involved in initial development plans, according to the company, the groundwork has been laid for it to see the project to fruition. “We anticipate that with this change, the project should continue forward on a more efficient track, including community and business collaborations,” Falls Ranch representative Robert Hand said. “This has always been a Wyoming project, but today it represents something even greater: an opportunity for Natrona County to shape its own economic future.” More details will be revealed in the near future, Hand added. Prometheus announced its departure from the project Wednesday. Originally, the $500 million, 1,250-megawatt complex was to be sited on Falls Ranch property spanning Natrona and Converse counties north of Interstate 25. In its latest configuration, it would sit entirely in Natrona County, south of the interstate. The move opened the door for developers to bypass a state-level Industrial Siting Council review and permitting process to instead empower Natrona County commissioners to vet the project. If green lit locally, however, the endeavor would still be subject to review from several state and federal agencies. That process had not advanced beyond initial discussions before Prometheus exited the project. artigo.texto: Wave of BESS augmentation financing expected in a few years The topic of battery energy storage systems (BESS) augmentation was a key one at the Battery Asset Management Summit UK & Ireland 2026 last month, held in London by our publisher Solar Media, part of Informa Connect. There may be a wave of BESS augmentation-linked financings in a few years’ time in the UK, a speaker at a recent Solar Media event said. The topic of battery energy storage systems (BESS) augmentation was a key one at the Battery Asset Management Summit UK & Ireland 2026 last month, held in London by our publisher Solar Media, part of Informa Connect. Speakers from various UK BESS owner-operators discussed the topic on stage at the two-day event. Here are the key takeaways, in a shortened write-up of a piece that originally appeared on our sister site Energy-Storage.news as part of its subscription-based ESN Premium offering. Build assumptions, track the market Javier Arrue, investment director at BW ESS, said you need some assumptions around augmentation built into your model from the start, that you need to track the market but also that BESS supply developments were making life a bit easier for augmentation planning. “It’s also interesting to see battery manufacturers now defaulting to 4-hour systems. That supports delaying augmentation as you’re adding extra capacity to your batteries, which is a benefit,” he said. Expect a wave of augmentation financings in the medium term Pablo Zalvide, structured finance and M&A lead for UK BESS at Fotowatio Renewable Ventures (FRV), expects a wave of financings for augmentation in a few years’ time. “In a few years, there will be a wave of projects needing refinancing. Even where debt sizing was based on a 15-year warranty duration, most financing in place today is structured as mini-perm, around seven years. That means a wave of projects will come up for refinancing, potentially with outdated duration assumptions by that point. I’d expect a good portion of those projects to pursue augmentation at the point of refinancing,” he said. LTSAs Ricardo Folgado, managing partner for owner-operator TagEnergy, essentially said that factoring augmentation into long-term service agreements (LTSAs) is a challenge and so, for multiple reasons, the company tends to stay away from such contracts. Folgado said: “You want to sell the assets, you want to recontract, you want to augment, you want to do something, and you’re locked in, so they’re not ideal. That’s probably an obvious thing to say, but my advice would probably be to not enter into a long-term contract.” Have a good energy management system Gore Street Capital’s senior asset manager, David Harris, said having a good EMS is key. “I think when it comes to state of health (SOH), the point where it really matters is when you start to augment your sites because then you have a site that’s in two halves where you might be able to dispatch at full power one half of your site for a full hour, but then your more degraded older part of the site might only last 50 minutes,” he explained. “So that’s where you really need to have a good EMS in place that can telemeter the right values and discharge each unit at different rates, perhaps, but maintain a declared level for that full hour, or where it can.” Augmentation risk is under-priced currently Harris’ colleague, project development manager Michael Darzi, highlighted augmentation and repowering as a key risk that is currently being under-priced. “Let’s say we might go with one technology provider when we build our system, but as technology evolves, maybe that supplier will no longer be relevant in the market, or maybe we like someone else’s technology. How does that play with the existing technology? How do the EMS and the PPC controller also have an impact?” he asked. Read more about:

artigo.texto: Energy storage emerged as a defining driver of lithium demand in 2026, with the rapid expansion of battery energy stationary storage (BESS) creating new requirements for supply. As global datacentre buildout adds another source of demand, understanding shifting lithium supply requirements for the next phase of energy storage growth is essential for future planning. Join Benchmark's end-of-year webinar to hear in-depth analysis of BESS lithium requirements, the outlook for emerging energy storage markets, and the impact of lithium prices on BESS and alternative technology uptake. This session will cover: - How much lithium the storage boom will require, including how many new mines BESS demand alone could support and the additional demand from datacentre expansion. - How the supply landscape changed in 2026, including new material entering the market and shifts in the lithium cost curve. - What price is needed to incentivise the next wave of supply, and where lithium inventory levels stand heading into 2027. artigo.texto: MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sungrow, a globally leading PV inverter and energy storage system provider, announced the Australian debut of its all-in-one residential energy storage system, PowerHarbour, at All-Energy Australia 2026. The platform responds to Australia's booming home battery market, with accelerating uptake driven by the federal government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program. Built around Sungrow's "Triple W" value proposition — Win More, Waste Less, Work Faster — PowerHarbour combines intelligent energy management, flexible storage and simplified installation in an integrated solution. It aims to simplify energy management for Australian households, whether installing a new solar-plus-storage system or upgrading an existing setup. Integrated EV Charging: Empowering the EV and V2X Era Australia's growing EV market is also reshaping household energy needs. According to the Electric Vehicle Council, battery electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles accounted for 34.5% of new vehicle sales in September 2026, highlighting the increasing relevance of home charging. Responding to this shift, the PowerHarbour Pro range introduces integrated EV charging in selected configurations*, bringing the inverter, energy management system and charging hardware together within a compact power core. Designed with future V2X applications in mind, it reflects Sungrow's approach to connecting home energy management with electric mobility. High Flexibility & Scalability: Tailored for Australia's Large Residential Loads For many Australian households, solar generation peaks during the day, with Solar Sharer offering free midday electricity in some regions; household electricity demand often surges in the evening. To address this mismatch, PowerHarbour incorporates AI-driven energy management that analyses weather forecasts, solar predictions, consumption patterns, and electricity pricing to optimize energy scheduling—helping homeowners, especially those in larger properties with higher electricity demands, make the most of the energy they generate. Heavy-Duty Protection: Built for Extreme Australian Climates From coastal salt mist to harsh inland conditions, PowerHarbour is engineered for high durability across Australia's environmental extremes: Optimized Installation: Streamlined for Local Clean Energy Contractors For Australian installers, PowerHarbour's integrated architecture streamlines new installations and existing system upgrades. Its stackable battery modules and plug-and-play design help reduce installation complexity and additional wiring requirements. "Australia's transition towards more connected home energy systems presents a significant opportunity for the industry. We believe the next step is not simply adding more features, but making solar, storage and energy management work together more effectively. With PowerHarbour, our focus is on bringing these technologies together in a practical, flexible solution that can support different household needs as the market evolves." said Scott Su, Technical Service Director, Sungrow Australia. As Australia's residential energy landscape evolves, Sungrow aims to support smarter home energy systems through PowerHarbour and close collaboration with local distributors and installers, helping households meet changing energy needs and move toward a more sustainable energy future.

artigo.texto: Sila Nanotechnologies Leading pure-play silicon anode developer According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Silicon Anode Additives market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global silicon anode additives market is at a pivotal inflection point as battery makers accelerate the shift toward higher-energy-density lithium-ion cells. Silicon's theoretical capacity, roughly ten times that of graphite, makes it the most promising pathway to extend electric vehicle range and enable faster charging. As of 2026, the market is transitioning from pilot-scale validation to early commercial adoption, with silicon-carbon composites and silicon oxide variants leading integration into graphite-dominant anode formulations. The competitive landscape remains fragmented, spanning nanotechnology specialists and established chemical conglomerates, and is increasingly shaped by strategic partnerships across the value chain. This report provides a data-driven outlook for 2026–2035, covering product types, end-use segments, regional dynamics, and the technical and economic factors that will determine adoption speed. Demand is concentrated in Asia-Pacific battery manufacturing hubs, while North America and Europe are building domestic capacity in response to electrification policy and supply-chain resilience goals. Key uncertainties include silicon's volume expansion during cycling, first-cycle efficiency losses, and the pace at which cost reductions and recycling infrastructure mature. The baseline scenario for the world silicon anode additives market anticipates accelerating adoption through 2035, supported by automaker commitments to higher-range and fast-charging electric vehicles. In the near term, silicon additives will remain a minority component blended into graphite anodes, with silicon-carbon composites and silicon oxide materials capturing the largest share of commercial demand due to their balance of capacity and cycle life. As cell designs and electrolyte systems mature, silicon loading levels are expected to rise, lifting additive consumption per kilowatt-hour. The market index is projected to reach 420 by 2035 (2025 = 100), equivalent to a 15.4% CAGR, reflecting expansion from a relatively small base. Price premiums over graphite are expected to narrow as production scales and yields improve, though high-purity silicon nanoparticle capacity remains a constraint. Regionally, Asia-Pacific will retain the dominant share, led by China, Japan, and South Korea, while North America and Europe add capacity amid local-content requirements. Downside risks include slower EV demand growth, technical setbacks in cycle life, and competition from alternative anode chemistries. Upside potential stems from energy storage systems and fast-charging consumer electronics, which could diversify demand beyond automotive. Electric vehicle batteries are the primary growth engine for silicon anode additives. Automakers are demanding higher energy density to extend range and reduce battery pack size, and silicon additives enable incremental capacity gains within existing graphite-dominant cell designs. Through 2035, adoption will shift from low-silicon blends in premium vehicles to higher loadings across mass-market models as cycle-life and cost challenges are mitigated. Demand-side indicators include EV production volumes, average battery pack size, silicon content per kilowatt-hour, and the share of fast-charging-capable models. The mechanism is straightforward: each percentage point increase in silicon loading raises additive consumption per cell, and growing EV output multiplies that effect. Silicon-carbon composites and silicon oxide are expected to dominate this segment, with suppliers qualifying materials through multi-year cell testing cycles. Current trend: Rapid adoption, rising silicon loading. artigo.texto: The hotbed issue striking statewide for local communities and Tennessee state leaders is AI data centers. On Oct. 27, Gubernatorial candidates faced off at the Tennessee Press Association’s hosted forum. Democratic nominee and Memphis City Councilmember Jerri Green and Independent candidates David Hatley and Lauren Pinkston attended the event. Candidates discussed their response to local communities imposing moratoriums on future data center expansions — an issue that currently faces MTSU’s own Rutherford County. Rutherford County Commission unanimously recommended a 12-month moratorium Oct. 12 for a new Rutherford County data center development, pausing its advances and moving the proposal closer to county officials’ consideration. Set for Nov. 3, the Rutherford County Public Works and Planning Committee will discuss “a resolution establishing a one-year moratorium on the acceptance and processing of any land use applications for data centers,” per their meeting agenda. Whichever candidate secures Governor in this election will decide how this issue will be carried out in Tennessee communities. Candidate response Memphis journalist and co-forum moderator Otis Stanford asked candidates, “What specifically would be your policies, as valid, for state government oversight of these data centers?” Given two minutes each for a response, all three candidates agreed to placing limitations on data center advancements but with differing approaches. Hatley said state leaders owe it to citizens to protect them and make sure the data centers are the ones paying for property taxes, power, water and other utilities. The Independent also echoed data centers should have limitations on where they can be placed and how loud they can be. “If they want to come to Tennessee, they’re gonna play by our rules. We have to have these guardrails,” Hatley said. Once data centers can abide by legislation, Hatley said, then counties have the opportunity to vote if they want moratoriums or allow advancements. Green said she’s been against data centers for years and is currently fighting for a moratorium on the Memphis City Council. Green said the next step is to take this statewide before there is “human harm.” “We’re talking about our air and our water. There is nothing more vital to our life, much less the livelihoods of the people whose jobs will be taken by AI,” Green said. Pinkston also calls for a statewide moratorium on data centers, due to technology “outpacing our ability to legislate it.” “The last thing that I want to see is someone in the middle class, in the working class, have to foot the bill for the expansion of the utility systems, and of the water systems that are going to be required to actually keep these businesses up and running in Tennessee,” Pinkston said. Republican candidate and current Sen. Marsha Blackburn did not accept the invitation to TPA’s forum, but she has shared publicly that communities should be able to decide if they want data centers. Blackburn said communities have the right to decline center advancements while some other county mayors are actively recruiting data centers, according to WSMV 4. “There are county mayors that are saying we’ve got excess capacity when it comes to water and utilities and yes, we want them. We’ve got space for them. And they are actively trying to recruit them because they want the jobs,” Blackburn said to WSMV 4. Instead, Blackburn proposes her support for a rate payer protection plan that would let citizens know their water utility and electric power rates are “not going to go up with the advent of any kind of data center” and that the “data center is going to pay for that cost.” Other moratoriums placed this year and public outcry In August, Metro Nashville voted to impose a moratorium on data center advancements at its location next to the Nashville Zoo. The temporary moratorium pauses permit approvals until after Dec. 1, after Nashville Zoo claimed that the data center would cause detrimental harm to its animals, conservation efforts and community. “While this is meaningful progress, our work isn’t over. We remain committed to ensuring the proposed data center is not built adjacent to Nashville Zoo,” according to the zoo’s website. Memphis’ one-year moratorium recently failed to pass Oct. 20, but instead city council members reached for a substitute ordinance that halts data center construction for 135 days. After Tennessee elects its new governor, Tennesseans will have a clear path on how state government oversight will tackle data center advancements and public discourse. Election Day is Nov. 3. artigo.texto: Alpena County approves data center moratorium resolution Encourages local governments to enact ordinances Trending ALPENA -- Alpena County Board of Commissioners approved a resolution encouraging local units of government to enact ordinances, restricting the development of data centers in Northeast Michigan. According to County Administrator Jesse Osmer, the commissioners had been approached by community members regarding a data center moratorium. Osmer said that the county doesn't have much say in a moratorium, rather the City of Alpena and townships have to set their own ordinances. "Speaking with the majority of you I found that most of you were opposed (to data centers)," he said. Osmer added that the county can only encourage local units of government to take certain stances when it comes to data centers and moratoriums. "We ourselves cannot put much into place as far as any type of ordinances or anything like that," he said. Osmer explained that the resolution encourages local units of government, townships and the City of Alpena, to create systems that would allow for full transparency in the event that a data center approaches a municipality in the area. "I don't know of any data centers coming to the area, but basically putting on a pause and putting that framework into place in the coming months," Osmer said. In September, Osmer explained that townships enforce their own ordinances, planning development, zoning, et cetera. In the case of a data center, it would be up to the local unit of government to set procedures. If a data center company was looking at county land to develop, the county and company would have to comply with whichever municipality it falls under. He added that in the case of county owned property or in a situation where county property would have to be rezoned, then the county would have an advisory role only though the coordinating zoning committee. “Local cities, villages, and townships actually have the jurisdiction over planning zoning, site plan reviews, approvals, code enforcement related to data centers and their affiliated uses,” Osmer said. “In accordance with their adopted plans, ordinances and procedures, the county does not have jurisdiction over planning development or approval for those data centers.” He explained that the county can draft a “nice letter” making recommendations to local municipalities. “Because it's not really an ordinance or anything. It's a nice letter, basically, to the municipality, it asks, ‘Please refrain from any action that would bring those facilities into our area anytime soon,'" he said. The Alpena County resolution states that local units of government should adopt a moratorium on the planning, construction, permitting, or expansion of any data center. It also states that in the event that a proposed data center comes to the area, a comprehensive study is done to ensure the local ecosystem is protected from potential pollution and/or damage. "It is in the best interest of Alpena County residents that any data center development occur within a clear and comprehensive regulatory framework that protects public resources, ensures transparency, and prevents unintended financial or environmental consequences," the resolution stated. The adopted resolution defines a data center as a specialized facility that houses computing systems and stores large volumes of data. The resolution also notes the rapid growth of cloud storage and artificial intelligence (AI) across the country which places an increased demand on data centers real estate. The resolution also encourages transparency and public disclosure regarding data center projects, including the following considerations: - The source of electrical power for the facility; - The anticipated water usage of the facility and protective measures; - How electric utilities will meet the increased energy demands; - Contractual protections, minimum usage requirements, or exit provisions; - Measures to ensure environmental compliance, equitable cost allocation, and meaningful community benefit. Kayla Wikaryasz can be reached at 989-358-5688 or kwikaryasz@TheAlpenaNews.com.

artigo.texto: Nvidia in Talks to Guarantee Debt for Nscale’s $44.6B Anthropic Data Center Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions of dollars in debt financing for AI cloud provider Nscale’s planned Anthropic data center in West Virginia, The Information reported, with Bloomberg later confirming. Anthropic has signed a $44.6 billion contract for the campus’s first 460-megawatt building, which will use Nvidia’s Vera Rubin chips, and the two are discussing a second deal of roughly $45 billion. Under the proposed residual value guarantee, Nvidia would step in if Nscale defaulted on construction payments, temporarily take over the site and help find a new buyer and tenant. Nvidia’s past support for cloud providers has mostly covered leases and chip purchases rather than construction. It has extended around $170 billion in investments and credit support to neoclouds and major customers, including $1 billion to Nscale in September. The stakes are high for Nscale, which is seeking a public listing at up to $35 billion. It had about 25,000 advanced AI chips running in August against plans for nearly 500,000, its West Virginia site has caused flooding of nearby homes, and Microsoft recently withdrew from a planned site in England. The talks come as neocloud shares slide and Anthropic faces questions over financing its expansion, with Blackstone reportedly warning it may receive a junk credit rating after its IPO.

artigo.texto: Newswise — Binghamton University is a member of a new national consortium to accelerate the transition of energy storage innovations from discovery to domestic manufacturing. The new Battery Manufacturing (BattMan) Accelerator, led by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL), will bring together national laboratories, universities, and industry partners to address critical barriers in scaling next-generation battery technologies. Jie Xiao, a Binghamton University alumna, serves as accelerator director. “Breakthroughs in battery science must be matched by our ability to manufacture them at scale,” said Jie, the Boeing Martin Professor of Mechanical Engineering at the University of Washington and a Battelle Fellow at PNNL. “This effort brings together the tools, data, and partnerships needed to design manufacturable solutions from the start and accelerate their transition into industry.” The BattMan Accelerator will bridge the gap between discovery and manufacturing while establishing comprehensive manufacturing systems with super intelligence that integrate materials development, process design, and production in a seamless manner. Nobel laureate M. Stanley Whittingham, SUNY distinguished professor of chemistry, will serve as the lead investigator from Binghamton. He noted that the accelerator’s goals align closely with efforts of the Binghamton-led battery ecosystem that includes New Energy New York and the NSF Energy Storage Engine in Upstate New York. “Incorporating super intelligence into both research and manufacturing allows us to move from trial-and-error to predictive design,” Whittngham said. “This capability is key to accelerating innovation while ensuring technologies can be produced reliably and affordably at scale.” Whittingham said he expects close interactions between the New York efforts and BattMan. Binghamton is one of five university partners; the others are the University of Washington, University of Alabama, Arizona State University, and the University of Michigan. Argonne and Oak Ridge National Laboratories are also partners. The BattMan Accelerator aligns with the DOE’s Genesis vision to integrate super intelligence, materials science, and advanced manufacturing into a coordinated, data-driven innovation ecosystem. The initiative seeks to lower manufacturing costs, speed up development from lab to scale, and boost U.S. leadership in energy storage manufacturing through scientific innovation. About Binghamton University Binghamton University is a nationally ranked public research university and one of four university centers in the State University of New York (SUNY) system. Founded in 1946 and located in Vestal, N.Y., Binghamton is an R1 research institution, tackling complex challenges and driving innovation in areas that shape our world – from next-generation energy storage to responsible AI. Binghamton enrolls more than 18,000 students in 130+ majors across six schools, providing clear pathways for undergraduate students to future careers, supporting graduate students as they advance boundaries of innovation and discovery, and building partnerships that serve the public good from Binghamton to the rest of the world. artigo.texto: O sul da Malásia, em áreas que antes abrigavam plantações de óleo de palma e abacaxi, testemunha a rápida expansão das ambições tecnológicas globais da China. Guindastes e canteiros de obras se multiplicam em dezenas de hectares onde empresas constroem enormes complexos para atender companhias de tecnologia. A estratégia da neutralidade Nesses novos centros de dados, operam alguns dos chips de inteligência artificial mais avançados fabricados pela Nvidia. Embora essas peças tenham exportação proibida para o território chinês pelas regras dos Estados Unidos, as restrições geralmente não impedem que empresas como a ByteDance acessem os mesmos semicondutores em instalações situadas fora da China. Essa distinção impulsionou o país de 35 milhões de habitantes no boom tecnológico global. Motivadas por terrenos baratos, eletricidade acessível e conexão com cabos submarinos, corporações estrangeiras despejam bilhões de dólares na região. O estado de Johor tornou-se o epicentro desse movimento, acumulando dezenas de projetos aprovados ou em construção. “É algo impressionante e difícil até de imaginar”, afirmou Steven Tan, CEO da Pro3c, empresa taiwanesa que fabrica componentes ópticos usados nos chips da Nvidia. “Todo mundo está vindo para cá.” Gigantes dos Estados Unidos, a exemplo de Microsoft, Google e Oracle, investem pesado no território malaio para atender clientes asiáticos. Simultaneamente, o local virou um centro de processamento para marcas chinesas como Tencent e Alibaba, posicionando infraestruturas rivais praticamente lado a lado. “Este é o único lugar do mundo onde estamos vendo isso acontecer”, afirmou Lee Ting Han, integrante do governo de Johor envolvido na aprovação dos projetos. “O que torna a Malásia tão especial para essa onda da IA é justamente sua posição neutra e não alinhada.” O avanço chinês e as brechas regulatórias O movimento começou em 2021, impulsionado por restrições energéticas em Singapura. A DayOne, ligada a uma das maiores operadoras de data centers chinesas, liderou a chegada de companhias daquele país à região, transformando até mesmo campos de golfe em complexos tecnológicos. A expansão coincidiu com o endurecimento dos controles comerciais americanos, mas a captação de recursos internacionais permitiu que a empresa mantivesse fortes laços com Pequim. Autoridades dos Estados Unidos monitoram de perto o papel do Sudeste Asiático nessa dinâmica. Relatórios internos apontam que a capacidade computacional disponível para empresas chinesas em países da região rivaliza com a da China continental. Críticos apontam que as políticas americanas deixaram lacunas significativas. “Nada disso é ilegal”, disse Jimmy Goodrich, pesquisador da Universidade da Califórnia em San Diego e ex-executivo do setor de semicondutores. “É uma enorme lacuna nos controles de exportação que ninguém corrigiu. Essas brechas dão à China acesso a capacidade computacional gigantesca e espaço para alcançar os concorrentes na corrida pela IA.” Desafios locais e regulação O ritmo acelerado gerou alertas internos. O governo malaio passou a adotar exigências mais rígidas, dificultando novas aprovações ao cobrar fontes independentes de água e energia. Apesar disso, os empreendimentos já licenciados seguem transformando a economia e a paisagem local, alimentados pelas próprias rivalidades internacionais que marcam a tecnologia moderna. “Só quando a situação fica complicada é que temos trabalho para fazer”, afirmou Eric Yong, corretor imobiliário e desenvolvedor do setor na região.

artigo.texto: Chemist who transformed energy storage nabs Canada’s top science prize University of Waterloo chemist Linda Nazar is 2026 winner of $1M Herzberg medal When Linda Nazar learned she would receive Canada’s most prestigious scientific award, she could hardly believe it. “I felt quite honestly both humbled and inspired,” the University of Waterloo chemist told Quirks & Quarks. “It’s a real honour and I’m thrilled and deeply appreciative of receiving this and frankly I was surprised.” But the award might not come as a surprise to anyone familiar with her track record. Nazar has been collecting honours throughout her career. She’s a fellow of the Royal Society of Canada, the Royal Society (U.K.) and was made an Officer of the Order of Canada in 2015 for her contributions to battery research. On November 4, she’ll add another to the collection: the $1-million Gerhard Herzberg Canada Gold Medal, the highest honour awarded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC). The medal was one of 26 prizes announced by the federal agency on Thursday. It recognizes Nazar’s pioneering work developing next-generation batteries, with discoveries that have helped advance the design of safer, more efficient batteries for electric vehicles, energy storage for power grids and beyond. Awarded annually, the medal celebrates researchers “whose work has had a transformative impact on their field,” according to a statement from NSERC. “Through visionary leadership, industry collaboration and mentorship, Dr. Linda Nazar has built a globally influential research enterprise at the intersection of chemistry, materials science and engineering,” said NSERC President Professor Alejandro Adem in the statement. “We celebrate her remarkable contributions and the profound influence she continues to have on science and the research community.” Those contributions, her counterparts say, have helped tackle one of the biggest challenges in the transition to renewable energy: developing batteries that can store more power, last longer, cost less and operate safely. Michael Pope, an associate professor at the University of Waterloo who co-directs the university’s Ontario Battery and Electrochemistry Research Centre alongside Nazar, says her cutting-edge research and “pioneering discoveries have advanced our fundamental understanding of battery chemistry.” “[Her discoveries have] led to the development of entirely new battery materials and technologies,” Pope said in a statement to CBC. “Having worked closely with Linda, I have witnessed first-hand her extraordinary passion for science, unwavering dedication to discovery and genuine love of research, making this recognition incredibly well deserved.” How Nazar got here Nazar's path into battery research wasn't necessarily part of some big grand plan. In fact, it began, she says, with a side quest on Friday afternoons. After earning a bachelor's degree in chemistry from the University of British Columbia in 1978, and a PhD from the University of Toronto six years later, Nazar went on to complete a postdoctoral fellowship at Exxon Research Labs in Annandale, N.J. At the time, she says the lab was among the first working to develop rechargeable lithium-ion batteries. As a side project, Nazar says she would head into the lab every Friday to run battery experiments. “It was just a great opportunity to kind of have some fun on a Friday afternoon,” she said. That side project would soon help spark a career at the forefront of battery innovation. By the early 2000s, Nazar's research was helping advance the understanding of lithium iron phosphate — a material that has since become widely used in rechargeable batteries, including those powering electric vehicles and laptops. An EV charging station is seen in Montreal on Friday, Feb. 20. Nazar's research has contributed to developments that could one day allow electric cars to travel farther on a single charge. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press) According to Ontario's Universities, Nazar's research has contributed to developments that could one day allow electric cars to travel farther on a single charge. Ultimately, Nazar says what excites her most isn't just the science itself, but what it could make possible. She says the long-term potential for her research to benefit the environment — and humanity more broadly — is what keeps her motivated. “Charging electric vehicles via renewable sources and mitigating climate change as a result is…extremely important, extremely important,” she said. artigo.texto: Elon Musk Elon Musk calls Earth’s data centers “peanuts” next to what SpaceX is planning in orbit Elon Musk says SpaceX capex efficiency is underestimated as orbital data centers loom by 2028. Elon Musk is pushing back on one of the biggest worries hanging over SpaceX stock. In a reply on X on Sunday, Musk said the company’s capital expenditure efficiency is severely underestimated. He was responding to a Milk Road Stocks post citing analyst Kyle Reidhead, who estimates SpaceX will need to spend roughly $470 billion over the next five quarters. Reidhead built that figure around the target SpaceX set on its third quarter earnings call: 13 gigawatts or more of compute by the end of 2027. In his breakdown, Nvidia captures 83 to 89 percent of the spending. SpaceX ended the quarter with 1.7 GW of nameplate compute and guided to $35 billion to $40 billion in fourth quarter capex, as Teslarati reported. Musk did not attach a number to his claim, but the earnings call shows the argument. CFO Bret Johnsen said new compute currently pays for itself in under a year at today’s pricing, and Musk said that window could shrink to six months next year. Using that pace, Reidhead argues about $230 billion of the $470 billion could come from operating cash flow and about $60 billion from SpaceX’s roughly $90 billion cash pile, leaving around $180 billion to borrow. Musk confirmed last week that SpaceX had already closed a new $40 billion debt raise to buy GPUs. The ground buildout is not the end goal. It is what is meant to pay for the move to orbit. Replying on Friday to charts built from Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire’s SpaceX model, Musk wrote that “Terrestrial compute will be peanuts compared to orbital compute,” adding that orbital compute deployed per month “probably exceeds terrestrial around the end of 2028 and then far exceeds it in 2029.” Maguire’s model shows how steep that path is. It has capex climbing from $88 billion this year to $290 billion in 2027 and $369 billion in 2028, with SpaceX burning $77.8 billion in cash this year and $122.6 billion next year before turning $114.9 billion cash positive in 2028. Musk’s response to the model was, “I think we can do better.” The orbital half runs through Starmind. SpaceX plans to operate up to 1 million AI satellites flying in clusters of about 10, linked by roughly 10 terabits of bandwidth, with deployment of thousands of units starting as soon as late 2027 out of its Gigasat factory in Bastrop, Texas, according to SpaceX’s space safety page. Musk has said each Starmind spacecraft will carry more than 250 kW of solar power. Getting there depends on launch volume. Maguire’s model assumes 250 Starship flights in 2028, up from two this year and 38 next year. The nearer test is financial: SpaceX guided to $33 billion to $37 billion in first quarter 2027 revenue, more than double the $14.58 billion it booked in Q3, and Musk reposted that guidance again on Sunday morning.

artigo.texto: Hinojosa, Abbott outline differing plans on data centers, housing ahead of Election Day SHERMAN, Texas (KXII) - Rep. Gina Hinojosa and Gov. Greg Abbott described different approaches to data centers and housing costs ahead of Election Day on Tuesday. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Abbott visited Gainesville and Sherman in September. Hinojosa spoke with KXII’ 12s Ava Gibson on Friday. Candidates discuss turnout and polls Hinojosa said the turnout gives her reason to be hopeful. “I feel good. People are voting. That’s a great thing. Young people are back voting. People who didn’t vote in the last presidential election are voting because they feel like this is a change election year and they want to be a part of it. It’s a historic time,” Hinojosa said. Abbott downplayed the polls. “Polls don’t win elections, and polls are often wrong. What I’m confident about is exactly where my campaign stands and the outcome, that I’m going to win this race,” Abbott said. Data centers Data centers have become a major issue in the race. Both candidates said local communities should have a say, but they disagree on how to get there. Abbott wants the Legislature to give cities and counties the final say. He said he wants “rules and regulations that will empower local governments, such as counties or cities, to be the decision makers about whether or not any data center is ever going to be able to go up in their county or city.” Abbott said state permits are on hold. “And in the meantime, everything is on hold because of the mandates and restrictions that I have put in place, denying permits, denying the capability of going forward,” Abbott said. Hinojosa wants a moratorium or ban on new approvals until laws are passed to protect Texans. “Most importantly, Texans need a seat at the table to decide if and how data centers come into their communities,” Hinojosa said. Housing costs Housing costs are another top issue. In Grayson County, home prices have about doubled since 2015, while wages have grown about 40%. Both candidates were asked how they would make home ownership attainable again for working Texans. Hinojosa pointed to private equity firms buying single-family homes. “Texas has the worst problem with private equity coming in and buying up single family homes, middle income homes. And that’s wrong. That should not be happening because then regular Texas families can’t compete,” Hinojosa said. Abbott said more homes mean lower prices. He said cities that violate state laws on housing will face consequences. “Any city that violates these laws that we passed, they’re going to have their sales tax withheld until they come into compliance with these laws that we passed that actually does make it more affordable,” Abbott said. artigo.texto: 247 – A indústria química brasileira garantiu sua inclusão na primeira etapa do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SBCE), prevista para começar em 2027. A medida foi oficializada pela Portaria SEMC/MF nº 3.199, publicada pelo Ministério da Fazenda no Diário Oficial da União em 29 de outubro de 2026. A norma estabelece o cronograma de obrigações relacionadas ao monitoramento, à mensuração, ao relato e à verificação (MRV) das emissões de gases de efeito estufa nos setores abrangidos pelo mercado regulado de carbono. O planejamento inicial do governo federal previa a entrada da indústria química apenas na segunda etapa de implementação do SBCE, com início previsto para até 2029, em razão da diversidade e da pulverização das atividades do setor. A antecipação ocorreu após a Associação Brasileira da Indústria Química (Abiquim) elaborar um estudo técnico interno que identificou os segmentos responsáveis pelas maiores emissões de gases de efeito estufa (GEE). Com base nesse levantamento, a entidade apresentou uma proposta à Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono, que acolheu o pedido de inclusão antecipada. Com a alteração, a primeira fase do SBCE contemplará atividades relacionadas à fabricação de intermediários para fertilizantes e plastificantes, produtos petroquímicos básicos, resinas, fibras, resinas termoplásticas e produtos químicos orgânicos. Os demais segmentos da cadeia química continuarão previstos para a segunda etapa de implementação do sistema. Cronograma de MRV e regras do SBCE Instituído pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, o SBCE será implementado gradualmente. Nesta etapa inicial, as obrigações estarão concentradas na estruturação dos procedimentos de monitoramento, mensuração, relato e verificação das emissões. A definição dos limites de emissão e a distribuição das Cotas Brasileiras de Emissões (CBEs) ficarão para uma fase posterior, no âmbito do Plano Nacional de Alocação. De acordo com o cronograma estabelecido, as empresas deverão apresentar seus planos de monitoramento ao órgão gestor durante o primeiro ano, para análise e aprovação. No segundo ano, terá início a mensuração das emissões e remoções de gases de efeito estufa, conforme os procedimentos definidos nos planos aprovados. A partir do terceiro ano, as companhias deverão manter a mensuração e apresentar relatórios verificados referentes às emissões e remoções registradas no ano-calendário anterior. O processo permitirá acompanhar os dados ambientais das atividades abrangidas pelo sistema e estabelecer uma base técnica para a aplicação das regras do mercado regulado. A Abiquim também passará a integrar a Câmara de Assuntos Regulatórios (CAREG), contribuindo com informações e subsídios técnicos para a elaboração e a implementação das diretrizes do novo mercado de carbono. Para André Passos Cordeiro, presidente-executivo da Abiquim, o acolhimento da proposta evidencia a importância da articulação institucional acompanhada de fundamentação técnica. “Nosso compromisso agora é continuar contribuindo para que o mercado regulado de carbono seja implementado com segurança técnica, transparência e regras adequadas às características dos setores abrangidos”, afirmou. O executivo ressaltou ainda que a associação atuará na capacitação das empresas associadas, com o objetivo de assegurar o cumprimento das exigências do sistema e contribuir para o alcance das metas ambientais estabelecidas. O que muda com o mercado regulado de carbono O Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões, criado pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, estabelece um modelo de regulação das emissões de gases de efeito estufa no Brasil. O mecanismo tem como objetivo contribuir para a redução dessas emissões por meio de regras aplicáveis aos setores econômicos definidos pelo governo federal. A implementação ocorrerá em etapas, começando pela organização dos processos necessários ao acompanhamento das emissões e remoções de gases de efeito estufa. Nesta primeira fase, a prioridade será consolidar os procedimentos de Mensuração, Relato e Verificação (MRV), que servirão de base para o funcionamento do mercado regulado. Na prática, as empresas abrangidas deverão elaborar planos de monitoramento, realizar a mensuração de suas emissões e remoções e apresentar os resultados conforme as metodologias e os procedimentos definidos pelo órgão gestor. Essas informações permitirão estruturar o acompanhamento das atividades reguladas e subsidiar as próximas etapas de implementação do SBCE, incluindo a definição de limites de emissão e a distribuição das Cotas Brasileiras de Emissões previstas no Plano Nacional de Alocação.

Armenia Solar Armenia adds interest subsidies for solar-plus-storage loans Subsidies cover 6 to 10 points Support runs for up to seven years Stock video by Los Muertos Crew via Pexels Nov 2, 2026 Armenia Introduces Interest Rate Subsidies for Solar-Plus-Storage Loans and Leases The Armenian government has introduced interest rate subsidies for loans and leasing arrangements used to acquire storage devices paired with solar systems, according to pv magazine. The provisions, which took effect last week, apply when the storage systems are intended to hold energy generated by solar plants or panels. Under the incentive, eligible businesses can receive subsidies ranging from 6 to 10 percentage points, depending on the financing arrangement and currency, for a period of up to seven years. A notice on Arlis, Armenia's online legal information system, indicates that a loan covering batteries and their components can receive an 8% subsidy when denominated in Armenian drams, while a lease can receive a 10% subsidy. For foreign currency financing, the subsidy stands at 6% for loans and 8% for leases. To qualify in each case, the battery storage systems must be used exclusively for storing energy produced by solar plants or solar panels. Armenia's Minister of Economy, Gevorg Papoyan, described the mechanism in a social media post, explaining that owners of solar plants who wish to store the energy they produce can purchase accumulators through the new state support toolkit, which subsidizes the interest rate on a loan or lease. Armenia's storage market remains at a relatively early stage. The country's Energy Law was amended in May to allow the development of energy storage systems for the first time, subject to licensing. Systems smaller than 1 MW, as well as those above 1 MW designed for self-consumption, are exempt from licensing. Renewable energy installations in Armenia are meanwhile expanding. Government statistics show that solar accounted for 16.3% of the country's electricity generation last year, and 2025 was a record year for solar deployment, taking cumulative solar capacity past 1 GW. artigo.texto: Um ataque de drone reivindicado pela Guarda Revolucionária do Irã provocou incêndio e interrupção de energia em um data center da Amazon Web Services (AWS) em Dubai no domingo (1º), segundo a agência Fars, nesta segunda-feira (2). De acordo com a Amazon, “objetos desconhecidos” atingiram uma das zonas de disponibilidade do centro de dados, gerando faíscas que deram início ao incêndio. As autoridades locais precisaram desligar a energia, incluindo os geradores de emergência, para conter o fogo. A interrupção afetou parcialmente serviços da AWS na região, que atende mais de 1,5 milhão de clientes ao redor do mundo. O incidente ocorre em meio à escalada do conflito entre Irã, Israel e Estados Unidos. No sábado (28), Israel realizou ataques contra alvos no Irã, alegando neutralizar ameaças ao país, com explosões relatadas em diferentes regiões de Teerã. O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, confirmou a participação norte-americana na ofensiva. Em retaliação, o Irã lançou múltiplos ataques com mísseis balísticos contra Israel e bases americanas na região. A tensão aumentou após a morte do Líder Supremo iraniano, aiatolá Ali Khamenei, e de altos oficiais do governo durante a operação conjunta, ampliando preocupações internacionais sobre a estabilidade regional. *Compartilhe esta reportagem do Diário da Guanabara, o melhor site de notícias do Rio de Janeiro.

artigo.texto: The Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission (GERC) has adopted the tariffs discovered through a competitive bidding process for the development of a 450 MW / 900 MWh standalone Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Gujarat. The approval covers projects allocated to NLC India Renewables Limited and Sun Drops Energia Limited under Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited’s (GUVNL) Phase-IX battery storage procurement initiative. The petition was filed by GUVNL before the Commission under Sections 63 and 86(1)(b) of the Electricity Act, 2003, seeking approval for the discovered tariffs. The procurement process was initiated after a developer selected under the earlier Phase-VII tender failed to execute the required Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreement (BESPA) for the 900 MWh capacity. Following approval from the Ministry of Power, Government of India, GUVNL issued a fresh Request for Selection (RfS) on June 22, 2026, under Phase-IX. The projects are supported through Viability Gap Funding (VGF) provided under the Power System Development Fund (PSDF), aimed at encouraging the deployment of battery storage infrastructure. The tender received 11 online bids, of which 10 bidders successfully met the technical and financial qualification requirements. Subsequently, an e-reverse auction was conducted on August 11, 2026, with nine eligible bidders participating in the competitive bidding process. The successful capacities were allocated through a bucket-filling approach based on the L1 discovered tariff, with a two percent margin. Under the final allocation, NLC India Renewables Limited has been awarded 275 MW / 550 MWh of battery storage capacity at a discovered monthly storage rate of ₹231,989 per MW. Sun Drops Energia Limited has secured the remaining 175 MW / 350 MWh capacity at a monthly storage rate of ₹231,990 per MW. Both successful bidders submitted affidavits before the Commission confirming that they had no objections to the adoption of the discovered tariffs. After examining the bidding process and submissions made by the parties, GERC approved the tariffs for both developers under the provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003. GUVNL highlighted that the proposed battery storage projects will support Gujarat in meeting its Energy Storage Obligations (ESO) and Renewable Purchase Obligations (RPO). The installations are also expected to strengthen grid stability, improve power balancing and address the variability associated with renewable energy generation. As part of its directions, GERC has instructed GUVNL to execute the BESPAs with the successful developers within the stipulated timeframe. The agreements must incorporate appropriate provisions under the Electricity (Late Payment Surcharge) Rules. GUVNL has also been directed to submit copies of the executed agreements to the Commission and publish the final tariff structures on its official website to ensure transparency. With the tariff adoption approved, GERC has disposed of the petition, clearing the way for the implementation of the 450 MW / 900 MWh standalone battery storage projects in Gujarat. artigo.texto: Some residents of a proposed large data center in Enid are planning a petition drive for a recall of the City Council and Mayor who supported a data center project proposed by some local business officials while Yukon voters will decide this week on the fate of their mayor in a similar protest. While the Project Thunderbird data center proposed by Jason Singer, Aaron Singer, Chad Dillingham and Troy Phillips who make up the firm Plainsmen Holdings, has the support of the Enid Regional Development Alliance, it doesn’t have the support of some residents. The group, No Data Centers in Enid, is led by Jacob McNew, who recently said the organization has launched efforts to recall Mayor David Mason and most city commissioners. A petition effort was held Sunday in Enid to force a vote of residents to overturn the rezoning of two properties where the data center project would be located. We are seeking committed volunteers who can get involved in this campaign. As we enter a new phase of this fight, we are needing folks who can help out. There are tons of ways to get involved. Many of which don’t require a lot of time. If you or anyone you know would like to get experience in activism, please reach out! This is a great opportunity for young and old to make a difference in our community,” shared the group in a social media posting over the weekend. It followed an earlier posting. “We would like to take the time to address the biggest piece of misinformation that we frequently see online and hear in person. It is imperative that we oppose this project using only facts. Project Thunderbird is not a “done deal”. While Mayor David Mason, City Manager Jerald Gilbert and City Attorney Melissa Blanton have been in contact with Plainsmen Holdings LLC since at least January 2026, as their NDAs prove, they do not have the power alone to accept this proposal. Although they have made it quite apparent, they are not impartial to this project, it still requires city commissioners to decide whether it gets approval or not. There are more opportunities to fight back on the proposal, and we will share those opportunities on this page as they are announced. As of now, we are collecting signatures for recalls as well as a referendum to overturn the city council vote that approved the rezonings.” No Data Centers in Enid originally announced its opposition saying it wants to keep health and quality of life and that no possible tax income was worth the sacrifice. “People want to stay living in their homes, farming on their farms to provide healthy food for our people and running the ranches that provide food. We want to continue to know our kids are healthy and able to focus at school. We want to keep looking up at night to enjoy our beautiful clear and clean pollution free sky!” Project Thunderbird would sit on a 1,735 acre site and the developers say it would use behind-the-meter electricity generation. In their original announcement in September, they said the project would rely on raw pipeline water from Kaw Lake located 8 miles east of Ponca City. A similar recall election petition was successful in the city of Yukon over a proposed Beltline Energy data center that drew large opposition. City voters will decide Tuesday, November 3 on a recall of Mayor Brian Pilmore. Residents launched their recall petition in May. In addition, a petition to require voter approval for the proposed data center was recently filed with the Yukon City Clerk, according to the Yukon Progress. “It’s the most democratic way to deal with these things,” explained petition proponent Charles Scott. He said the vote would not be for a prohibition but for approval. Scott also said the petition contained 354 signatures while only 162 were required. City officials were reported to be in the process of verifying the validity of the signatures. The recall drive in Yukon already resulted in the resignation of Vice Mayor Jeff Wooton shortly after the recall effort targeted him and Mayor Pilmore. He resigned June 6, 2026.

artigo.texto: BYD recorded its strongest monthly sales performance of the year in October, with battery electric vehicle (BEV) deliveries exceeding 300,000 units for the first time. Strong demand for fully electric models helped offset declining plug-in hybrid sales, highlighting a continued shift in the Chinese automaker’s sales mix toward battery-powered vehicles. The Chinese automotive giant sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, representing a 10.97% increase compared with the same month last year and a 5.74% improvement over September, according to the company’s latest sales data. October marked BYD’s sixth consecutive month of year-over-year sales growth and its eighth consecutive month of higher sales compared with the previous month. However, the annual growth rate continued to moderate, falling from 16.98% in September. Despite the slower growth, October was BYD’s strongest sales month since December 2024 and the fourth-highest monthly total in the company’s history. Battery electric vehicles were the biggest contributor to BYD’s October performance. The company sold 305,743 battery electric passenger vehicles, an impressive 37.38% increase from October last year and an 11.94% rise compared with September. This marked the third consecutive monthly record for BYD’s fully electric passenger vehicle sales. BEVs accounted for 63.28% of BYD’s passenger vehicle sales in October, compared with 59.81% in September and 50.95% during the same month last year. The figures demonstrate how rapidly BYD’s product mix is changing as demand for fully electric models continues to grow. The trend is particularly significant because BYD has traditionally relied heavily on plug-in hybrid vehicles alongside its fully electric lineup. October’s results suggest that battery electric models are becoming an increasingly important part of the company’s overall business. While fully electric vehicle sales reached new heights, BYD’s plug-in hybrid business faced another difficult month. The automaker sold 177,382 plug-in hybrid passenger vehicles in October, down 17.23% year-over-year and 3.37% compared with September. This represented the second consecutive month of annual declines for the plug-in hybrid segment, following a 2.36% decrease in September. Looking at the first 10 months of the year, BYD sold 1,935,700 battery electric passenger vehicles, up 5.86% compared with the same period last year. Plug-in hybrid passenger vehicle sales, meanwhile, dropped 11.02% to 1,625,969 units. Overall, BYD delivered 483,125 passenger new energy vehicles in October, an increase of 10.59% year-over-year and 5.78% month-over-month. Commercial NEV sales contributed another 7,043 units, representing a substantial 45.22% annual increase. International markets continued to play an increasingly important role in BYD’s expansion. The company exported 170,194 new energy vehicles in October, up 102.84% compared with the same month last year. However, exports were down 5.81% from September. From January through October, BYD’s NEV exports reached 1,513,154 units, representing a 93.75% increase compared with the same period last year. The export figures highlight BYD’s growing international ambitions as the company expands its presence in markets across Europe, Southeast Asia, Latin America and other regions. Although monthly exports fluctuated slightly, the nearly doubled year-to-date total demonstrates the importance of overseas markets to BYD’s long-term growth strategy. Alongside its expanding sales, BYD has been refreshing several important models across its vehicle lineup. On October 20, the company introduced the second-generation BYD Seagull, a compact electric car that received a larger body and flash-charging technology on selected versions. Just one week later, on October 27, BYD launched the third-generation Qin Plus DM-i. The updated plug-in hybrid sedan features a larger body, improved electric driving range and optional LiDAR technology. The next major launch is scheduled for November 5, when BYD is expected to introduce the second-generation Seal 07. The updated model will be offered with both fully electric and plug-in hybrid powertrains, continuing the expansion of the company’s Ocean series. These product updates are expected to help BYD maintain its competitive position in China’s increasingly crowded electric vehicle market. BYD’s October results reveal an important development in the company’s business. While overall NEV sales continue to grow, battery electric vehicles are increasingly driving that expansion, while plug-in hybrid models are losing momentum. The milestone of surpassing 300,000 electric passenger vehicles in a single month is particularly significant, demonstrating the scale BYD has achieved in the global EV industry. However, the company still faces challenges, including slower annual sales growth and intensifying competition in China. Its ability to sustain BEV momentum, refresh its product lineup and expand international deliveries will be crucial in the months ahead. With several updated models entering the market and overseas sales continuing to climb, BYD is positioning itself for another important phase of growth.

artigo.texto: [Cover photo credit to Elizabeth Landry] UK artist Bess Atwell has announced her new album, Cut A Figure, arriving February 5th, 2026, via Nettwerk. Atwell has also shared the single “Glass” alongside a video, and confirmed full world tour dates in 2027. For her follow-up to 2024’s Aaron Dessner-produced album Light Sleeper, Bess Atwell retreated from the UK to Quebec, where she lived for nine months, conceiving and writing what would become Cut a Figure. To bring the album to life, she worked with Los Angeles-based Producer and mixer Chris Coady (Beach House, Future Islands, DIIV, Foals, and more). “Glass” is “the emotional heart” of the new record, and its lyrics even inspired the album’s title. “Glass” is an Indie Pop song with lyrics “exploring how an eagerness to be understood can make someone invisible.” Bess explains: I knew I wanted to name the album after a line in this song as it feels like the heart of the record. Sometimes, an eagerness to be seen and understood can have the opposite effect – you can be so transparent that you end up invisible. When I was a teenager, I was really into doing ‘personality tests’. One test had you imagine a cube and then describe it (the cube supposedly representing how you express yourself). All my friends and family pictured various different sizes and colors, while I saw a transparent glass box floating in space.

artigo.texto: A Botetourt County citizen’s lawsuit alleges that the county violated Virginia’s Freedom of Information Act when it approved documentation advancing the Google data center project in Troutville. Robert Dallas, a retired anesthesiologist who said he lives near the Botetourt Center at Greenfield site, filed the suit on Monday, seeking to invalidate the county’s economic development performance agreement with the limited liability company behind the project. The suit asks the Botetourt County Circuit Court to “rescind all actions” carried out in connection with the June 2025 economic development performance agreement. Dallas identifies the Botetourt County Board of Supervisors, the county itself, its economic development authority and Helio Capital LLC as respondents. All were part of the performance agreement, which set in motion the land sale and the county’s support of the Google development, among other items. According to the suit, the county’s board of supervisors did not disclose on its published agenda that it would be discussing the agreement or a resolution to enact it in a closed meeting on June 24, 2025. After the board returned to public session, it voted 5-0, with no discussion, to approve them, after they were added to the agenda during the meeting, the case alleges. After a recess, the board returned to address another “walk-on” item — announcing the data center project. A final item that didn’t appear on the agenda was a board resolution approving Google’s agreement with the Western Virginia Water Authority, Dallas alleges. “At no time … did the board reasonably identify the substance of the performance agreement resolution or the performance agreement itself, despite having agreed to both at the closed meeting immediately preceding the performance agreement resolution’s being added to the agenda as a walk-on item,” the lawsuit reads. The agreement set in motion Google’s $14 million deal with Botetourt County for 312 acres in Greenfield. The tech giant plans a data center campus including three data centers, three substations, an office building, access roads, utilities, parking areas and stormwater management facilities, according to a March 10 Army Corps of Engineers notice soliciting public comment on the project. The board of supervisors engaged in “subterfuge” by adopting what the lawsuit called the key contract related to the data center, without adequate disclosure, “not only undermining the will of the people but violating the Virginia Freedom of Information Act,” the suit states. The open government and records law in question requires localities to identify such projects. Quoting Virginia law, the suit states, “Except as specifically authorized by law, in no event may any public body take action on matters discussed in any closed meeting, except at an open meeting for which notice was given as required by” the law. Dallas spoke during a Monday afternoon news conference at the Roanoke law firm Fishwick & Associates, which filed the suit on his behalf. He said that he has lived in Botetourt County for 36 years. His home is about a half-mile from the proposed Google complex, where work has already begun. He said his land is protected by a conservation easement he had recorded about three years ago. “I know this community well, and like many, I was surprised when the county suddenly announced the data center project with no public input in June of 2025,” he said. “I filed this petition because I strongly believe that the Botetourt County Board of Supervisors should follow all the rules of procedure and give citizens like me and many others the chance to make our voices heard. “The board did not do so on June 24, 2025, when they agreed to the performance agreement for the Google data center, outside of the public eye, in a closed session, and then voted to adopt it without offering even a hint of what it was. This case is about holding our leaders responsible and having open and transparent government.” Nor had it been open with county residents in the year and a half preceding that day, during which Botetourt officials “cultivated” an “atmosphere of secrecy” concerning negotiations about the project, Fishwick’s firm stated in both the lawsuit and a news release. Dallas is asking the court to rescind actions including the county issuing expedited permits and granting Google eligibility to participate in the county’s third-party inspection program. If the county chooses to adopt a similar resolution in the future, it should comply with the Freedom of Information Act, according to the suit. Botetourt County, through its spokesman, sent an email to reporters on Monday. “As this matter involves pending litigation, Botetourt County will not comment on the specific allegations or discuss legal matters,” the email read. “The county respects the legal process and remains committed to providing accurate and appropriate information to the public as the matter moves forward.” $1 billion investment from Google per data center A nondisclosure agreement was part of the process leading up to the deal, County Administrator Gary Larrowe has said. Google will pay a property tax rate of 70 cents per $100 of assessed value, same as any other landowner in the county, Larrowe has said. The county has made the performance agreement public, however. It includes Google’s commitment to make capital investments of at least $1 billion to develop each data center on the property, while promising to invest $4 million over five years in community projects that include public safety and parks and recreation items. John Fishwick, talking to reporters during the news conference, said that the law calls for a hearing on the case within seven working days. artigo.texto: An out-of-town data center development firm has locked down a 180-acre site approved last year for a data center campus on the Powhatan-Chesterfield line. An entity tied to Vantage Data Centers out of Colorado last month paid roughly $9.4 million for an assemblage that’s planned to eventually house the Powhatan Technology Park. The property, the majority of which is located at 1318 Page Road, was approved two years ago for a 120-acre data center project that was proposed by California-based Province Group. Then, in October of 2025, Province Group received approvals to tack on 60 additional acres to the original project site for an overall 180-acre campus. The fully assembled site is on the east side of Page Road, just north of the intersection with Anderson Highway, abutting Chesterfield County. As detailed last year in county staff reports, the total roughly 180 acres were slated to eventually house up to four detached data center buildings with a total of 2 million square feet, in what has been described as the biggest data center project the county has ever had on the table. Per a Powhatan County representative, the sale of the original 120-acre tract closed Oct. 21 for $5.7 million. A sale of the additional roughly 60-acre parcel closed on the same day for $3.65 million. The buyer was Powhatan Technology Park LLC. Vantage Data Centers confirmed its purchase of the Powhatan Tech Park site in an email on Friday. “We are evaluating opportunities for future development at the location, but we do not have any additional details to share at this time,” a company representative wrote to BizSense. “We look forward to engaging with local stakeholders and the community as planning progresses and will share more information when available.” The sale had not yet been reflected in online property records as of Friday afternoon. The previous owner of the 120-acre tract is listed in online property records as New County Line Farm LLC, an entity tied to Harold and Christina Ellis, while the previous owner of the 60-acre parcel is listed as JMS Investments LLC, which is tied to Mark and Deborah Sowers. The nature of the relationship between Province Group and Vantage Data Centers regarding the Powhatan project is unclear; however, in an email late Friday afternoon, a Powhatan County representative confirmed Province Group remains involved in the project. The Powhatan County representative also stated that the county has not yet received a site plan for the project. Province Group CEO Mark Kerslake presented the application for the 60-acre addition to the Powhatan Planning Commission a year ago. In his presentation, he noted that Province Group had an end user lined up for the previously rezoned 120-acre parcel, though it was not clear who that end user was. As of last year, buildout of the overall project from Province Group was anticipated to occur in multiple phases and take at least five years to complete. Vantage was founded in 2010, and has developed dozens of data center campuses across the U.S. and around the world. According to company’s website, it has developed or is developing three data centers in Ashburn in Northern Virginia and one in Fredericksburg. Province Group was founded in 1991 and is headquartered in Newport Beach, California. The website states that it has developed, renovated, acquired or entitled more than 75 projects with a combined value of more than $850 million, including projects in states like California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia and Washington. The proposed Powhatan project was seemingly the company’s first development in the Richmond area. Elsewhere in the region, data center news abounds. Google revealed publicly last week that it is currently doing due diligence on a roughly 1,000-acre site within West Creek Business Park in Goochland County for a potential, 1,200-megawatt data center development. The announcement comes as several other data center developments within Goochland’s tech overlay district are being weighed, to the concern of hundreds of residents on both sides of the Goochland-Henrico county line. Google has also begun construction on a data center campus on a 300-plus-acre site at 2700 Bermuda Hundred Road in eastern Chesterfield next to Meadowville Technology Park, and has several other data center facilities planned for the western end of Chesterfield.

artigo.texto: A Lackawanna County judge recently denied a developer’s court challenge that sought to compel Jessup to approve plans for six data centers along Breaker Street after the borough denied them. Judge Terrence R. Nealon rejected West Conshohocken-based Breaker Street Associates LLC’s contention that its proposal for a nearly 210-acre data center campus should be deemed approved due to issues with the timing and substance of Jessup’s denial of its plans last year. Although Breaker Street Associates could have successfully argued deemed approval because Jessup did not properly deny its initial application submitted in June 2025, the developer lost the ability to do so by voluntarily submitting revised plans in July 2025 and October 2025, restarting the 90-day window for the municipality to rule on the applications, Nealon’s Oct. 22 order states. “The owner has not established that it is clear and free from doubt that there is no genuine issue of material fact and that it is entitled to mandamus relief in the form of a deemed approval,” Nealon wrote. “Accordingly, the owner’s motion for peremptory judgment will be denied.” Breaker Street Associates, which shares a West Conshohocken address with Catalyst Commercial Development LLC, wants to build six data centers, ranging from 148,480 square feet to 187,500 square feet, south of Breaker Street off Hill Street, in addition to a 10,000-square-foot admin/security building and a 17.44-acre switchyard/substation area, according to court filings on the project. The location of the switchyard/substation played a key role in Jessup’s denial of the project. Data centers were previously principally permitted in the borough’s mixed-use zoning district south of Breaker Street until council amended its zoning ordinance last year to regulate and restrict data centers. However, the switchyard/substation fell into residentially zoned land north of Breaker Street, which never permitted data centers. The Jessup Zoning Hearing Board denied an appeal from Breaker Street Associates last year that sought zoning relief for that electric infrastructure; the developer is appealing the denial separately. Another firm linked to Catalyst Commercial Development, Sunnyside Road Associates LLC, also proposes a data center next to the Lackawanna Energy Center natural gas power plant on Sunnyside Road near Alberigi Drive. Although Jessup council conditionally approved preliminary land development plans in June for Sunnyside Road Associates to build a 50-foot-tall data center next to the power plant, the developer is appealing the zoning hearing board’s denial of a 20-foot height variance that would have allowed it to build a 70-foot-tall data center. Attorneys Richard M. Williams and Kevin M. Walsh Jr. of Hourigan, Kluger & Quinn in Kingston filed the mandamus complaint June 18 asking the court to approve Breaker Street Associates’ plans and to compel Jessup to approve them. Attempts to reach Williams and Walsh were unsuccessful Monday afternoon. Breaker Street background Breaker Street Associates submitted its initial land development application June 11, 2025, followed by revised applications and plans July 23, 2025, and Oct. 2, 2025, in response to comments from the Lackawanna County Regional Planning Commission. Jessup’s zoning officer denied the initial application June 16, 2025, because of the infrastructure in a residential area. The planning commission sent Breaker Street Associates a letter June 24, 2025, informing the developer that the commission had reviewed its application but would not be accepting it because of the non-permitted use in the residential zone. The planning commission has 90 days to rule on an application, with the countdown beginning after the commission’s next meeting, or in this case, on June 18, 2025, setting a Sept. 16, 2025, deadline. In its mandamus complaint filed this year, Breaker Street Associates argues that the planning commission’s letter was improper under the Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code, or MPC, which provides the legal framework for municipal zoning, because it failed to cite specific provisions of Jessup’s Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance, or SALDO, used to deny it. The lawsuit further argues that the borough never ruled on its July 23, 2025, application. As a result, both the June 11, 2025, and July 23, 2025, applications should be deemed approved, according to the filing. The complaint does not reference the revised application submitted in October 2025. Nealon’s order Nealon recognizes in his order that Jessup denied Breaker Street Associates’ initial June 2025 application “without describing the unsatisfied requirements or citing the relevant provisions of the statute or ordinance supporting that denial.” “The Planning Commission’s letter decision does not cite the provisions of the MPC, SALDO, or Zoning Ordinance upon which the Planning Commission relied in rejecting Breaker Street’s land development application,” he wrote. If Breaker Street Associates had relied on only its initial application, it could have sought deemed approval. By voluntarily submitting revised plans with significant changes, it twice reset the 90-day timer, leading to Jessup properly denying the third application in October 2025, according to Nealon’s order. “Breaker Street could have chosen to rely upon its original application on June 11, 2025, and if it considered the Planning Commission’s letter of June 24, 2025, to be insufficient … it had the option to stand firm through September 16, 2025 (i.e., 90 days after the Planning Commission’s next regular meeting on June 18), and assert that its original land development application was deemed approved as of September 17, 2025.
