artigo.texto: Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has said that some Michigan voters are "deathly afraid" of the rapid growth of data centers. Artificial intelligence and the rapid construction of data centers have emerged as key issues ahead of the midterm elections. Citizens across the country have raised concerns about their potential impact on electricity bills, water consumption, and noise disrupting nearby neighborhoods. Speaking on CBS News' 60 Minutes, El Sayed discussed the most important issues facing Michiganders that he had witnessed during his campaign. "Had you asked me five years ago, I would have said healthcare. It still is really really high on people's minds. I think right now we are barreling toward a world where the most important issue I hear about every day is AI," he said. Read More on News He said that AI could transform the economy so rapidly that society would be unable to adjust, and warned of the risks of the technology escaping human control and being used by terrorists to develop a biological weapon or fueling an arms race that threatens humanity. "All of these outcomes are really really quite scary. I hear it in so many different ways," he said. El-Sayed added that students were fearful of the disruption the technology could bring to the jobs market, and cited rural voters who were concerned about the impact of data centers on utility bills. "These are these are issues that people are deathly afraid of and it shows up in just all kinds of ways," he said. El-Sayed is competing against Republican Mike Rogers in a closely watched Senate contest that will help decide the balance of power in Congress. This is a developing story. More to follow.

artigo.texto: Marvell compra Lumentum por US$ 115 bilhões e aposta em data centers Aquisição reforça a aposta da fabricante de chips na expansão da infraestrutura óptica para data centers e intensifica a disputa com a Broadcom pelo mercado de inteligência artificial A Marvell Technology anunciou um acordo para comprar a fabricante de componentes ópticos Lumentum em uma transação de US$ 115 bilhões inteiramente em ações, incluindo dívidas, à medida que a fabricante de chips personalizados intensifica seu desafio à rival de maior porte, a Broadcom, em meio a um boom de gastos com IA. O negócio, anunciado nesta segunda-feira (2), é um dos maiores de 2026 e está entre as apostas corporativas mais ousadas até agora no boom da IA, que os executivos do setor de chips esperam que sustente a demanda da indústria por muitos anos. Ao adquirir a Lumentum — uma empresa com cerca de metade do seu tamanho —, a Marvell aposta que o boom de gastos com IA das grandes empresas de tecnologia veio para ficar e que a demanda por componentes ópticos usados para transmitir dados em alta velocidade continuará superando a oferta. Segundo o acordo, a Marvell pagará US$ 1.132 por ação em ações, um prêmio de 23,9% em relação ao último preço de fechamento não afetado da Lumentum em 28 de outubro, antes que as negociações fossem divulgadas pela primeira vez. Isso confere ao negócio um valor patrimonial de US$ 102,54 bilhões. A Marvell afirmou que a transação ampliará o mercado total acessível da empresa resultante da fusão para US$ 550 bilhões. Suas ações subiram 2,8% no pré-mercado, enquanto as negociações com as ações da Lumentum foram suspensas. A Nvidia, gigante dos chips de IA, investiu US$ 2 bilhões tanto na Marvell quanto na Lumentum no início deste ano. Há apenas três anos, a Marvell era uma fabricante de chips relativamente desconhecida. Mas, desde então, seu valor de mercado disparou para mais de US$ 170 bilhões, graças ao seu papel em ajudar gigantes da tecnologia, como a Amazon , a desenvolver chips de IA personalizados e tecnologia de rede para data centers. O acordo firmado nesta segunda-feira também pode fortalecer ainda mais a Marvell em sua disputa com a rival Broadcom, que há muito tempo é a principal parceira de chips personalizados do Google, de propriedade da Alphabet , e oferece aos clientes uma gama mais ampla de hardware de IA para data centers sob o mesmo teto. A Marvell conquistou uma de suas maiores vitórias em agosto, ao assinar um acordo para fornecer chips que atuam em conjunto com os processadores de IA do Google, com um valor de vendas de até US$ 120 bilhões até o ano fiscal de 2033, concedendo ao gigante das buscas o direito de adquirir uma participação de US$ 12,2 bilhões.

artigo.texto: Principais Conclusões - A chefe de energia de data centers da Alphabet, Google, diz que data centers no espaço podem custar até 100 vezes mais do que os na Terra, e que o fornecimento de energia dos EUA é suficiente, sendo as licenças a parte lenta. - Jim Chanos diz que essa discrepância deve fazer qualquer pessoa que esteja modelando a SpaceX pensar duas vezes, e que os lucros da computação de IA irão para os fabricantes de GPUs, como a NVIDIA. - Analistas esperam que a receita da SpaceX atinja US$ 336 bilhões em 2028, e até mesmo o otimista Shaun Maguire não vê a computação orbital como sua principal linha de receita antes de 2030 ou 2031. - A computação orbital não merece nenhum crédito em uma avaliação da SpaceX até que o Starship mostre quanto custa. Os otimistas sobre a SpaceX (SPCX) passaram o fim de semana discutindo sobre a rapidez com que a computação orbital poderia dominar seus negócios. Então o Google entrou na discussão com um número. No domingo, The Information informou que Amanda Peterson Corio, chefe de energia de data centers da unidade Google da Alphabet (GOOG), coloca o custo de data centers no espaço em até 100 vezes o dos na Terra. Ela também teria dito que o fornecimento de energia dos EUA é suficiente, e a parte lenta são as licenças. "Vamos explorar todas as opções terrestres antes de irmos extraterrestres", disse ela. O vendedor a descoberto Jim Chanos interpretou isso como US$ 5 trilhões por gigawatt de computação, e acrescentou em uma postagem no X: "O fato de a chefe de energia de data centers de uma hiperescaladora estar tão distante das estimativas da administração/otimistas da $SPCX deve fazer qualquer pessoa que esteja tentando modelar esse negócio pensar duas vezes." São muitos zeros para modelar. A TIKR acompanha 39 analistas da SpaceX. Quantos dizem "Comprar"? Veja a análise completa das recomendações de Compra, Manter e Vender da SpaceX, junto com as estimativas de receita e lucro de Wall Street, tudo em um só lugar. Mais de 500.000 investidores usam a TIKR para pesquisar ações como esta. Veja as Recomendações dos Analistas da SpaceX A receita da órbita está a anos de distância Analistas esperam que a receita da SpaceX suba de US$ 48,9 bilhões este ano para US$ 336 bilhões em 2028: Elon Musk diz no X que a computação orbital implantada por mês "provavelmente excede a terrestre por volta do final de 2028". Mas Shaun Maguire, sócio da Sequoia Capital, cujo modelo da SpaceX iniciou a discussão do fim de semana, diz que a computação orbital é "simplesmente não a linha de receita dominante até 2030 ou 2031". Para a órbita, a SpaceX precisa do Starship. Maguire diz que cada lançamento carrega cerca de 10 megawatts de computação, e ele está prevendo "cerca de 280 lançamentos de computação orbital até o final de 2028". Se não for então, ele diz, "será em 2029". Na teleconferência do terceiro trimestre da SpaceX, Musk deu como previsão voos semanais do Starship no primeiro semestre de 2027 e voos duas vezes por semana até o final daquele ano. Duas vezes por semana durante todo o ano de 2028 dá cerca de 100 voos, para tudo o que o Starship carrega, incluindo os satélites Starlink. Multiplique o retorno por 100 Os gastos de capital da SpaceX mais do que quadruplicaram de 2023 para 2025: E a SpaceX gastou US$ 48,1 bilhões apenas nos primeiros nove meses de 2026, com mais US$ 35 bilhões a US$ 40 bilhões de gastos de capital previstos para o quarto trimestre. O CFO da SpaceX disse na teleconferência do terceiro trimestre que a nova capacidade de computação se paga em menos de um ano aos preços atuais de aluguel. Construa essa capacidade de computação em órbita a até 100 vezes o custo, alugue-a pelo mesmo preço, e um retorno de menos de um ano se torna um de até um século. (Mesmo com um décimo do limite superior do Google, você está esperando cerca de uma década.) E se a energia dos EUA é suficiente e as licenças são o entrave, a vantagem da órbita sobre o solo se resume a pular a fila de licenças, a até 100 vezes o preço. A NVIDIA é paga primeiro Chanos fez um segundo ponto, respondendo a outro usuário do X: "Com o tempo, os aluguéis econômicos irão para os fornecedores de GPUs, não para os locadores/proprietários dos equipamentos. Eles são condutos financeiros." A SpaceX se encaixa nessa descrição hoje. Ela está captando US$ 40 bilhões em dívida que Musk chama de "principalmente dívida resgatável para compras de GPUs", e os chips vêm da NVIDIA (NVDA). A NVIDIA é paga quando esses chips são enviados, e a SpaceX apenas enquanto os clientes continuarem alugando-os. A Anthropic, que concordou em seu prospecto de IPO a gastar até US$ 120,5 bilhões com a SpaceX até 2029, pode sair com 90 dias de aviso assim que seus primeiros períodos não canceláveis terminarem no início do próximo ano. Dê zero para a órbita por enquanto Claro, o Google supostamente está testando chips de servidor de IA em órbita ele mesmo, então dificilmente é uma parte neutra, e o Starship foi construído para reduzir exatamente os custos de lançamento que tornam o espaço tão caro. Mas Chanos está certo de que uma discrepância tão grande deve fazer pensar. A 45x os lucros futuros no fechamento de sexta-feira, os investidores já estão pagando caro pelo Starlink e pela capacidade de computação que a SpaceX aluga no solo. Eu avaliaria a ação com base nesses dois e daria zero para a computação orbital até que o Starship mostre quanto realmente custa um gigawatt no espaço. A primeira pista vem em breve: o Voo 15, que Musk espera para novembro, tentará capturar tanto o booster quanto a nave. Um ritmo próximo do de Maguire seria o primeiro sinal real de que a órbita pode ser viável financeiramente. Então, quanto vale realmente a ação da SpaceX? artigo.texto: China exempts sodium-ion batteries from tax as Hina targets 10 GWh commerical EV push A Chinese electric heavy truck equipped with a sodium-ion battery retained more than 90% of its usable capacity at minus 40°C during testing, according to FAW Jiefang, providing evidence of the chemistry’s low-temperature performance in heavy-duty vehicles. Hina Battery is expanding its commercial vehicle push, with a planned 10 GWh production base in Wuhan and a partnership to develop electric sanitation trucks. The expansion comes as China introduces a consumption tax on specified lithium-ion batteries while exempting qualifying sodium-ion batteries through 2028. The policy gives the alternative chemistry a temporary tax advantage, even as falling lithium prices have narrowed its potential cost advantage over lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. China creates a tax gap between lithium and sodium batteries China’s Ministry of Finance, General Administration of Customs and State Taxation Administration issued Announcement No. 20 (2026) on July 16, revising consumption tax treatment for several battery categories. From September 1, 2026, specified lithium-ion batteries became subject to a 2% consumption tax, rising to 4% on September 1, 2027. Sodium-ion batteries, solid-state batteries and fuel cells are exempt through December 31, 2028, provided they meet applicable national standards. The tax difference comes as lower lithium prices put pressure on sodium-ion’s potential cost advantage. On October 28, battery-grade lithium carbonate averaged around 97,000 yuan (13,500 USD) per tonne, while square LFP cells for electric vehicles averaged 0.41 yuan (0.057 USD) per Wh on October 22. The exemption gives qualifying sodium-ion batteries a tax advantage, but does not establish that they are cheaper to manufacture than LFP batteries. Sodium-ion also offers a different raw-material supply profile. Sodium-based feedstocks are more geographically distributed than lithium resources, although the downstream supply chain remains heavily concentrated in China, including cell, cathode and hard-carbon production. Hina takes sodium-ion technology into commercial fleets Hina signed an agreement with Wuhan’s Jiangxia District on October 14 to establish a sodium-ion battery production base with a planned annual capacity of 10 GWh. Signed during the fourth National Sodium Battery Symposium, the agreement covers a first phase of 3 GWh. Construction is scheduled to begin in early 2027, with initial production expected before the end of that year. Under a separate agreement, Hina and Chengli Special Automobile Group will develop sodium-ion-powered sanitation vehicles, including refuse collection, hook-lift, dust-suppression and food-waste collection trucks. The partners expect to submit an initial chassis approval application in early 2027. After prototype development, they plan demonstration vehicles, followed by vehicle approval and small-volume orders. Wuhan is expected to host the initial demonstrations. Sanitation and engineering trucks offer potential early applications because their chassis can accommodate larger battery systems and their defined operating routes allow performance to be assessed under specific working conditions. Passenger cars face different requirements, particularly for energy density and packaging. Heavy trucks provide a proving ground for sodium-ion batteries Energy density remains a limitation compared with established lithium-ion batteries. Hina’s published specifications for its sodium-ion products list a gravimetric energy density of at least 145 Wh/kg and an operating temperature range of minus 40 to 80 degrees Celsius. The company has already tested the technology in heavy-duty vehicles. In June 2026, a battery-electric FAW Jiefang J6P tractor equipped with a 339 kWh Hina sodium-ion battery completed nearly seven months of testing and more than 15,000 km of driving. At minus 40 degrees Celsius, FAW Jiefang reported that the battery retained more than 90% of its usable capacity. In August, Hina and Tonly Heavy Industries delivered an electric mining truck equipped with a 676 kWh sodium-ion battery system to the Tangshan Sanyou mine in Hebei Province. These deployments show sodium-ion technology entering heavy-duty applications, where low-temperature performance, frequent charging and high battery utilisation can be important. They do not establish its suitability for every electric vehicle segment. Hard-carbon anodes remain a cost challenge Sodium is abundant, but inexpensive raw materials do not automatically translate into cheaper battery cells. Commercial sodium-ion batteries commonly use hard-carbon anodes made from coal, biomass and other carbon-rich feedstocks. Producing hard carbon with the required structure and electrochemical properties involves controlled processing, adding cost and manufacturing complexity. Sodium-ion batteries have yet to establish a consistent cost advantage over LFP. Their lower energy density may also require larger or heavier battery packs to deliver comparable vehicle range, making their commercial viability application-dependent. China sets new safety requirements for sodium-ion batteries China is also establishing technical requirements for sodium-ion batteries. GB/T 48072-2026, published on August 28, specifies safety requirements for sodium-ion cells and batteries used in electrical energy storage systems. It is scheduled to take effect on March 1, 2027. The standard covers stationary energy storage, not automotive traction batteries, and is not an electric vehicle approval standard. Separately, the tax exemption requires qualifying products to meet applicable national standards.

artigo.texto: Prévia do Balanço do 2T da Arm: Royalties de Data Centers Podem Continuar Dobrando o Crescimento? Maior Preço-Alvo de Wall Street É de US$ 480 A Arm Holdings divulgará seus resultados do segundo trimestre do ano fiscal de 2027 em 4 de novembro, com projeção de receita entre US$ 1,37 bilhão e US$ 1,38 bilhão e LPA ajustado de US$ 0,48. O crescimento é impulsionado pela expansão em data centers e pela adoção da arquitetura Armv9 e dos Subsistemas de Computação. No entanto, o valuation elevado e a execução da nova CPU de AGI exigem cautela dos investidores quanto à sustentabilidade das metas de longo prazo e ao ritmo de conversão da receita. TradingKey - Arm Holdings (ARM) divulgará seus resultados financeiros do segundo trimestre do ano fiscal de 2027 após o fechamento do mercado norte-americano em 4 de novembro, no horário da Costa Leste. Com a expansão contínua dos data centers de IA, a demanda do mercado pela arquitetura de processadores da Arm está se estendendo dos smartphones para a computação em nuvem, servidores e infraestrutura de IA, trazendo novas oportunidades de crescimento para a empresa. No entanto, diante dos recentes recuos no preço das ações e de um valuation ainda elevado, os investidores não apenas focarão em se a receita atende às expectativas, mas também examinarão de perto o crescimento dos royalties de data centers, o desempenho do negócio de licenciamento e se a recém-lançada CPU de AGI pode gerar receita real. Atualmente, Wall Street espera que a receita da Arm no segundo trimestre fique entre US$ 1,37 bilhão e US$ 1,38 bilhão, uma alta de cerca de 21% na comparação anual, com o lucro por ação ajustado esperado em torno de US$ 0,48, alta de aproximadamente 23% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior. O guidance anterior da Arm previa uma receita de US$ 1,38 bilhão, mais ou menos US$ 50 milhões, e lucro por ação não-GAAP de US$ 0,47, mais ou menos US$ 0,04. Os royalties de data centers podem manter o crescimento rápido? Para entender o desempenho da Arm, é preciso primeiro distinguir suas duas fontes tradicionais de receita: a receita de licenciamento e a receita de royalties. A primeira decorre principalmente de taxas pagas pelos clientes para adquirir direitos de uso das arquiteturas de processadores da Arm e propriedade intelectual relacionada, com o reconhecimento da receita dependendo tipicamente de valores contratuais, cronogramas de entrega e acordos estabelecidos. A segunda está vinculada aos envios de chips baseados na tecnologia Arm, em que a empresa recebe royalties a uma taxa acordada para cada lote de chips relevantes vendido pelos clientes. Os dois negócios refletem ciclos de mercado que não são inteiramente idênticos. A receita de licenciamento reflete melhor os investimentos atuais dos clientes no design de chips e no planejamento de produtos futuros, enquanto a receita de royalties está mais ligada a chips que já entraram nas fases de produção e vendas. Portanto, o negócio de licenciamento ajuda a avaliar os requisitos futuros de design dos clientes, ao passo que o negócio de royalties reflete de forma mais direta a escala real de adoção da tecnologia Arm em produtos finais. No trimestre anterior, a Arm gerou uma receita de US$ 1,289 bilhão, alta de 22% na comparação anual, registrando um recorde para um primeiro trimestre fiscal. Desse total, a receita de royalties cresceu 22%, atingindo US$ 715 milhões, enquanto a receita de licenciamento e outras receitas subiu 23%, para US$ 574 milhões. A receita de royalties proveniente de data centers mais que dobrou em relação ao ano anterior, tornando-se o destaque mais sobressalente do seu desempenho. Diferente da AMD ou da Intel, que vendem chips diretamente, a Arm depende principalmente de taxas de licenciamento e royalties para obter receita. Esse modelo significa que o crescimento da Arm em data centers depende não apenas do volume de envios de chips, mas também é influenciado pela taxa de royalties por chip. À medida que os clientes migram de arquiteturas antigas para a Armv9 e passam a adotar os Subsistemas de Computação (CSS), a Arm consegue aumentar a receita gerada por chip sem um aumento equivalente no volume de remessas de chips. A empresa revelou que a arquitetura Armv9 representa atualmente cerca de um terço da receita de royalties, o que significa que a maioria dos produtos existentes ainda opera em arquiteturas mais antigas com taxas de royalties menores. A taxa de royalties dos Subsistemas de Computação é aproximadamente o dobro daquela do licenciamento de processadores Armv9 avulsos, e produtos subsequentes podem chegar a três vezes essa taxa. Desde que as atualizações de arquitetura continuem progredindo, espera-se que a melhoria no mix de produtos atue como um dos principais motores do crescimento dos royalties nos próximos anos. No entanto, a Arm projetou que o crescimento da receita de royalties no ano fiscal de 2027 ficará na faixa superior de 15% a 20%, um pouco abaixo da meta de crescimento composto de longo prazo da empresa, de aproximadamente 20% até o ano fiscal de 2031. CPU de AGI da Arm abre novas áreas de crescimento Além de seu negócio tradicional de licenciamento de propriedade intelectual e royalties, a Arm está buscando se expandir ainda mais no segmento de produtos de chips. Em março de 2026, a empresa lançou sua primeira CPU Arm AGI para cargas de trabalho de IA agêntica, sinalizando que seu modelo de negócios não se limita mais ao licenciamento de arquitetura e à cobrança de royalties sobre chips, mas também começa a gerar receitas mais diretas ao vender seus próprios produtos de processadores. Essa mudança é de grande importância. Embora o modelo tradicional de licenciamento e royalties ofereça margens brutas mais elevadas, a Arm consegue capturar apenas uma parcela do valor na cadeia de valor de chips. artigo.texto: Holly Ridge residents weigh leaving homes as Meta Data Center construction disrupts community Neighbors report frequent water outages, rising utility bills and heavy traffic, while Meta says it enforces strict site rules and dust controls. HOLLY RIDGE, La. — Ongoing construction of the Meta data center is creating severe growing pains for Holly Ridge neighbors, driving some longtime residents to consider leaving the area entirely. Residents living directly across from the site say construction crews frequently strike underground utility lines, cutting off running water to nearby homes. Neighbors also report surging utility bills, relentless dust and heavy construction traffic that blocks residential driveways. “It’s just way more traffic and everything — more traffic, more dust,” said Kevin Dove, a Holly Ridge resident living near the project. “It’s just a whole totally different country. I mean, this is not country anymore. It’s like turning into town.” Randy Dove, who has lived on his property for more than five decades, said the heavy congestion directly interferes with his daily routine. “They don’t give no respect to let you out of your own driveway that we’ve been using our driveway for 50-something years,” he said, adding that he now plans to move. Meta stated that all project drivers must follow strict traffic regulations or face removal from the job site. The company also said crews actively manage dust levels and maintain close communication with local leaders. However, several neighbors say those measures fall short of addressing their day-to-day disruption. “We haven’t been expecting anything because they haven’t seemed to show any concern on what they’ve done,” resident Lisa Hopkins said. “Yeah, they’re giving the school scholarships and stuff and that’s great, but what have they done for the residents right here dealing with this traffic and noise every day?” Hopkins and Randy Dove both noted that the ongoing disruption is forcing an outcome they never anticipated: abandoning their roots. “We’ve done a lot here and we’ve made it home,” Hopkins said. “And the thought of having to move and start over, it’s sad. Of course we want to get out of here now because it’s not going to get any better.” “Who wants to live amongst all this here?” Dove added. “It ain’t even got started yet because it’s going to get worse as it goes throughout time. So we’re not looking forward to that, having to leave our home place, the place that we’ve known all our life.” Copyright 2026 KNOE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Questions remain after city council tightens oversight of data centers with 9-2 vote SAN ANTONIO - The city has adopted new rules that tighten oversight of data centers, a move supporters say will give residents more say in projects that can affect neighborhoods, while critics warn the changes could push jobs and investment elsewhere. City Council voted 9-2 to require public review and council approval for new data center projects. The rules took effect immediately and apply to the industry’s footprint in San Antonio, where there are 75 data centers operating or planned for operation. The changes also add restrictions on where data centers can be built and the rules they must follow. A key piece of the new policy requires projects to go before City Council for public approval before moving forward in the process. “We’re able to deliver today as the largest city in Texas to push on the best regulations possible here in the state of Texas,” Ric Galvan said after the vote. Supporters say the new rules give residents a voice amid concerns about water use, electricity demand and noise. But critics of the tighter regulations say the restrictions could drive jobs and investment out of the city. Officials with District 6 and the city’s zoning and policy staff said projects with existing permits can move forward. Councilman Marc Whyte said he understands why some residents are worried about data centers near their homes. “We know that there’s a lot of fear out there about these data centers. People don’t want them placed right in the middle of their neighborhoods, and I understand that,” Whyte said. Questions remain about whether the new rules will protect communities from issues other parts of the country have faced, whether the regulations could discourage businesses from building in San Antonio, and how the new process will work for projects already in the planning stages.

artigo.texto: A new USC Annenberg survey finds broad concern about the expansion of artificial intelligence and the infrastructure powering it, with large majorities calling for greater regulation and questioning whether technology companies and government will act in the public interest. As Americans prepare to vote in the 2026 midterm elections, these issues have emerged as a significant national concern, crossing partisan, generational and geographic lines. Nearly one-third of Americans rank AI and data centers among the three most important issues facing the country, according to a new probability-based national survey from the USC Annenberg Center for Climate Journalism and Communication utilizing the Understanding America Study. That places the issue behind only inflation and the cost of living, selected by 86% of respondents, and political polarization, selected by 35%. It ranks ahead of immigration, financial well-being, climate change, crime and unemployment. The findings suggest that as AI becomes more deeply embedded in the economy and daily life, voters are thinking not only about what the technology can do, but also about who will oversee its growth, who will benefit, and which communities will bear its costs. Seventy-six percent of respondents say the government is doing too little to regulate AI, and 77% say it is doing too little to regulate data centers. At the same time, 71% do not trust Big Tech companies at all to act in society’s best interest when it comes to data center development. Fifty-nine percent say the same of the federal government. “Our research has focused on the origins of community pushback against the expansion of data centers since the summer of 2025,” said Allison Agsten, director of USC’s Center for Climate Journalism and Communication, scholar at the Leonard D. Schaeffer Institute for Public Policy and Government Service, and executive producer of the podcast, Electric Futures. “With the midterms around the corner, the timeliness of these issues requires understanding the public’s opinions today.” Concern Extends Across Party Lines The survey reveals political differences, but it also finds a notable degree of concern across party affiliations. Democrats express the greatest skepticism: 86% say the government is doing too little to regulate AI, compared with 72% of independents and others and 68% of Republicans. Similarly, 88% of Democrats, 73% of independents and others, and 69% of Republicans say data centers are underregulated. Distrust of Big Tech is also widespread. Seventy-nine percent of Democrats, 72% of independents and others, and 61% of Republicans say they do not trust technology companies at all to act in society’s best interest when developing data centers. “Although we find that Republicans and daily users of AI are slightly less negative about AI and data centers, they are still mostly negative,” said Wändi Bruine de Bruin, Provost Professor of Public Policy, Psychology and Behavioral Science and senior scholar at the USC Schaeffer Institute for Public Policy and Government Service. The pattern extends across the country. The survey found little to no regional variation in most attitudes toward AI and data centers, indicating that the concerns are not confined to communities where new facilities have received the greatest public attention. Americans Question Who Benefits Most respondents have either negative or mixed feelings about AI: 32% describe their feelings as somewhat or very negative, while another 40% report mixed feelings. Just 20% feel somewhat or very positive. They are also skeptical about the effects of the data centers needed to support AI. Sixty percent believe data centers are somewhat or very bad for nearby communities, while 67% say they are bad for the environment. Only 13% see data centers as beneficial to nearby communities, and 7% consider them beneficial to the environment. Looking a decade ahead, 36% expect AI to have a mostly negative effect on their own lives, compared with 24% who anticipate a mostly positive effect. Nearly half expect AI to negatively affect Americans’ financial well-being, while only 16% foresee a positive effect. Opposition to data center construction is strongest close to home, with 62% opposing development in their area. But the findings suggest that this sentiment is not simply a case of residents wanting facilities built somewhere else. Forty-six percent oppose data center construction in the United States more broadly, and among those who oppose local construction, most also oppose it nationally. That distinction could become increasingly important to candidates and policymakers as data center proposals raise questions about electricity demand, water use, land development, economic growth and local control. Even Frequent AI Users Express Reservations The survey also complicates the idea that familiarity with AI necessarily translates into confidence about its broader effects. Twenty-seven percent of Americans report using AI tools daily. Daily users are more positive than people who use the technology less often, but significant concerns remain within this group. Nearly three-quarters of daily users say the government is doing too little to regulate AI, and three-quarters say the same about data centers. Among respondents who use AI at any frequency, 44% say they use it more often than they would like. Only 7% would like to increase their use. Age differences are similarly modest. Adults 45 and younger are somewhat more likely than older Americans to identify AI and data centers as a leading national concern and to oppose data center construction. Yet the two groups report nearly identical levels of distrust toward Big Tech and the federal government. A New Approach to Sharing Timely Research The findings are part of Electric Futures: AI, Data Centers, and Trust, an October 2026 survey of 2,980 Americans developed by Agsten and Charles Zukoski, former USC provost and host of the Electric Future

artigo.texto: The One-Way Street Runs the Other Way: Clinton’s WTO Forecast and the BYD Reality On March 8, 2000, President Bill Clinton went to the Paul H. Nitze School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins to make his closing argument for granting China Permanent Normal Trade Relations and supporting its entry into the World Trade Organization (Johns Hopkins Gazette). I reprinted that speech in full in The Biden Administration Confronts Global Change, and concluded there that it is hard to find any foreign policy forecast as wrong as this one. That judgment can now be tested against a single company. When China became the 143rd member of the WTO on December 11, 2001 (WTO), BYD did not build cars. It was a Shenzhen battery maker, founded in 1995 by the chemist Wang Chuanfu, that made rechargeable cells for mobile phones (CNBC). It entered the automobile business only in January 2003, when it bought a struggling carmaker, Xi’an Qinchuan Automobile, from the state-owned defense conglomerate Norinco (Wikipedia, BYD Auto). In April 2026 alone, BYD exported 135,098 vehicles, every one of them fully electric or plug-in hybrid (Yahoo Finance). BYD is, in other words, a company whose entire life as an automaker falls inside the WTO era. It is as clean a test case as one could design for the claims Clinton made in 2000. Taking those claims one at a time shows how thoroughly reality reversed them. Forecast One: “A One-Way Street” Clinton’s central economic claim was blunt: “Economically, this agreement is the equivalent of a one-way street.” China would open its markets; the United States would merely maintain the access China already enjoyed. American firms would be able to sell into China “without being forced to relocate manufacturing to China.” In his words, “We’ll be able to export products without exporting jobs” (IATP full text). The street did turn out to be one-way. It simply ran in the opposite direction. As Ross Babbage has laid out, China’s manufacturing output was half that of the United States in 2004. Twenty years later it is double, and China’s trade surplus has reached $1.2 trillion, the largest ever recorded by any country. BYD is that reversal in automotive form. SNE Research put BYD’s non-China deliveries at roughly 497,000 units in the first half of 2026, up 81 percent year on year (BYD Today). The company is targeting 1.6 million overseas sales this year, supported by new or expanding plants in Hungary, Brazil, Thailand, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Turkey (Boston Brand Media). Clinton imagined American workers building products for Chinese consumers. What emerged is a Chinese firm building factories inside other countries’ borders, with assembly jobs going to the host nation while the battery cell, the chemistry, and the software stay anchored in China. The jobs were exported. So, increasingly, is the factory. Forecast Two: No More Forced Technology Transfer Clinton told his audience that, “for the first time,” American companies would be able to sell in China without being forced to “transfer valuable technology.” The automobile sector shows how hollow that promise was. From 1994, China required foreign automakers to enter the market through joint ventures with Chinese partners and capped foreign ownership at 50 percent. The rule was designed to protect domestic players and give them access to foreign automakers’ technology (Caixin Global). WTO accession did not end it. Ten years after China joined, foreign carmakers were still “forced to team up with local partners” and could own at most half of those ventures (Reuters factbox). The cap was not lifted for passenger-car manufacturing until January 1, 2022 (International Trade Administration). The U.S. Trade Representative had long criticized the joint-venture regime as a means of forced technology transfer (HKTDC Research). The timing tells the story. Beijing opened the door to full foreign ownership only once its own electric-vehicle champions were strong enough not to need the protection. The two decades in which foreign automakers trained China’s automotive ecosystem were the same two decades in which BYD learned how to build cars. Forecast Three: The State Would Recede The most revolutionary claim in the speech was that WTO membership would push the Chinese state out of economic life. Clinton described the state-owned enterprises as “dinosaurs that are least likely to survive in the global economy.” By lowering the barriers that protected them, he said, China would be “removing government from vast areas of people’s lives,” leaving the Party with “fewer instruments” of control. The state did not recede. It changed instruments. BYD’s entry into the car business was itself a product of state and local politics. When Wang bought Qinchuan, local authorities wanted to keep the ailing factory open and preserve employment, and BYD reportedly received a large piece of land for free along with loans at marginal interest rates (CarNewsChina). That pattern then scaled up nationally. The Center for Strategic and International Studies calculates that Chinese government support for the EV sector totaled $230.9 billion from 2009 to 2023 (CSIS). CSIS calls this a highly conservative estimate, because it excludes local-government rebates, cheap land and utilities, and subsidies to the battery supply chain (Quartz). Babbage identifies four structural levers behind China’s export machine: a protected home market of 1.4 billion consumers, state subsidies the OECD estimates at three to five times those of other major economies, a currency the IMF assesses as undervalued by 20 to 40 percent, and a state apparatus of commercial intelligence, IP theft, cyber operations, and influence that works alongside Chinese firms abroad. Clinton saw a state trying to shovel coal into the furnaces of a sinking Titanic. What Beijing actually built was a state that picks the industries of the future and funds them at a scale no market competitor can match. Forec

artigo.texto: Data centers have become one of the nation’s defining political issues ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. As tech giants invest hundreds of billions of dollars to build behemoth facilities and use vast amounts of power to support their artificial intelligence race, communities have pushed back. Candidates on the federal, state and local levels have responded to data center opposition by proposing stringent regulations on the industry — and by painting their opponents as data center supporters. This contentious issue could influence the control of Congress and reshape statehouses across the country. But for all the focus on data centers on the campaign trail, industry experts say the election’s actual impact on the development boom may be less widespread than the rhetoric would suggest. In Congress, even if a wave of anti-data center Democrats take control of both chambers, they would still struggle to pass significant legislation that could receive the signature of President Donald Trump, a vocal supporter of the industry. In many states, candidates on both sides of the aisle are supporting stricter data center rules — meaning the industry is in for a tougher road no matter who wins. But there are state-level races in the key digital infrastructure markets of Texas, Pennsylvania and Georgia where candidates have staked out different positions, and the election could determine how much data center development will be allowed to move forward. Just in those three states, Morgan Stanley estimates the planned development of 284 data centers totaling more than 33 gigawatts of capacity are at risk pending the results of these races. “I don't think at the federal level the policy is going to shift much,” MOCA Economics Chief Economist Brandon Michalski told Bisnow. “If we go to the state level, that shifts dramatically and could change the trajectory significantly.” The Battle For Capitol Hill From Ohio and Michigan to Wisconsin, Texas and Maine, data centers have emerged as a major campaign issue in high-profile House and Senate races ahead of this week’s midterms. Data centers are deeply unpopular, and congressional candidates from both parties have made proposals to rein in development or limit its impacts a core element of their campaigns as voters voice growing concerns over electricity costs, environmental impacts and the broader consequences of the AI data center boom. The trend is especially visible in political advertising. As of the beginning of October, House and Senate campaigns had spent more than $29M on ads mentioning data centers, almost always negatively, according to AdImpact data analyzed by Bisnow. Although opposition to data centers cuts across party lines, Democrats have more aggressively nationalized the issue, contrasting calls for oversight of the sector with the Trump administration’s support for accelerating AI infrastructure development. Prominent congressional Democrats have already proposed measures like a national data center moratorium and released an investigation arguing that hyperscalers aren’t paying their fair share of grid costs. Now, party leaders are signaling their intent to make more aggressive oversight of the industry a prominent part of their policy agenda following the midterms, particularly if the party gains control of one or both houses of Congress. Last week, the Senate’s top Democratic tax writer announced plans to pursue an additional excise tax on data centers while eliminating the industry’s ability to tap a range of existing tax benefits tied to depreciation, research spending, opportunity zones and REIT structures. Although Republicans have also pursued measures aimed at addressing voter concerns over data centers driving up electricity prices, GOP leaders have privately acknowledged that data centers have become a winning issue for Democrats. The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned major technology and AI firms in August that Democrats were successfully making data centers the “centerpiece” of the Senate race in Ohio and that deteriorating public sentiment toward the industry was becoming a broader risk to Republican candidates specifically. “This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle,” the letter warned. The data center industry has taken notice of this partisan dynamic. AI infrastructure super PAC Leading the Future and connected groups have spent significantly more supporting Republicans than Democrats, according to Forbes, while hyperscalers and AI giants like OpenAI have reportedly ramped up lobbying in anticipation of more aggressive Democratic oversight of data center development and the AI trade. Investors and analysts focused on the data center industry have similarly warned that the potential for Democratic victories in the House and Senate poses a threat to the industry’s growth and would bring greater regulatory and political risk. “There will be congressional hearings. There will be investigations,” said Brian Gardner, chief Washington policy strategist at Stifel, according to Reuters. “You never know where that stuff leads, and there can be negative headlines.” Yet despite the rhetoric and the flood of money pouring into congressional races, not everyone is convinced that even a Democratic sweep would materially change the federal regulatory environment for data centers. A report published this week by MOCA Economics examining data center construction spending projected that Democratic control of at least one chamber would be a “nothingburger for policy.” Michalski, who authored the report, said Democrats could introduce more restrictive bills, but Trump’s veto power would make measures such as a national moratorium, sweeping new grid cost requirements or additional tax burdens extremely difficult to enact. artigo.texto: MISSOULA — Data centers are a hot and controversial topic across the country right now. Much of the controversy centers around the impacts of data centers on both human and ecological health. The University of Montana’s Bureau of Business and Economic Research (BBER) has now published a study on the economic impacts of data centers. WATCH THE VIDEO BELOW: It is solely focused on impacts to jobs, tax revenue and energy for hyperscale data centers - centers 500 Megawatts (MW) and above. Jeff Michaels, director of the BBER, says the study was largely conducted through economic modeling (through the use of REMI modeling) of what Montana may look like with differently sized hyperscale data centers. “That's the kind of facility we don't have right now in Montana. We got nothing like it. So we sort of created some models of what that could look like here and estimated, you know, job creation, income creation and a lot of work on property taxes because that's a big part of what Data centers could bring to the state,” said Jeff Michael. “The findings overall were that, we looked at data centers and in terms of their capacity,” said Michael. Michael says that depending on the size of the data center, the number of jobs created and taxes generated vary. The study looked at 500 MW increments, examining both what each increment could bring in terms of direct and construction jobs. It also had estimates for personal income growth and tax revenue generation. The study found that impacts from a 1,000 MW data center that takes four years to build could directly result in 500 construction jobs and up to 1,500 statewide jobs. Those jobs may result in up to a total personal income increase of $93 million. Once the 1,000 MW data center is fully built and furnished with several billion dollars worth of Nvidia chips, the study estimates that the data center could have 250 direct jobs at the facility and a total of 452 jobs statewide. That would result in a total personal income increase of an estimated $34.2 million. “Still a big employment generator, but maybe not in terms of thousands, but in hundreds of jobs,” said Michaels. The potential tax revenue increases would also be significant, with a 1,000 MW data center projected to generate $47 million in annual property taxes. The property tax payments could also increase with co-developed new power generation, with the potential result of $54 million. “The biggest benefit of Montana, all these jobs would be a benefit, but the biggest potential benefit in the long run would just be a huge expansion in the property tax base,” said Michaels. With that benefit to the tax base, individuals’ property taxes could see a decrease, depending on how much their county decides to mill. “A certain amount of it is sort of in statute, and that's we follow the statute, which generally results in this sort of 50-50 split of new revenue and some reduction in the mills. So that's sort of how we follow it. I mean, it would be at the discretion of the county; they could go beyond that if they wanted to,” said Michaels. He also says, however, that the increases in property taxes could vary over the years. He says this is because the billions of dollars worth of chips contained within a data center depreciate rapidly, ultimately decreasing the overall value of the property. With all of the potential monetary benefits data centers could bring, it is important to note that all the findings were under the guidance of current state law, which could change in the upcoming legislative session.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de placas de resfriamento líquido: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de placas de resfriamento líquido até 2035: demanda por servidores de data center impulsiona expansão Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de placas de resfriamento líquido, o setor entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de suprimento mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de placas de resfriamento líquido atravessa um ponto de inflexão crítico, à medida que as exigências de gestão térmica se intensificam nas indústrias de alta tecnologia. Em 2026, o segmento já superou o nicho da computação de alto desempenho e alcançou a adoção mainstream, impulsionado pelo crescimento exponencial da intensidade de dados e pela eletrificação dos transportes. As placas de resfriamento líquido, ou cold plates, são trocadores de calor especializados que fazem circular o fluido refrigerante por canais internos para absorver e transferir o calor residual de componentes com alta densidade térmica. Sua eficiência afeta diretamente o desempenho e a confiabilidade dos sistemas, o que as torna indispensáveis em servidores de data centers, baterias de veículos elétricos, eletrônica de potência e computação de alto desempenho. O período até 2035 será marcado por mudanças estruturais: o aumento da densidade de potência dos servidores, a proliferação de aceleradores de IA e a transição para arquiteturas de veículos elétricos de 800 volts exigirão projetos de placas mais avançados, incluindo variantes de microcanais e de duas fases. Os avanços em ciência dos materiais com ligas de alumínio e cobre, a usinagem de precisão e a vedação à prova de vazamentos moldarão a dinâmica competitiva. Este relatório oferece uma visão orientada por dados sobre tamanho de mercado, segmentação, cadeia de suprimentos e perspectivas regionais, proporcionando às partes interessadas um arcabouço analítico transparente para navegar por um cenário em evolução. O cenário-base para o mercado mundial de placas de resfriamento líquido projeta expansão robusta entre 2026 e 2035, com taxa de crescimento anual composta (CAGR) de 8,2%, elevando o índice de mercado a 220 em 2035 (2025=100). Essa perspectiva se apoia na aceleração da transição do resfriamento a ar para o resfriamento líquido nos data centers, onde a densidade de potência por rack ultrapassa 20 kW e torna necessário o resfriamento líquido direto no chip. O setor de veículos elétricos também dará contribuição relevante, à medida que os sistemas de gestão térmica de baterias adotam cada vez mais placas de resfriamento líquido para ampliar a capacidade de recarga rápida e prolongar a vida útil das baterias. Geograficamente, a Ásia-Pacífico manterá sua liderança, sustentada pela base industrial chinesa de veículos elétricos e eletrônicos, enquanto América do Norte e Europa registrarão crescimento acima da média, graças aos investimentos em data centers e a regulamentações rigorosas de eficiência. Restrições de oferta, incluindo a volatilidade do preço do cobre e a capacidade de usinagem de precisão, podem conter o crescimento, mas devem ser mitigadas por inovações de projeto e substituição de materiais. O mercado permanecerá moderadamente consolidado, com especialistas em gestão térmica e novos entrantes de setores adjacentes competindo com base em projeto personalizado e integração de sistemas. No conjunto, a perspectiva é positiva: os vetores de demanda superam as restrições e o mercado está posicionado para gerar valor significativo até 2035. Vetores e restrições da demanda Principais vetores de demanda - Aumento da densidade de potência dos servidores de data centers, impulsionado por IA e computação em nuvem, o que exige placas de resfriamento líquido para dissipação eficiente do calor. - Necessidades de gestão térmica das baterias de veículos elétricos, já que a recarga rápida e a maior densidade energética demandam placas de resfriamento líquido para manter a temperatura ideal. - Crescimento da computação de alto desempenho e dos aceleradores de IA, contextos em que o resfriamento a ar é insuficiente e que impulsionam a adoção de cold plates avançadas. - Confiabilidade e densidade de potência da eletrônica de potência em aplicações de energia renovável e industriais, que exigem resfriamento líquido para sistemas compactos de alta potência. - Sistemas de aviônica aeroespacial e de diagnóstico por imagem demandam estabilidade térmica precisa, viabilizada por placas de resfriamento líquido diante de restrições de tamanho, peso e potência. - Equipamentos de telecomunicações, incluindo estações-base 5G, requerem placas de resfriamento líquido para controlar o calor em ambientes externos e de alta densidade. Possíveis restrições ao crescimento - Custos iniciais elevados e maior complexidade dos sistemas de resfriamento líquido em comparação com o resfriamento a ar, o que limita a adoção em segmentos sensíveis a custo. - Riscos potenciais de vazamento e preocupações com confiabilidade, que exigem vedação e testes robustos e podem afastar usuários finais avessos a risco. - Volatilidade dos preços de matérias-primas, sobretudo cobre e alumínio, com impacto nos custos de fabricação e nas margens de lucro. - Falta de projetos padronizados e de interoperabilidade entre unidades de distribuição de refrigerante (CDUs) e placas, o que retarda a implantação. - Restrições na cadeia de suprimentos de usinagem de precisão e fabricação de microcanais, especialmente para projetos avançados de placas. artigo.texto: Michigan trails neighboring states in data center power as governor candidates discuss moratorium SAGINAW, Mich. (WNEM) - Data centers are a flashpoint in the race for Michigan’s next governor. They could affect electric bills and water and take up acres of property. A review of data from several data center research groups shows Michigan has 2.5 gigawatts of power planned, approved or running for data centers. Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, Texas and Virginia each have more. One researcher said the trend is like a gold rush. Companies are proposing hyperscale data centers across the country, but builders will finish only a fraction of them. What hyperscale data centers are Each hyperscale data center covers hundreds of acres, uses a large amount of water, and pulls a large amount of energy. Erik Nordman, director of the Institute of Public Utilities at Michigan State University, said this new generation of hyperscale data centers is causing the controversy. He said they are built specifically for artificial intelligence computing. Nordman said his institute has received interest over the past year from people in Michigan and across the country about how data centers might affect electric and water utilities. Two projects approved in Michigan Michigan has cleared two hyperscale projects. In Washtenaw County, crews are building “The Barn” for Oracle and OpenAI. Nordman said the site in Southeast Michigan will use about as much electricity as the city of Detroit, about 25% of DTE’s current load. Google plans a project called “Project Cannoli” in Wayne County. Nordman said it is based on a template Google has developed and implemented in other states. He said the template is considered one of the best practices among industry leaders. Together, the two projects will use 2.4 gigawatts of power. Both are in DTE Energy’s territory. Nordman said Michigan’s investor-owned utilities, including Consumers Energy and DTE, say they have enough electricity and resources for the initial hyperscale data center in Southeast Michigan. If more growth happens, he said, more resources would need to be built. How Michigan compares with other states The U.S. Data Center Map tracks the gigawatts powering data centers that are planned, approved or running in each state. Michigan has 2.5 gigawatts, according to the map. Michigan’s neighbors have more: - Illinois: almost 12 gigawatts - Indiana: about 10 gigawatts - Ohio: almost 19 gigawatts Nationwide, Texas leads with almost 104 gigawatts. Virginia ranks second with more than 40 gigawatts. Nordman said several factors can affect where data centers are sited. He listed the cost of electricity, access to transmission lines, available land near transmission lines, the business environment, and tax breaks. He said Michigan has community resistance to data centers, which he called a headwind for developers. He said Michigan has abundant clean water that is useful for cooling, but residents are protective of the resource. Nordman said the state’s sales and use tax incentives are meant to attract data center owners, but it is unclear whether they will be enough. Nordman said Texas has a “very liberal approach to permitting and facilities.” He said a data center can build and connect to the electric grid more easily there than in a place like Michigan. Nordman said Virginia has a lot of data centers because it is the national hub where the internet started and is connected to the Pentagon and government agencies. He said AI data centers are appearing in other places. Nordman said Michigan is lagging, but more developers could still come. He said it is hard to tell which direction those decisions will go. He said both candidates are trying to walk a fine line. He said there is grassroots dissatisfaction with how data center development has progressed in Michigan and elsewhere, but the candidates also see an economic development opportunity they don’t want Michigan to miss. Benson said, “I think data centers threaten the fabric of many of our communities, particularly our rural communities, and do threaten the possibility of driving up water rates, energy rates, and using or abusing our natural resources like our water.” She said she has called for a moratorium “until we put guardrails in place.” James said, “No new data centers until we have a plan to protect our people.” He said he has said this for a long time and on the debate stage in the primary. “Local control comes first,” James said. “And then we need to make sure our electricity bills don’t go up, that we protect our water.” Consumers Energy response Consumers Energy said earlier this year that a hyperscale data center is coming to its service area. The company declined an interview request. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call, someone asked Garrick Rochow about the candidates’ stances. Rochow is president of CMS Energy Corporation and Consumers Energy. The question was how to think about the data center opportunity window. “Politics do not equal policy,” Rochow said. “And some of the spin that you see leading up to the election does not equal reality.” Rochow said there is common ground on affordability and data centers. artigo.texto: Neopulse Energy Private Limited has been appointed as the Owner’s Engineer by Coal India Limited (CIL) for its 80 MW / 320 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project in Odisha. Its responsibilities will also include technical supervision and oversight during equipment manufacturing, project construction, testing and commissioning. The 80 MW / 320 MWh BESS project is expected to support grid flexibility and improve the integration of renewable energy into India’s electricity network. Battery storage plays an important role in managing the intermittent nature of solar and wind power while supporting reliable electricity supply. Through this appointment, Neopulse Energy will contribute its technical expertise to CIL’s expanding renewable energy and energy storage portfolio. artigo.texto: Solid-state battery race: Sunwoda tests polymer cells with automakers as CATL targets 2027 Sunwoda is advancing a polymer-composite approach to solid-state batteries as CATL pursues sulfide chemistry. The two Chinese suppliers are developing different electrolyte technologies and production timelines. Sunwoda’s latest disclosure confirms that its battery has completed design and process verification and remains under customer evaluation, while CATL continues to target small-batch production in 2027. Sunwoda Electric Vehicle Battery Co., Ltd. (SEVB), the automotive battery subsidiary of Sunwoda Electronic Co., Ltd., disclosed the update on October 30 through the Shenzhen Stock Exchange’s investor interaction platform. The company did not identify the automakers evaluating its cells or disclose sample volumes. It had already reported customer testing in May 2026, making the latest response an update on ongoing work rather than the start of a new testing programme. CATL reaffirmed its 2027 small-batch production target in an October 27 investor response. CATL previously reported its 20 Ah solid-state prototype in 2024. While CATL is developing sulfide-based cells, Sunwoda’s Xin Bixiao programme uses a polymer-composite electrolyte. Polymer cells operate at pressures below 1 MPa Sunwoda’s 20 Ah Xin Bixiao cell has a reported energy density of 400 Wh/kg and a cycle life exceeding 1,200 cycles under external pressure below 1 MPa. Its disclosed design includes a 12-micron polymer-composite membrane and a nanoscale high-entropy silicon anode. The company has also reported that the cell passed a 200°C hot-box test. The low-pressure requirement relates to maintaining contact between electrodes and the solid electrolyte as materials expand and contract during charging and discharging. Some sulfide-based designs require sustained external pressure to limit interface deterioration. Sulfide materials also require moisture-controlled manufacturing because reactions with water can release toxic hydrogen sulfide (H₂S). Sunwoda says its polymer-composite design can accommodate electrode movement while maintaining contact between cell components. Operating below 1 MPa could reduce a battery pack’s structural requirements, but the cell-level results do not show that additional support can be eliminated. The reported cycle life and thermal results also do not demonstrate equivalent performance in a complete vehicle battery. For illustration, increasing a hypothetical battery from 55 kWh to 80 kWh could raise range from 550 km CLTC (approximately 450 km WLTP) to 800 km CLTC (approximately 660 km WLTP), assuming unchanged vehicle efficiency. This is an illustrative calculation, not a Sunwoda vehicle projection. Pilot production and aviation applications SEVB has connected a solid-state battery pilot line with an annual design capacity of 0.2 GWh. Its roadmap includes a second-generation sulfide battery targeted for 2027 and a future cell exceeding 500 Wh/kg targeted for 2030. Both remain development targets, not confirmed commercial production dates. Sulfide electrolytes also cost more. Shanghai Metals Market has assessed lithium phosphorus sulfur chloride (Li₆PS₅Cl), a sulfide electrolyte, at approximately 3,500 to 4,500 yuan per kilogram, compared with around 30 to 50 yuan per kilogram for conventional liquid electrolytes. The materials are not direct substitutes, but the difference illustrates the price gap between the two materials. Sunwoda is also involved in the Guangdong Engineering Research Centre for Aviation Power Batteries, which has set a target of at least 450 Wh/kg for aviation battery cells. Its eVTOL development targets include continuous discharge power density of at least 1,000 W/kg. Aviation is one potential application for high-energy-density batteries, although the disclosed targets do not establish commercial orders or production volumes. Li Auto and Xiaomi’s battery plans The October 30 investor exchange also raised questions about Li Auto and Xiaomi developing in-house battery packs for selected models. Sunwoda said it respected customers’ decisions and would seek to expand its business through product development and service. Both automakers are also significant SEVB shareholders. Li Auto agreed to invest 2.65 billion yuan (approximately 395 million USD) for an initial 8.79% stake. Xiaomi subsequently proposed a 1.7 billion yuan (approximately 253 million USD) investment for a 5.34% stake, subject to shareholder approval. After the proposed transaction, Li Auto’s stake would fall to about 8.32%, making it the second-largest shareholder, with Xiaomi third. Neither company has been identified as an evaluator of the current solid-state samples. Their in-house battery plans provide commercial context, but do not establish lost orders or a direct connection to Sunwoda’s solid-state development. Next steps include vehicle-level validation and repeatable production. Sunwoda’s polymer approach offers an alternative to sulfide chemistry, but manufacturing yield, cost, durability and pack integration will determine its commercial prospects.

artigo.texto: Coal India Limited (CIL) has appointed Neopulse Energy Pvt. Ltd. as the Owner’s Engineer for its 80 MW / 320 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project in Odisha. CIL awarded the contract a month after issuing the BESS tender for the project in Odisha. With this, CIL continues the trend of PSU's counting on external expertise when it comes to renewable energy projects. Other than NTPC through NTPC Green, most PSU's have usually struggled to execute green projects on their own. As CIL expands its renewable energy and energy storage portfolio, Neopulse will provide independent technical support across both stages of the Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contract. Under the pre-award scope, Neopulse will undertake technical specifications, define equipment requirements, and provide technical bid evaluation support for EPC tendering. As part of the post-award scope, Neopulse Energy will review the EPC contractor’s engineering designs, vendor documents, and quality plans. It will also provide technical oversight during manufacturing, construction, testing, and commissioning of the energy storage system. These activities are central to ensuring the project's technical compliance and supporting the integration of more renewable energy into India's grid. About The Tender The BESS tender issued for this project is spread across four locations in Odisha—Bhatli, Basta, Padampur, and New Bolangir. It also provides for 15 years of comprehensive Operation and Maintenance (O&M). For developing the BESS system and its associated power evacuation infrastructure, the EPC contractor is required to undertake the entire scope of work. Under the contract, the contractor will be responsible for setting up the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and making the energy storage facility available to GRIDCO on an 'on-demand' basis. Earlier this year, SECI, on behalf of GRIDCO, had initiated and awarded a tender for a 500 MWh (125 MW x 4 hours) grid-connected Battery Energy Storage System project. Subsequently, GRIDCO issued a Letter of Award (LoA) to Coal India Limited on April 30, 2026, for developing a 40 MW / 160 MWh BESS project across two locations in Odisha. The project comprises a 20 MW / 80 MWh BESS connected to the 132/33 kV GSS Padampur and another 20 MW / 80 MWh BESS at OPTCL's 220/132/33 kV GSS New Bolangir.

artigo.texto: HIZENERGY, a China-based supplier of commercial and industrial (C&I) BESS solutions, has presented its C&I BESS portfolio in a keynote presentation at Frankfurt, Germany. The portfolio is led by the ENERBOX series, which is an all-in-one AC-coupled cabinet with 125 kW of power and 261 kWh or 313 kWh of energy capacity. That capacity can be expanded by connecting the cabinets in parallel, and each unit can be operated on the grid, off the grid or with a seamless switch between them. The units have passed UL 9540A safety testing, and they can be fully commissioned on site within two hours. They are intended for factories, industrial parks and commercial premises, where they can be used for PV self-consumption, peak shaving, energy arbitrage and critical-load backup. These sites are being supported from a central hub in the Netherlands and through 12 after-sales service points in Europe, where the company has live deployments. artigo.texto: CNTE Named in BloombergNEF's Q4 2026 Tier 1 Energy Storage Manufacturers LONDON, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Contemporary Nebula Technology Energy Co., Ltd. (CNTE) has been included in BloombergNEF's (BNEF) Q4 2026 Tier 1 Energy Storage Manufacturers List, marking an important milestone in its global expansion and growing international market recognition. BloombergNEF's Tier 1 classification is a widely recognized industry benchmark based on manufacturers' commercial project deployment records, including project scale, independent customer relationships, and verified project experience. As project bankability and delivery capabilities become increasingly important, the classification provides a valuable reference for developers, investors, and industry stakeholders. CNTE's inclusion reflects its expanding international project experience and growing market acceptance, highlighting its continued progress in the global energy storage industry. Full-Scenario Energy Storage Solutions and Global Deployment Established in 2019 with investment from CATL, a global leader in battery technology, CNTE provides full-scenario energy storage solutions covering power generation, grid, and end-user applications, including utility-scale storage, commercial and industrial systems, microgrids, and integrated energy storage and EV charging solutions. CNTE has successfully delivered multiple utility-scale energy storage projects across Europe, particularly in Germany, demonstrating its capabilities in system integration and international project execution. Looking ahead, CNTE will continue advancing energy storage innovation, strengthening global partnerships, and expanding localized service capabilities to support renewable energy integration and the global energy transition. Who We Are CNTE (Contemporary Nebula Technology Energy) was founded in 2019 by Mr. Huang Shilin, co-founder of CATL, and today its second-largest shareholder. We integrate CATL LFP cells into complete systems in-house, with 12 GWh of production capacity, more than 10 GWh shipped worldwide across 2,600+ projects, a European service centre and a 500 MWh project reference in Germany.

artigo.texto: [SMM ESS Flash] CATL Opens Argentina Office and Supplies 1,025 MWh to Central Puerto CATL has opened a commercial and technical office in Buenos Aires staffed for sales, engineering and project management, and is already supplying batteries to two Central Puerto projects totalling 205 MW and 1,025 MWh of storage capacity. The projects are Nuevo Puerto at 150 MW/750 MWh and Central Costanera at 55 MW/275 MWh, both using CATL lithium iron phosphate batteries with five-hour duration and both awarded under the AlmaGBA storage programme, with Nuevo Puerto holding a 15-year supply contract with distributor Edenor and Central Costanera serving Edesur. Nuevo Puerto is close to 80% complete, and Central Puerto plans to energise one project before the end of 2026 and the other in January 2027, with batteries installed but commissioning dependent on transformers from China delayed in transit. Argentina has awarded 713 MW under AlmaGBA and a further 700.5 MW across 20 projects under AlmaSADI at an estimated investment of US$700 million, while CATL says it has more than 15 GWh of awarded storage projects in Latin America and has shipped over 330 GWh of energy storage batteries globally to June 2026.

artigo.texto: Five key takeaways from the renewable energy company's September-quarter results Juniper Green Energy reported consolidated revenue from operations of ₹344.66 crore in Q2 FY27, up 2.4 times year-on-year, while EBITDA rose 2.6 times to ₹339.55 crore. Total income increased 132% to ₹371.64 crore, and EBITDA margin expanded to 91.36% from 81.02% a year earlier. The company posted a consolidated profit after tax (PAT) of ₹53.56 crore, against a loss of ₹18.40 crore in Q2 FY26. Cash PAT rose 3.9 times to ₹152.55 crore. The results point to five key developments. 1. Operating scale is driving record earnings The sharp increase in revenue and EBITDA reflects the expansion of Juniper's operating portfolio. The company commissioned 1,036 MWp of renewable energy capacity and around 503 MWh of BESS during the first seven months of FY27. Its operational portfolio has reached 2,844 MWp of renewable capacity and 604 MWh of BESS. 2. Profitability is improving, but financing remains a major cost While EBITDA rose sharply, consolidated finance costs increased to ₹201.14 crore in Q2 FY27 from ₹96.52 crore a year earlier. Depreciation also rose to ₹98.99 crore from ₹57.99 crore. A rising interest rate cycle could impact those numbers further. With the capital-intensive nature of the business, the company's ability to translate operating earnings into sustained net profit will remain an important indicator as its portfolio expands. 3. BESS is emerging as a major growth driver Juniper is targeting approximately 4,500 MWh of BESS installations by June 2027 and 10,000 MWh by March 2028. Its total portfolio already includes 8,989 MWh of BESS capacity, operational and under construction. The targets point to a substantial expansion of storage alongside renewable generation, although the company has not provided a separate revenue or earnings outlook for the storage business. 4. A large project pipeline offers visibility Juniper's total portfolio stands at 11,218 MWp of renewable capacity and 8,989 MWh of BESS. The company says 98% of its portfolio is secured through long-term power purchase agreements, typically spanning 25 years, while 98% of offtakers carry ratings of A or above. It also has surplus grid connectivity of more than 5,200 MW available for future bids. 5. Growth continues to demand substantial capital Juniper has incurred ₹18,895 crore in cumulative capital expenditure through September 2026, including ₹2,591 crore in Q2 alone. Its consolidated borrowings remain substantial, reflecting the investment required to build its operating portfolio. The company also received an upgrade in its credit rating to AA- (Stable) from ICRA.

artigo.texto: Humanoid robots are an emerging technology that promises to revolutionize society. Designed and modeled on the human form, humanoid robots can navigate a world made for humans, and it is their versatility that sets them apart from specialized robots, such as automated guided vehicles (AGVs). Similar to AGVs, humanoid robots need an energy source that can reliably supply power to ensure full operation for as long as required. While current battery technology has been successful in demonstrating humanoid robot potential, IDTechEx’s new report Batteries for Humanoid Robots 2027-2037: Technologies, Players, and Forecasts focuses on the technologies that will lead humanoid robots into widespread adoption in the market, reaching 10.5 GWh of battery demand by 2037. IDTechEx highlights the suitability of current and emerging battery chemistries for humanoid robots. The comparisons illustrate trade-offs between battery performance and technological maturity across different chemistries. Which battery technologies are employed in humanoid robots today? The energy density of a battery used to power a humanoid robot needs to be high enough that it can complete power-intensive tasks and continue operating afterwards. Currently, NMC-based lithium-ion batteries are the most common technology employed by humanoid robots. They balance a suitably high energy density with the prerequisite specifications of humanoids, that is that they require batteries with the potential to be fast-charged, a good cycle life, and a technology mature enough that they are already, or close to being, commercialized. The energy density of NMC cathodes can also be improved by increasing the nickel-content in the cathode, which can boost performance and reduce dependence on costly and supply-constrained cobalt. LFP cathodes are a chemistry considered not energy dense enough to be able to support the general demand of humanoid robots. Since NMC batteries are widely adopted for use in a plethora of other applications, NMC-based lithium-ion batteries are in great supply to support the growth of the humanoid robot market today, and beyond. IDTechEx’s new “Batteries for Humanoid Robots 2027-2037: Technologies, Players, and Forecasts” report compares lithium-ion NMC cathode chemistries (mid-, high-, and ultra high-nickel) as current technology that can support humanoid robot growth. The report also assesses solid-state and lithium-sulfur batteries as key future technology options for implementation in humanoid robots. What are the benefits of adopting emerging technologies? Solid-state Solid-state batteries are a technology that has seen huge capital investment in their development, especially from the automotive industry. A solid-state battery differs from a conventional lithium-ion cell in so much as it removes the liquid electrolyte and replaces it with a solid one. The cell is then composed of an anode, a cathode and solid electrolyte, which also removes the need for a separator. The benefit of using solid-state batteries is primarily their increased energy density of~400-500+ Wh/kg. Lithium metal, which has a high specific capacity, can be utilized as the anode and paired with high-voltage, high-energy-density cathodes (including NMC), thereby increasing the overall energy density of the cell. The removal of the flammable electrolyte improves the overall safety of the cell. Since humanoid robots will operate in close proximity to humans, enhancing safety will reduce the harm to humans in the case of cell failure. In addition, removing the separator allows for tighter packing of materials in the cell, which can improve volumetric energy density. This means a greater proportion of the battery volume within the humanoid can be occupied by active material, enabling the storage of more energy and an extension of operational capacity. However, mass production of solid-state batteries is not due to begin until the end of the 2020’s with key battery manufacturers such as BYD and Toyota driving this. With no scalable production of reliable solid electrolytes, and problems with the interface contact between the electrode and solid electrolyte, the adoption of solid-state batteries into humanoid robots is still some years away; however, it is a matter of when, not if, they will be adopted. Lithium-sulfur Lithium-sulfur cells also employ a lithium metal anode which is paired with a carbon/sulfur cathode. Together, these deliver a high theoretical energy density, which translate to longer operational times for the humanoid. This is also one of the key drivers for humanoid manufacturers opting for lithium-sulfur over solid-state in the future. Moreover, their potential to lower the overall cost of the battery due to the use of abundant and cheap sulfur in the lithium-sulfur cathode also makes them an attractive alternative to solid state batteries will include more complex materials. However, there exist many limitations to their widespread adoption, including poor cycle lives and an inability to withstand fast charging – both caused by a parasitic process termed “polysulfide-shuttle”. This triggers prolonged and sometimes rapid degradation of the cell by reducing the amount of active material over successive cycles. The consequence for the humanoid will be more frequent replacements of the battery packs. The continued research and development of lithium-sulfur batteries is crucial to overcoming this effect. Their commercialization is not expected until the early 2030’s leading to them making up only a small amount of the market by 2037. Main image: Courtesy of Longsing Energy
