The global flow battery market is transitioning from a niche, demonstration-phase technology to a commercially bankable solution for long-duration energy storage (LDES), driven by the structural inadequacy of lithium-ion batteries for applications exceeding 4-6 hours. Demand is architecting around utility-scale renewable integration mandates and grid modernization projects, where the technology's inherent safety, long cycle life, and power/energy decoupling offer a compelling total cost of ownership proposition over a 20-year asset life. Supply chain resilience is a critical vulnerability, with key electrolyte materials (vanadium, organic compounds) and specialized components (membranes, pumps, stack assemblies) facing concentration risks, scale-up challenges, and qualification timelines that lag behind demand projections. Project economics are dominated by upfront capital expenditure, with electrolyte cost representing a significant, recoverable portion of the system value. Bankability hinges on proven system performance, robust warranties, and the credibility of off-take agreements for ancillary grid services. The competitive landscape is bifurcating between vertically integrated technology developers controlling core IP (electrolyte, stack) and system integrators/EPCs specializing in balance-of-plant engineering, grid interconnection, and project delivery. Geographic deployment is clustering in regions with aggressive renewable penetration targets, supportive LDES policy mechanisms, and grids experiencing congestion or stability challenges, creating distinct demand hubs. Safety and standardization are emerging as key market enablers. The non-flammable aqueous electrolyte of most flow batteries significantly reduces fire suppression costs and insurance premiums, but a lack of uniform international standards for performance reporting and testing creates friction in procurement. The technology stack's success is inextricably linked to the power conversion system and energy management system. Efficiency losses at the PCS and suboptimal control logic can erode the core economic advantages, making integrator expertise a critical differentiator. Investors and developers must model scenarios based on electrolyte price volatility, local content requirements, and the evolving policy landscape for long-duration storage procurement. The baseline scenario for the global flow battery market through 2035 anticipates robust expansion, with deployment accelerating as utilities and grid operators increasingly recognize the limitations of lithium-ion chemistry for long-duration applications. The market is forecast to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 15.2% from 2026 to 2035, reaching a market index of 410 by 2035 (2025=100). This growth is underpinned by the structural need for storage durations exceeding 4-6 hours, where flow batteries' independent scaling of power and energy capacity provides a distinct cost advantage. The baseline assumes continued policy support in key markets, particularly China, the United States, and Europe, where LDES procurement targets and capacity remuneration mechanisms are being established. However, the pace of manufacturing scale-up and the industry's ability to standardize modular systems will determine the actual growth trajectory. Project economics will improve as electrolyte leasing models and recycling infrastructure mature, reducing upfront capital burdens. The competitive landscape will see consolidation among technology developers, with vertically integrated players controlling core IP gaining market share. Geographically, Asia-Pacific will maintain its dominance, driven by China's aggressive renewable build-out and grid modernization investments, while North America and Europe will see accelerated deployment supported by policy frameworks. artigo.texto: Marvell compra Lumentum em negócio de US$ 115 bilhões em aposta no mercado de data centers para IA A Marvell Technology anunciou um acordo para comprar a fabricante de componentes ópticos Lumentum em uma transação de US$ 115 bilhões inteiramente em ações, incluindo dívidas, à medida que a fabricante de chips personalizados intensifica seu desafio à rival de maior porte, a Broadcom , em meio a um boom de gastos com inteligência artificial (IA). O negócio, anunciado nesta segunda-feira, é um dos maiores de 2026 e está entre as apostas corporativas mais ousadas até agora no boom da IA, que os executivos do setor de chips esperam que sustente a demanda da indústria por muitos anos. Ao adquirir a Lumentum — uma empresa com cerca de metade do seu tamanho —, a Marvell aposta que o boom de gastos com IA das grandes empresas de tecnologia veio para ficar e que a demanda por componentes ópticos usados para transmitir dados em alta velocidade continuará superando a oferta. Segundo o acordo, a Marvell pagará US$ 1.132 por ação em ações, um prêmio de 23,9% em relação ao último preço de fechamento não afetado da Lumentum em 28 de outubro, antes que as negociações fossem divulgadas pela primeira vez. Isso confere ao negócio um valor patrimonial de US$ 102,54 bilhões. A Marvell afirmou que a transação ampliará o mercado total acessível da empresa resultante da fusão para US$ 550 bilhões. Suas ações subiram 2,8% no pré-mercado, enquanto as negociações com as ações da Lumentum foram suspensas. A Nvidia , gigante dos chips de IA, investiu US$ 2 bilhões tanto na Marvell quanto na Lumentum no início deste ano. Há apenas três anos, a Marvell era uma fabricante de chips relativamente desconhecida. Mas, desde então, seu valor de mercado disparou para mais de US$ 170 bilhões, graças ao seu papel em ajudar gigantes da tecnologia, como a Amazon , a desenvolver chips de IA personalizados e tecnologia de rede para data centers. O acordo firmado nesta segunda-feira também pode fortalecer ainda mais a Marvell em sua disputa com a rival Broadcom, que há muito tempo é a principal parceira de chips personalizados do Google, de propriedade da Alphabet , e oferece aos clientes uma gama mais ampla de hardware de IA para data centers sob o mesmo teto. A Marvell conquistou uma de suas maiores vitórias em agosto, ao assinar um acordo para fornecer chips que atuam em conjunto com os processadores de IA do Google, com um valor de vendas de até US$ 120 bilhões até o ano fiscal de 2033, concedendo ao gigante das buscas o direito de adquirir uma participação de US$12,2 bilhões.

artigo.texto: From Carbon Compliance To Carbon Commerce: India’s Market Enters A New Phase India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme is shifting emissions management from voluntary ESG reporting to a regulatory requirement, creating new compliance obligations and potential revenue opportunities for businesses A few years ago, if you asked a company why it was buying carbon credits, the genuine answer would be "to look good." Carbon Credits were added to the company’s annual Sustainability Report alongside the tree planting picture so that the ESG slide deck felt finished. And that era is over and it’s going to end much quicker in India than most people realize. The change is not philosophical. It is regulatory, and it has a timeline attached to it. On 28 June 2023 the Ministry of Power announced the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, 2023 under section 14(w) of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001, which set the stage for what has now become the Indian Carbon Market. The Offset Mechanism, which was a second track to be added by amendment in December 2023, enables non-obligated companies to submit voluntary emission reduction, removal or avoidance projects and earn tradable credits. CCTS idea was that energy-intensive firms to be assigned a target for greenhouse gas emitted per unit of output, firms that meet the target earn tradable Carbon Credit Certificates, and firms that do not meet it must buy certificates or pay a penalty. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) had set binding emission intensity targets for 7 energy-intensive sectors, aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp and paper, petroleum refining, petrochemicals and textiles, and more than 490 industrial entities from 2025-26 compliance year. Two more sectors, iron and steel and fertilisers, were also incorporated, taking the overall number to 740 companies and more than 700 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent, making it the biggest emissions trading systems in the world. Cement is a good place to see what this shift means on the ground. The sector accounts for about 177 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent a year, or about 6 per cent of India’s industrial output, and that’s through 186 companies. These plants are now required to set emission intensity targets, which typically start with 2 to 3 per cent cut in 2025-26 and can increase to 3 to 15 per cent the following year, depending on the sub-sector. Steel has a similar challenge. Plants doing blast-furnace basic-oxygen-furnace are benchmarked against 1.46 tonnes of CO2 equivalent per tonne of crude steel and the targets only get tighter from here on out. As Carbon Credit Trading Schemes (CCTS) take shape globally, adherence will increasingly influence how Indian companies compete in export markets. The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) contains a carbon-linked tariff on cement, steel, aluminium, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity from countries that do not price carbon domestically. By putting a domestic price on those sectors, CCTS gives Indian exporters a way to show they are already paying for their emissions at home, which directly lowers what they owe at the EU border. For emissions-intensive industries, building carbon efficiency and credible emissions management into operations can become a strategic advantage—helping businesses meet evolving international requirements, protect market access and strengthen their position in global supply chains and is more than compliance departments. The international carbon credit market is opening up a significant opportunity, with India’s emerging partnership with Japan offering one of the first real examples of how this market could evolve. On 8 June 2026, the two countries signed the Rules of Implementation for their Joint Crediting Mechanism, a joint effort under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement providing Indian project developers with a way to bring in Japanese investment and technology for renewable energy, green hydrogen, sustainable aviation fuel and carbon capture and to issue credits that both countries can count on when it comes to meeting their own climate targets. It’s the sort of bilateral plumbing that seems dry initially until you realise that it is the money that gets into projects. Green hydrogen is where this gets interesting for Indian industry. Companies like Reliance Industries, Indian Oil and Adani Enterprises already have serious investment in this area. Government officials have also said that India is in talks with Japan and other partners on bilateral deals to link carbon credits with green hydrogen production in exchange for investment and firm offtake. In that case, if these deals actually happen, they solve two problems for a hydrogen developer at once: the buyer for the credits and the buyer for the fuel. All of this doesn’t work if the credits are not credible, and the market has learned that lesson the hard way. Years of loosely verified offsets, double-counted reductions and vague methodology have made buyers far more wary of what they are actually purchasing. The response in India has been to put verification into the system itself, satellite monitoring, digital registries and third-party validation are now standard features instead of nice-to-have features, and CCTS’s offset mechanism has been designed to be accessible to small project developers and rural communities, not just large industrial players at the heart of compliance. For a company that is producing verified emission reductions, such as renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, ecosystem restoration or industrial decarbonisation, credits have become a revenue line that investors would like to see properly modelled - not just a footnote. And for the energy-hungry companies that are now in CCTS, it is no longer whether to be active in carbon markets. artigo.texto: Contemporary Amperex Technology stock retains EV battery lead at 39.1% Published on 11/02/2026 at 09:04 | Editorial responsibility: Rafael Müller, Editor-in-Chief AD HOC NEWS Global battery demand stays strong - CATL's battery installations grew faster than the global market through September. - CATL continued expanding its overseas automaker customer base while retaining a substantial lead over BYD. - Chinese manufacturers increased their combined presence among the world's leading battery suppliers. Contemporary Amperex Technology retained its position as the world's largest electric-vehicle battery maker through September, according to CnEVPost, which cited figures from South Korean market researcher SNE Research published on Monday, November 2, 2026. CATL widens its global lead CATL recorded 389.2 gigawatt-hours of battery installations in the first nine months of 2026, up 24.9 percent from a year earlier. Its global share reached 39.1 percent, compared with 37.5 percent in the same period of 2025. Global battery usage rose 19.7 percent to 994.5 gigawatt-hours during the period. CATL therefore expanded faster than the overall market, although its share slipped from 39.4 percent in January through August as September growth moderated. Chinese suppliers dominate rankings BYD ranked second with 150.9 gigawatt-hours of installations and a 15.2 percent share. CATL and BYD together accounted for 54.3 percent of global usage, while seven Chinese companies in the top ten held a combined 73.0 percent. The market data also showed a widening difference in business exposure. SNE Research said CATL continued to expand its overseas automaker customer base, while BYD's battery supply remained largely linked to its own vehicle sales. CATL's lead is therefore supported by both scale and a broader customer mix, but monthly share movements underline the competitive pressure in China's battery market. Investor focus shifts to execution The figures strengthen CATL's standing in a growing global market, yet the slower September expansion and intense competition remain relevant for investors. The company's ability to convert international demand into profitable production will be important as Chinese battery makers compete for automaker contracts and energy-storage growth. China's broader market backdrop can be followed through current reports on the Shanghai Composite. More news and analyses on Contemporary Amperex Technology stock are available in the CATL stock topic. artigo.texto: Chemists have developed a graphene-armoured anode designed to overcome sodium-ion batteries’ trade-off between charging speed and lifespan. Interest in sodium-ion batteries has grown in recent years as researchers seek more sustainable alternatives to lithium-ion technology. Sodium is approximately 1000 times more abundant than lithium, potentially easing supply-chain constraints and reducing battery costs, although overall environmental impact depends on other components in the battery, supply chains and manufacturing. Sodium-ion batteries also offer several advantages, including high power output, rapid charging and reliable operation at low temperatures. However, sodium-ion batteries currently still exhibit lower power density and energy density than their lithium-ion counterparts. Researchers in China have now addressed this trade-off by using ultrathin nanosheets of titanium dioxide wrapped in a graphene-based protective shell to create a battery anode. This offers a potential route to high-power sodium-ion batteries, with the key advance being not a new battery ingredient but a structural design that combines fast charging and long life under more demanding electrode conditions. This architecture, says Wei Li at Fudan University, China, does several jobs at once. The nanosheets allow sodium ions to move in and out easily, helping the electrode charge and discharge quickly, while the graphene coating improves electrical conductivity and helps protect the anode’s structure. ‘Our design combines fast energy storage with long cycle life, even when considerably more active material is packed onto the electrode,’ he adds. In tests, the electrode retained more than 90% of its capacity after 3000 cycles at a relatively high active-material loading. ‘Practical charging speed also depends on the cathode electrode and electrolyte,’ says Li. ‘Both must keep pace with our electrode and remain stable during repeated fast charging.’ The anode was made using established processing steps: forming the particles, coating them with carbon and heat-treating the material. ‘However, familiarity does not establish industrial scalability,’ says Li. ‘Maintaining the same thin sheets and uniform graphene wrapping across large batches remains unproven. We would need to demonstrate consistent quality, yield and performance using larger equipment, while assessing energy use and processing costs.’ Tengfei Song, a research fellow at the University of Birmingham, UK, who was not involved in the study, agrees. ‘This is a strong piece of fundamental research,’ he says. ‘The authors show that careful nanoscale and interfacial design can give a titanium dioxide anode unusually fast sodium-ion storage kinetics and very long cycle life, even at relatively high mass loading. However, I would see it mainly as a high-power materials concept rather than a commercially ready anode material.’ Although the material’s large surface area helps it store sodium quickly, it could make manufacturing more difficult and costly at scale, Song adds. ‘The main next step would be testing under more realistic full-cell conditions,’ says Song. This would mean testing the material in larger batteries, using practical amounts of active material and without the need for extra sodium to compensate for early losses. A test cell to emulate a normal battery environment would help establish whether the anode’s fast charging and long cycle life translate into useful energy storage in a practical battery, he concludes. References Y Wan et al, J. Am. Chem. Soc., 2026, DOI: 10.1021/jacs.6c13892

artigo.texto: Global energy storage owner-operator BW ESS has started commercial operations for the first phase of its Hams Hall battery energy storage system (BESS) in the West Midlands. The milestone brings 350 MW/1243 MWh of storage capacity into commercial operation, the largest BESS by storage capacity (MWh) in Europe and a significant step forward in the delivery of infrastructure supporting the UK’s transition to a cleaner, more resilient energy system. Located adjacent to National Grid’s Hams Hall substation, the project will help balance variable electricity demand and intermittent renewable generation, supporting greater integration of renewable energy while strengthening grid resilience and energy security. The project reached commercial operation just 20 days after energisation. From commissioning and testing to operational readiness, BW ESS worked closely with partners including Sungrow, Energy-IO, National Grid, and NESO. Achieving this milestone safely and efficiently reflects the engineering expertise, rigorous preparation, and close co-ordination behind Hams Hall, as well as the technical capability and commitment of everyone involved. Hams Hall’s capacity will increase to 400 MW/1424 MWh following completion of its second phase. At full capacity, the project will be capable of supporting the electricity needs of around 1.3 million homes for up to 3.5 hours, which is approximately equivalent to the number of households across Greater Manchester. Erik Strømsø, CEO and Co-Founder of BW ESS, commented: “The start of commercial operations at Hams Hall is a landmark moment for BW ESS and a significant addition to Europe’s energy infrastructure. The project was built and commissioned on budget and ahead of schedule, which is a remarkable achievement for a system of this scale and complexity and a testament to the dedication and expertise of our team, and the commitment and collaboration of our partners.” Long-term revenues for the project are underpinned by a 10-year floor and optimisation agreement with EDF and financing was recently secured from lenders OCBC, Rabobank, and Société Générale. Hams Hall forms part of BW ESS’ 2.6 GWh Ardenham portfolio, co-owned with leading energy and decarbonisation investor AIP Management. Its entry into commercial operations expands BW ESS’ operating presence in the UK, alongside the 331 MWh Bramley BESS in Hampshire. The company also has 857 MWh under construction at Berkswell and a broader UK development pipeline spanning multiple gigawatt hours. artigo.texto: Italy connected 1.74 GW of new solar photovoltaic (PV) capacity in the third quarter of 2026, registering a 37% increase compared to the 1.269 GW added during the same period in 2025. The country’s solar market continued to expand during the first nine months of the year, with total new installations reaching 4.834 GW through 147,632 newly connected systems. According to data compiled by ITALIA SOLARE from Terna’s Gaudì database, Italy had 2,314,113 connected photovoltaic systems as of September 30, 2026, representing a cumulative installed capacity of 48.347 GW. During the third quarter alone, 58,459 new systems were connected, compared to 38,660 in the previous quarter, marking a 34% increase. Newly connected capacity also increased by 5% compared to the second quarter. The growth was mainly driven by utility-scale and commercial and industrial (C&I) installations. During the first nine months of 2026, utility-scale projects with capacities of 1 MW and above added 2,241 MW through 473 installations, accounting for 46% of the total new capacity. The C&I segment, covering systems between 20 kW and 1 MW, contributed 1,697 MW from 11,905 installations, representing 35%. Residential installations of up to 20 kW added 897 MW through 135,254 connections, accounting for 19%. During the third quarter, utility-scale installations contributed 858 MW, including 394 MW from projects between 1 MW and 10 MW and 464 MW from projects above 10 MW. C&I installations added 543 MW, while residential systems contributed 341 MW. Geographically, Sicily led Italy in newly connected solar capacity during the first nine months, adding 686 MW. Lombardy followed with 644 MW, ahead of Piedmont with 498 MW, Veneto with 463 MW, Emilia-Romagna with 443 MW and Lazio with 432 MW. Lombardy recorded the highest number of new installations, with 22,999 systems, followed by Veneto with 18,099. Italy’s energy storage market also continued to expand, approaching the 20 GWh milestone. By September 30, 2026, the country had connected 984,829 electrochemical storage systems with a combined capacity of 19,983 MWh and a power output of 8,338 MW. Of the total capacity, 12,552 MWh was associated with photovoltaic installations, while 7,368 MWh came from standalone storage systems. During the first nine months, 1,953 MWh of new storage capacity was connected, including 1,486 MWh associated with solar installations and 467 MWh from standalone systems. In the third quarter, photovoltaic-linked storage added 480 MWh of capacity and 252 MW of power through 31,039 new connections. This represented a 15% increase in capacity compared to the same quarter in 2025. Lombardy also led the photovoltaic-linked storage segment, adding 206 MWh during the first nine months, followed by Emilia-Romagna with 155 MWh, Veneto with 146 MWh and Sicily with 144 MWh. ITALIA SOLARE highlighted the growing importance of utility-scale solar and energy storage in Italy’s energy transition, while emphasising the need to continue supporting distributed generation, self-consumption and regulatory improvements to accelerate storage deployment. artigo.texto: In the summer of 2025, upon announcing a $20 billion investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure from tech giant Amazon, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro declared the commonwealth was “all in on AI.” The democratic governor said data centers would become “the largest sector investment in the history of Pennsylvania” and lead to hundreds of high-paying jobs and new revenue for local communities. But, four years earlier, in 2021, Pennsylvania put in motion an incentive to attract data center buildout that would also deprive the state of critical income — a tax exemption program that eliminates the 6% sales tax and use tax on computer equipment purchases by eligible data centers. The Computer Data Center Equipment Exemption Program started as a tax refund initiative, requiring companies to pay sales tax before requesting reimbursement by the state government. It originally came with a cap of $5 million each year and took effect in 2017 under Gov. Wolf’s administration. Act 25 of 2021 replaced that with a tax exemption program, meaning no sales tax would be paid at all for eligible purchases. The change made the program “less transparent and less accountable,” said researcher Kasia Tarczynska from the non-profit Good Jobs First. She said, under the previous design, public officials knew more about the actual cost of the program. To qualify, the state requires operators of data centers to invest millions. In a host county with less than 250,000 residents, a minimum of $75 million in new spending is required, along with 25 jobs created. In more populated counties, that figure goes up to $100 million and 45 jobs. The companies are also required to compensate workers at least $1 million every year. Right now, according to the Department of Revenue, 16 data center facilities in development or already operating in Pennsylvania hold these active certificates. In exchange for the data center investment, the state estimated that it would lose nearly $1.9 billion in tax revenue over seven fiscal years starting in 2024-25. That’s according to a February 2026 report by the Department of Revenue. At that time, there were just 12 companies holding the exemption. The department told the News Lab in an email that the state doesn’t have a direct way of tracking these losses. One thing the department referenced was expenditure reports produced by Ohio’s statement government. But Tarczynska said a lot of states are underestimating how much revenue they are losing to these programs. In 2025, Ohio’s own data center tax break cost $1.6 billion, which was eleven times more than the original estimate of $136 million, according to the Associated Press. When data centers come to town In November 2024, Governor Shapiro introduced and signed an executive order that launched his PA Permit Fast Track program. The initiative, meant to streamline state approvals for development and promised economic growth, featured Project Hazelnut in Luzerne County, a data center site owned by NorthPoint Development. Amazon Web Services was later revealed as the end user. NorthPoint Development’s vice president of development Brian Stahl joined Shapiro for the ceremonial signing of the executive order. “This really was his baby,” Ginny Marcille-Kerslake, a senior organizer with Food and Water Watch Pennsylvania, said, referring to Shapiro. Marcille-Kerslake said Shapiro’s initiative sped up state permitting for the developer to bypass local approval. At the 1,300-acre site in Hazle Township, NorthPoint allegedly cut down hundreds of acres of woodland. “That is a real failure of our state government to allow that to happen,” Marcille-Kerslake said. Ashley Bahrt was born and raised in the Hazleton area, which has quickly become one of the epicenters of data center development in Pennsylvania. Over the past year, she found herself fighting the construction of Project Hazelnut. Bahrt said she remembered the day she saw the trees cleared. “The visual reality of what was to come,” she said, “It just, like, stopped me in my tracks.” With Marcille-Kerslake’s help, Bahrt got involved. She attended public meetings at Hazle Township to ask questions about Project Hazelnut. She learned about the state’s open records law and how to file a request. Eventually, Bahrt found what she believed to be a violation of the local zoning ordinance and brought the issue to Hazle Township’s Board of Supervisors. At that point, Project Hazelnut already received more than a dozen state permits. Amazon, as the operator of the site, had been awarded a tax exemption certificate for the facility. Regardless, the township denied NorthPoint Development a zoning approval, halting the project. “Community involvement that should have been awarded through public zoning hearings … that was never given to us,” Bahrt said. “Nobody really knew what was going on until it was the final hour.” NorthPoint sued, and the county court upheld the township’s decision. NorthPoint has appealed that ruling to the Commonwealth Court. The News Lab reached out to both NorthPoint and Hazle Township supervisors, but they did not return comments. After the county court’s decision, NorthPoint started a campaign to change community perception around the project, Bahat said. It hosted events with the Chamber of Commerce as well as the Rotary Club. It announced a $165 million community benefit offer, which includes funding a brand new local police department for the township, and $10,000 for each eligible household in the township. The package made national headlines. Some residents called it a bribe. It became a symbol of local level pushback against behemoth tech development. Bahrt said developers are trying to “bulldoze [their] way in” without actually changing the scale of the project or mitigate environmental impacts. artigo.texto: NORTHAMPTON — With unanimous recommendations from the Planning Board and the council’s Committee on Legislative Matters, the City Council Thursday will take up a proposed yearlong moratorium on commercial data centers. The council formed a committee last month to study data centers’ potential impact on their host communities — a topic that arose as the proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers sparks concerns across the region, prompting municipalities such as Greenfield, Easthampton and Westfield to enact moratoriums. Meanwhile, Shutesbury and Holyoke have banned such developments. Environmental experts and researchers frequently point to data centers’ potential to use large amounts of energy, pollute nearby waterways, and release substantial heat, making the facilities a target of controversy in areas where they have been proposed. For instance, large data centers can consume up to 5 million gallons of water in a single day, according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute — a volume equivalent to the daily water usage of a town populated of 10,000 to 50,000 people. At the Oct. 29 public comment portion of a joint hearing of the Planning Board and the Legislative Matters Committee, members of the public, such as Smith College student Scarlet Labbé-Watson, came out to speak in support of the moratorium. Referencing the emergence of “forever chemicals,” known as PFAS, left behind by former industrial sites across her home state of Maine as an example of how shortsighted decision-making can lead to long-term pollution, Labbé-Watson asked city officials what harm a moratorium could have on the city, compared to the potential long-term harm data centers could impose. “What would we be destroying if we put a moratorium within the bounds of Northampton?” Labbé-Watson asked. “Would we be interfering with old buildings that could potentially be repurposed for low-income housing? What would we be destroying to put a data center in and also what kind of harm would that open us up to long term?” Resident Zain Salim said environmental impacts were a secondary concern for him. He said he was more worried that the large amounts of data stored at these centers could be used for corporate or government surveillance. Salim argued that AI models that operate on the cloud, rather than on individuals’ devices, would allow large tech companies to surveil individuals’ use of AI. “What data centers do is they allow large amounts of data to be stored in one place, and that’s primarily something that large corporations such as Google or Microsoft would want to do in order to, for example, surveil user queries of AI agents,” Salim said. “They will have AI models that can only be run on the cloud, not locally on people’s devices … that allows these companies to surveil user interactions with AI — that’s what I’m against, that’s what everyone should be against.” Planning Board and the Committee on Legislative Matters members generally supported the moratorium, but deliberated over whether to implement size or electricity usage limitations. Ward 3 City Councilor Laurie Loisel voiced concerns that overly specific language within the ordinance might inadvertently create loopholes for potential data center applicants. “Sometimes when you define something more specifically then people think ‘well, it’s not that so I get to do it,'” Loisel said. “That’s my hesitation — accidentally using a definition that then gives people a reason to say ‘well, it’s not that so let me do it.'” Ward 6 City Councilor Christopher Stratton said he would prefer to set a minimum size or electricity use in the ordinance’s definition of a data center, so the moratorium does not block less harmful businesses from coming to the city. Stratton referenced South Hadley’s stalled effort to produce a data center moratorium as being an outcome he wished to avoid in Northampton, adding that he hoped the council could pass a moratorium that clearly defined what kinds of data centers it would temporarily ban. “I would like to get a moratorium in. I would like it to be a moratorium that I can feel good about. Easthampton wrote their [moratorium] in terms of square feet … maybe that’s a more intuitively familiar unit,” Stratton said. “I was at a 500-kilowatt [energy use limit], today I’m at a 250-kilowatt [limit]. I like laws and regulations that establish a clarity of expectation.” The two bodies ultimately decided to refer debate over whether to allow smaller, or less energy-consuming, data centers to City Council, which will further discuss the ordinance at its Thursday meeting.

artigo.texto: Utility scale solar developers are increasingly co-locating battery storage with new solar photovoltaic capacity. As of September 2026, over 16% of new utility scale solar capacity added this year is co-located with operable battery storage, compared with 2% in 2017, according to data reported to U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) by operators. Reported plans for solar additions scheduled to come online in the last three months of 2026 show that the share with co-located battery storage could increase to 19% this year. Longer-term plans indicate that this trend will continue, with the portion increasing to more than 30% in plans submitted for 2027 and 2028. When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices. Wholesale prices in regions with large solar participation tend to fall when solar contributions are high and rise as they decrease. Plants with both solar and battery storage can manage the combined output of their generating resources to maximise their value in a changing wholesale price environment. Although battery storage and solar units at the same plant often enter commercial service at different times, the EIA-860 and EIA-860M data collection programme tracks these developments and provides a monthly summary that can be used to identify co-located technologies. Southwest states have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility scale solar and battery capacity. As of September, 13% of the total US utility scale generating capacity is solar photovoltaic, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage. The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average. artigo.texto: The federal government has announced $6.77 million in funding for Melbourne-based Clutch Industries to help manufacture batteries that can be used at home or taken on the road. Melbourne-based Clutch Industries will use the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) funding to design, construct and commission a scalable manufacturing line in Coburg North, Victoria, supporting Australian capability in an emerging battery technology. The $19.35 million project is expected to create at least 16 ongoing skilled jobs and strengthen Australia’s battery manufacturing capability. The new facility will incorporate automated assembly, testing, quality assurance and traceable supply chains, helping to establish advanced manufacturing capability in Australia. The project will focus on Clutch Industries’ PowerNet – a 20-kilogram portable 4kWh battery pack that can operate independently or be combined with multiple units to create a home battery system. Units can also be detached and used as portable power sources. “We don’t want Australia to simply export the raw materials needed for the industries of the future. We want to build more things here, create more skilled jobs here and capture more of the economic opportunities created by the global energy transition,” Minister for Industry and Innovation and Minister for Science Tim Ayres said. “Australia has a growing demand for home batteries and off-grid power solutions. This project can demonstrate how the next generation of modular battery technology can meet this requirement. “This investment will help grow Australian manufacturing capability, support skilled jobs in Victoria and strengthen our ability to produce advanced battery technologies here in Australia.” The project will also test the batteries’ safety and performance across different uses, helping refine the product and meet the requirements needed to bring it to a wider market. “Batteries are critical to Australia’s energy future, and we want to see more of this technology designed, manufactured and developed here at home,” member for Wills Peter Khalil said. “By supporting Clutch Industries to establish a scalable manufacturing line right here in Coburg North, we’re backing local industry, creating opportunities for skilled Australian workers and building our advanced manufacturing capability. “It’s great to hear this $19.35 million project is expected to create at least 16 ongoing skilled jobs, which demonstrates how Australian innovation can translate into real economic opportunities.” Want to see more stories from trusted news sources? artigo.texto: Home › Renewable energy ›Roofsol Energy Signs PPA with Lloyds Metals and Energy for 19.9 MWp Solar + 14.7 MWh BESS Projects Roofsol Energy Signs PPA with Lloyds Metals and Energy for 19.9 MWp Solar + 14.7 MWh BESS Projects Roofsol Energy has signed a PPA with Lloyds Metals and Energy to develop 19.9 MWp of solar projects integrated with 14.7 MWh of BESS across three locations in Maharashtra. November 02, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey Solar EPC company Roofsol Energy has announced that the company has signed a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with Lloyds Metals and Energy for 19.9 MWp solar projects integrated with 14.7 MWh of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Maharashtra. The projects will be located at Ghugus, Hedri and Konsari in the state. “Located in Ghugus, Hedri and Konsari in Maharashtra, the projects reflect Roofsol Energy’s engineering expertise and execution capabilities across diverse solar applications — from rooftop installations to floating solar solutions,” stated the company. In a separate agreement earlier last month, Roofsol Energy signed a PPA with Exedy India, a subsidiary of Japanese multinational EXEDY Corporation, for a 2 MWp solar power project at Kolar in Karnataka. The Exedy Group manufactures automotive clutch systems and drivetrain components. Roofsol Energy will implement the project under its OPEX model to supply solar power to the company's manufacturing operations. Last month, Roofsol Energy also signed a PPA with RAK Ceramics to develop a 3 MWp solar power project at Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh, under its OPEX model. In September 2026, Roofsol secured a repeat 4.48 MWp solar project order from Metro Decorative (CROSSBOND) for installations in Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh, following an earlier 3.2 MWp project. In August 2026, Roofsol Energy signed a Power Purchase Agreement for a 5 MWp solar plus 4 MWh BESS OPEX project for pharmaceutical packaging manufacturer Associated Capsules Group in Maharashtra, marking Roofsol's entry into the commercial and industrial (C&I) energy storage market. In July 2026, the company signed a 10.44 MWp rooftop solar PPA with steel manufacturer Shyam Steel Industries under the OPEX model, for the latter’s factory in Durgapur, West Bengal. The company also signed a 17 MWp rooftop solar PPA with Foxconn to develop an OPEX-based solar project for the smartphone manufacturer's facility in Bengaluru, Karnataka. In FY27, the company’s target is to invest in 200 MWp of rooftop solar assets through PPAs, out of which over 50 MWp has already been signed and is under execution, the company stated. In June 2026, Roofsol Energy secured INR 260 crore in funding from Aseem Infrastructure Finance to develop solar IPP projects, including installations for JK Tyre and Industries and an additional 100 MWp of C&I solar capacity across India. artigo.texto: "Ficará no fundo do jardim": compraram uma casa nos arredores de Paris e agora terão um data center que consome quatro vezes mais do que a Disneyland O caso resume uma contradição cada vez mais visível na expansão da IA: as infraestruturas precisam de grandes quantidades de espaço, e alguém deve "pagar" por isso Moradores de Ballainvilliers, nos arredores de Paris, foram surpreendidos pelo projeto da incorporadora Goodman de construir um gigantesco data center colado a uma área residencial. Prevista para 2028, a instalação de 27 metros de altura ocupará seis hectares e terá 84 sistemas de refrigeração e 44 geradores. O complexo, voltado à infraestrutura de IA, deve consumir quatro vezes mais eletricidade que a Disneyland Paris, gerando forte preocupação na vizinhança sobre os impactos da megaestrutura. Nos arredores de Paris, uma família vive há 26 anos em uma casa com jardim. Agora, do outro lado da cerca, tudo indica que será erguido um gigantesco centro de dados de 27 metros de altura, equipado com dezenas de sistemas de refrigeração e geradores elétricos. A instalação teria capacidade para consumir mais de quatro vezes a eletricidade anual da Disneyland Paris. É a face mais próxima de uma transformação que está levando a infraestrutura de IA até as portas de bairros residenciais franceses. No fundo do jardim A história se passa em Ballainvilliers, uma localidade com menos de 5.000 habitantes situada ao sul de Paris, próxima a Épinay-sur-Orge. O jornal Le Parisien relatou, nesta semana, que Gilles — um profissional de TI que comprou sua casa há 26 anos — vê agora o terreno situado atrás de sua propriedade correr o risco de se transformar em uma enorme instalação industrial. "Ficará no fundo do nosso jardim", lamenta ele na reportagem publicada. A incorporadora australiana Goodman pretende transformar uma antiga plataforma logística da editora Seuil em um centro de dados, ocupando uma área de mais de seis hectares, com obras previstas para começar a partir de meados de 2028. Um vizinho de 27 metros O projeto prevê um edifício de 22 metros de altura, chegando a 27 metros se contadas as chaminés. No telhado, seriam instalados 84 equipamentos de refrigeração, e o complexo contaria com 44 grupos geradores de emergência. Em outras palavras, os moradores temem ter de conviver com ... 'Não vamos sobreviver': Calor recorde e contas altas ameaçam deixar famílias sem eletricidade nos EUA
Aumento do consumo de energia, devido ao uso de ar-condicionado durante o verão, deixa moradores de Oklahoma endividados e sob risco de cortes no fornecimento
Quando Genia Weitz, de 58 anos, saiu para enfrentar o sol implacável do estado americano de Oklahoma, no mês passado, ela encontrou uma nova carta na caixa de correio. “Aviso de corte de energia”, dizia. A conta somava US$ 1.340,96 (cerca de R$ 7.270), muito acima de sua renda mensal. As regras estaduais impediam cortes quando o calor passava de 38,3 °C, mas agora a temperatura havia caído para 37,2 °C, e ela tinha nove dias para pagar.
- Veja também: Aprovação de Trump atinge novo mínimo duas semanas antes das eleições de meio de mandato nos EUA, aponta pesquisa
- Quer ler mais notícias de Mundo? Acompanhe o canal no WhatsApp
- Quer morar fora? Veja guia interativo do GLOBO que reúne informações sobre 36 países
Weitz e o marido, Daryl Mason, haviam se confinado à sala de estar da casa de três quartos para economizar eletricidade. Cobertores pendurados nas portas retinham o ar frio de um ar-condicionado de janela. Ela dependia de um aparelho de oxigênio; ele usava um aparelho médico (CPAP) para tratar a apneia do sono. Weitz dormia no sofá e Mason numa poltrona reclinável. Às vezes, os netos se amontoavam em colchões na sala. Nas noites mais úmidas, o calor e a umidade mantinham o ar-condicionado ligado até de manhã.
— Não consigo respirar se ficar sem oxigênio — diz Weitz. — Acho que não aguentaria passar uma única noite.
— Provavelmente teríamos um AVC de qualquer maneira com todo esse calor — afirma Mason. — Se perdermos este cômodo, não vamos sobreviver.
Com a chegada do outono nos EUA, chegou também a conta do verão mais quente já registrado no país. As temperaturas dos últimos três meses ficaram 1,7 °C acima da média, superando as do verão de 1936, durante o desastre de Dust Bowl, e as da onda de calor de 2021. Dezenas de milhões de pessoas não conseguem pagar pelo ar-condicionado que as protegeu do calor. Dados federais indicam que um em cada seis domicílios está com contas de serviços públicos atrasadas. Mais de uma dúzia de estados restringem cortes de energia durante ondas de calor. Por isso, os desligamentos costumam atingir o pico em outubro, quando a crise climática vira cobrança de dívidas.
A Companhia de Serviços Públicos de Oklahoma (PSO, na sigla em inglês), responsável pelo fornecimento de energia elétrica, já havia cortado a luz de Weitz antes. A empresa havia informado que também enfrentava custos crescentes: com combustíveis e equipamentos, modernização da rede elétrica e com o aumento da demanda provocado por eventos climáticos extremos e por novos grandes consumidores, como centros de dados usados para inteligência artificial. Embora suas tarifas ainda estivessem abaixo da média nacional, a PSO atribuiu boa parte das contas elevadas do verão ao uso contínuo do ar-cond

O CEO da OpenAI, Sam Altman, afirmou que manter grandes quantidades de memória RAM em computadores pessoais é um desperdício diante da atual escassez global do componente. Para o executivo, concentrar esses recursos em data centers permitiria aproveitar melhor a capacidade disponível.
A declaração foi feita durante uma entrevista ao podcast Cheeky Pint, em conversa sobre os gargalos nas cadeias de suprimentos de tecnologia. Altman criticou especialmente a ideia de que modelos de inteligência artificial (IA) de código aberto, executados diretamente nos computadores dos usuários, poderiam reduzir a necessidade de grandes centros de processamento.
Segundo ele, muitas pessoas acreditam que a possibilidade de rodar modelos localmente resolveria parte da demanda por infraestrutura de IA. O executivo, porém, argumenta que essa estratégia não representa necessariamente a melhor forma de distribuir um recurso que está em falta.
“Do ponto de vista da alocação global, é realmente péssimo que todo mundo tenha uma parte da oferta limitada de DRAM do mundo parada no próprio computador, sendo utilizada apenas 5% do tempo”, afirmou Altman.
Na avaliação do CEO, a memória disponível deveria ser aproveitada com o máximo de eficiência possível. “Você quer a utilização máxima na nuvem se está tentando lidar com esse ambiente de oferta extremamente restrita”, acrescentou.
Leia mais:
- Corrida da IA está enriquecendo até fabricantes de tinta
- Nvidia sobe preços de servidores de IA por alta da memória
- Sam Altman visita Samsung para discutir futuro dos chips de IA
Data centers pressionam oferta de memória
- A declaração ocorre em momento de forte disputa por componentes utilizados em infraestruturas de IA;
- Fabricantes, como Samsung e SK Hynix, firmaram acordos de longo prazo com operadoras de serviços em nuvem e projetos, como o Stargate, iniciativa da OpenAI;
- Esses contratos reservaram parcela significativa da produção mundial de memória RAM para os próximos anos. Com grandes empresas dispostas a desembolsar bilhões de dólares pelos chips, a disponibilidade de componentes para outros segmentos do mercado fica pressionada;
- O impacto também chega aos consumidores. A disputa por memória contribui para o encarecimento de produtos eletrônicos, incluindo notebooks, smartphones e outros dispositivos.
Declaração reacende debate sobre IA local
A defesa de Altman contrasta com o interesse de usuários e desenvolvedores em executar modelos de IA diretamente em computadores pessoais. Essa alternativa pode reduzir a dependência de serviços hospedados na nuvem e permitir que determinadas tarefas sejam realizadas sem recorrer continuamente à infraestrutura de grandes empresas.
O argumento do executivo, por outro lado, parte da ideia de que a memória instalada em data centers pode ser utilizada de maneira mais intensa, enquanto computadores pessoais permanecem ligados a maior parte do tempo sem aproveitar toda a capacidade disponível.
